research.q: FTC "Nixing the Fix" (2021) report and later FTC actions: what repair restrictions did it find, what evidence did OEMs give, what did it conclude about cost and safety?
research.headline: The FTC's 2021 "Nixing the Fix" report found eight kinds of repair restriction, of which only some are knowledge barriers. The others are access and authority locks: parts not for sale, parts pairing, firmware signing, EULAs, warranty steering and design. Across 22 empirical submissions and 68 comments, OEMs gave "scant evidence" for their safety, security and liability arguments, and no submission rebutted the claim that restrictions raise prices. Later actions (the 2021 policy statement, the 2022 warranty orders, the 2024 warning letters, and the Deere suit that settled in July 2026) all fixed the problem by forcing access to dealer-equivalent diagnostic and pairing tools, not by replacing the knowledge.
research.bottleneck: The scarce layer is the OEM's software authority plus its proprietary diagnostic database, not general know-how. That means the full-function diagnostic tool (Service ADVISOR), the right to pair or serialize a part, the right to clear emissions or safety lockouts, and the accumulated troubleshooting database (DTAC). Firmware signing, EULAs and parts that are not sold enforce it. Regulators had to compel access to these. Knowledge alone does not unlock them.
research.money_time: The FTC report has no total cost figure. Its price evidence points to OEM parts and dealer-only repair premiums: alternative parts are 15-50% cheaper, and repair could cut household spending 22%. In heavy equipment, the best available estimate (PIRG, an advocacy source) puts downtime waiting for a dealer technician with the only fully functional diagnostic tool at about 70% of the cost ($3B of $4.2B a year), against an excess repair price of $1.2B. So in this domain the costly stages are diagnose and authorize: reading fault codes, pairing parts and clearing derates all wait on a dealer visit. Parts price is secondary.
shapes: Independent diagnostics and authorization layer for heavy equipment (ag, construction, generators, energy assets). The Deere order now guarantees owners and independents 'fair and reasonable' access to dealer-equivalent tools for 10 years, so a company can build AI troubleshooting and fleet uptime services on top of compelled OEM data instead of fighting for it. Expect copycat orders against CNH and AGCO.
Downtime-minimization for capital equipment: predictive diagnosis plus pre-positioned parts and a mobile technician, because evidence says downtime, not repair price, is the dominant cost.

Compliance-safe independent repair with an audit trail. The strongest OEM argument is emissions and safety tampering (the EDA/AEM survey). A company that certifies, logs and attests independent repairs, especially emissions and safety-critical work, answers the one legitimate OEM objection and fits C6.

Repair-access compliance tooling for OEMs that must now offer owners and independents the same resources dealers get under consent orders and state laws (portal, licensing, part-pairing service). This sells to manufacturers rather than fighting them.
surprises: A Republican-led FTC (Ferguson and Meador, 2-0) finished the Biden-era Deere case with a 10-year compelled-access order, so US right to repair is bipartisan.
The settlement names part 'pairing' and emissions 'limp mode' restart as covered resources, which shows the lock is software authority rather than knowledge.
OEMs offered a single safety incident (a 2011 phone in Australia) despite being asked directly for data.
Magnuson-Moss has had 3 tying-waiver requests in 46 years, all denied, and the FTC cannot get civil penalties under its MMWA rules.
The best OEM evidence was about tampering and emissions deletes, not repair, a real regulatory-compliance issue the FTC set aside.
In ag, estimated downtime cost (about $3B) is 2.5x the repair price premium ($1.2B).
Apple's $29 battery program was big enough that the CEO blamed it in part for weaker iPhone sales.

stances.why: The FTC's barriers map onto diagnose, understand, source and repair. But the Deere remedy shows a step the chain leaves out: software authorization or re-commissioning (part pairing, clearing emissions limp mode). Return to service is gated by OEM software, not only by inspection.

Information and diagnostic access (manuals, Service ADVISOR, DTAC) is central. But most of the 8 barriers are legal or technical control: parts not sold, pairing, firmware signing, EULAs, warranty steering, design. This is an access and authority monopoly more than a knowledge one.

Regulators fixed the problem by compelling OEMs to give access to their tools and parts-pairing authority. AI knowledge cannot clear a cryptographic pairing lock, license an EULA or sell an unavailable part. The FTC's finding that independent repair is as good is conditional on that access.

Price evidence shows 8-50% savings (parts competition) and 22% (household repair), not 10x. But downtime is the largest cost in ag (about $3B of $4.2B), so collapsing time to diagnose and get parts could be larger than any price cut.

The report says nothing to suggest bespoke parts are solved. Design patents on collision parts, trademarks, parts pairing and VIN-burned modules block substitute parts even when they can be physically made.

OEMs lean on authorized-network certification for quality. Advocates question its value, and the FTC floats certifications and trainings independent businesses can advertise. Assurance clearly matters, but there is no data on how certification should evolve.

Supports the incentive story: Apple's battery program cannibalized sales, Deere allegedly held a 100% repair share, and warranty tying persists despite a 1975 ban. But auto (70-75% independent share) and the Deere order show the system was opened by access mandates rather than a ground-up rebuild.

research.q: EU right-to-repair directive (2024) and ecodesign spare-parts/repair-information rules: what inefficiencies did the impact assessments quantify (costs, lifetimes, repair rates)?
research.headline: The EU impact assessments find large waste from premature replacement. For example, phones are used 1.7 years against a 7-year design life, and consumers lose at least EUR 5.1bn a year (plausibly EUR 5-25bn). But they attribute it mainly to repair price versus buying new, hassle and time, trust, design and preference for new goods, with information only one driver among several. The EU's own interventions are modelled to raise repair take-up by only about 2-21%, and to deliver EUR 176.5bn in consumer savings over 15 years, mostly by consumers buying fewer new goods rather than by cutting the cost of a repair. That argues against an order-of-magnitude collapse driven by knowledge alone.
research.bottleneck: According to the EU evidence, the scarce layer is the economics of repair versus replacement at the point of failure. That means parts and labour cost relative to a cheap new product, combined with OEM control over parts, calibration and parts-pairing software and IP, plus convenience and downtime. Knowledge or information is a real but secondary barrier. For consumer goods, demand-side preference for new goods (39.5% of consumers) caps what any supply-side efficiency can achieve.
research.money_time: For consumer goods, the decision hinges on the repair price relative to a new product: consumers accept about 20% of the purchase price (17-27% depending on product). That price is dominated by parts plus labour; a smartphone display costs 42% of a new phone's price and a battery about 14%. Diagnosis is a separate, upfront and uncertain cost, 7-22% of common repairs, which deters people before they ever get a quote. Time and logistics each dissuade roughly 9-14% of non-repairers: getting the item to a repairer, waiting for parts (5-10 working days for phones, up to 15 for white goods) and being without the product. Searching for information or a repairer is measurable but smaller, about 19% for smartphones. The largest 'waste' is never attempting repair at all, driven by preference for new goods and design-related irreparability. Policy savings come mostly from buying fewer new goods rather than from cheaper repair execution.
shapes: Diagnosis-and-quote layer: instant, free or near-free remote diagnosis with a binding repair quote. The R2R IA identifies paid upfront diagnosis (7-22% of repair cost) and price uncertainty as a reason consumers abandon repair, and the directive now mandates a standard repair information form (quote).

Parts liquidity and logistics for independent repairers, especially for products now under EU 7-10 year spare-parts obligations: a marketplace or broker that makes the 5-15 working-day delivery mandates cheap and fast, and supplies non-OEM or refurbished parts.

Tooling against parts-pairing and calibration lock-in for independent repair, now that Directive 2024/1799 prohibits techniques that impede repair: compliance, enforcement and evidence tooling for regulators and repairers.
Verification and certification of repairability and durability scores, which are self-declared in France and inflated: a third-party testing layer in line with C6.

Higher-value assets (industrial machines, energy equipment, vehicles), where labour and downtime dominate and repair already beats replacement. The consumer-goods evidence suggests that market is weak for a knowledge-only play because repair must cost under about 20% of a new product.
surprises: The EUR 176.5bn 'consumer savings' headline comes mostly from buying fewer new goods. It is not a reduction in the cost of performing a repair, and the IA frames business losses as a transfer to consumers.
The EU's strongest repair options raise repair take-up by only about 13-15%, and a repairability score adds about 1 month to smartphone lifetime.
France's subsidised repair bonus used only 19% of its 2024 budget, which suggests subsidies and information alone do not unlock repair demand.
White-goods ecodesign never quantified its repair or resource savings; regulators assumed they were 'modest' compared with energy savings.
Professional repair success rates barely move: 54.7% in 2014 versus 57.7% in 2021, so about 40% of attempts still fail.
The R2R IA explicitly put repair prices, the single biggest driver, outside its scope.

stances.why: The IAs implicitly follow a defect, decide, find repairer, diagnose/quote, parts, repair, return chain. But the dominant inefficiency sits in a step C1 omits: the repair-or-replace decision. 39.5% are enthusiastic replacers and only about 10% of broken phones get repaired, so most items never enter the chain.

The smartphone IA explicitly documents that information, diagnostics, calibration software and parts are restricted to OEM networks, and 26% of Austrians with broken phones 'did not know how to repair'. But the R2R IA ranks price versus new (an acceptable repair is about 20% of the new price), hassle and time, trust, irreparable design and taste as equal or larger drivers. The monopoly is as much about parts, software locks and IP as about knowledge.

Indirect. The barriers the IAs identify (parts pairing, OEM-only calibration software, IP, missing parts, about 40% of repair attempts failing on physical grounds, consumer preference for new goods) are not removed by AI-provided knowledge.

Repair cost is dominated by parts and labour: a display repair is 42% of a new phone's price, while diagnosis is 7-22% of common repair costs. The EU's strongest measures raise repair take-up only 13-15%. For cheap consumer goods, even 10x cheaper diagnosis and sourcing would rarely bring repair under the roughly 20% threshold. The EUR 176.5bn in savings comes from buying fewer new goods, not from cheaper repairs.

The IAs address parts availability through mandatory stocking (7-10 years) and delivery-time rules, not on-demand fabrication. 'No spare parts available' is a top Repair Café barrier, which signals demand but is not evidence for an AI parts factory.

Trust in repair quality scores 8.2/10, comparable to price, and France's repairability index is self-declared and unverified, which shows verification is a weak link. But the IAs barely address inspection or certification as an industry.

The IAs state the dominant business model relies on selling new goods and gives producers little incentive to change. Ecodesign would cut smartphone revenue by 24-26%, a structural incentive against repair, and the FTC is cited for 'scant evidence' behind repair restrictions. Caveats: regulators chose incremental fixes over a rebuild, and demand-side preference is also a cause.

research.q: US state right-to-repair laws (NY Digital Fair Repair, Minnesota, California SB 244, Colorado ag and wheelchair laws, Oregon parts pairing): what do they require and what early evidence of effect exists?
research.headline: US state right-to-repair laws (NY 2022/23, MN and CA 2024, CO ag 2024 and wheelchair 2023, OR parts-pairing ban 2025) mostly require OEMs to make manuals, diagnostics, tools and parts available to owners and independents on dealer-equivalent terms. Their many carve-outs (vehicles, medical, aviation, off-road, energy, security bypass) mean they mostly cover consumer goods. Early evidence of effect is thin and is about compliance rather than outcomes: PIRG found no manual for 48% and no parts for 44% of covered products, and no state attorney general has publicly enforced an electronics law. The measurable wins so far came from Deere litigation and the FTC, not from the state laws.
research.bottleneck: The authorization and permission layer: OEM software keys, parts pairing and calibration, dealer-only tools, and liability for safety, emissions and security. Enforcement capacity is thin on top of that: attorneys general have brought essentially no actions, so litigation and the FTC did the real work. In thin markets (wheelchairs, rural ag) a second bottleneck is skilled technician capacity and dispatch. It is not a lack of knowledge.
research.money_time: Ag: dealer-only diagnostics and programming drive both a price premium and downtime. Deere's estimated overcharge is $190-387M across 200k+ farmers since 2018, and a PIRG/NFU survey puts downtime losses at about $3,348 per farm per year. Wheelchairs: time goes to waiting for a technician and for authorization (62% wait 4+ weeks), not to diagnosis. Electronics: the barrier is parts availability (44% had none), then parts pairing and calibration, then manuals. No study measures cost or time changes after any state law took effect.
shapes: Diagnostics and repair tooling for independent heavy and ag equipment shops, built on the access Deere now must provide for 10 years (trouble codes, ECU programming, calibration). The access is legally guaranteed, and AI can add value on top of it.

OEM-side compliance infrastructure for a 13-state patchwork plus FTC-style orders: portals that deliver manuals, diagnostics and pairing tools to independents, with audit trails for CEO-certified reports.
OEM-neutral calibration and part authentication as a service, because pairing bans move the control point to calibration and identity.
Mobile technician and dispatch networks for powered wheelchairs and mobility devices in states with new laws, where the bottleneck is labour and logistics, not knowledge.

Caution for energy and deeptech: energy, construction, aviation, medical and vehicle equipment are mostly exempt from state repair laws, so there is little regulatory tailwind there. The path there runs through contracts and certification.
surprises: The largest measurable effect came from antitrust litigation (Deere's $99M settlement and the FTC order), not from any state repair statute.
Apple supported California's SB 244 because it already owned a compliant channel, so an access mandate can entrench the OEM's own parts channel.
No state attorney general has publicly enforced an electronics repair law, and newer laws (Texas cure notice, Kansas injunctive-only) are weaker than older ones.
Oregon's parts-pairing penalties cannot be imposed until July 2027.
The control point has moved from manuals to cryptographic part identity and calibration, which AI does not unlock.
Colorado's electronics law explicitly excludes energy-related and aviation equipment.

stances.why: The laws line up with the diagnose, understand and source-parts stages. But the delays in the evidence sit in stages the chain leaves out: authorization and unlocking (pairing, ECU programming, immobilizer resets), payer approval, and technician dispatch (wheelchairs).

The FTC found restrictions mostly unjustified, PIRG found 48% of products had no manual, and Deere's estimated overcharge was $190-387M. The refinement is that the monopoly is now over software keys, calibration and dealer-only tools, not just know-how.

What is gated is cryptographic pairing, signed firmware, immobilizer resets and emissions overrides. Only legal mandates and settlements opened them, AI did not. The statutes also exclude materials that bypass security, so some gates stay closed even with the laws.
No law has a measured cost effect. The Deere overcharge points to rents of tens of percent, not a 10x gap. The laws also do not touch parts delivery or labour.

Parts pairing and calibration enforce OEM part identity in software. California and Colorado make independents disclose non-genuine parts. Aviation, medical and vehicles are excluded, so third-party fabricated parts still face technical and regulatory gates.

The laws carve out safety, security and emissions modifications and require disclosure of non-OEM parts. Certified sectors (aviation, medical) are excluded because their certification regimes govern repair.

NY's law was gutted at signing, Massachusetts' auto law has been delayed 5+ years, and newer state laws carry weaker enforcement. The FTC found restrictions unjustified. The system looks built for rent capture through access control, and antitrust law rather than technology is what moved it.

research.q: Agricultural right to repair (John Deere, CNH; FTC v Deere 2025; farmer surveys from US PIRG): quantify downtime and dealer-repair cost premiums and what the knowledge/software lock actually is.
research.headline: In US farming, the "knowledge monopoly" is mainly a permission and access lock: Deere's dealer-only reprogramming, calibration and engineering-helpdesk tools (Service ADVISOR, CCMS/DTAC payload files). It is used deliberately to steer service, and through service OE parts, into consolidated dealers charging $130-200/hr. PIRG estimates it costs about $3B/yr in downtime plus $1.2B/yr in excess repair costs. 2025-26 litigation, the FTC consent order and EPA guidance, not AI, opened the lock, and technician scarcity and timeliness remain the binding cost.
research.bottleneck: The scarce layer is authorization plus hands, not knowledge. On authorization: OEM-signed ECU payload files, calibration routines, emissions-override rights and the DTAC case base, all gated by software and contract and now being opened by FTC and EPA action. On hands: technicians able to reach the machine in the field during the window, with the dealer technician shortage at an 11% opening rate. Data access, meaning telematics and fault histories, determines who can apply AI diagnosis, and today it sits with the OEM and dealer.
research.money_time: Time is mostly downtime in narrow planting and harvest windows ($500-1,400 per breakdown day per ISU; PIRG's $3,348 per farm per year). It comes from waiting for scarce dealer technicians, hauling machines 30-60 miles, and uncertainty over whether a fault needs a dealer: only 6% of dealer-required DTCs say so. Money comes from the dealer labor premium ($130-200/hr, about $59/hr above independents), the OE-parts premium that dealer service captures, and the tool gate. PIRG's split of $3B downtime plus $1.2B excess cost implies about 70% of the harm is downtime, not the repair bill.
shapes: Independent repair-network enabler built on the 2026 FTC order: a multi-brand diagnostic and reprogramming layer licensing the newly mandated Repair Resources, with AI triage that answers 'does this DTC need a dealer?' (the uncodified 94% gap)
Field-service dispatch and mobile technician marketplace for harvest-window downtime, since hands and travel distance dominate time cost

Emissions/safety repair attestation: a software-logged, auditable record that DEF and safety functions were restored after independent repair. This addresses the OEMs' main objection (C6) and could become the compliance currency
Multi-brand telematics fault prediction with pre-staged parts and techs, competing with Deere Expert Alerts on owner-controlled data
All-makes parts plus electronic pairing service: generics are cheaper and near parity, but ECU parts need pairing, which the order now forces Deere to offer
surprises: Deere priced the customer repair tool to be 'cost prohibitive for nearly all customers but then we can't be accused of not making it available' (internal document cited by the FTC)
Deere itself has no dictionary of which fault codes need a dealer, and only 6% of dealer-required DTCs say so: a real knowledge gap that even the OEM has not codified
Tool access price fell about 16x ($3,160 to $195 per machine per year) within months of the FTC suit, through regulatory pressure, not technology
The $99M class settlement works out to about $500 per class member over about 8 years, small next to PIRG's $4.2B/yr harm estimate
The software lock was technically shallow (weak crypto, root everywhere per the DEF CON 2022 jailbreak); the barrier is legal and contractual
Emissions DEF derates are a second regulatory software lock that needed EPA guidance in 2025-26, at Deere's own request, to permit overrides
77% of surveyed farmers bought older equipment to avoid the software, so the lock is priced into used-equipment demand

stances.why: The chain fits, but ag adds non-physical steps the rubric omits: authorization or entitlement, software pairing and calibration, emissions re-enablement, and hauling heavy machines 30-60 miles. Timeliness, meaning downtime in the planting and harvest window, dominates cost rather than any single step.

Deere documents show a deliberate dealer-only gate on reprogramming, calibration and the DTAC knowledge base, used to 'Control the Wrench' and capture parts. Correction: it is mainly an access/permission monopoly enforced by software and contract and amplified by 82% dealer chain consolidation. It is only partly a know-how gap: 94% of dealer-required DTCs do not say so, and there is no DTC dictionary.

AI cannot generate Deere's signed payload files or reach its DTAC case base. The gap was closed by the 2026 FTC order, the $99M class settlement and EPA DEF guidance. AI could help with fault triage and troubleshooting only once access is granted, and the OEM already runs its own predictive telematics (Expert Alerts).

Tool access price fell about 16x ($3,160 to $195 per machine per year) because of regulation. But the labor premium is about 30-45% ($59/hr), the OE-parts premium is moderate, and downtime is tied to technician scarcity and distance. A 10x combined drop is not supported; a 1.5-3x cut in restricted repair cost plus timeliness gains is plausible.

Ag parts are not unavailable: Deere has about 500k OE parts, and generics are cheaper and increasingly comparable. The issue is steering. Electronic parts need pairing and reprogramming that a parts factory cannot supply without software access. 2021-22 delays came from supply chain shocks.

OEMs' core defense is emissions, safety and cybersecurity integrity. The settlement explicitly governs emissions inducement overrides, and EPA is redefining lawful repair and DEF derates. Certification of restored compliance is the durable choke point.

Internal Deere documents show the customer tool was designed to be 'cost prohibitive' while avoiding accusations of withholding it, and service capture was designed to drive parts. But it is being reformed incrementally through litigation and contract, and Kubota and AGCO show far less consolidation, so the structure is one firm's strategic choice rather than inherent to repair.

research.q: Automotive repair data access: Massachusetts 2013 and 2020 telematics ballot laws, the 2014 national MOU, REPAIR Act; independent vs dealer share of repair; what is actually locked (data, tools, parts, calibrations)?
research.headline: In US auto repair, the knowledge layer (manuals, wiring diagrams, standard diagnostics) has mostly been for sale since the 2013 Massachusetts law and the 2014 national MOU. What is still locked is permission, not know-how: secure-gateway authentication, VIN-paired modules and security functions, telematics data (still not open six years after Massachusetts' 2020 vote, with the case now at the First Circuit), ADAS calibration capital, EV tooling, and warranty tie-in. AI can speed up diagnosis, but it cannot remove these credential, legal and capital gates, and the measured data-access tax (about $3.1B a year) is under 1% of a roughly $414B light-duty aftermarket.
research.bottleneck: Authorization and trust infrastructure, not knowledge. The scarce pieces are: credentialed and cybersecure access to the vehicle (secure gateways, VIN-paired module coding, immobilizer and security functions, telematics); the neutral standards and credentialing body that Massachusetts and Maine required but nobody built; and the capital, equipment and labor needed to calibrate and verify ADAS and EV systems. Underneath it all is the warranty-plus-dealer-profit incentive.
research.money_time: The cost and delay don't come from 'understanding'. They come from four places. (1) Labor hours, with a technician gap of about 20.8k a year. (2) Unpaid diagnostic time before a car gets referred to a dealer (2-4 hours per vehicle) when a shop hits a gateway, coding or security wall. (3) Post-repair ADAS calibration, about $360 on a windshield job and $150-250k to set up a bay. (4) Warranty-period and EV work captive to dealers. Parts sourcing and delivery for mainstream cars is already same-day. The quantified access tax is about $3.1B a year against a roughly $414B light-duty aftermarket.
shapes: Neutral cybersecure vehicle-data access and credentialing layer (the 'inter-operable open access platform' and 'independent entity' Massachusetts and Maine mandated but nobody built). Security tech pulled by regulators; risks are OEM cooperation and ongoing litigation.

ADAS calibration plus a digital verification-record network that insurers accept: mobile calibration rigs, automated targetless verification, and a tamper-evident return-to-service certificate (this rides on C6).
EV high-voltage service enablement for independents: lower-capex tooling, safety training and a procedure copilot, attacking the $30-70k barrier and the more than 75% dealer EV share.

Diagnostic copilot for fleets and independents, defensible only with proprietary confirmed-fix and telematics data. Must beat incumbents (Bosch, Solera/Identifix, Snap-on, Mitchell1) that are already shipping AI.
Part-pairing and coding as a service (remote, credentialed module programming), positioned for laws like New Jersey's part-pairing-code bill and a codified MOU.
surprises: Automakers chose to disable telematics in Massachusetts (Subaru, Kia) rather than open it, and the AG accepted that as compliance, so a data 'right' can mean that no one gets the data.
Six years after a 75% vote and more than $43M in spending, the Massachusetts open telematics platform still does not exist, and the case sits at the First Circuit.
The House committee stripped the REPAIR Act down to codifying the 2014 MOU, which NADA backs.
EVs are re-concentrating service at dealers (more than 75% of EV service spend, single source).

The headline advocacy pain figure ($3.1B a year) is under 1% of the light-duty aftermarket, and the knowledge layer was already commoditized by aggregators and crowdsourced fix databases long before LLMs.

stances.why: Auto repair fits the chain. But the car itself increasingly does the 'notice' step through OEM-controlled telematics, and calibration and verification is a distinct post-repair gate. The locks sit unevenly across steps.

OEM control is real (84% of shops rank data access their top issue, 51% refer cars to dealers, $3.1B/yr). But since 2013-2014 most knowledge is purchasable. The 'monopoly' is over credentials, gateways, part pairing, telematics, warranty and capital, not understanding. Independents already do most post-warranty ICE work.

AI can digest manuals that are already available. It cannot authenticate to secure gateways, code VIN-locked modules, open telematics that OEMs disable, or replace a $150-250k calibration bay. Thirteen years of laws have not opened telematics.

Auto parts sourcing and delivery is already fast and commoditized. The measured data-access tax is under 1% of the aftermarket, and labor shortage, calibration and EV capex dominate. AI diagnostic savings are anecdotal and apply to one step only.
The barriers are electronic pairing and coding of parts and design-patent protection of captive parts, not the ability to fabricate. A bespoke-made part still has to be coded and legally sold.

Verification and credential layers are growing: ADAS calibration verification, SERMI accreditation (ISO 17020), NASTF registry, AutoAuth. Laws failed precisely because no trusted access and certification body was built (Maine).

Incentives are misaligned (fixed ops are about 50% of dealer gross profit, OEMs disable telematics and litigate for years). But the FTC calls auto relatively successful self-regulation, and the independent channel is large and growing for ICE. This is rent-seeking at specific choke points rather than systemic slop.

research.q: Medical device servicing: FDA 2018 report on servicing by third parties, ISOs vs OEMs for imaging equipment, the 2020 ventilator repair crisis; cost and safety evidence.
research.headline: In medical devices, the evidence (FDA 2018, ECRI's review of 2.1M MAUDE records) says independent and in-house servicing is about as safe as OEM servicing. What blocks it is access: service keys, calibration software, gated training, parts refusals and DMCA suits. A shortage of knowledge is not the main problem, so AI can shrink the know-how gap but cannot remove the locks. The savings on offer from opening access look like 20-40% on service spend plus big cuts in time-to-repair in specific cases, not an order of magnitude. The 2020 ventilator 'crisis' was mostly a stockpile contracting lapse and a demand overshoot, not a failure to repair.
research.bottleneck: The scarce layer is not general repair knowledge. It is control of access to the machine itself: diagnostic data behind service keys and DMCA, calibration/activation software for new parts, OEM-gated training and parts distribution, plus an ageing and shrinking biomed workforce. A second gap is the lack of a trusted evidence and traceability layer, since ISOs have no adverse-event reporting and service outcomes go unmeasured. OEMs use that gap to argue safety, and regulators cite it to decline action.
research.money_time: For hospital capital equipment, money goes to OEM service contracts (about 10% of purchase price per year on imaging; service is about a third of GE HealthCare revenue at about 52% gross margin). Expensive proprietary parts (CT tubes can approach the residual value of the machine) and downtime (about $6k/day for CT and $15k/day for MRI by Siemens's own calculator) add to it. Time is lost mainly waiting for an OEM engineer, or for keys, software and parts the OEM releases only to its own channel. Diagnosis itself is fast, and half of imaging faults are resolved remotely by OEMs. Scheduled PM and inspection is a large, fixed, mandated labor cost.
shapes: Multivendor AI copilot for in-house biomeds and ISOs that ingests manuals, CMMS histories and the error logs reachable under the DMCA 1201 repair exemption. It works only if paired with a legal data-access strategy, since telemetry ownership is the moat.

Service-quality evidence and traceability platform: service records, parts provenance and voluntary adverse-event reporting for ISOs. It answers the OEM safety argument and the FDA's 'foster evidence' agenda, and could become the inspection/certification layer (C6).

Parts-provenance and refurbished-parts exchange for imaging after OEM end-of-service letters. It would need QMS-compliant test and certification to stay on the servicing side of FDA's remanufacturing line.
Workforce-multiplier tools (remote expert plus AI guidance) aimed at the BMET shortage, especially for rural hospitals facing end-of-service letters.

Avoid: a generic 'AI parts factory' for medical devices. The FDA remanufacturing rules, IP and validation dominate, and the high-value parts (X-ray tubes, detectors, MRI coils) are not generically fabricable.
surprises: 4,240 of the 4,301 MDRs mentioning third-party servicers were filed by manufacturers.
FDA servicing complaints named OEMs about three times as often as ISOs (29 vs 10).
Two of the three deaths definitively caused by servicing were field engineers killed while servicing CT and MRI scanners, so a worker-safety problem rather than a patient-safety one.
One device's training course cost about 80% of the device price ($28k vs $35k).
The 2020 US ventilator shortage became a glut (about 96k stockpiled, about 38k cancelled). About 2,109 stockpile units were offline because of a maintenance-contract bid protest.
OEMs already resolve about half of imaging faults remotely, so AI diagnosis tends to strengthen whoever owns the device telemetry.

stances.why: The hospital work-order flow does match notice, diagnose, parts, repair, then performance and electrical-safety verification. But medical adds a calendar-driven PM and inspection loop that CMS and TJC require at 100% for high-risk gear. It also adds a regulatory classification step (servicing or remanufacturing?), and OEM remote monitoring often does the 'noticing'.

OEMs gate manuals, service keys, calibration software, training and parts (91.8% of biomeds denied info), and courts found antitrust violations (Red Lion, Kodak). FDA and ECRI show independents can repair safely, so the gap is created by OEMs rather than inherent. It is better described as an access monopoly than a knowledge monopoly.

AI can interpret manuals and error codes (an LLM reached 100% on error codes but 80% on fixes). The binding locks are the device's own data behind passwords and the DMCA, part-activation software, training gates and parts refusals. AI cannot remove these. OEMs also own the telemetry, and AI diagnosis may entrench them.

Evidence points to 20-40% savings on service spend from competition and large cuts in time-to-repair in specific cases. No source supports a 10x cost drop. Hard parts (tubes, coils, detectors), labor shortages and mandatory PM and inspection remain.

The 2020 3D-printing episodes show fabrication is fast. But a non-OEM part that changes the spec can turn a repair into FDA-regulated remanufacturing, IP and certification limit sharing, and the expensive imaging parts are not fabricable by generic shops.

CMS and TJC mandate PM and inspection completion, FDA is pushing quality management and evidence generation, and both OEMs and ISOs agree there is no systematic outcome data or ISO adverse-event reporting. An AI-era traceability and inspection layer is the gap both sides name.

The evidence supports deliberate aftermarket rent capture: about 52% services margin at GE HealthCare, plus antitrust and DMCA cases. It does not support 'built to be inefficient, needs a full rebuild'. FDA says the mixed OEM/ISO/in-house system works and is critical, and the ventilator crisis was procurement and demand, not repair.

research.q: iFixit, Repair.org (Gay Gordon-Byrne), US PIRG, Restart Project, Repair Cafe: what are their core arguments about why repair is inefficient, and what data do they cite?
research.headline: The five main repair advocates (iFixit, Repair.org, US PIRG, Restart Project, Repair Cafe) argue that repair is inefficient because manufacturers deliberately lock down the aftermarket: parts, manuals, diagnostic software, service keys, parts pairing and unrepairable design. They push legal fixes, not technology. Their best hard data, from more than 200,000 logged community repairs, shows parts (unavailable or too expensive) and design as the dominant barriers, with missing information the smallest named barrier at 12%. That cuts against the idea that AI closing a knowledge gap is the main lever.
research.bottleneck: Access and authorisation: OEM control of parts supply and pricing, software and cryptographic locks (parts pairing, service keys, dealer-only diagnostics), plus design for non-disassembly. Knowledge capability is not the bottleneck. These locks are legal and economic, and are being dismantled by legislation (coverage moving from about 26% to 35% of Americans in 2026) rather than by AI.
research.money_time: In the advocates' data, the time and cost go to sourcing parts: unavailable (25% of failures) or too expensive (18%). Next come physical design (16%) and wait times for parts and authorisation; 62% of wheelchair users wait 4+ weeks, and hospitals and farms wait on dealer and OEM diagnostic access. For consumer goods, the cost of labour plus parts relative to a cheap new product (a 15-20% tolerance threshold) decides repair-or-replace. Diagnosis and understanding are a minority of failures (12%).
shapes: Independent parts supply and aftermarket marketplace for categories newly opened by right-to-repair laws (wheelchairs, farm equipment, medical devices): parts are the #1 barrier, and laws now force OEMs to sell parts, tools and manuals

Compliance and ingestion layer: OEM-mandated manuals and diagnostic tools (NY, CA, MN, OR, CO, TX laws) turned into an AI service copilot for independent technicians in heavy equipment and medical devices, where the information is newly legally available but scattered

Medical-equipment uptime and ISO servicing business with AI diagnostics, competing with OEM service contracts (91.8% of biomeds report being denied service information, so legal access plus AI is a wedge)
Independent ag-equipment repair network with legally obtained diagnostic software, building on the FTC v. Deere case
Repair cost-reduction tooling (design-for-repair analysis or remanufacturing) to bring repair under the 15-20%-of-new-price threshold
surprises: In the largest real-world repair dataset (208k attempts), missing repair information is the least common named barrier (12%), behind no spare parts (25%), parts too expensive (18%) and unopenable design (16%)
iFixit, the canonical 'repair knowledge' company, already shipped an AI repair assistant (FixBot) and still frames the battle as parts pairing and parts access
Advocates treat OEM 'safety' arguments as pretext, and the FTC agreed (scant evidence), which complicates the idea that inspection is the enduring bottleneck for consumer goods
Phone repairability went from F to B- in three years mainly through legislation, which suggests the dominant lever is legal, not technological
PIRG's headline $49.6B savings figure is contested; the CEI estimate is roughly 7x lower

stances.why: No group disputes the chain. But the evidence puts the waiting in sourcing and authorisation (insurer approvals, OEM service keys, software unlocks), a step the founder's chain leaves out.

All five groups centre an OEM monopoly, but over access to information that already exists (paywalled manuals, service keys, dealer software, pairing), not a capability gap. In community repair data, missing information is only 12% of failures.
AI cannot bypass cryptographic parts pairing, dealer-only calibration software or service keys. Parts and design barriers (about 59%) dwarf information barriers (12%). iFixit's own AI admits errors.

The evidence points to parts price and availability, labour cost relative to the new-product price (the 15-20% tolerance), wait times and dealer distance as the dominant costs, not diagnosis or understanding.

Parts unavailability is the #1 barrier, which supports demand for alternative parts supply. But many parts are serialised, electronic or too expensive, and no advocate claims on-demand fabrication solves this.
For consumer goods, advocates and the FTC treat OEM safety claims as largely pretextual (scant evidence). Inspection is not presented as a bottleneck outside regulated sectors such as medical.

The advocates argue the inefficiency is deliberately engineered for aftermarket profit. Their remedy, though, is legal and economic (right-to-repair laws, pairing bans, FTC enforcement), and laws are measurably changing OEM behaviour.

research.q: Antitrust history of aftermarket lock-in: Kodak v Image Technical Services (1992), Xerox, IBM tying cases, Apple parts pairing; what economics did courts and economists (Shapiro, Borenstein) find about aftermarket monopolies?
research.headline: Courts and economists agree that aftermarket lock-in is real: Kodak (1992) held that a firm with little power in the equipment market can still monopolize its own parts and service, and Borenstein, MacKie-Mason and Netz showed aftermarket prices stay above cost even when the equipment market is competitive. Shapiro and Cabral argue the welfare harm is narrower or ambiguous when terms are known in advance. In every major case (Kodak, Xerox, IBM, Intuitive/SIS, Deere, Apple pairing), what was locked up was access to parts, IP, software keys and approval gates, not repair know-how, so AI closing the knowledge gap would not by itself break these monopolies.
research.bottleneck: Access rights and authorization, not know-how: the right to buy parts, copyrighted manuals and diagnostic software (lawful to withhold under Xerox), cryptographic pairing or authorization keys (Apple, Deere payload files, EndoWrist usage chips), and regulatory approval for non-OEM parts and service (FAA PMA, FDA). The binding constraints are legal, cryptographic and certification layers, which have loosened only through regulation and settlements since 2024-2026.
research.money_time: In the antitrust record, the money goes to aftermarket rents on parts and service: dealer service around 70% gross margin against 5-6% on equipment, 50% K-Cup margins, sole-source aerospace markups of 17-4,451%, and EndoWrist and Kodak parts at near-100% share. The time goes to access, not diagnosis. Owners wait for dealer-only tools and authorization keys (Deere planting and harvest delays), OEM-only parts and service, and approvals and certification for alternatives (PMA, FDA). Fixing it through litigation takes about 10 years (Kodak 1987 to 1996+), and plaintiffs mostly lost.
shapes: AI-native certification and evidence engine for non-OEM parts and repairs (FAA PMA/STC data packages, FDA 510(k) for remanufactured instruments, UL/IEC). The approval gate, not fabrication, is the scarce layer.

Independent diagnostics and authorized parts pairing as a service, riding new access mandates: the Deere FTC order (10 years of dealer-parity tools), the Oregon pairing ban and the EU Directive 2024/1799 transposed in 2026.

Independent service and repair network for medical and industrial robots (EndoWrist-type instruments), now that the Ninth Circuit's Aug 2026 SIS ruling reopens tying claims and hospitals have a certified class.
PMA-style alternative-parts supplier for heavy equipment, energy and mining machines, where sole-source markups resemble TransDigm's but certification regimes are lighter than in aviation.
Lifecycle-cost transparency and procurement tool for buyers of equipment fleets. It attacks the information cost Kodak identified, at the time of purchase, before lock-in.
surprises: The excluded independents almost always already had the repair know-how. Kodak ISOs were cheaper and sometimes better. What they lacked was parts, software keys and legal rights, so the knowledge monopoly is mostly an access monopoly enforced by IP law.
Borenstein et al.: aftermarket prices can be higher when the equipment market is more competitive.
Kodak's practical legacy was near zero for 20 years: defendants won almost every follow-on case because courts required a policy change after lock-in.
2026 was a turning point: the $99M Deere class settlement (April), the FTC/five-state Deere order including parts-pairing tools (July), and the Ninth Circuit reviving SIS v Intuitive (August).
Cabral shows aftermarket power can raise consumer surplus under increasing returns, while still entrenching incumbents.
When patents were weakened (Lexmark 2017), lock-in moved to chips and software pairing rather than disappearing.

stances.why: The antitrust record does not test the stage chain. It implicitly adds stages the chain omits: getting authorization or pairing keys and IP clearance.

Monopolies over repair are well documented (Kodak 80-95%/~100%, Deere 100% of tool-dependent repairs, Intuitive 100%, TransDigm sole-source). But the rivals who were shut out already had the know-how. What is monopolized is access: parts, copyrighted manuals, diagnostic and authorization software, and approval gates. It is an access monopoly, often legally protected (Xerox), more than a knowledge gap.

The locks are legal (patents and copyright, upheld in Xerox), cryptographic (Apple pairing, Deere payload files, EndoWrist chips) and regulatory (FAA PMA, FDA). AI understanding does not remove any of them. Only regulation and settlements (Deere 2026, Oregon, EU directive) have opened access.

Large rents exist: service margins around 70%, parts markups up to 4,451%, and PMA parts 25-50% cheaper. So big price cuts are possible once access opens. But economists (Shapiro, Cabral) show part of the rent is a transfer offset by cheaper equipment, so welfare gains are smaller than the price gaps suggest, and the costs are not mainly in diagnosis or knowledge.

Making alternate parts has been technically routine for decades (PMA, ISOs, K-Cup rivals). The barriers are certification (FAA PMA, FDA), IP (patent holders may refuse to sell or license under Xerox) and software pairing that rejects non-authorized parts. An AI factory solves fabrication, not those barriers.

Certification and approval gates (FAA PMA, FDA servicing versus remanufacturing, Intuitive's 'illusory' approval process) are both genuine safety functions and the place where lock-in now hides. The FTC and FDA found OEM safety claims weakly evidenced, which argues for a better, evidence-based inspection layer.

Incentives are deliberately built around the aftermarket: equipment sells at 5-6% margin while service earns about 70%, and IBM, Kodak, Keurig and Deere all follow a razor-and-blades design. That is a deliberate profit design, not an absence of 'smart'. Change has come piecemeal through law (EU directive, Oregon, FTC orders), not a wholesale rebuild.

research.q: Section 1201 DMCA repair exemptions (Copyright Office triennial rulemakings 2015-2024): what did the record show about software locks blocking diagnosis and repair across vehicles, appliances, medical, industrial?
research.headline: Across the 2015-2024 rulemakings, the record showed software locks really do gate diagnosis and repair: dealer-only ECU tools for cars and tractors, hidden error codes on Taylor soft-serve machines, and tiered, licensed service software and manuals for medical imaging, where OEM labour runs $600-800/hr against $150-200/hr for independents. But what holds the lock in place is law, cryptography and certification more than missing know-how. The DMCA lets owners circumvent but bans selling the tools or the service; industrial and B2B exemptions were refused twice for thin evidence; aviation data fell outside copyright entirely; and in 2026 the medical lock is moving to OEM clouds as a priced product.
research.bottleneck: The scarce layer is legal and cryptographic authorisation to act on knowledge, not the knowledge itself. That means service keys and credentials, OEM-hosted servicing software and manuals (moving to the cloud as tiered paid licences), the DMCA's ban on selling tools or services, and regulatory sign-off (FAA, FDA, EPA). Even with a 1201 exemption, an independent cannot legally buy a bypass tool. Industrial and B2B locks are tied up in contracts the Copyright Office will not override.
research.money_time: The record never measures cost by repair stage. Qualitatively, both time and money concentrate where the diagnose and understand steps meet authorisation. You need OEM tools, service keys or credentials to read error codes, open service menus, or recalibrate and re-authorise parts after a repair, and the OEM holds those. Medical shows an OEM labour premium of roughly 3-5x ($600-800/hr with a 4-hour minimum versus $150-200/hr), per-technician training and access fees (around $7,000 for ventilators), and per-engineer hardware. Downtime from waiting for authorised technicians recurs across farms, hospitals and restaurants. Parts sourcing and delivery come up less often as software-lock problems; appliance makers argue those repairs are mechanical. The record has no good figures on downtime cost.
shapes: An authorised multi-vendor service network that buys OEM-licensed access (Level 1 credentials, Carestream-style subscriptions) and adds AI triage on top. This works within the law, since the record shows these licences are for sale.

Open diagnostics for equipment the OEM no longer supports, or whose maker is defunct, built on data that is not copyrightable (machine telemetry, fault data). The 2018 avionics ruling shows such data is outside 1201, so the lock is only contractual.

Tools for owners to diagnose and fix their own industrial equipment: a self-help kit (not a circumvention device, which would be trafficking) combined with evidence-gathering to support a commercial and industrial exemption in the 2027 or 2030 cycle. The Office twice said it lacked evidence.

Re-certification and return-to-service verification (calibration and verification records) that FDA, FAA and EPA would accept from independents. This targets the safety argument OEMs use to justify locks.

Analytics on fleet maintenance data the operator already owns (aviation, heavy equipment), built on the finding that the data is factual and not copyrightable, so the remaining barrier is contractual.
surprises: The 2018 avionics petition was denied because aircraft maintenance and fault data is factual, arranged to the ARINC/SAE standard, and not copyrightable. The DMCA does not reach aviation; contracts and the FAA do.
The DMCA lets owners circumvent but forbids anyone selling them the tool or service. That blocks a market for repair tools from forming, and only Congress can fix it.

In Sept 2026, medical OEMs openly described a tiered, priced, cloud-hosted market for repair knowledge: Philips Levels 0-3 (Levels 2-3 never licensed), GE Class M trade-secret service software, Carestream per-person, per-unit subscriptions.
Industrial and B2B equipment, the category closest to a deeptech startup, was refused twice (2021, 2024) for a thin evidence record.
An OEM-authorised diagnostic tool misdiagnosed a fault that reverse engineering found (2015 power-window case).
Appliance makers told the Office that 'almost all' appliance repair is mechanical and needs no circumvention.

stances.why: Repairs in the record follow diagnose, get info or software, parts, repair, verify. But the record adds a step the chain lacks: re-authorising, recalibrating or pairing after a repair (ECU recalibration, parts pairing, medical 'verify before clinical use'). The Office also repeatedly found commercial and industrial categories too varied to treat as one class.

The strongest support is in medical: a 3-5x labour price gap, 91.8% of technicians denied service information, and OEMs openly running tiered, licensed, cloud-hosted service knowledge. Vehicles, ag, Taylor machines and enterprise IT show the same gating. The caveats: appliance makers say appliance repair is mostly mechanical, and aviation's gate is data contracts plus the FAA. The monopoly is enforced by law and cryptography, not just by ignorance.

The binding constraints are legal (anti-trafficking ban on tools and services, licences, NDAs), cryptographic (service keys, PKI, multi-factor logins, cloud-hosted service software) and regulatory (FDA quality rules, EPA, FAA). AI can interpret error codes, but it cannot derive a withheld key or lawfully distribute a circumvention tool.

The only price evidence is a 3-5x OEM-vs-independent labour premium in medical, which reflects monopoly pricing rather than the cost of diagnosis. No record shows how much repair cost locks cause versus parts or logistics, and nothing supports a 10x drop across categories.

The 3D printing exemption history shows regulated parts (FAA, FDA) are gated by certification, not by the ability to fabricate. Proponents said the regulatory carve-out nearly voided the exemption, and closed material systems were defended on safety grounds.

EPA, DOT and FDA concerns delayed the 2015 exemption by a year. FAA certification put avionics software off-limits even to the petitioner. OEM servicing software exists in part to verify a device before it returns to service. The Office handed safety questions to agencies with those mandates.

The Office said 1201 was never meant to enable tying or lock-in, and the triennial, product-by-product process is slow (proponents called it 'scattershot'). But in B2B the Office twice credited real alternatives (service agreements, password recovery, negotiated licences) and found the evidence thin. 'Built to be inefficient' overstates what the record shows.

research.q: Military right to repair: FY2024-FY2026 NDAA proposals, Army right-to-repair policy (2025), GAO reports on technical data rights and contractor-locked sustainment (F-35 ALIS/ODIN, ship maintenance). Quantify cost and readiness impacts.
research.headline: US military repair is a well-documented case of contractor lock-in. GAO finds DOD lacks the data rights, software and manufacturing data needed to repair systems it paid for. The result is cannibalisation, weeks-long waits for the original manufacturer (OEM), sole-source premiums (e.g. Stryker's $534M support deal) and falling readiness: the F-35 mission-capable rate fell from 67% to 44% between FY21 and FY25. But the monopoly is legal and contractual, not cognitive. The FY26 NDAA right-to-repair language was stripped under industry lobbying, and the largest ship-maintenance losses (15,000+ lost submarine days, $3.4B) come from shipyard capacity and workforce, not from knowledge.
research.bottleneck: Legal and contractual control of technical data and software, especially detailed manufacturing data, which statute excludes from DOD's unlimited rights to operation and maintenance data. Behind that sit physical depot and shipyard capacity, skilled labour, and the slow qualification of non-OEM parts. Knowledge exists but is fenced off by contract. Repair throughput is limited by docks, people and certification.
research.money_time: Sustainment dominates life-cycle cost: about $1.3-1.6T of the F-35's roughly $1.7T. Time is lost mainly in two places. The first is the physical repair and depot stage: shipyard capacity, workforce, dry docks and unplanned work account for 75% of late periods, more than 15,000 lost submarine days and $3.4B. The second is parts availability: a 10,000-part F-35 repair backlog, cannibalisation and parts scarcity. Contractor lock-in on data and software adds OEM waits of weeks, sole-source premiums (a $534M Stryker deal; parts margins up to 4,451%) and lost depot capability (44 of 68 F-35 components). Information systems also impose overhead, such as about 45,000 workaround hours a year at one unit on ALIS. Diagnosis as such is rarely the cited bottleneck.
shapes: Data-rights and technical-data intelligence for program offices: AI that audits contract deliverables and markings (F/A-18 rejected 80% of deliveries, Stryker had 1,274 unreviewed items) and builds IP strategies. GAO found every reviewed program failing here.
Qualified reverse engineering and replacement parts for obsolete military parts, sold to DLA and depots, where the moat is the qualification data package rather than the printer.
Deployable or forward repair cells with certification workflows for low-criticality printed parts (Navy commanding-officer approval model), expanding as qualification rules evolve.
Shipyard and depot planning tools that predict unplanned work, since unplanned work and workforce capacity cause most Navy delay-days.
A neutral escrow or broker for technical data: an alternative to OEM 'data-as-a-service' that gives guaranteed wartime access while protecting contractor IP, which is the political compromise space.
surprises: The right-to-repair provisions had White House, Secretary of Defense and service-secretary support plus bipartisan bills in both chambers, and were still stripped in conference in December 2025.
GAO itself says reverse engineering and additive manufacturing are less efficient than buying data rights up front, which undercuts the 'just make it' thesis.
The biggest readiness losses (submarines) come from dry dock and shipyard capacity, not knowledge or IP.
The F-35 contractor was paid incentive fees while readiness fell.
The data-rights problem was documented by GAO in 2006 for the C-17, F-22 and C-130J and remains unresolved.

stances.why: The chain fits roughly, but GAO shows the 'understand' step splits into data rights and software licences (legal), and that unplanned work found mid-repair loops back to diagnosis. Ship delays come from discoveries during the repair itself.

There is strong GAO evidence that OEMs hold the technical data, software and manufacturing data, causing cannibalisation, OEM waits and sole-source premiums. But the monopoly is legal and contractual over knowledge DOD paid for, not a lack of understanding.

AI cannot grant legal rights to drawings or source code. Software locks (e.g. Avenger) and the statutory exclusion of manufacturing data persist. GAO says reverse engineering is less efficient than owning the rights.

Individual parts show 10-100x savings (16 cents vs $20; $55 vs $700). But the largest system losses (submarines: $3.4B and 15,000 days; F-35 backlog) sit in depot and shipyard capacity, workforce and parts scarcity, outside the four knowledge steps.

Routine printing is limited to low-criticality parts. Flight-critical additive manufacturing qualification is still in R&D a decade after the first demonstration. Obsolete parts such as B-2 components still require slow reverse engineering.
Qualification and airworthiness are the gate on printed and reverse-engineered parts. Commanding-officer approval and NAVAIR qualification are bottlenecks, and certification itself needs to evolve.

Contractor incentives were not tied to readiness, sole-source acquisition is a business model (TransDigm), and the data-rights problem has persisted since 2006. Industry lobbying killed the FY26 reform even with White House and service support.

research.q: OEM aftermarket economics: share of revenue and profit from services/spares in industrial and aerospace OEMs (GE Aerospace, Rolls-Royce, Caterpillar, Siemens Energy); what do OEM executives say is the strategy (razor-blade, lifecycle lock)?
research.headline: In heavy-asset OEMs, services and spares make up 60-77% of segment revenue and most of the profit. GE CES is 75% services, Siemens Energy Gas Services is 66% service with 77% of its backlog in service, and Rolls-Royce Civil's 20.5% margin is driven by the aftermarket. Executives describe this as an installed-base or lifecycle model, not a razor-blade one. The lock rests on IP, design authority, licensing and physical parts capacity, not on scarce diagnostic knowledge: in an engine shop visit, materials and OEM-controlled repairs are 80-90% of cost, and labour or diagnosis is only about 5-10%.
research.bottleneck: Design authority plus certified physical supply. The OEM owns the type design, the instructions for continued airworthiness, repair data and licensing terms. Only OEM-qualified capacity can make life-limited and hot-section parts such as castings, forgings and HPT blades. Alternative parts and repairs (PMA, DER, USM) need regulatory approval one part at a time. Shop capacity and skilled MRO labour are the secondary constraints.
research.money_time: The money goes to parts and materials, and the time goes to waiting for parts and shop slots. In aero engine shop visits, materials are about 60% of direct cost (65-80% when life-limited parts are replaced), OEM and approved repairs are 20-30%, and labour is about 5-10%. OEMs earn 70-77% of revenue from this stage. Time is lost to parts scarcity and MRO capacity: GE says it is 'all about our ability to move spare parts', Rolls-Royce is adding 20% shop capacity and new joint-venture shops, and IATA reports grounded fleets and 20-30% higher lease rates. Diagnosis and understanding are a small share of both cost and delay.
shapes: Independent PMA/DER repair developer that uses AI and digital inspection data to speed up the approval package for alternative parts and repairs. This attacks the certification gate that actually protects OEM margin, not the knowledge gap.

Certified additive and advanced-manufacturing supplier for obsolete or constrained non-hot-section parts on long-lived fleets (defense, power-gen, mining), where the OEM no longer supports the part. The value is in qualification data, not the printer.
Engine-agnostic USM/teardown and parts-harvest marketplace with condition data. Used serviceable material is the main way independents escape OEM pricing.
Durability and time-on-wing analytics sold to independents and lessors running power-by-hour-like risk contracts, where avoiding shop visits is worth more than cheaper repairs.

Independent long-term service provider for gas turbines and industrial assets (data-center power, mining). Siemens Energy's more than 90% own-fleet service share and €400m/GW lifecycle value show the size of the prize, and Caterpillar's flat services growth shows the lock is beatable.
surprises: Labour and diagnosis are only about 5-10% of engine overhaul direct cost. Materials and repairs dominate, so cheaper knowledge alone cannot cut repair cost by 10x.
Caterpillar missed its own aftermarket goal ($24bn vs $28bn by 2026) and reset to $30bn by 2030, even with 1.6m connected assets.
Rolls-Royce publicly stopped selling engines at a loss to recover the money in maintenance, and pays for durability because it earns per flying hour.
Engine OEMs took 47% of the 2025 aerospace profit pool while MRO shops earn only about 7%. Independent repair is a low-margin business.
The IATA-CFM conduct agreement shows OEMs can be pushed to open manuals and honor warranties regardless of where parts come from, without new technology.

stances.why: OEM data organizes repair around contracts (power-by-hour, LTSA, shop visits, time-on-wing) rather than a linear chain. The steps exist, but the economics are bundled under one lifecycle contract, and the costly step is the parts and materials inside the repair.

IATA/Oliver Wyman and AlixPartners say OEMs capture aftermarket value through control of design data, repair instructions, test equipment, licensing and parts. Siemens Energy has more than 90% service share on its own fleet. However, the monopoly is legal and IP-based (design authority, certification, licenses), not just an epistemic gap.

The gap is enforced by IP rights, design-approval and certification rules, and license terms that prohibit DER, PMA and USM use. AI does not remove these. Independents already have the knowledge to build PMA and DER repairs, but approval and licensing gate them. GE says it is constrained by parts output, not know-how.

In engine overhauls, materials are about 60-80% of direct cost and repairs 20-30%, while labour and diagnosis are about 5-10%. Cutting diagnosis and understanding 10x barely moves the total. Sourcing and delivery costs are set by OEM pricing power and physical capacity, not information costs.

Specialized parts (life-limited parts, HPT blades, castings) are capacity- and certification-constrained. The existing alternative path (PMA, DER repairs) takes approval per part, and the report says independents gain share only slowly over a platform's life.

The certification and approval regime (FAA 8110.54A ICAs, Part 21, DER, PMA) is the gate that preserves OEM capture, and IATA asks regulators to speed repair approvals. Inspection and approval capacity is central.

Aftermarket rent capture is structural: OE is sold at or below cost and the aftermarket carries 70% or more of economics, and IATA says the model is 'unbalanced'. But per-flying-hour contracts give OEMs a reason to improve durability (Rolls-Royce's 100% time-on-wing target), the IATA-CFM deal opened competition, and Caterpillar's missed services goal shows lock-in is leaky. The system is built to capture rent, not to be inefficient.

research.q: Consulting literature on aftermarket service (Cohen, Agrawal, Agrawal HBR 2006 "Winning in the aftermarket"; Bain, McKinsey, BCG, Deloitte service reports): what inefficiencies and margins do they report?
research.headline: The consulting literature agrees that aftermarket service is 20-25% of OEM revenue but 40-50% of profit, at margins 1.4-2.5x those of new equipment, and that spare parts alone run about 50% gross margin. The inefficiencies it reports are parts logistics (wrong or missing parts, 1-2 inventory turns, 23% annual obsolescence), technician availability and utilisation, and management neglect, not a knowledge gap. The gains it documents are 10-50%, not 10x.
research.bottleneck: The scarce layer is the right part, pre-positioned near the failure, plus a skilled technician on site within the response window, under sporadic, probabilistic demand across 15-20x more SKUs than manufacturing, plus OEM commercial lock-in over parts pricing and installed-base access. Knowledge matters, but it already leaks (OEMs capture only 10-25% of potential service) and incumbents are absorbing AI to widen parts margins.
research.money_time: The money goes to spare parts and contracts. Parts are about 49% of service revenue at ~50% gross margin. Service is 20-25% of OEM revenue but 40-50% of profit, at 1.4-2.5x equipment margins (EBIT 25% vs 10%). The time goes to parts availability and technician dispatch. Missing parts at the dealer caused ~50% of problem-repair delays at one automaker, and half of US farmers say the technician takes too long to arrive. Inventory turns only 1-2x a year with 23% annual obsolescence, and technician utilisation ranges from <50% to >90%. Diagnosis and 'understanding' are not named as the dominant cost or time stage in any consulting source, and Bobst already fixes 80% of electrical faults remotely.
shapes: Independent parts-availability and pre-positioning layer: probabilistic multi-OEM spare-parts forecasting and stocking for owners and independents. Only 5-8% of OEMs have even piloted AI parts forecasting, and inventory turns are 1-2x.

Long-tail and obsolete-parts on-demand supply (reverse engineering plus additive or CNC): 23% of parts go obsolete yearly and suppliers lose tooling, as in the Daimler Trucks case. A narrow, certifiable niche, not a general 'AI parts factory'.

Multi-brand service operator for a fragmented installed base (the Sears model of shared technicians across brands): OEMs leave 75-90% of service potential on the table, and AI-guided troubleshooting lets lower-skill technicians cover more brands.

Uptime-contract and outcome-based service provider for energy and robotics fleets: the industry is moving from 75:25 products-to-outcomes toward 50:50. Price on uptime rather than fill rate, which is Cohen's core prescription.
Watch out: incumbent OEMs (Airbus Skywise, AI parts pricing at +3-4 pts EBIT) are deploying the same AI. A wedge must own parts access or the dispatch and logistics layer, not just diagnosis.
surprises: Deloitte's data shows the services share of US industrial revenue barely moved in 13 years (21.9% in 2005 to 23.6% in 2018) while service margins rose from 15.5% to 23%. OEMs are extracting more margin, not more volume.

OEMs capture only 10-25% of installed-base service potential (Bain 2012), so for industrial gear the 'knowledge monopoly' is already leaky. Most repair spend already goes to independents, in-house crews or deferral.
Consultants' main AI use case for the aftermarket is value-based spare-parts pricing (+3-4 pts EBIT), which raises the cost of repair to owners.

Cohen et al. were selling after-sales supply-chain software (MCA Solutions), and their own fix was probabilistic inventory planning, not knowledge. They also call service knowledge a durable moat rivals 'can't easily acquire'.
Europe's elevator OEMs grew EBIT 56% in 2008-09, the strongest example of inspection-mandated service lock-in.
Only 4% of OEMs earn recurring digital-service revenue even though 28% of new machines are connected (BCG 2025).

stances.why: The literature models service as a supply chain of parts, people and infrastructure plus reverse logistics and a response-time promise. It does not use a linear chain. The economics sit in pre-positioning inventory and technicians before failure, and steps run in parallel, so the chain is roughly right but misses where the value is.

Cohen and Airbus Skywise confirm OEM service knowledge is a moat. But the inefficiencies consultants document are parts logistics, labour and management neglect. OEMs capture only 10-25% of installed-base service potential, so independents and owners already do most of the work and the monopoly leaks in industrial categories.

About a third of OEMs already run AI in guided troubleshooting, and they use AI to raise parts prices (+3-4 pts EBIT). AI is being absorbed by incumbents, and the binding constraints (parts availability, technician arrival, contracts) are not knowledge problems.

Documented improvements are 5-15% opex, 10% opex, 25-50% inventory investment (vendor-reported) and 2-4 pts EBIT. No source suggests a 10x drop. Delays are dominated by missing parts (50% of problem repairs at one automaker) and technician arrival time, not diagnosis.

Daimler Trucks uses 3D printing where suppliers lack tooling or lead times are long, but only for small parts. Nothing suggests bespoke part-making is solved. The problem consultants describe is 15-20x the SKU count and 23% obsolescence, which on-demand making could chip at, but only partially.

Elevator service, which is inspection-mandated, shows the most entrenched and resilient OEM economics (+56% EBIT in a crisis), so inspection anchors incumbent lock-in. Deloitte notes virtual AR/VR quality checks, but evolving certification is barely discussed.

Supports: the system is built for OEM margin. Aftermarket margins are 2.5x and rising, parts run ~50% GM, equipment is sold to feed aftersales, and satisfaction is 10-15% below expectations. Contradicts 'rebuild': consultants see the waste as fixable by better incumbent management, and say so for profit reasons.

research.q: Power-by-the-hour and outcome-based service contracts (Rolls-Royce TotalCare, GE TrueChoice, Pratt EngineWise, Caterpillar CSAs): how do they change who owns knowledge and repair, and what evidence on cost and availability?
research.headline: Outcome-based contracts such as power-by-the-hour, TotalCare, TrueChoice, EngineWise and Cat customer service agreements don't remove the knowledge monopoly; they put it into the contract. The operator stops diagnosing and sourcing parts, and the manufacturer owns the health data, repair data and repair volume. Where these contracts raise availability, the cause is aligned incentives (Rolls-Royce engine data shows 25-40% better reliability, from prior knowledge, not re-checked). The big failures (the Pratt GTF engine recall, Trent 1000, F-35) came from shop capacity, parts supply and data rights, not slow diagnosis.
research.bottleneck: The scarce layer is certified physical capacity: castings and forgings, life-limited part production, and licensed shop slots. Behind it sits the IP and certification regime. The type-certificate holder owns the repair data. Non-OEM parts and repairs (PMA and DER) need regulator approval. Power-by-the-hour contracts and lessor return conditions exclude non-OEM parts. Data rights decide who can repair at all (F-35). Knowledge is held by contract and law, not because it is scarce.
research.money_time: In high-value engine repair, money goes mostly to parts: life-limited parts and hot-section material are up to about 80% of a shop-visit cost, priced to recover heavy discounts on new engines. Time goes to shop queues and parts lead times. The GTF crisis shows this: about 350 aircraft on the ground and 250-300-day inspection cycles. In the Trent 1000 case, regulator inspection intervals and ETOPS limits did the same. Diagnosis and understanding are fast, centralised at the manufacturer and already data-driven. Outcome contracts move the cost risk to the manufacturer, which then reprices it. They do not reduce the physical repair or parts time.
shapes: Certification-evidence engine for non-OEM parts and repairs: use AI to cut the engineering and test-package cost and time of FAA/EASA approvals. The bottleneck is approval, and the economics are 30-50% savings versus OEM parts.

Independent outcome-contract provider for mid-life and older fleets or industrial assets, like JSSI or third-party power-by-the-hour. It underwrites availability using its own health monitoring and a non-OEM supply chain, competing where OEM agreements lapse.

Rapid certified manufacturing for long-lead and obsolete parts (castings, forgings, out-of-production defence parts). It targets diminishing manufacturing sources and the queue of 10,000+ F-35 components awaiting repair, sold to defence sustainment, which is actively pulling work back from contractors.

Data-rights and sustainment intelligence for defence and owner-operators: help owners capture and structure technical data so they can take repair back in-house (the DoD must transfer F-35 sustainment elements by 2027-28).
Shop-capacity and parts-flow orchestration across MRO networks (slot booking, used serviceable material, lease engines). It works on queue time, which is where availability is lost.
surprises: The best empirical result (25-40% reliability gain) credits outcome contracts with better repair through incentives, not knowledge diffusion. Ownership of risk matters more than access to knowledge.
GAO found the DoD's performance-based logistics cost more in the only direct comparisons, and the cost data needed to judge them was missing.

In the biggest recent repair crisis (the GTF engine) the manufacturer controlled the whole chain and knew the fault, yet aircraft waited 250-300 days. Owning the knowledge did not help when shop and parts capacity were short.
Rolls-Royce's recent margin recovery came largely from repricing its long-term service agreements, so customers pay for the risk transfer. The 'efficiency' is captured by the manufacturer.
The F-35 shows the starkest knowledge monopoly: the owner of a $1.7T programme lacks the technical data to repair its own jets, and the fix is IP negotiation, not information.

Web search budget was exhausted before this agent ran. Several numbers (Rolls-Royce share of hours, GE ~70% services share, Cat $24B/$28B, PMA pricing, IATA's $11B) come from prior knowledge and need verification.

stances.why: The steps all exist, but outcome contracts bundle them under one provider and make the chain predictive (planned removals) rather than starting from someone noticing a fault. The real time goes into queues between steps, such as shop slots and parts lead times.

Manufacturers do capture the data and know-how: the F-35 lacks technical data, and power-by-the-hour moves health data and repair to the manufacturer. But the monopoly rests on contracts, IP and certification, plus deliberate razor-and-blades pricing, not just a skills gap.
The gaps are data rights, IP and approvals. In the GTF and Trent 1000 cases the fault was understood fast; the binding limits were physical capacity and regulator inspection limits.

Engine repair cost is mostly parts (life-limited parts up to ~80% of a shop visit) and time is mostly shop and parts capacity (250-300 days on the GTF). Diagnosis and understanding are a small, already centralised share.

Non-OEM parts and repairs (PMA and DER) already exist and are limited by certification, testing, lessor and insurer acceptance, and contract exclusions. Life-limited and hot-section parts need certified materials and processes.
Regulator inspection intervals and ETOPS limits set availability in the Trent 1000 case. Inspection is the gating step and becomes data-driven through engine-health monitoring.

The aftermarket's economics are designed on purpose (subsidised hardware, profitable aftermarket) and lock customers in; GAO shows performance-based contracts don't automatically save cost. But outcome contracts do measurably improve reliability, so the system is optimised for manufacturer profit and risk transfer, not for inefficiency.

research.q: Servitization literature (Vandermerwe, Baines, Neely): what fraction of manufacturers succeed at service businesses and why do OEMs keep control of repair knowledge?
research.headline: Only a minority of manufacturers that push into services succeed, roughly 20-30%. Studies from Neely, Fang et al., Suarez et al. and Bain all find no gain, or a loss, until service reaches large scale. OEMs keep control of repair through several locks, not just know-how: rent capture, dealer-only software and authorisation, data and telemetry ownership, certification, and field-service scale. Know-how is the one lock AI weakens most, and when knowledge spreads, the literature shows 'deservitization' rather than a system rebuilt for efficiency.
research.bottleneck: The scarce layer is authorised access plus scale, not raw knowledge. That means dealer-only diagnostic and calibration software, parts pairing, OEM-owned telemetry, certified repair data in regulated sectors, and the installed-base density needed to make field-service labour and parts logistics profitable. Knowledge asymmetry is the lock that is easiest to commoditise, and OEMs are already moving toward software, data and outcome-contract locks.
research.money_time: The servitization evidence puts the economics in the installed-base phase, meaning parts plus field labour plus risk-bearing. Diagnosis is not where the money is. Profit comes only with scale: a 20-30% service share for firm value (Fang), over 50% for margins in software (Suarez), and density-driven economies of scale (Visnjic Kastalli & Van Looy). Service businesses fail on internal operational risks (Benedettini). OEMs extract the margin mostly through parts pricing and dealer-exclusive labour that tool access enforces (Deere: branded parts, dealer-only software), and in aerospace through risk-transfer contracts priced per flying hour. Diagnosis and knowledge serve as the gatekeeping step that lets OEMs capture the parts and labour stages, rather than being the largest cost stage themselves.
