shapes: AI-native independent service organisation (diagnosis, parts sourcing and technician dispatch) for fragmented or orphaned installed bases where OEM service is weak (industrial machinery, medical imaging, equipment from defunct OEMs). Why: the literature shows most OEMs fail at service, leaving share to win, and deservitization moves rent to independents.

Third-party uptime or outcome contracts (power-by-the-hour for non-OEM fleets) with AI used to price failure risk. Why: the profitable form of servitization is risk transfer at scale, not information.
Open diagnostic, calibration and parts-pairing tooling plus compliance with right-to-repair laws. Why: FTC and Deere show the binding constraint is software authorisation, not know-how.
Avoid a pure 'AI repair knowledge' layer. Why: knowledge is the lock that is easiest to commoditise, and OEMs keep control through data, certification and access.
surprises: Most OEMs are bad at monetising service. The supposed knowledge monopolists often earn lower profit and fail more often after servitizing (Neely; Benedettini).
Deservitization is documented: when service knowledge spreads to customers or third parties, OEM service businesses shrink. This is a direct historical analog of the AI thesis.
Separating service from product innovation causes 'long-term knowledge loss' (Visnjic et al.). Repair knowledge feeds design, so independents with AI lack the design-feedback loop.

Note: the shared WebSearch budget was used up before this agent ran, so several widely cited numbers (Bain's 21%, Neely's 3-4% vs 6-7% margins) are from prior knowledge and could not be verified this run.

stances.why: The servitization literature frames repair as installed-base services and outcome contracts, not as a stage chain. Oliva & Kallenberg's stages describe the service business, not the repair process.

Knowledge asymmetry does underpin OEM service rent (Valtakoski, Vandermerwe). But the locks that bind hardest are access and authorisation (Deere), data ownership (Rolls-Royce), certification, rent-seeking design (FTC), and field-service scale economics. Also, most OEMs fail to monetise their knowledge at all.

AI can close the cognitive gap but not software authorisation, parts pairing, telemetry ownership, certification, or labour and logistics scale. History shows OEMs move to other locks when knowledge spreads, and deservitization moves rent to independents rather than removing it.

Service profitability and failure turn on scale, labour and internal operational risk (Visnjic Kastalli & Van Looy, Benedettini). Diagnosis and knowledge are not the dominant cost, so a 10x cut there does not mean a 10x cut in total repair cost.
Not addressed. The only related point is that Rolls-Royce remanufacturing relies on the OEM's design data.

Indirect support: certification and approved data stay a durable OEM lever, especially in aerospace. The FTC notes safety and liability are cited as justifications, even if poorly evidenced outside regulated sectors.

The aftermarket is deliberately designed for OEM rent (FTC finds 'scant evidence' for the justifications; Deere). But most OEMs are poor at service ('afterthought', the service paradox), so the system is fragmented and badly managed rather than a coherent structure that needs a rebuild.

research.q: TransDigm and HEICO business models: pricing, DoD IG findings on TransDigm markups, HEICO PMA discounts; what do they reveal about where value sits in aftermarket parts?
research.headline: In aerospace aftermarket parts, the value comes from certification, sole-source IP and data rights, the price-inelastic demand of a grounded aircraft, and procurement rules that hide cost data. It does not come from knowledge or from making the part: TransDigm earns about a 47% operating margin with DoD IG-documented markups of up to thousands of percent, while HEICO, which already has the engineering know-how, wins only about 30-40% PMA discounts and a small market share. NOTE: no web searches ran because the shared budget was used up and most primary sources returned 403, so several numbers are from background knowledge and need checking.
research.bottleneck: The right to install: type-certificate and PMA approval, data rights or IP, and contractual acceptance (lessor return conditions, engine-OEM service agreements). Together with grounded-aircraft (AOG) price-inelasticity and procurement rules that hide cost data, these turn cheap-to-make parts into sole-source rents. Knowledge and fabrication are not the scarce layer.
research.money_time: In aerospace aftermarket parts, the excess cost sits at the sourcing step, but it is rent, not physical effort: sole-source pricing on parts that cost little to make. Time and cost for alternatives go into certification (PMA or DER approval, production audits) and into getting lessors, engine agreements and insurers to accept the part. Diagnosis and understanding are not where the money is.
shapes: AI-accelerated PMA/DER-as-a-service: reverse engineering plus automated certification packages to cut the cost and time per approved part number, since HEICO's model is limited by certification throughput
Should-cost and price-transparency engine for DoD and airline buyers: estimate fair price from geometry, material and process, to address the cost-data blind spot the IG documented
Technical-data reconstruction and data-rights tools for defence sustainment (the F-35 IP gap, the 10,000+ component repair backlog), enabling government depots and second sources
Avoid a pure 'parts factory': without the approval and acceptance layer, fabrication commoditises and does not capture the rent
surprises: HEICO, the PMA disruptor, earns roughly half TransDigm's margin while undercutting OEMs by only a third, so certified competition narrows the rent but does not remove it.
TransDigm refunded money in 2019 but not after the 2021 IG report. The legal gaps (TINA threshold, commercial-item rules) let the pricing continue.
The F-35 'knowledge monopoly' is contractual data rights the government never bought, not a missing understanding that AI could fill.
Research limits: no web searches ran (shared budget used up) and most primary PDFs returned 403, so several figures are from background knowledge and need checking.

stances.why: The pricing and business-model evidence says nothing about the order of repair steps.

There is a monopoly, but it rests on IP, data rights, certification and sole-source installation rights, not on know-how. HEICO shows independents can reverse-engineer parts, and the F-35 gap is legal data rights, not understanding.
HEICO already has the knowledge and still wins only about 30-40% off price and a small share. AI does not remove certification, data-rights law, lessor conditions or engine-agreement lock-in.

For regulated aerospace parts, the best observed case for competing parts is about 30-50% off price, not 10x. The TransDigm rent comes from sole-source plus grounded-aircraft (AOG) pricing, not from diagnosis or sourcing costs.
Making the part is the cheap step (the 9,400% pin). The slow, costly step is airworthiness approval and the production quality audit, which is needed for every part number.
Certification and approval are the chokepoint and where the value sits. Any rebuild has to speed up or go through FAA/EASA approval and inspection.

The rents are deliberately built in through certification, procurement thresholds and contracts, and TransDigm exploits them on purpose. That is a rational incentive structure, not missing intelligence or 'slop'.

research.q: Commercial aviation MRO cost structure: breakdown of MRO spend by engine, component, line, airframe; labor vs material share; OEM share of MRO market (Oliver Wyman MRO survey/forecasts, IATA MCX).
research.headline: Commercial MRO was about $104-119B in 2024-25, about 11.5% of airline costs. About 52% of it is engines, where 80-95% of a shop visit is materials and OEM repairs and labor is only 5-10%. OEMs and their JVs hold about 79% of engine MRO through IP, licences and parts supply rather than a know-how gap, so AI attacking diagnosis and understanding touches a thin slice of cost; the binding constraints are piece-part availability, certification and licence terms.
research.bottleneck: OEM-held IP and licence control over repair data, approved repairs and parts, combined with scarce certified production capacity for high-value piece parts (LLPs, hot section) and certified shop slots. A shrinking certified-mechanic workforce and slow PMA/DER approval and acceptance compound it.
research.money_time: Money: about 52% of MRO is engines, and 80-95% of an engine shop visit is materials and OEM piece-part repairs. LLPs can be 50-60% of an LLP visit, and labor is only 5-10%. Components (18%) are also 60%+ materials. Only airframe and line work (about 30%) are labor-dominated. Time: piece-part availability (top cause of TAT growth for 80% of respondents) and shop capacity, with engine visits up to 300+ days against a 30-60 day norm. Diagnosis and understanding are a minor share of both cost and time.
shapes: AI-accelerated DER repair / PMA part substantiation and approval platform: it attacks the legal and certification moat directly, where the margin is
Engine shop-visit workscope and LLP optimiser: the biggest dollar lever (materials are 65-80% of LLP visits), an optimisation-knowledge problem
USM / part-out yield intelligence plus back-to-birth records automation: USM is supply-constrained and blocked by paperwork
Technician inspection and records copilot: addresses the 24-27% labor gap, the 2-3 year ramp and paper-heavy certification (C6)
Long-tail component, cabin and BFE repair and parts maker for sunset fleets, where OEM support is thin and certification lighter
surprises: Labor is only 5-10% of a narrowbody engine shop visit; LLPs alone can be 50-60%
Asked why turnaround times grew, 80% named piece-part availability, ahead of OEM control of repairs
Engine OEM gross margins are -5% to 10% on new engines vs 20-35% on MRO, so the aftermarket is the business model
Where competition rules opened (CFM56), the OEM does only about a third of overhauls across about 40 shops
80% of MRO players investing in AI reported little value so far (2024)
Dispatch reliability is already 98.86%, so day-to-day notice and fix works well; the pain is in shop visits
The web search budget was already used up, so evidence comes from directly fetched IATA/OW primary documents and sibling notes

stances.why: Most MRO dollars go to scheduled, interval- or LLP-driven events (engine overhauls, heavy checks), which OW calls 'highly predictable'. There, notice and diagnose barely apply, and inspection happens inside the repair as teardown. The chain fits unscheduled line and component work.

OEMs hold 63% of engine MRO (about 79% with JVs). They capture 20-35% MRO margins through control of manuals, repair instructions, test equipment, licences and parts. But the monopoly is legal and contractual plus physical supply, not missing know-how; where the rules opened (CFM56), about 40 shops compete.
The gap is IP, certification (DER/PMA approvals), licence terms and lessor acceptance, none of which AI removes. 80% of the industry reports little AI value so far.

In engines (52% of spend), labor is 5-10% and materials plus repairs are 80-95%. 80% name piece-part availability as the top cause of TAT growth. Diagnosis and understanding are a thin slice, and sourcing cost is set by OEM part prices and capacity.

PMA and USM already exist and are limited by approval, availability and lessor/airline acceptance. LLPs (50-60% of an LLP visit) are among the most heavily certified parts. Some opening exists in long-tail BFE interiors and sunset fleets.

Labor in engine and component work is concentrated in disassembly, inspection and test. There is a 24-27% technician gap and new hires take 2-3 years to become productive, and certification is paper-heavy, so inspection and records are both a real bottleneck and an AI-relevant target.

The structure is deliberately designed: OE discounts of up to 80% are recouped through aftermarket margins, and licences restrict PMA, USM and DER use. That is costly for airlines, but it delivers 98.9% dispatch reliability. IATA proposes targeted competition and capacity fixes, not a rebuild.

research.q: Aircraft-on-ground (AOG) events: frequency, cost per hour, how AOG support works (OEM AOG desks, field service reps, parts logistics); quantify how much of AOG time is diagnosis vs waiting for parts vs repair vs sign-off.
research.headline: An aircraft on the ground (AOG) costs roughly $10k-$150k per hour (Boeing's often-quoted 2008 estimate). The longest AOG and fleet groundings today come from parts, shop capacity and certification paperwork, not diagnosis: about 700 aircraft were parked for engine inspections in Dec 2024, and the F-35 had more than 10,000 components awaiting repair. AI can shrink diagnosis and no-fault-found waste, but no public data splits AOG time by stage, and the evidence points to parts and approvals, not knowledge, as the long pole.
research.bottleneck: Certified physical supply: approved parts with traceable release paperwork, engine and component shop slots, and casting and forging capacity. On top of that sits the design-authority approval monopoly (OEM sign-off on repair schemes and parts, enforced by IP and tech-data rights). Knowledge of what is wrong is rarely the scarce layer.
research.money_time: The time goes to sourcing and delivering parts, including the paperwork that makes a part usable, and to OEM engineering approval of non-standard repairs. It does not go to diagnosis. At fleet level the big money is capacity: about 700 aircraft parked for engine inspections in 2024, F-35 with more than 10,000 parts awaiting repair, and an estimated (unverified) $11bn per year cost to airlines from supply-chain problems. Diagnosis costs money mostly indirectly, through misdiagnosis: no-fault-found removals drive rotable-pool and shop costs. No public stage-by-stage split of AOG time exists; my estimate is parts at 50-70% for outstation AOGs and over 90% for engine groundings.
shapes: AI troubleshooting and no-fault-found reduction for line maintenance, using fault isolation manuals plus fleet history. Diagnostic waste is measurable and this sells to airline maintenance control and MROs, but the OEM manual licence is needed.

Network for finding certified parts and AOG logistics: real-time inventory and traceability across pools, brokers and the used-parts market, with automated checking of 8130-3 / Form 1 paperwork. Parts wait dominates AOG time.

A 'digital design authority' that speeds up repair dispositions and replacement-part approval (designated engineering representatives plus AI drafting repair schemes and substantiation). It targets the approval bottleneck rather than the knowledge gap.

Military sustainment: tech-data reconstruction, reverse engineering and qualified additive manufacturing for obsolete parts, since GAO documents >10,000-part backlogs and data-rights gaps and DoD is a buyer.
AI-assisted inspection (borescope and drone image analysis) that speeds up the human sign-off rather than replacing it.
surprises: The headline AOG cost-per-hour figure ($10k-$150k) everyone repeats comes from a 2008 Boeing page; no audited modern dataset is public.
The biggest grounding event of 2024-25 (about 700 aircraft parked for engines) is a problem everyone understands; it is limited by hardware and shop capacity, not knowledge.
The MEL system means most faults are deliberately not repaired at once, so AOG covers only the faults that cannot be deferred or happen away from base.
The F-35 case is the clearest real 'knowledge monopoly': the government lacks tech-data rights to its own jet, and the result is a backlog of physical repairs.
The WebSearch budget was exhausted before this agent started, so several items are prior knowledge flagged as unverified.

stances.why: The stages exist, but aviation adds a defer-under-MEL branch, so most faults are deferred, not fixed at once. It also adds engineering-approval and parts-paperwork stages, and swapping parts is used as a diagnostic tool, so the chain is not linear.

A monopoly is real in legal and contractual form: F-35 tech-data and IP gaps, OEM-licensed manuals, repair schemes that need OEM design-authority sign-off. But the largest current groundings (700 aircraft parked for engines) are hardware and capacity problems where everyone knows the fix.

The gatekeeping is regulatory (design authority, PMA, 8130-3 traceability) and data-rights based, not cognitive. OEMs are pulling fleet data into their own platforms (Skywise, AHM), so the moat is shifting from knowledge to data rather than disappearing.

Diagnosis and no-fault-found waste could fall sharply, but diagnosis is a small share of AOG time. Sourcing and delivery are limited by where physical, certified inventory sits and by global supply. A 10x cut in total AOG cost is implausible.

Aviation parts need approved design data plus production approval and conformity, so on-demand replacement is a certification problem lasting months to years. Exceptions are possible for non-critical cabin parts, tooling and military sustainment.
Release to service, required independent inspections, design-authority approval of repairs and parts traceability are the binding gates and remain human-signed.

Much of the apparent inefficiency (rotable pools, MEL, stationed field reps) is rational redundancy against unpredictable failures. OEM aftermarket margins and data control do create incentives to keep repair OEM-centric, which supports a weaker form of the claim.

research.q: Airline maintenance engineering: how do airlines use OEM tech support (Boeing Field Service, Airbus AIRTAC/AOG), structural repair manuals and repairs outside the SRM requiring OEM approval; time and cost data.
research.headline: In airline maintenance, the slow part of a repair outside the Structural Repair Manual (SRM) is approval authority and liability: an OEM, DER/ODA or DOA must sign approved data. The bigger costs are physical: AOG downtime, parts and shop capacity (GTF shop visits of 250-300 days; ~$11bn in 2025 supply-chain costs), and certified labor. AI can speed up the engineering-disposition step but does not remove the need for accountable sign-off and inspection. Caveat: the shared web-search budget was used up before this agent started. Findings come from directly fetched pages (marked [FETCHED] in the notes) plus prior knowledge (marked [BACKGROUND], to verify).
research.bottleneck: Accountable approval authority (who may sign repair data and release the aircraft, and carry the liability), gated by ownership of type-design data and FAA/EASA delegation. Alongside it sit physical capacity: engine and structures shops, certified parts, and licensed mechanics and inspectors. The knowledge itself exists; the right to certify it and the capacity to act on it are scarce.
research.money_time: The biggest costs are AOG and out-of-service downtime ($10k-$150k per hour; ~350 GTF aircraft parked for months), then physical shop capacity and parts lead times (engine shop visits of 250-300 days; >$11bn in airline supply-chain costs in 2025), then certified labor and inspection. The OEM engineering-disposition step (tech request, RDAS / 8100-9) is a real but bounded delay: hours to days for AOG, weeks to months for permanent non-SRM approvals. It matters most for AOG structural damage but is not the dominant cost.
shapes: AI engineering co-pilot for airline and MRO engineering departments and DER/DOA firms: drafts non-SRM repair dispositions and substantiation from SRM data, damage photos and scans for a human signer. It sells AOG hours saved.

Automated damage capture and inspection (drone or robot visual, NDT, borescope AI mapped to SRM allowable damage limits) that produces regulator-grade evidence. It targets the scarce inspection labor and the notice-and-diagnose steps.
Certification-evidence platform for PMA and additive-manufactured replacement parts, cutting months-long qualification. The moat is certification, not fabrication.
AI-native approved repair-design organisation (DOA/ODA-like) that captures the regulated sign-off rent instead of trying to remove it.
surprises: The web-search budget was used up before this agent began, so the evidence base is thinner than planned.
JAL 123's faulty repair was done by Boeing's own team, so OEM knowledge did not prevent the failure. Execution and inspection were the weak links.
Faulty repairs can stay hidden for decades (22 years for CAL 611). That latency is why regulators will not accept removing human sign-off.
The OEM 'knowledge monopoly' is already legally contestable through DERs, DOAs and PMA. The friction is commercial lock-in and certification cost, not secrecy.

stances.why: Aviation broadly follows the chain, but adds legally separate steps it leaves out: approved repair data, MEL/CDL deferral (fly with the defect), temporary repairs with deadlines, and decades of follow-up damage-tolerance inspection. It loops rather than runs in a line.

OEMs do own type-design data and use the aftermarket for lock-in. But repair-design authority is legally spread across DERs, ODAs, DOAs and large airline engineering groups. The binding constraint is accountable approval and liability, and major accidents (JAL 123, Aloha 243) happened with the knowledge present.

FAA and EASA require a certificated human or organisation to approve data and release the aircraft, with personal liability. Approval needs fatigue and damage-tolerance substantiation tied to type data. Catastrophic failures that surfaced years later (CAL 611 after 22 years) keep human sign-off firmly in place.

Most cost and time is AOG downtime, shop capacity, parts lead times (GTF shop visits of 250-300 days; $11bn in supply-chain costs) and labor. Engineering disposition is a bounded delay of hours to weeks. AI can shrink it, but a 10x cut across diagnose, understand, source and deliver is not supported.

PMA and DER routes already allow third-party parts. The barrier is material and process qualification and FAA approval, taking months per part number, plus OEM contract restrictions, not the ability to make the part.

The fatal cases (CAL 611, JAL 123, Aloha 243) were failures of execution and inspection. Certified inspectors are scarce and inspection cannot legally be automated away, so this is where AI-enabled NDT and records can add value.

There are real OEM aftermarket rents and data control. But much of the friction is deliberate safety redundancy written after accidents, and aviation's maintenance safety record is strong. Speeding up evidence and approval inside the rules is more realistic than a rebuild.

research.q: No-fault-found / no-trouble-found rates in avionics, military electronics and industrial components; cost of removing good parts; causes.
research.headline: No-fault-found is the single largest waste in electronics-heavy repair: 30-60% of avionics repair actions and 30-70% of electronics/appliance returns, with DoD estimating over $2B a year. The best evidence says the cause is not a knowledge monopoly but physical intermittents (wiring, connectors, contamination, wear) that bench tests cannot reproduce, plus line-versus-shop incentives. The proven fixes are instrumentation and test hardware (GAO: about $62M saved, MTBF up 4x), not knowledge alone.
research.bottleneck: Observability under real operating conditions. The fault (wiring or connector intermittents, contamination, thermal or voltage wear) exists only in flight or field conditions and is never recorded. Bench test equipment runs static room-temperature functional tests that cannot reproduce it. Next come incentives: line maintenance is rewarded for dispatch, while the NFF cost falls on the shop or pool. OEM/contractor ownership of technical data rights is a smaller factor.
research.money_time: In electronics-heavy systems (avionics, military electronics, automotive and appliance electronics) the money and time go into the diagnose-and-verify loop, not the physical fix. That loop is: unjustified removals, shipping and shop-testing units that pass, repeat removals of rogue units, and aircraft downtime while technicians swap parts. NFF is 30-60% of avionics repair actions and 50-60% of failures in some field databases. Historical cost was about $22k per NPF event (ATA 1995), about $20M a year per 200-aircraft airline, and over $2B a year for DoD. Parts sourcing and delivery costs are largely caused by misdiagnosis: parts move because they were pulled, not because they were broken.
shapes: Intermittent-fault detection hardware made general-purpose (thousands of channels, nanosecond detection, vibration and thermal stimulus) for commercial MROs, rail, wind, EV and robot harnesses. DoD has shown $60M+ payback, but the market is still a niche defence vendor one.

Cross-operator serial-number tracking of rogue/bad-actor units: pooled removal and shop-finding data that flags repeat-NFF units before reinstall. No single airline or depot has this data, which makes it the moat.
Bringing flight and field data to the bench: pair in-service sensor and fault logs with shop tests that replay the stresses the fault appeared under.
NTF reduction for electronics OEMs' warranty returns (appliances, automotive, industrial, where 30-70% of returns are NTF): contamination and physics-of-failure analysis plus return triage.

Removal-decision support at the line: a probabilistic 'is this part likely NFF?' check before pulling, with the human in the loop. This is where AI/LLM log mining fits, but it needs real operator validation.
surprises: The strongest data says NFF parts are often not good: 93% of NFF-prone F/A-18 radar receiver chassis had latent wiring faults. 'Removing good parts' is often 'keeping bad parts the tests can't see'.
More automated diagnosis created NFF: F/A-18E/F built-in test false alarms wasted about 85,639 man-hours and 25,881 aircraft downtime hours.
Even with GAO-documented savings (about $62M, MTBF 4x), a DoD depot tester needed programme-manager approvals and a 2019 OSD memo to spread.
Cypress's ML analysis found NTF semiconductor returns statistically indistinguishable from good units.
Discarding can beat diagnosing: a US Army study estimated 25% maintenance cost savings by throwing away 70-80% of items instead of repairing them.
Headline NFF cost numbers are decades old (BA 1992, ATA 1995, DoD 2012) and rarely re-measured. The field itself says economics is under-studied.

Research limitation: the shared WebSearch budget was used up for the whole run before this agent started, so sources came from OpenAlex and Europe PMC catalogue lookups and direct fetches. Several key papers (Khan 2014, Söderholm 2007, Qi/Pecht 2008, ARINC 672) were paywalled and are cited only through secondary quotes.

stances.why: The stages exist, but NFF shows the process is a loop, not a line: remove, shop test, NFF, return to stock, reinstall, recur. Diagnosis also happens twice, in different environments (in flight and on the bench) that disagree. That iteration is where the cost is.

Some support: GAO says contractors retain the IP and data needed to repair, and an engineer survey says manuals and test equipment fail technicians. But NFF is equally high inside OEM and depot shops that hold all the knowledge. The dominant causes are physical intermittents and test-environment gaps: missing signal, not missing knowledge.

AI cannot recover a fault that was never measured (50 ns intermittents, faults that appear only under vibration or humidity). Smarter built-in test has historically added NFF (F/A-18E/F: 85k wasted man-hours). ML could not separate NTF semiconductor returns from good units. The AI results claimed so far are self-reported and depend on new sensor data.

NFF is 30-60% of repair actions, so removing it could roughly halve diagnosis, sourcing and logistics cost, not cut it tenfold across the board. 100x improvements exist case by case (460 hrs to 4 hrs; 11 months to 30 min), but they came from instrumentation hardware, not knowledge.
NFF is about too many parts being pulled and sourced, not about parts being unavailable or needing to be made.

Shop retest and inspection is the point of failure: room-temperature functional tests cannot see field faults, NFF units go back to service as rogue units with an airworthiness risk, and test standards (MIL-PRF-32516, ARINC 672) are evolving.

Supporting: split line and shop budgets, separate contracts per depot, programme-manager approvals, and an OSD memo needed to spread a proven $62M-saving tester. Against: swapping LRUs is a rational hedge against aircraft-on-ground costs under real uncertainty, and discarding is sometimes cheaper than diagnosis (Army: 25%).

research.q: Independent aviation MROs and the used serviceable material (USM) market: how teardown and USM lowered costs; what limits independents (OEM licenses, data, DER repairs)?
research.headline: Independent MROs cut costs mainly by attacking the price and availability of parts, not by closing a knowledge gap. Teardown USM caps what OEMs can charge, PMA/DER provide certified alternatives, and module-swap logistics do the rest. HEICO's FSG ($3.1bn sales, 24% margin), FTAI ($1.6bn aerospace revenue, roughly 3.5x in two years) and AerSale show these economics. What limits independents is legal, contractual and regulatory: OEM IP claims on manuals and tooling, licence contracts, warranty and lease-return clauses, per-part FAA approval capacity, personally liable DER sign-off, scarce feedstock, and the integrity of parts records. AI does not remove these.
research.bottleneck: Getting legal permission to install the part, and getting the physical part. The scarce layer has four pieces: (1) regulatory approval throughput for alternative parts and repairs (FAA PMA reviewers, DERs who carry personal liability); (2) OEM legal control of manuals, tooling and licences, reinforced by warranty and lease-return clauses that require OEM parts; (3) feedstock, meaning retired engines and airframes to tear down, plus the capital to hold inventory; (4) trusted traceability records for each part. Engineering knowledge is not the bottleneck.
research.money_time: Money goes to parts. Material (new OEM parts and life-limited parts) is the dominant share of engine and component repair cost, and OEMs price it high to recover engines sold at deep discounts. USM from teardowns and PMA parts save money by undercutting this, and the profit sits with whoever owns the parts: AerSale's gross margin is 35-39% on owned parts versus 17% on labour services. Time goes to waiting: for shop slots, scarce parts and certified repairs. IATA puts the 2025 cost at $2.6bn in extra engine leases and $1.4bn in extra spares, because engines sit in shops longer. Diagnosis and understanding are a small share of both cost and time in airline repair.
shapes: AI tooling that drafts PMA/DER substantiation packages (analysis, test plans, conformity data) so DERs and the FAA approve alternative parts and repairs faster. It targets the actual throughput bottleneck, and PMA houses and airline engineering departments are the buyers.

Provenance and records security for USM: automated back-to-birth records review, forgery detection on 8130-3 and EASA Form 1 certificates, and a digital chain of custody. The AOG Technics case shows the need, and it fits security tech.
Software-driven teardown and part-out arbitrage (which engines to buy, which modules to harvest, when to sell), modelled on FTAI and AerSale. It is capital-heavy but proven.
Lease-return and records compliance automation that lowers lessors' resistance to PMA/DER at redelivery, matching IATA's January 2026 lease-end guidance.
Cross-domain reuse: repurposing and maintaining aero-derivative engines as power turbines (FTAI Power) for data-centre and grid demand, which fits an energy founder.
surprises: FTAI's aerospace products revenue grew about 3.5x in two years ($455m to $1.6bn) on 25-year-old engine families. The independent opportunity is largest late in a platform's life, not at the frontier.
At AerSale, labour-based MRO services have the lowest margin (16.6%), while owned USM parts earn 35-39%. Knowledge and labour are not where the money is.
HEICO's roughly $3.1bn PMA/repair business has no material patents. Its moat is FAA approval track record and the capacity of FAA reviewers.
IATA names lease-return clauses and OEM agreements, not technical knowledge, as the main barriers to using PMA parts.
FTAI is converting CFM56 jet engines into power turbines, linking aviation repair to energy.

Process note: the shared WebSearch budget was exhausted, so all evidence came from direct fetches of known primary URLs (SEC 10-Ks, IATA, Wikipedia). The USM/PMA discount percentages and the AOG Technics details are background knowledge flagged as unverified.

stances.why: Aviation adds steps the chain leaves out: acquiring feedstock and tearing it down, records and traceability, approving repair data (PMA/DER), and lease-return compliance. Parts are often harvested from retired assets rather than ordered.

OEMs capture the aftermarket, but through legal and contractual control (IP claims on manuals, licensed tooling, warranty and lease clauses, access to continued-airworthiness instructions) and through capital, not because independents can't understand the hardware. Reverse engineering has been routine since the 1990s.
The gaps that bind are approval throughput, personally liable DER sign-off, licence rights and records provenance. HEICO's moat is FAA track record, not knowledge, and it has no material patents.

The savings come from material price and availability (USM, PMA), which are capital- and supply-bound. Diagnosis and understanding are small cost shares. Time is lost to shop slots, parts and engine leases, not diagnosis.

Making a part is not the bottleneck. A part can be installed only with PMA/DER approval and traceable documentation. HEICO built about 20,000 approvals over decades, adds about 500 a year, and FAA resources set the pace.
Approval capacity (PMA/DER, FAA reviewers), Part 145 releases and records authentication (AOG Technics) are the scarce layer. Cheaper parts flows raise the stakes of provenance.

Some inefficiency is designed in (razor-blade engine pricing, lease clauses), and IATA calls OEM dominance a cost driver. But a mature, profitable independent counter-system (HEICO, FTAI, AerSale) already exists, and change is incremental (the IATA-CFM deal, lease-end guidance), not a rebuild.

research.q: Field service management industry (ServiceMax, IFS, Salesforce Field Service, Aquant data): first-time fix rates, truck rolls, mean time to repair, causes of repeat visits; quantify waste.
research.headline: Field service data shows first-time fix stuck at about 75-77% for over a decade. Failed visits make up about 25% of service cost at the median, 44-52% for the worst organisations and 14% for the best, and 14-20% of truck rolls are unnecessary. The recoverable waste for a typical organisation is about 10-26%, not 90%, and parts and logistics failures are as large a cause as knowledge gaps. Vendor (mostly Aquant) data only. The search budget was used up, so every finding comes from fetching pages directly.
research.bottleneck: The real constraint is getting the right diagnosis and the right part together before the truck rolls. Parts availability, data quality for stocking and triage before dispatch interact multiplicatively with technician knowledge. Knowledge alone is not the limit: the industry average has not moved in 10+ years of digital tools, while top-quintile operators in the same structure do 8x better.
research.money_time: The money goes to failed and repeat visits: 25% of service cost at the median and 44-52% for lower performers. Each failure brings about 2.5 more visits and roughly 20 days to resolution, which drives mean time to repair (4.5 days at the median, 10 for the bottom). Unnecessary dispatches (14-20% of truck rolls) and admin (about 18% of technician hours) come next. By cause, parts and tools not being on the truck (40% of return visits) and wrong diagnosis or missing skills (27%) dominate. Most of the time is spent waiting between visits (parts lead time, rescheduling), not on the repair itself.
shapes: AI triage and remote resolution before dispatch, sold as avoided truck rolls (14-20% of dispatches) on outcome-based pricing. The waste is measurable and the buyer already tracks the metric.

Diagnosis-to-part prediction: use the symptom history of an asset or fleet to predict the exact parts kit before dispatch. This targets the largest stated cause of return visits (parts and tools, 40%).

Capture and transfer expertise from retiring senior technicians (voice or AR copilot) for equipment makers and their dealers. The gap between top and bottom technicians is the main driver of the 8x cost spread.
Job-closure verification and QA (photo or sensor evidence before close-out) to cut rework, warranty cost and early failures after preventive maintenance (25% of assets fail within 3 months).
surprises: First-time fix has stayed at about 75% for over a decade even as field service software (ServiceMax, Salesforce Field Service, IFS) became widespread. Digital tools alone did not move the average.
In the UK consumer survey, missing parts and tools (40%) cause more return visits than missing skills (27%).
The AI vendor's own claims are modest: savings 'typically in the low teens' and up to 26%, and AI 'gets us 80% of the way'. That is far from an order of magnitude.
Inside an organisation, the gap between top and other technicians is only 2.9 points in best-in-class teams. Process and system design seem to explain more than individual knowledge.
Measuring first-time fix over short windows (7 or 14 days) flatters the number. A 30-day window shows many hidden repeat visits.

stances.why: The data does follow a chain: triage, dispatch, diagnose, parts, fix, verify. But the real process loops (a failed first visit leads to 2.5 more visits), and it has a remote-resolution step before dispatch that can skip the chain for about 20% of cases.

Knowledge is concentrated in a few people: top vs bottom technicians are 75% vs 59% on first-time fix, the in-house gap is up to 10 points, and retirements loom. But parts and tools (40%) outrank skills (27%) as the stated cause of return visits, so knowledge is only part of the story.

First-time fix has stayed at about 75% for over a decade despite digital tools. Even the AI vendor says AI gets about 80% of the way and experts are still needed. Parts, access and customer readiness are not knowledge problems.

For a median organisation the recoverable waste is about 10-26% (failed visits are 25% of cost, best-in-class is 14%). An order-of-magnitude gap appears only between the worst and best organisations ($5,706 vs $688 per event).
No field service data on making bespoke parts. There was only a teaser saying spare-parts availability is a 'critical risk factor' and pointing to additive manufacturing.

Checking work quality before job closure is weak (ServicePower), and 25% of assets fail within 3 months of a preventive maintenance visit. That suggests verification matters and is underbuilt, but there is no data on certification evolving for AI.

Failures are systemic and multiplicative (parts logistics, data quality, scheduling, admin taking 18% of hours). But top-quintile organisations reach 88% first-time fix and 8x lower cost under the same industry structure, which points to an execution gap rather than a system built to be inefficient.

research.q: Industrial plant maintenance benchmarks (SMRP, reactive vs preventive vs predictive share, maintenance cost as % of replacement asset value, wrench time ~25-35%): where does maintenance labor time actually go?
research.headline: In industrial plants, technicians spend only about 25-35% of their time hands-on with tools. Most of the rest goes to logistics, coordination and waiting that come from reactive, unplanned work (about 45-55% of all maintenance), not to a lack of knowledge. The proven gains come from planning, scheduling, kitting and the shift to preventive and predictive work: about 12-40% lower cost and wrench time rising from about 35% to 50%. None of the sources shows a 10x drop, and the largest economic loss is lost production, not repair cost.
research.bottleneck: Work management and organisational discipline: converting reactive work into planned, kitted and scheduled work, and coordinating operations with maintenance. This sits alongside a shrinking skilled hands-on workforce (BLS +14% demand, mostly replacing retirees) and the cost of sensing and condition data for predictive maintenance. Knowledge of how to repair is a secondary constraint.
research.money_time: Labour time: only about 25-35% is hands-on work. The other 65-75% goes to travel, fetching parts, tools and permits, waiting for equipment to be released or for instructions, and breaks or late starts. Up to 20-30% may be diagnosis and planning thinking (IDCON). Money: the direct maintenance spend ($74.5B in US discrete manufacturing) is smaller than the losses it causes ($119B, mostly lost sales from delays). Unplanned downtime costs about 11% of Fortune Global 500 industrial turnover. The dominant cost is therefore time-to-restore during unplanned outages, driven by a reactive share of about 45-55% and poor planning and kitting, rather than diagnosis or the parts themselves.
shapes: An AI planner and scheduler that turns each work request into a ready job: job plan, parts kit, permits and a scheduled slot. This attacks the 65-75% of non-wrench time directly and could plausibly move wrench time from about 30% to 50%.
An automatic kitting and parts-staging service, possibly paired with robotics, that delivers parts and tools to the job before the technician arrives. It removes travel and parts-waiting time.
Low-cost retrofit condition monitoring for the long tail of mid-criticality assets, where today's predictive maintenance hardware (over $50k) does not pay. It shrinks the 45-55% reactive share.
A reliability copilot that runs RCM analysis on existing CMMS history to cut unnecessary preventive work and pick which assets should run to failure (the Nowlan & Heap insight at scale).
Outcome-priced uptime contracts (paying per avoided downtime hour) instead of selling software seats, since buyers measure lost production, not maintenance cost.
surprises: Losses from bad maintenance ($119B) are about 1.6x the maintenance spend itself, and $100B of that is lost sales, so the prize is uptime rather than cheaper repairs.
The reactive share has barely moved in 20 years: over 55% in the DOE's ~2000 study versus 45.7% in NIST's 2016 data, even with widespread CMMS use and 58% claimed AI adoption.
Practitioners (IDCON) say 90% of reliability improvement effort is people and behaviour, which runs against a technology-first thesis.
Some non-wrench time is valuable diagnosis and planning work, so maximising wrench time is the wrong goal.
The world-class to typical gap in maintenance cost as a share of asset value is only about 1.5-2x, nowhere near 10x.

Constraint: the shared web-search budget was exhausted, so every finding comes from direct fetches. A primary wrench-time category breakdown, Nowlan & Heap and SMRP's benchmark values could not be verified here.

stances.why: The chain broadly holds, but in industrial practice the time sits in steps it leaves out: screening, prioritising, planning, kitting parts, scheduling, permits and lockout, and coordinating with operations. Most non-wrench time is travel and waiting, not diagnosis. RCM also deliberately chooses run-to-failure for some assets.

In-plant inefficiency comes mainly from reactive culture and weak planning and logistics (IDCON, Palmer, NIST). A knowledge gap is not the main cause. Skills shortages are real (28% cite skills, 36% labour), but they are about people as much as knowledge, and plants mostly own their own maintenance rather than depending on OEMs.

58% of teams already report using AI, yet half still spend less than 40% of their time on planned work. Predictive maintenance needs sensors (over $50k), training and behaviour change, and IDCON puts 90% of the improvement effort on people.

Documented gains are 12-40% lower maintenance cost and wrench time rising from about 35% to 50%. No source shows 10x. Thinking work is only about 20-30% of technician time, and the largest economic cost is lost production during downtime, not the intermediate repair steps.
Emergency spares appear only as one downtime cost component, and buffer inventory is small ($0.9B in NIST). Nothing in this evidence covers bespoke manufacturing of parts.

Testing after repair is part of every job. Condition monitoring is effectively continuous inspection, and AI is already entering there, which supports the 'must evolve' part. There is no direct evidence on certification.

Low wrench time and a 45-55% reactive share support it. But the fixes (planning, RCM, predictive maintenance) have been known for decades, and best-in-class plants already reach under 10% reactive and 2-3% of asset value. The gap is management discipline, not structural design.

research.q: Wind turbine operations and maintenance: O&M cost share of LCOE, major component failures (gearbox, blades, main bearings), crane and vessel logistics, OEM full-service contracts vs ISPs; what is the bottleneck?
research.headline: O&M is about 18-27% of wind LCOE (NREL 2024: $43/kW-yr onshore, $135/kW-yr fixed offshore), but offshore OpEx is about 78% vessels and only about 5% technician labor plus materials. Cheaper diagnosis or knowledge barely moves cost; heavy-lift access and weather windows do. The deepest gap, main bearings failing at half their design life with no known root cause, is unknown to OEMs too, and AI prognostics have seen limited industrial adoption despite a decade of research.
research.bottleneck: Heavy-lift access is the bottleneck: scarce crane and jack-up vessel capacity, about 7 top-tier vessels at roughly $220k/day, plus weather windows to use them. Two things compound it: early-failing major components with unknown root causes (main bearings failing at about half their design life), and OEM data and full-service-agreement lock-in that keep failure data siloed, so repairs cannot be batched or predicted across fleets. Knowledge of how to repair is not the scarce layer.
research.money_time: O&M is roughly 18-27% of LCOE (NREL 2024), or 10-30% onshore and 16-25% offshore (IRENA); CapEx is the rest. Within offshore OpEx, NREL models vessels and heavy-lift equipment at about 78% ($105 of $135/kW-yr), insurance at about 14%, and technician labor plus materials at about 5%. UK statutory inspections are about 1% of OPEX. Onshore, major corrective events (gearbox, main bearing, blade) are dominated by crane mobilization plus lost production (background, unverified). In time, waiting for a crane or jack-up and a weather window, and for fleet defects regulator review and inspection campaigns lasting months, outweigh diagnosis time; faults are often detected 5-6 months ahead.
shapes: Lift-avoidance and uptower repair tooling (self-hoisting cranes, in-nacelle bearing and gearbox stage swaps): attacks the roughly 78% vessel and crane share directly.
Cross-owner anonymized failure and SCADA data clearinghouse with physics-informed prognostics: the value is batching repairs into vessel campaigns and spares planning, using data OEMs silo.
Robotic blade inspection and repair (leading-edge erosion, bond-line defects): cuts rope-access and weather dependence and fits the C6 inspection-evolution thesis.
Heavy-lift vessel and crane pooling marketplace or scheduler across owners and regions: targets the scarce asset itself.

Reverse-engineering and remanufacture of obsolete small parts (controller boards, pitch drives, sensors) for orphaned legacy 1-2 MW fleets: the only niche where an AI parts-factory idea plausibly fits.
surprises: Technician labor plus materials is only about 5% of NREL's modelled fixed-bottom offshore OpEx; vessels are about 78%.
Main bearings: 22-25% are projected to be replaced by year 20 against a 20-year design life, and no root cause is known to anyone, OEMs included.
Statutory inspections are only about 1% of UK offshore OPEX, yet a regulator halt after one blade failure took Vineyard Wind offline for about 6 months.
OEMs are not comfortably profiting: Siemens Gamesa's over-€1bn quality crisis needed a €7.5bn state guarantee.
Detecting faults was already possible 5-6 months ahead before modern AI; the binding constraint is acting on detection cheaply.

The shared web search budget was exhausted before this agent ran. Findings come from direct fetches of primary URLs, and the OEM vs ISP market-share figures are background knowledge, not verified this session (notes in /home/user/nuketime/research/repair/raw/m08.md).

stances.why: The chain fits a single corrective event. But much wind work is scheduled maintenance or fleet-wide serial-defect campaigns (Siemens Gamesa, Vineyard Wind), and booking a vessel or crane and waiting for a weather window are missing steps that dominate elapsed time.

OEMs control data, software and FSAs, and failure data is 'strictly protected', which supports a data monopoly. But the main bearing root cause is unknown to everyone, OEMs included, and large owners and ISPs do have repair know-how. Knowledge is not the main cost.

ML condition monitoring has been researched for about a decade, yet industrial prognostics adoption 'remains limited' because of false alarms, scarce fault labels, the explainability gap and uncertainty. Fault detection 5-6 months ahead already exists, so detection lead time is not the gap.

Offshore, technician labor plus materials is about 5% of OpEx and vessels about 78% (NREL). A 10x cheaper diagnosis or sourcing step barely moves cost unless it cuts heavy-lift use. Part delivery here means heavy-lift logistics, a physical asset constraint, not an information one.

Critical failing parts are multi-tonne gearboxes, main bearings and 100 m composite blades that need forging, heat treatment, grinding and certified layup. The Vineyard Wind failure was a manufacturing-quality defect. On-demand bespoke fabrication only plausibly fits small obsolete electronics and parts for legacy fleets.

At Vineyard Wind, the regulator halt and fleet inspection set a roughly 6-month timeline. Statutory inspection is cheap (about 1% of UK offshore OPEX) but decisive for timing. Drone and robotic blade inspection is the evolving layer.

FSA lock-in, data siloing and high OEM service margins look like rent-seeking. But the dominant costs are physics and logistics (scarce vessels and cranes, weather, the Jones Act), CapEx is about 75% of LCOE, and OEMs themselves are losing billions, which does not fit an industry comfortably extracting rents.

research.q: Semiconductor fab tool service (Applied, Lam, ASML, KLA service revenue; third-party refurbishers): how is the knowledge locked and what is downtime cost?
research.headline: Four Western OEMs (Applied, Lam, ASML, KLA) earn about $27B a year from fab tool service. It is locked in by tool qualification, multi-year subscription contracts, OEM ownership of tool telemetry and design data, and scarce field engineers, and governments now restrict servicing itself as a national-security chokepoint. Downtime costs a leading fab tens of millions of dollars a day: TSMC lost $85M on a 3-day malware outage and ~$110M on one photoresist contamination. But the evidence suggests the system is highly optimised for speed, not built to be inefficient, and that AI mainly strengthens the OEMs that already hold the data.
research.bottleneck: Qualified tacit expertise (field and applications engineers, scarce and now export-controlled) combined with process requalification of any part or repair, behind OEM ownership of tool telemetry and design data. For legacy tools, the binding constraint is obsolete components and retiring engineers, which ASML itself names.
research.money_time: Money: about $27B a year of OEM service spend (Applied $6.4B, Lam $8.3B, ASML ~$9.2B, KLA $3.1B), priced mostly for labour and parts logistics (Applied's service gross margin is 33%). The fab's dominant cost is lost output while a bottleneck tool is down (TSMC ~$13.9M revenue per hour company-wide; $85M for a ~3-day tool outage) and scrapped wafers from excursions (~$110M for one photoresist event). Time: diagnosis is already instrumented. Time goes to recovery, process requalification, and waiting for qualified parts on obsolete legacy platforms.
shapes: Lifetime-extension provider for legacy 150/200mm fabs: reverse-engineered, requalified replacement subassemblies and electronics for orphaned tools, plus AI capture of knowledge from retiring engineers. Demand evidence: ASML PAS-LTE, KLA end-of-life buys, 33% of non-ASML-serviced tools still active. Risks: OEM IP claims and OEM refurbishment businesses.
Fab-owned, multi-vendor tool-health and diagnostics layer that gives fabs leverage against OEM subscription lock-in. Hard part: getting data access through tight fab security gating.

Security and verification for tools and service actions entering fabs (malware screening, audit of AI-agent and remote-service actions). A C6 opening supported by the TSMC 2018 incident and Lam's warnings about AI agents.
Training and AI copilots for fab technicians at new CHIPS-funded and sovereign fabs facing engineer shortages, where qualified field expertise is the scarce input.
surprises: Applied's service segment has a lower gross margin (33%) than its new-tool segment (54%). ASML's service margin is about equal to systems. Service is not an outsized monopoly profit pool.
ASML says it is losing domain knowledge as its own engineers retire, so the knowledge holder is also losing knowledge.
Export controls regulate servicing, maintenance and repair as a strategic weapon, which is the clearest proof that repair know-how is an asset in its own right.
The TSMC 2018 shutdown was caused by the service and installation channel itself: malware on a newly installed tool.
ASML already prices some service contracts on system performance, so outcome-based service exists today.
The search budget was exhausted before this agent started, so the findings rest on primary filings read directly. Practitioner and analyst opinion is thin.

stances.why: The steps exist, but fabs run them in parallel: monitoring is continuous, parts are on consignment and engineers are already on site. Return to service means process requalification. A large share of service revenue is upgrades, not repair.

Qualification lock-in, trade secrets, subscription contracts, OEM-only telemetry, and export controls that treat servicing as a chokepoint all show the knowledge lock is real. Two caveats: service margins at or below systems margins, and the OEMs' own knowledge loss as engineers retire, both soften the 'monopoly rent' reading.

Newer tools need more service, OEMs own the data and already use AI for diagnosis, and China's rebuild took years, billions of dollars and former OEM engineers. The gap is not gone at the leading edge, though it may narrow for documented legacy tools.

These steps matter because downtime is so expensive (about $28M per day at TSMC scale), but fabs already buy speed with on-site engineers and consignment spares. The remaining cost is in recovery and requalification and in bottleneck downtime, not in diagnosis.

Obsolescence is real (KLA end-of-life buys, ASML redesign programs, Applied's reused-equipment parts problems). But parts must meet purity and contamination standards and be requalified, OEMs make IP claims, and ASML's answer is engineered redesign, not rapid fabrication.
Requalification, contamination analysis, tool malware screening (after TSMC 2018) and AI-agent security risks (Lam 10-K) point to a growing verification layer.

Fab service is among the most optimised repair systems anywhere: about 10,000 ASML field staff working around the clock, uptime-linked contracts, fleet analytics, and 95% of 30-year-old tools still running. It is concentrated and expensive because downtime is expensive, not because it was built to be inefficient.

research.q: Elevator maintenance oligopoly (Otis, KONE, Schindler, TK Elevator): service margins, proprietary diagnostic tools, independent maintainer complaints, EU and US cases.
research.headline: In elevators the whole profit pool is the service annuity. Otis earns a 25.1% margin on service against 4.8% on new equipment, and service brings 91% of its segment profit; KONE+TKE's 2026 merger is justified mainly by service-route density. The incumbents' advantage is access plus structure: locked tools and parts, conversion of new installs into service contracts, cartels that also covered maintenance, licensed labour and mandated inspection. Pure knowledge matters less, since independents already maintain about 50% of units, so AI-led diagnosis alone will not produce a 10x cost cut.
research.bottleneck: Access and structure rather than knowledge: OEM-locked controller software and service tools, OEM-controlled parts supply, a scarce licensed and unionised technician workforce (route density), the mandated inspection and certification regime, and long service contracts reinforced by converting new installs into service contracts. That conversion lets OEMs sell new equipment at near break-even to secure decades of service.
research.money_time: Profit sits almost entirely in the maintenance annuity: 91% of Otis segment profit at a 25% margin, and service plus modernization at ~65% of TKE sales. Cost is dominated by technician labour and travel, which is why the KONE+TKE synergies are mainly route density; by mandated preventive visits and periodic inspections; and by modernization of obsolete, often proprietary controllers. Owners lose time mainly waiting for licensed technicians, parts and inspectors, not on figuring out the fault. Diagnosis and parts information are a small share of total cost.
shapes: Vendor-neutral retrofit IoT plus AI fault-triage layer for independent maintainers and owners: gives the ~50% of units serviced by independents the same 'connected' capability Otis and KONE sell; risk is OEM controller lock-out.

Owner-side contract audit and procurement software: verifies visits and maintenance logs against ASME A17.1 8.6 or EN 13015, benchmarks pricing and runs re-tenders, exploiting long contracts and 'favorable' service pricing.
Certified interoperable replacement controllers and parts for obsolete units as an alternative to full OEM modernization; the type-examination and certification pipeline is the moat.
Risk-based and remote inspection tooling for regulators and notified bodies, moving fixed-interval inspection to evidence from monitoring data.
Track the KONE+TKE merger review (close Q2 2027 at earliest): service-portfolio divestitures or remedies on access to tools and parts could open a software-enabled roll-up of independents.
surprises: Independent service providers already hold about 50% of global service units (per Otis's own 10-K), so the 'monopoly' is over high-value units and value share, not over units.
KONE's contract win/loss balance against competition was slightly negative outside China in 2025; the OEMs are not fully insulated.

The EU's 2007 cartel case explicitly covered maintenance, with the Commission estimating effects lasting 20-50 years. The inefficiency was literally engineered, by collusion rather than a knowledge gap.
In April 2026 KONE agreed to merge with TK Elevator (EV EUR 29.4bn, 3.2m serviced units), and the stated main synergy is technician route density, not diagnostics.

OEMs are already the leading deployers of connected and AI maintenance (Otis 1.1m units connected; KONE >40% of its base, plus Dynamic Maintenance Planning), so AI may widen rather than close the incumbents' advantage.

stances.why: Elevators fit the chain, but most value is contracted preventive maintenance plus mandated periodic inspection and planned modernization at 20-25 years, not reactive incident chains.

OEMs control tools, parts and documentation, and EFESME asks for 'fair access to data, tools, and documentation'. But independents already maintain ~50% of units, and KONE is net-losing contracts outside China. The moat is also collusion (EUR 992m cartel), contract lock-in and conversion of new installs, which are not knowledge.

The barrier is locked controllers and service tools, parts access, licensed labour and inspection, none of which AI removes. The OEMs are themselves deploying IoT and AI (1.1m Otis connected units, >40% of KONE's base) and keeping the gains as margin.

The industry's own merger case puts the main cost lever in technician route density and labour productivity; labour is the stated risk; mandated visits set a cost floor. The information steps are a minority of cost, so a 10x cut there does not mean 10x overall.

Obsolete controllers do drive costly modernization (Otis +9%, KONE +17% growth), but safety components need type-examination under EN 81 or ASME A17.1, so certification, not fabrication, is the binding step.

Mandatory periodic inspection anchors the market and incumbents' resilient service economics; data-driven visit scheduling (KONE DMP) shows inspection and maintenance intervals starting to shift toward monitoring evidence.

New equipment sells at a 4.8% margin to lock in service at 25.1%; cartels covered maintenance with effects lasting decades; consolidation continues (KONE+TKE); service pricing is 'favorable'. The inefficiency is structural, but it comes from economics and law, not ignorance.

research.q: Naval ship maintenance: GAO findings on Navy depot maintenance delays (days of maintenance delay, causes: parts, unplanned work, workforce, planning); submarine idle time.
research.headline: GAO data from 2008 to 2026 show that Navy maintenance delays are driven mainly by capacity and execution limits, not a knowledge monopoly. Attack submarines lost more than 15,000 operational days ($3.4B) to depot overruns and waiting for a shipyard slot in FY2016-2025, and only about 11% of submarine depot maintenance finished on time. The top causes are unplanned "new work" found mid-repair, too few skilled workers, parts shortages and obsolescence, and too few dry docks. AI could help with condition prediction and parts demand forecasting, but it cannot remove the physical, workforce and certification limits.
research.bottleneck: The scarce layer is certified physical and human repair capacity: dry docks (including those needed to defuel reactors), skilled shipyard trades, and qualified spare parts for obsolete systems. It is made worse by poor knowledge of a ship's condition before work starts, which shows up as unplanned "new work", and by rigid funding and planning rules. Information about how to repair is not the constraint.
research.money_time: Most lost time and money go to waiting for capacity and to overruns from discovery work and labor shortfalls, not to diagnosis as a separate step. For attack submarines in FY2016-2025: 18,687 days and $4.17B in total, of which about 12,200 days ($2.7B) were idle waiting for shipyard or dry-dock capacity and 6,494 days ($1.46B) were depot overruns. Within carrier and submarine overruns in FY2015-2019 (causes overlap): unplanned "new work" 4,100+ days, workforce 4,000+ days (capacity 2,500+), and parts as the #2 submarine cause. On the capital side, shipyard infrastructure (SIOP) will exceed $200B. Fleet-wide, 33,700 excess days in FY2014-2019 and rising cannibalization and casualty reports.
shapes: Pre-availability condition assessment and growth-work prediction (sensors, digital twins, ML on past work packages): attacks unplanned work, the largest single delay cause (4,100+ days).

Obsolete and diminishing-source parts as a service: reverse engineering, technical data package creation, and qualified additive manufacturing. Cannibalization trends and sailor workarounds prove the demand; the moat is qualification and certification, not printing.
Spares demand and allowance-list modelling (onboard fill rate below the 65% goal; lists out of date): software sold to fleets and operators of military sealift and other government-owned vessels.

Shipyard throughput tools: AR and AI work instructions to bring inexperienced trades up to speed, workforce and capacity scheduling, and digital inspection and certification evidence (departures from spec rising).
Capacity-adding hardware: modular or floating dry docks, and defueling outside dry docks, which GAO explicitly recommends evaluating, against $3.1B of projected idle cost.
surprises: Active submarine idle time fell about 90% (1,518 days in FY2022 to 166 in FY2025) through hiring, training and moving work to private yards, but depot delays kept growing and only about 11% of submarine depot periods finished on time.
The newest idle-time problem is decommissioning: boats wait up to 4 years for a dry dock to defuel, with $3.1B in idle costs projected for FY2026-2030.
The Navy is its own OEM and owns its shipyards, and still shows the same delay pattern, which suggests a knowledge monopoly is not the root cause here.
One submarine gave 222 parts to 17 other submarines in a single maintenance cycle; sailors buy door handles at hardware stores and reverse-engineer motors.
The Navy did not even collect delay data for surface ship and carrier intermediate maintenance until GAO pushed for it.
The shipyard infrastructure estimate grew roughly tenfold, from $21B over 20 years to more than $200B over 50+ years.
Method note: the shared web-search budget was used up, so these findings come from GAO pages and PDFs fetched directly, not searches; non-GAO sources (CBO, CRS, industry) were not covered.

stances.why: The stages exist, and certification gates return to service. But most lost time is queueing for scarce dry docks and shipyard slots, planning 2.5 years ahead, funding approvals, and work discovered mid-repair, with feedback loops (deferred maintenance creates more unplanned work; cannibalization breaks the donor ship). It is not a linear per-repair chain.

The Navy owns its shipyards and largely its technical data, so no outside OEM monopolizes the knowledge, yet delays persist. The knowledge gaps that do exist are unknown ship condition (the root of unplanned work), tacit hands-on skill, and outdated documentation and spares lists, not proprietary monopoly.
Practitioners point to hands-on training, headcount, parts and dry docks. AI could help on predicting unplanned work and modelling parts demand, but certified physical skill and capacity gaps remain.

Better upfront diagnosis could cut part of the unplanned-work delay (4,100+ of 7,424 days), and parts sourcing is a top submarine cause. But a large share of cost is idle waiting for capacity and workforce limits (12,200 of 18,687 submarine days, plus 4,000+ workforce days), which a 10x drop in information costs does not fix.

Demand is huge: obsolete parts, backorders of up to 2 years, rising cannibalization, sailors reverse-engineering parts. But nothing is solved, and SUBSAFE and nuclear parts need qualification. The Navy already does emergency part manufacture at its maintenance facilities.

Expiry of SUBSAFE certification is what turns a submarine into an idle boat. Departures from specification are rising, and cannibalized parts need re-inspection, so certification gates are where time accumulates.

Structural rigidities are real: annual budgets and approval rules, hiring with no surge capacity, acquisition that ignores sustainment, poor data. But targeted management changes cut active idle time by about 90%, and the remaining limit is physical capacity (dry docks, aged shipyards).

research.q: Rail rolling stock and locomotive maintenance: OEM vs operator vs independent; parts obsolescence on long-life fleets; cost and availability data.
research.headline: Rail rolling stock runs for 30-50 years (the GB passenger fleet is 15,348 vehicles averaging 16.7 years; HSTs ran 41+ years). Most cost goes on scheduled maintenance labour, depot capacity, and obsolescence redesign of electronics with re-approval, not on diagnosis or finding knowledge. OEM capture is real, especially in the North American locomotive aftermarket, but it is enforced by contracts, IP and design/approval authority rather than by a pure knowledge gap. Caveat: the search budget was exhausted, so only some findings were verified this session.
research.bottleneck: Design authority and approval for replacement or modified parts (safety case, vehicle authorisation, ECM sign-off, data and IP rights held by the OEM), together with depot capacity and skilled fitters. These matter more than knowing what is wrong.
research.money_time: Most cost is scheduled maintenance labour and depot or shop capacity, plus heavy overhaul and mid-life refurbishment, plus obsolescence programmes such as re-engining (e.g. £110m for 54 HST power cars) and electronics or signalling redesign with re-approval. Maintenance is often cited at 30-50% of lifecycle cost. Diagnosis is already largely digitised by OEMs, and parts sourcing becomes a long-lead problem mainly for obsolete electronics and low-volume legacy parts.
shapes: Obsolescence-as-a-service for rail electronics: form-fit-function replacement of legacy control and traction boards, delivered with the approval dossier. This targets the most costly class of obsolescence.
AI-assisted builder of approval and ECM dossiers for replacement or modified parts, aimed at the real bottleneck (the safety case and conformity evidence).
A qualification broker for AM spare parts serving ROSCOs and operators running unsupported 30-40 year fleets, starting with non-safety-critical parts where DB has proven the model.
Depot automation and robotic underframe or wheel inspection to relieve the depot labour and capacity constraint.
surprises: In the UK, the asset lessor (a ROSCO), not the OEM or the operator, often runs the major obsolescence programmes, such as HST re-engining.
Obsolescence pain in rail is mainly electronics with 5-10 year lives in 30-40 year vehicles, not mechanical parts.
US railroads cut maintenance spend under Precision Scheduled Railroading mainly by parking and cannibalising locomotives, not through smarter diagnosis.
The WebSearch budget was exhausted before this agent started, so several numbers are background knowledge flagged as unverified in research/repair/raw/m12.md.

stances.why: The chain fits corrective repairs, but most rail maintenance is scheduled (mileage- or time-based exams, heavy overhauls every 8-12 years) or done as fleet-wide modification programmes (re-engining, ETCS retrofit) driven by obsolescence or regulation rather than by noticing a fault.

OEM capture is real (Wabtec/GE and Progress/EMD aftermarket; 25-30 year OEM maintenance contracts on new fleets), but it is enforced by contracts, IP, software and design authority. In the UK, ROSCOs and third parties (Angel/MTU re-engining, Wabtec Doncaster) routinely do major work without the original OEM.

The binding gaps are legal design authority, data rights and the approval or safety case, plus depot capacity. AI does not transfer IP or approval authority, and OEM digital diagnostics already exist.
Diagnosis and parts ordering are a small share of cost. Labour, depot capacity, heavy overhaul and electronics redesign dominate, and predictive maintenance claims run 10-30%, not 10x.

DB's printed spare parts show AM works for non-critical obsolete parts, with lead times cut from months to days. The costly obsolescence, though, is electronics needing redesign and re-approval, and safety-critical parts need certification.
The EU ECM certification regime was strengthened after Viareggio, and FRA mandates 92-day inspections. Certification and approval is the gate even for open-market independents.

Incentives favour OEMs (high-margin, decades-long service backlogs, aftermarket duopoly in NA locomotives), but the structure is largely a rational response to safety regulation and 30-50 year asset lives, not plain sloppiness.

research.q: Mining and heavy equipment (Caterpillar, Komatsu dealers, component rebuild centres): mechanical availability targets, dealer lock, rebuild economics.
research.headline: In mining and heavy equipment, the lock-in comes from exclusive dealer territories, dealer-only diagnostic and calibration software, OEM reman and core programmes, and availability-guaranteed service contracts that miners buy for risk transfer, not from knowledge alone. The real bottlenecks are rotable component capital, parts and tyre supply, and skilled technicians at remote sites. AI-cheap diagnosis would not cut total repair cost 10x, and incumbents are using AI and telemetry to deepen lock-in. Caveat: the shared search budget was exhausted before this agent ran, so only a few findings were verified this session and the rest are flagged as background knowledge in /home/user/nuketime/research/repair/raw/m13.md.
research.bottleneck: Rotable component capital and core supply, skilled technicians at remote sites, and OEM control of diagnostic and calibration software, warranty and the parts channel through exclusive territorial dealers. It is an access, capital and labour bottleneck rather than a knowledge bottleneck.
research.money_time: The dominant cost is lost production from unavailability. One idle ultra-class truck forgoes thousands of dollars per hour, and maintenance is roughly 30-50% of mine opex. Within direct maintenance spend, parts and components (including rebuilds and exchange units) are likely the largest share, ahead of labour. Time is lost waiting for components and parts, technicians and shutdown windows. Diagnosis is a small share for telemetry-equipped large fleets, but larger for mid-tier and older mixed fleets and for electrical and electronic faults. (Directional; mostly background figures, not verified this session.)
shapes: An OEM-agnostic diagnostic and maintenance-planning copilot for mid-tier miners, quarries and contractors with mixed-brand fleets. Diagnosis still costs them time, and they lack the dealer-level MARC support of the majors. Telematics access via ISO 15143-3 exists but is limited.
A pooled rotable and component-exchange network for independent rebuilders. It attacks the capital and logistics bottleneck that underpins dealer lock-in.

Qualified on-demand manufacturing (reverse engineering plus AM and casting plus a certification pack) for obsolete and long-lead parts at remote mines. Lead time and obsolescence are real, but qualification is the moat.
A labour-multiplier toolset for fitters (AI and AR guided procedures, job planning) aimed at the heavy-diesel technician shortage.
Functional-safety and assurance tooling for autonomous and retrofit mining fleets, the inspection angle of C6.
surprises: The shared search budget ran out before this agent started; only about 5 findings were verified by direct fetch.
Miners often choose dealer lock-in voluntarily through availability-guaranteed MARCs, buying risk transfer and capital rather than knowledge.
OEMs are the leading users of AI and telemetry in mining (connected fleets, autonomy, RPMGlobal acquisition), which concentrates knowledge rather than spreading it.
Heavy and off-road equipment is the largest US remanufacturing sector: 'rebuild instead of replace' is already the norm, under OEM control.
Right-to-repair law and enforcement have targeted agricultural equipment (FTC v. Deere) but largely exempt mining and construction equipment.

stances.why: Unplanned failures follow the chain. But mining is dominated by planned component-life change-outs from pre-positioned rotable pools, which split the chain into a fast swap loop and a slow off-site rebuild loop and pre-empt the 'diagnose then source' sequence.

Real lock-in exists: exclusive dealer territories, dealer-only diagnostic tools, a proprietary reman spec and parts profit pool. But it is an access and channel monopoly more than a knowledge gap. Big miners have deep in-house expertise yet still buy availability contracts, and simple wear parts are already contestable.

The barriers are authenticated software, encrypted ECUs, warranty terms, the parts channel, labour and capital, which AI cannot unlock. OEMs are using AI, telemetry and autonomy to deepen lock-in (connected assets, RPMGlobal acquisition).

Cost is dominated by lost production from unavailability and by physical parts and component supply and labour. Diagnosis on large fleets is already telemetry-driven, so cheaper information would not cut total cost 10x, though forecasting and pooling gains are possible.

On-demand manufacturing helps with obsolete and long-tail parts at remote mines, but critical parts need material qualification. Component rebuild is already a mature, OEM-led industry at 40-70% of new price.
Isolation and safety, statutory mine inspections and new autonomy functional-safety assurance (ISO 17757) remain central. Evidence that inspection itself is evolving for AI is thin in this domain.

The system is built for OEM and dealer margin capture and territorial exclusivity. But availability guarantees, exchange pools and on-site dealer crews are a rational response to extreme downtime costs: it is inefficient on price but efficient at delivering uptime.

research.q: Data centre hardware repair and hyperscaler practices (Google/Meta fleet repair, sparing, RMA, robotics in DC repair, Open Compute): how did hyperscalers make repair efficient at scale and what can generalise?
research.headline: Hyperscalers made repair efficient mainly by taking it off the critical path, not by knowing more. Redundancy and spares (about 1-2% overhead) turn every failure into batched, non-urgent work, cutting repair cost from 5-15% of equipment value per year (OEM on-site contracts) to about 0.75%. Continuous telemetry, automated isolation, homogeneous fleets, standard fault reporting and harvested spares do the rest. Per-unit diagnosis is still hard even for Google and Meta: SMART signals miss 36-56% of disk failures, half of human-flagged bad cores turn out to be false leads, and silent data corruption has risen from about 1 in a million to about 1 in a thousand devices.
research.bottleneck: Observability and isolation built into the hardware and the system, plus redundancy that makes repair non-urgent. The scarce layer is not general repair knowledge but trustworthy machine-readable fault signals. Silicon often does not expose them (chip test structures stay with vendors, SMART misses most disk failures), and making use of them needs a homogeneous fleet with enough data and spare capacity. Standards that force OEMs to expose fault data (OCP fault management, RAS requirements) and orchestration that decouples failure from service are what unlocked efficiency.
research.money_time: Money goes into urgency: keeping parts and technicians ready for fast on-site response (5-15% of equipment value per year, about double for 4-hour response). Batched repair costs about 0.75%. Downtime (capacity out of service) also costs more than parts or labour. Once redundancy removes the urgency, the remaining time goes into noticing and localising subtle faults (silent data corruption, stragglers, lemon nodes, intermittent faults), not into fixing them.
