At scale, MTTF falls to hours or minutes (0.23 hours projected at 131K GPUs), so detect, isolate and restart is the critical path and swapping the part is cheap and deferred. Diagnosis errors are a large waste line: 43% of returned drives were No Trouble Found, and every false prediction costs a full repair cycle.
shapes: Fleet reliability OS for physical assets (Borg/OpsPlanner-style): continuous health checks, automatic isolation, spare-capacity and maintenance-buffer orchestration, and batched work-order dispatch for robot fleets, battery storage, wind, EV/robotaxi and telecom. This is what made hyperscaler repair cheap, and most non-IT fleets lack it.

Cross-operator fault data network (a 'Backblaze stats' or OCP-fault-management for machines): pool field failure and No Trouble Found data across operators to correct OEM datasheets, cut false RMAs and plan spares; the data network effect breaks the vendors' knowledge hold.

Lemon-unit and silent-fault detection for AI/GPU fleets and other dense electronics: in-production screening, straggler and SDC detection, RMA evidence packages. The problem is growing (about 1 in 1,000 devices) and hyperscalers built it in-house while neoclouds and enterprises lack it.

Refurbished/harvested parts exchange and certification for standardised hardware, extending Google's 29% refurbished-component model to the mid-market, with automated test-to-certify as the inspection layer.
Design-for-fail-in-place / serviceability tooling: help OEMs make assets that report standard fault codes and tolerate failures in place, since redundancy beats fast repair.
surprises: Microsoft's Natick ran with no repair at all and had 1/8 the failure rate of land; people in the repair loop cause failures.
Even Google lacks the knowledge it needs: it has no access to chip makers' test structures and cannot root-cause mercurial cores. The knowledge gap is with the silicon maker, not the repairer.
Meta handled 416 of 419 unexpected failures automatically, but automation here means isolate and restart; the physical fix still happens later, off the critical path.
Vendor datasheets understate field failure rates by 3-30x, and 43% of returned drives are not faulty; RMA waste comes from diagnosis error, not missing knowledge.
Silent data corruption got 1,000x more common in dense AI silicon (1e-6 to 1e-3 per device); AI hardware makes diagnosis harder, not easier.
Google found that ML failure prediction pays off only at very high accuracy when software tolerates faults, so better diagnosis can be worth less than more redundancy.

The WebSearch budget ran out before this agent started, so findings come from directly fetched primary sources; robotics-in-data-centre-repair evidence is missing and Microsoft Circular Centers figures are unverified.

stances.why: The steps exist, but hyperscalers decouple and reorder them. Notice, isolate, swap in spare capacity and return to service happens in minutes; diagnosis and physical repair are batched later or skipped entirely (fail-in-place in Natick, decommission and harvest).

Real two-way knowledge gaps exist. Google lacks chip makers' test access, vendors lack fleet data, datasheets understate field failure rates 3-30x, and 43% of returned drives show no fault. But the biggest savings came from redundancy, batching and automation, not from closing a knowledge gap.

Google has used ML diagnosis for well over a decade, yet per-unit prediction stays weak (36-56% of disk failures give no SMART signal). Novel failure modes need human root-causing, silent data corruption is getting more common, and the hardware often does not expose the signals a model would need.

Hyperscalers did get roughly 10x cheaper repair than OEM service contracts (0.75% vs 5-15% of capex per year). The cause was scale, homogeneity, redundancy, batching and owned spares, not cheaper diagnosis. It depends on fleet scale and does not carry over to one-off assets.

No hyperscaler fabricates bespoke replacement parts, and the parts that fail most (GPUs, HBM, DIMMs, PCIe) need a fab. Sourcing was solved by standard SKUs and harvested refurbished spares (29% at Google).

Automated return-to-service gating (health checks every 5 minutes, host verification, SDC screening via Fleetscanner, Ripple and Hardware Sentinel) is central and keeps evolving. Inspection has become continuous and in-production rather than a one-off sign-off.

Hyperscalers did rebuild repair end to end, and OEM-style urgent service costs 7-30x more, which supports the claim for the vendor-service model. The rebuild worked by redesigning the asset and the system around expected failure, which needs fleet scale and control of the design.

research.q: Home appliance repair economics: repair vs replace decisions, technician call-out cost vs appliance price, parts availability windows, decline of repair shops; Whirlpool/Samsung/LG service models.
research.headline: Home appliance repair loses to replacement mainly because the fixed cost of an in-home visit is high against cheap new machines, parts waits are slow (the EU legally allows 15 working days), and designs like sealed drums and bundled spares raise the price floor, not mainly because knowledge is missing. AI can cut diagnosis and repeat-visit costs, but a 10x drop in total repair cost is unlikely because labor and the truck roll dominate. Caveat: no web searches ran (the shared search budget was used up) and many fetches failed, so only the FTC, EEB, Whirlpool 10-K and Minnesota statute findings plus the Wikipedia summaries (EU directive, design examples, Sears) were checked; the cost, workforce, Samsung/LG and subsidy findings are unverified background knowledge.
research.bottleneck: The real bottleneck is skilled in-home technician labor and the visit cost it carries. That cost is high relative to falling or tariff-volatile new-appliance prices, and the workforce is shrinking. Parts logistics and design-driven bundling come next, then OEM gating of service software, parts terms and warranty pay rates. Knowledge is a secondary constraint.
research.money_time: In appliances, the fixed cost of the in-home visit (call-out about $75-150, roughly 10-25% of a mid-range machine's price) and labor dominate the ticket. Elapsed time is driven by parts waits (the EU tolerates up to 15 working days) and by second visits when the part is not on the truck. Product design that forces whole-assembly replacement, such as sealed drums and bundled spares, sets a high parts floor. Diagnosis is relatively cheap and increasingly guided by error codes. Consumers cite cost and service quality, not missing know-how, as why they replace.
shapes: Remote AI triage and dispatch for appliance service networks: diagnose from error codes and video before the truck rolls, so the right part is on the first visit. This hits the real cost driver (repeat truck rolls), not just knowledge.

Long-tail parts supply for discontinued SKUs: reverse-engineered or on-demand parts (plastics, gaskets, latches, brackets) once OEM legal windows of 7-10 years lapse. Electronic control-board repair or remanufacture is a related wedge.

Compliance and parts-portal infrastructure for OEMs facing EU Directive 2024/1799 and US state right-to-repair laws: public parts catalogues, repairer registration, delivery-time SLAs. A regulatory deadline creates demand.

Caution: home appliances are a low-ticket domain where labor caps the gain. The same triage-plus-parts thesis probably earns far more where downtime is expensive (commercial refrigeration, HVAC, industrial machines).
surprises: OEMs appear to make little money from appliance repair. Whirlpool's warranty expense is about 2.1% of sales with no service profit reported, and AHAM says 87% of servicers are independents. The 'monopoly' is a gate on access and pay terms, not a profit pool.
EU law itself treats a 15-working-day parts delivery and a 2-year post-launch grace period as acceptable (detail from background knowledge), which shows how slow the baseline is.
To offset its production emissions, a washer would need to last 25-40 years against an actual 11, so the social case for repair far exceeds the private one.
Rising 2026 appliance prices (Whirlpool's +10% increase) improve the economics of repair over replacement.
The largest national brand-agnostic repairer, Sears Home Services, went down with Sears, which suggests standalone appliance repair is structurally thin-margin.

stances.why: Appliance repair does follow notice-diagnose-parts-repair. But the steps collapse or loop: the diagnostic visit and the repair visit are separate truck rolls, a missing part triggers a second visit, and there is rarely a formal safety inspection for household appliances beyond the technician's own check. The dominant decision node is repair-vs-replace, which the chain omits.

The FTC confirms OEM restrictions on parts, manuals and diagnostics, and Minnesota and California now legislate access. But AHAM says 87% of 20,000 servicers are local independents, and consumers cite repair cost and service quality (77% Eurobarometer), not lack of knowledge. The gate is on access and pay terms rather than on who holds the knowledge.

The binding constraints are labor and visit cost, parts logistics, design such as sealed drums and bundled spares, and OEM-gated service software and parts. AI does not remove these, and some parts and information remain legally professional-only in the EU.

Diagnosis and understanding are a small share of an appliance repair ticket. The truck roll, labor and part price dominate. AI can raise first-time fix rates and cut parts delays, but a 10x drop in combined cost is implausible for in-home appliance repair.

There is a real long-tail gap. Legal parts windows end 7-10 years after a model stops being sold (EU) or once the OEM stops supplying its network (Minnesota). But many failures involve bundled or sealed assemblies, electronic control boards or safety-critical parts, which on-demand fabrication does not easily solve.

The EU keeps some parts professional-only and requires repairer registration. France's bonus requires certified repairers. OEMs require technician vetting and traceability. Certification is the lever regulators use and is evolving.

Markets are biased toward replacement: the FTC says restrictions steer consumers to replace, and repair's environmental value is underpriced. But OEMs do not profit much from repair (Whirlpool's warranty cost is about 2.1% of sales), and regulators are already reworking the system incrementally (EU 2024/1799, state laws) rather than it being deliberately built to be inefficient.

research.q: Smartphone and electronics repair: Asurion, uBreakiFix, Apple Self Service Repair and parts pairing, independent repair provider program; market size and what drives cost.
research.headline: In smartphones, the bottleneck is control over who may repair, not knowledge of how. Parts pairing tied to Apple's servers, genuine-part pricing that undercuts independents ($270 for the part vs $280 installed at Apple), IRP contract terms and insurance-plan pricing decide cost and volume, while repair manuals are already public and most diagnoses (cracked screen, worn battery) are trivial. Regulators (FTC 2021, EU Ecodesign 2025, Oregon SB 1596) are reshaping the market, and AI does little against cryptographic and legal gates. Caveat: the shared web search budget was used up before this agent's first search, so all findings come from direct fetches of known primary sources, and market-size figures are unverified.
research.bottleneck: Control of authorization and authentication. Server-side parts pairing, calibration and Activation Lock on parts, plus OEM control of genuine-part supply and price, decide who can complete a repair and at what cost. Contracts and insurance-plan distribution reinforce that control. Know-how is not the binding constraint.
research.money_time: Phone repair cost is dominated by the price of the genuine part (OLED screen or battery, often $150-300), skilled labor and OEM authorization, not diagnosis. Apple charges independents $270 for a screen it installs for $280. Device-protection plans (Asurion, AppleCare) capture a large share of consumer spending and steer where repairs go. Time is lost to serial-number checks and paired-part ordering, System Configuration steps and depot routing. Diagnosis is minutes for screen and battery jobs.
shapes: A neutral parts-authentication and provenance layer (a cryptographic parts history that is not controlled by the OEM, with anti-theft checks). It would fit EU and Oregon mandates for non-discriminatory software access and turn certification into infrastructure, which is where C6 points.
A marketplace for harvested and refurbished genuine parts, with grading and verification of Activation Lock status, since Apple now calibrates used genuine parts.
Repair-cost data and compliance tooling for OEMs facing the EU Ecodesign and R2R Directive 2026-2028 deadlines: 7-year parts availability and 5-10 day delivery logistics.
Avoid an AI diagnosis app for consumer phones: diagnosis is already trivial and is not where the money goes. The insurer/OEM channel (Asurion, AppleCare) controls distribution.
surprises: Apple charges independents nearly its own retail repair price for the bare screen ($270 vs $280 installed).
Cutting battery replacement from $79 to $29 produced more than 11M replacements against 1-2M expected, and visibly hurt iPhone sales. Repair demand is highly price-elastic.
As of the 2019 FTC workshop, no study compared the quality of authorized and independent repair.
Apple now justifies pairing partly as anti-theft (Activation Lock on parts), a legitimate security role that complicates the knowledge-monopoly story.
The largest U.S. independent phone repair chain (uBreakiFix) is now part of a private-equity, debt-financed insurance company (Asurion).

stances.why: Apple's own Self Service flow (manual, order part, repair, System Configuration, return part) follows the chain. Phones add an OEM pairing or authorization step before return to service, and diagnosis is trivial for most jobs.

OEMs did restrict information (DMCA takedowns of manuals), but the stronger levers now are serialized parts, pricing that undercuts independents, IRP contracts and insurance-plan pricing. Know-how for screens and batteries is largely public via iFixit and Apple's own manuals.

The gap that matters is a server-side cryptographic handshake plus Activation Lock on parts. AI cannot produce OEM authorization, and board-level work is limited by microsoldering skill and tools, not information.

Diagnose and understand are already near-zero cost for common phone repairs, and parts cost is mostly part price set by the OEM. The $79-to-$29 battery cut shows a cheaper gate releases a lot of latent demand, but the lever was price and policy, not AI. The EU already mandates 5-10 day parts delivery.

OLED panels, batteries, cameras and chips cannot be made bespoke, and pairing would reject a fabricated part. The practical substitute is harvested or used genuine parts, which Apple now allows within anti-theft limits.

In phones, certification has become cryptographic authentication of parts (pairing, parts history, Activation Lock), which has a real anti-theft and anti-counterfeit role. The FTC found no study comparing authorized and independent repair quality, so who certifies is the open question.

The FTC found restrictions steer consumers to OEM networks and to early replacement, on scant evidence, so the system is built for capture. But change is coming from regulation (EU, CA, NY, MN, OR) and consolidation (Asurion), and the system works efficiently for OEMs and insurers, if not for society.

research.q: HVAC and plumbing trades: technician shortage numbers, how diagnosis is done, callbacks, ServiceTitan data, AI copilots for technicians (e.g., XOi, Bluon); evidence of AI improving first-time fix.
research.headline: In HVAC and plumbing, the scarce thing is skilled technicians on site (about 82,600 openings a year, mostly replacing retirees) and the senior judgement they carry. AI copilots such as Bluon, XOi, ServiceTitan Atlas and Aquant mainly cut escalations and sales friction; the best data, from vendors, puts the prize from closing the knowledge gap at about 10-26% of service cost, not 10x. NIST field data shows most installed systems run with undetected faults and that standard field diagnostic heuristics are unreliable, so there is a real knowledge and procedure gap, but closing it needs instruments, time on site and incentives, not only information. Caveat: the shared web search budget was used up, so these findings come from direct fetches of known primary URLs, and items marked unverified in the notes are leads only.
research.bottleneck: Experienced technicians: licensed hands with instruments and senior judgement. About 82,600 openings a year across HVAC and plumbing are mostly replacement as the workforce ages, and know-how sits with a few senior techs and service managers. Beyond that is proprietary structured equipment data (model to BOM, parts and known fixes, built from support calls and job records) plus the incentive and verification to measure correctly on site. Generic AI does not supply either.
research.money_time: Mostly in getting a qualified person on site and in visits that fail. Aquant puts failed visits at 25% of median service cost (44% for bottom performers), finds about 1 in 5 cases could be resolved remotely, and estimates about 1 in 7 truck rolls are unnecessary. Diagnosis quality is the hidden cost: most installed systems run with faults, about 20% efficiency is lost, and the cost shows up as energy waste and callbacks rather than invoice lines. Parts are mostly commodity and stocked locally, so physical delivery is a minor cost; part identification is the friction. Software spend (ServiceTitan, XOi) goes mainly to demand capture, dispatch and ticket size, which shows owners feel labour and revenue pain more than diagnostic pain.
shapes: A 'senior tech in your pocket' copilot built on a proprietary equipment, parts and fixes graph (the Bluon/XOi pattern). The moat is curated data from support calls and jobs, not the LLM; the evidence is that generic AI scores 11% on parts identification.

Instrumented diagnosis: connected sensors and probes (pressure, temperature, airflow) feeding AI fault detection and diagnosis, so faults get noticed and charge and airflow are measured correctly. This targets NIST's 57-72% mis-charge problem and the unreliable field heuristics.
Remote triage that avoids truck rolls (about 1 in 5 cases remotely resolvable, failed visits 25% of cost) for commercial HVAC or OEM service organisations, sold on cost per resolved case.

Verification and commissioning layer: AI plus measurement that proves an install or repair was done right, for utilities, insurers, A2L compliance or PE roll-ups. This fits C6 and the history of RCA programmes where technician-reported fixes didn't deliver savings (unverified lead).
Tooling for private-equity roll-ups of trades: standardising knowledge across acquired shops to push bottom-quartile first-time fix (60%) toward the top quartile (88%).
surprises: The largest trades platform (ServiceTitan) and XOi publish AI outcomes in close rates, ticket size and revenue, not first-time fix. AI in the trades is being sold mainly as a sales tool.
Bluon's own benchmark: generic AI with web search scores only 11-12% on replacement parts and procurement but 75% on troubleshooting. Sourcing is the harder knowledge problem, not diagnosis.
Even Aquant, which sells this outcome, models only up to 26% service cost savings from closing the knowledge gap, nowhere near 10x.

NIST field data: 95% of residential AC units failed a diagnostic test, and the profession's standard field methods give wrong answers under common low-airflow conditions. Diagnosis is wrong at scale, not only slow.
Shortage headlines are industry-sourced; BLS shows openings are mostly replacement, and median pay is moderate (about $61-64k).
Search budget was exhausted for this run; independent (non-vendor) first-time-fix evidence for AI copilots in HVAC was not found and may not exist publicly.

stances.why: The steps exist, but in HVAC the main failure is faults that are never noticed (57-72% of systems mis-charged and running degraded), and installation quality drives much of it. Diagnosis, parts and repair often collapse into one truck roll from van stock, and most residential repairs have no separate safety inspection beyond permits for gas, plumbing and installs.

There is a 28-point first-time-fix spread between top and bottom organisations, escalations to senior techs are a bottleneck (Bluon: 80% of service-manager calls avoidable), and NIST documents widespread mis-diagnosis. But the gap is mostly junior vs senior inside firms and about procedure and measurement, not an OEM monopoly; residential HVAC docs and parts are fairly open.

Bluon's own benchmark shows generic AI at 11-12% on parts identification and procurement. Practitioners say AI gets '80% of the way', and ServiceTitan warns of hallucinations and slow adoption. Knowledge is moving to owners of curated data, not vanishing.

Aquant, which sells this outcome, models savings from closing the knowledge gap at low double digits up to 26%, and failed visits are 25% of median cost. No source shows an order-of-magnitude drop; labour on site stays dominant.

No evidence of on-demand fabrication in HVAC or plumbing. Parts are largely commodity and distributor-stocked; the pain is identification and cross-referencing (1B cross-references), not manufacture. Safety listings would constrain bespoke parts (general knowledge).
Plumbing and gas licensing, EPA 608 refrigerant certification and new A2L safety training are expanding, and ACCA is wrapping AI around its standards rather than replacing certification.

Structural waste is real: degraded installs, about 25% of cost in failed visits, and knowledge stuck in a few heads. But the industry is consolidating through private-equity roll-ups and digitising (ServiceTitan $961M revenue, retention over 95%), and AI is being added incrementally. The incentive problems (upsell-focused AI, replace-over-repair) are business-model issues more than a reason to rebuild from scratch.

research.q: Automotive repair: diagnosis share of shop time, comebacks, misdiagnosis and "parts cannon" rates, technician shortage, ADAS calibration costs, EV battery repair; data from AAA, NIASE, consumer surveys.
research.headline: In car repair the knowledge monopoly was mostly broken by law back in 2013-14 (the Massachusetts law and the national MOU). Today's costs are driven by sensor-heavy hardware, calibration, labor hours and rates, cycle time and a shortage of hands (29-57% depending on sector), not by missing information. The knowledge gaps that remain are about data and access control (telematics, security gateways) and customer distrust (76% fear unneeded work). AI helps with triage and trust but cannot cut total repair cost by 10x.
research.bottleneck: Skilled labor capacity, worst in collision (57% gap) and diesel (52%), which is a pay and churn problem. Next come OEM-controlled access gates (telematics data, security gateways, module programming), which are legal and cryptographic rather than knowledge. Then verification and trust: customers can't check a diagnosis, and calibration needs proof. Then capital-heavy calibration and EV high-voltage equipment. Information itself has been largely purchasable since 2014.
research.money_time: In collision repair, money goes to labor hours (27.3 per claim, rising), labor rates (+4.5-7.5% a year), sensor-laden parts (ADAS up to 37.6% of the bill) and calibration (~$547 when needed, on ~30% of claims). Time goes to cycle time: weeks overall, 37.5 days for EVs, 4-5 days above 2020. Much of that is parts, approvals and supplements after hidden damage is found at teardown. Diagnostic scanning itself is routine and a small share. In mechanical repair, the consumer-side pain is trust and affordability. I found no hard data on diagnosis share of shop time, comeback rates or parts-cannon rates.
shapes: ADAS calibration verification and attestation (mobile calibration plus tamper-evident proof records): AAA tells consumers to demand proof, and CCC shows calibration on 30% of claims at about $547 each.
Pre-teardown damage triage using imaging and AI to catch hidden ADAS and structural damage before the supplement stage (56% of calibrations are found late), shortening a 37-day EV cycle time.
EV pack collision diagnostics and module-level repair to avoid total losses (record 22.9% total-loss share). Pack wear-out failures are rare (0.3%), so target crash damage.
Productivity and training multipliers for collision and diesel techs, where shortages are 52-57%: AI copilots that raise output per tech, not ones that replace the hands-on work.
Neutral repair-data and access layer (telematics and gateway access for independents) riding on Massachusetts-style mandates. Policy risk is high.
surprises: The workflow's shared web-search budget was used up before this agent ran. All evidence came from fetching known publisher URLs, and diagnosis share, comeback rates and parts-cannon rates could not be sourced.

The auto industry already broke its OEM information monopoly in 2013-14 (Massachusetts law and national MOU), and the FTC holds it up as the model sector. The 'knowledge monopoly' thesis is about a decade late for cars.
56% of ADAS calibrations are found only on supplements, after teardown. Late discovery, not lack of knowledge, is the costly diagnostic failure.
Battery replacement in 2022+ EVs is only 0.3%. EV repair pain comes from collisions and cycle time (37.5 days), not packs wearing out.
BLS openings (66k a year for auto service techs) are far below TechForce's 242k all-category figure. The shortage is real mainly in collision and diesel.

stances.why: The stages exist, but collision repair loops: estimate, teardown, supplement, re-diagnose (56% of calibrations are found on supplements). Insurer approval and financing are gates the chain leaves out.

The formal OEM information monopoly was largely broken in autos by the Massachusetts law and the 2014 MOU. What remains is control of data and access (telematics, security gateways, subscriptions) plus the owner-versus-shop credence gap (76% fear upselling). So C2 holds only if you recast it as asymmetry and access control.
Repair knowledge was already purchasable. The binding limits are hands (29-57% supply gaps), calibration equipment, access rights and incentives. 18-24 month apprenticeships show the skill is tacit.

Diagnosis is already near-universal and cheap (scans on 86% of estimates). Cost is dominated by hardware (sensor modules), calibration (~$547), labor hours and rates, and cycle time. Even a 10x drop in diagnosis and information cost would cut total repair cost only modestly. The real gains are in triage, parts logistics and cycle time.
The automotive evidence says little about bespoke parts. Modern auto parts are VIN-coded, security-paired, calibrated electronics, which fabricating a part does not solve.
AAA tells consumers to demand proof of calibration, and auto techs need no licence. The weak point is too little post-repair verification (ADAS, EV packs), so inspection and attestation must evolve.
Incentives (flat-rate pay, insurer DRP steering, OEM telematics steering) do create inefficiency. But the FTC calls autos the model open-repair sector, so 'built to be inefficient' overstates it.

research.q: Collision repair and insurance: how insurers (CCC, Mitchell, Audatex), DRP networks and OEM certification programs shape cost; AI photo estimating (Tractable) evidence on cost and cycle time.
research.headline: In collision repair, AI photo estimating already compresses the appraisal step from days to minutes. Tractable/Admiral reports 90% of estimates with no human appraiser and 98% of claims done in under 15 minutes. Repair costs still rose about 63% (2015-2024) because money and time sit in parts, labor, ADAS calibration and capacity, and the step is controlled by payers (CCC/Mitchell/Audatex data plus DRPs) and OEM gating, not by a knowledge gap. Caveat: the shared search budget was used up before this agent ran, so only directly fetched pages are verified. Several items (F8-F13) are prior knowledge marked VERIFY.
research.bottleneck: Control of the payment and price-setting layer: the CCC/Mitchell/Audatex databases plus insurer DRP networks set labor and parts terms. Alongside that, OEM gating of parts, repair procedures, diagnostic access and certification, plus a physical shortage of certified technicians, equipped bays and calibration capability. Knowledge is largely codified. Access, authority to pay and physical capacity are scarce.
research.money_time: Money goes to parts (13.5-22 per repair, costly sensor-laden assemblies), labor hours at rising rates (+4.5% to +7.5% a year, EV about +30%), and new mandatory scans (about $157) and calibrations (about $547). Time goes to parts delays, shop and technician capacity, and supplements after teardown: repair days are still 4-5 above 2020, and EVs average 37.5 days. Appraisal and estimating used to cost days of calendar time and are being compressed to minutes by photo AI, but they are a small share of total cost.
shapes: ADAS calibration and verification infrastructure (mobile calibration, automated post-repair sensor verification), because calibrations are frequent, often missed at estimate and increasingly mandated: an inspection play aligned with C6
Hidden-damage and teardown prediction (sensor and scan data fused with photos) to cut supplements, which is where photo AI fails
Independent post-repair inspection and certification for safety-critical repairs, serving consumers, lenders and insurers, as regulators add certification requirements
Avoid a plain 'AI photo estimating' company: CCC, Mitchell, Solera and Tractable already own distribution and data
Capacity tech for MSOs (robotic or automated paint, frame and calibration cells) that addresses the technician shortage, the real time bottleneck
surprises: 56% of ADAS calibrations are added on supplements, not the first estimate, so even incumbents' estimates miss the work that matters
Collision severity rose 63% in a decade while estimating has been digital and oligopolised for decades, so information efficiency has not bent cost
Courts rejected the body-shop antitrust MDL against insurers, so the structural inefficiency is lawful payer power, not collusion
Tractable distributes partly through Mitchell, an incumbent, rather than displacing it
The web search budget ran out before this agent ran, so findings F8-F13 need verification

stances.why: The chain broadly fits, but collision adds payer valuation and total-loss decisions plus an iterative teardown-supplement loop (56% of calibrations are found later), so the process is not linear.

There is a three-firm information oligopoly and OEM gating of parts, procedures and scan tools. But the dominant inefficiencies are payer power (DRP concessions, labor-rate setting) and physical capacity, and much repair knowledge is already codified in databases and OEM procedures.
Photo AI handles visible damage, but hidden damage, calibration requirements, OEM access rights and certification are not closed by AI. Supplements remain common.

Estimate time can drop more than 10x (days to minutes), but the estimate is a small share of dollars. Severity rose 63% despite decades of digitised estimating because parts, labor and calibrations dominate.

Collision parts are mass-produced. The constraints are commercial and legal (OEM-only structural parts, insurer aftermarket rules, Avery litigation) and safety certification, not the ability to fabricate.
States are adding ADAS technician certification and appraisal rights, OEM certification is expanding, and scans and calibrations are now on most repairs.

The incentives are structural (insurer-controlled payment, DRP steering upheld in court), but the industry is highly digitised and consolidating. It is built for payer cost control rather than being 'not built for smart'.

research.q: Home warranty and home repair marketplaces (Frontdoor/American Home Shield, Angi, Thumbtack, Sears Home Services decline): unit economics, why technician dispatch is hard to scale.
research.headline: In home repair, the scarce, costly layers are technician hours, route density and customer acquisition, not knowledge. About 45% of Frontdoor's revenue goes to contractor labor and parts (~$246 per dispatch), Angi spends ~49% of revenue on marketing, and the tech-first attempts to own dispatch (Angi Services, Handy, Homejoy) lost money, retreated or shut down. AI does threaten the lead-generation and information rent these firms earn, but in-house AR/ML remote diagnosis at Frontdoor since ~2019 has not visibly moved cost of services. That argues against an order-of-magnitude drop from fixing the knowledge steps alone. (Note: the shared web-search budget was used up before this agent ran, so the evidence is mainly SEC EDGAR filings pulled directly, plus Wikipedia background.)
research.bottleneck: Licensed, skilled technician hours, together with local route density. That is scarce supply of Pros and contractors, and the drive time and utilization of each truck. On top of it sits the cost of customer acquisition and disintermediation risk. Knowledge and diagnosis is a minor and already partly automated layer.
research.money_time: The money and time go mainly into the physical repair: on-site labor plus parts, the truck roll. At Frontdoor that is ~45% of revenue, with direct parts spend about 22% of that. The second big cost is customer acquisition: Angi spends ~49% of revenue on selling and marketing, and Frontdoor spends $315M on it plus $117M on customer service. Diagnosis is bundled into the dispatch visit, typically paid for by a trade service fee, rather than being a separate cost. Margins move with parts and labor inflation, weather-driven HVAC volume and pricing. Technician throughput caps at roughly 4–5 calls a day, and drive time and density decide cost per call.
shapes: Field-technician productivity tool: AI-guided diagnosis plus the right part on the first visit, aimed at cutting repeat truck rolls (the real cost). Caveat: crowded by ServiceTitan and OEM portals.

Telemetry-driven warranty underwriting and predictive dispatch: connected appliances and HVAC predict failures, lower claims cost and batch jobs for route density. This attacks Frontdoor-style claims economics.
Labor-multiplier robotics or remote-hands: one licensed technician supervising several junior or robotic workers on site. This targets the actual bottleneck of licensed technician hours.
Avoid: a new lead-gen or matching marketplace. It is ad-funded with ~50% marketing spend, exposed to AI search, and history shows owning fulfillment loses money (Angi Services, Handy, Homejoy).
surprises: Angi, the best-known 'repair marketplace', has a 95% gross margin and spends ~half its revenue on marketing. It is a media and lead business, not a repair business.
Frontdoor owned an AR/ML remote-diagnosis platform (Streem) for years and folded it into its core products rather than building a business on it, with no disclosed figure for visits avoided.
Sears halved its technician fleet in a decade while still the #1 appliance repairer; calls per technician fell ~26%, which points to density loss, not lost knowledge.
Angi's January 2025 'homeowner choice' change cut network leads by 74%, revealing how much prior volume was low-intent lead resale.
Angi lost $52M Adjusted EBITDA in 2022 when it owned fulfillment, and then contractually pushed the job back onto the Pro.

stances.why: Warranty claims do follow notice → request → dispatch → diagnose → parts → repair. But the chain leaves out two of the costliest stages here, customer acquisition and matching (~49% of Angi revenue) and coverage adjudication (authorize or deny, repair versus replace), and most consumer repairs have no formal safety inspection.

Incumbents earn from aggregation, risk pooling and lead brokerage, not from proprietary repair knowledge. The scarce inputs are technician hours (Angi active Pros −19%, 'Pro capacity' funnel), route density (Sears calls per technician −26%) and marketing spend. Sears even sold DIY parts with instructions.

Frontdoor has had AR/CV/ML remote diagnosis since ~2019, scaled back the standalone product, and its cost of services still tracks labor, parts and weather. AI mainly threatens the lead-gen and search rent (Angi's own risk factor), not the knowledge or labor needed to fix the thing.

Most of the ~$246 cost per dispatch is on-site labor plus parts. Parts sourcing is already consolidated with national suppliers. Cutting diagnosis and sourcing toward zero would still leave the truck roll and labor, so an order-of-magnitude drop is not supported.

Home warranties and marketplaces replace rather than fabricate. The only related evidence is Frontdoor's risk factor that finding alternate parts sources is 'time consuming, difficult and costly' if a supplier discontinues.

Quality control is a real cost and control point (preferred-contractor scoring, guarantee expense, the FTC lead-quality case), but formal safety inspection is largely absent in consumer repair beyond permits and licensing.

Supports it: incentives are misaligned (leads are paid regardless of whether the job is done, warranty firms minimize claims, FTC action). Contradicts it: every tech-first rebuild that owned fulfillment failed or retreated (Homejoy, Handy, Angi Services −$52M Adjusted EBITDA), while the rebuild that works is contractor-side productivity software (ServiceTitan).

research.q: Bicycle, e-bike, mobility scooter and wheelchair repair: wait times (wheelchair repair delays studies), parts availability, manufacturer lock; what is the bottleneck?
research.headline: In wheelchair repair, lost time comes mostly from the payer-and-vendor system rather than missing knowledge: prior authorization, too little repair funding, a thinning and consolidating vendor network, and vendors who don't complete the job. Results are a median 14 days to repair, 14% of users getting no repair, and US rural Medicare power-chair vendors down 51% from 2015 to 2022. In e-bikes the scarce layer is proprietary electronics and safety-certified batteries from brands that keep going bust (VanMoof, BionX, Rad Power); AI knowledge alone fixes neither.
research.bottleneck: For wheelchairs, the scarce layers are: funded, authorized technician labor delivered to the user, given that rural Medicare vendors halved and payers require prior authorization for repairs; and OEM-dealer control of parts and firmware. For e-bikes, the scarce layer is safety-certified, firmware-compatible replacement batteries and drive units for proprietary systems whose makers keep failing. Knowledge matters, but it isn't the binding constraint.
research.money_time: For wheelchairs, time goes into the gap between noticing a failure and a technician showing up with the part: getting authorization or funding, vendor dispatch backlogs, and dealer-held parts. That gap gives a median of 7-14 days, often weeks. The cost falls on the user as confinement at home, a backup chair, and a median $150 out of pocket, and it is worse for people on public insurance or in rural areas. Diagnosis itself isn't reported as the long pole. For e-bikes, the money goes into proprietary battery and motor replacement, plus warranty liabilities that can bankrupt the brand and leave owners with orphaned bikes. For plain bicycles, the pinch points are mechanic labor and supply-chain lead-time shocks.
shapes: A rural-first mobile repair network for power wheelchairs that works with any insurer, carries parts stock and loans backup chairs. Colorado-style right-to-repair makes it possible, and rural vendor counts have halved.

Telemetry and predictive maintenance for power chairs and e-bike fleets. Drive-time data already predicts failures (AUC 0.71), which turns reactive repair into scheduled service and builds the evidence needed for prior authorization.
AI that automates prior authorization and claims for durable medical equipment (DME) repairs. It targets the measured administrative time sink rather than diagnosis.

Certified universal replacement battery packs and battery management systems for orphaned e-bike brands (VanMoof, Rad, BionX). UL 2849/2271 certification is the moat, and the EU's 2027 battery-replaceability rule creates demand.
A cross-brand open diagnostic layer for e-bike motors, an 'OBD' for Bosch, Shimano and Bafang, aimed at independent shops.
surprises: The median time to repair does not vary by wheelchair component, so the delay is organisational rather than technical.
Wheelchair users under the VA wait about half as long (median 7 days) as the SCI Model Systems cohort (14 days), so payer design looks like the main lever.
The top reason repairs go undone is that the vendor didn't do the job after being contacted, not that parts were missing.
The first US right-to-repair law of any kind (Colorado, 2022) covered only wheelchairs.
Rad Power Bikes went bankrupt partly because it couldn't afford a battery recall. Battery safety, not knowledge, is the e-bike pinch point.
There are no data-driven inspection schedules for wheelchairs at all, which leaves the 'notice' stage under-instrumented.

Method limit: the shared web search budget ran out before this agent started, so the evidence relies on PubMed (NCBI API), the Colorado legislature page and Wikipedia. The PIRG survey, EU battery rule and Bosch/Shimano items come from memory and are unverified.

stances.why: The chain roughly fits, but it leaves out the stages that dominate here: payer prior authorization and funding approval before parts can be ordered, and sending a technician to someone immobilized by the broken device. 'Notice' is also weak, since there are no data-driven inspection schedules.

Real for power chairs and e-bikes: Colorado had to legislate access to firmware, tools and manuals, dealer-only diagnostics exist, and self-repair falls from 40% to 14% for power chairs. But the measured delays trace mostly to vendors and payers, and for plain bicycles the knowledge is already open.

Even with full knowledge, users still face prior authorization, missing funding for labor and backup chairs, firmware locks, and too few technicians. Informal repairers in low-resource settings already have the know-how and still lack parts.

The median 14-day delay doesn't vary by component and halves under the VA, which points to organisational causes rather than technical ones. A tenfold cut in diagnosis cost wouldn't shrink the authorization and dispatch queue tenfold. Telemonitoring does give a real but modest gain (11-18% fewer repairs).

Orphaned brands (VanMoof, BionX, Rad) show the need is real, but the critical orphaned parts are lithium batteries, motor controllers with firmware, and clinically fitted seating. These need UL or ISO 7176 certification and firmware keys. Simple mechanical parts are plausible to make.

Battery fires (CPSC: 31 fires; Rad couldn't fund a recall), UL battery mandates in NYC and SF, and the lack of data-driven wheelchair inspection schedules show that inspection and certification is a binding layer that needs modernising.

Researchers themselves cite 'structural inadequacies'. But the inefficiency comes from incentives (Medicare competitive bidding, prior authorization, PE consolidation, OEM dealer channels) rather than a lack of 'smart'. Reform of payment and access rules matters more than technology.

research.q: Predictive maintenance reality check: published evidence on PdM ROI, false alarm rates, adoption rates and failed deployments (Uptake, C3, GE Predix); what share of failures are actually predictable (P-F curve, Nowlan & Heap random failure patterns)?
research.headline: The evidence points to a ceiling. Even in aviation, only about 10-20% of failure modes are age-related, and condition monitoring works only where a detectable, long-enough P-F interval exists. A decade of heavily funded horizontal AI predictive-maintenance platforms (GE Predix, Uptake, C3.ai) produced restructurings, falling valuations and persistent losses rather than order-of-magnitude gains. The value is lost mostly after the alert (false positives, CMMS integration, parts and crew within the P-F window), not in the analytics. Caveat: the shared web-search budget was exhausted before this agent ran, so several key numbers come from prior knowledge rather than fresh fetches and are flagged as recalled.
research.bottleneck: The scarce layer is labelled run-to-failure data for each asset and failure mode, together with the operational ability to act inside the P-F window: trusted low-false-alarm alerts tied into planning, plus parts and labour on hand. The scarcity is not algorithms or general knowledge. Physics caps what can be predicted at all, because many failure modes have no detectable precursor.
research.money_time: The evidence puts the losses after detection, not in diagnosis. False positives trigger needless inspections and teardowns. Alerts are not wired into work-order and planning systems (CMMS/EAM). Parts, crew and outage windows are not available within the P-F interval. Every site needs custom data integration. Unplanned downtime itself (lost production, ~$1.4T/yr for the Global 500 per Siemens) dwarfs the cost of analytics. Since roughly 80-90% of failure modes are random, much of the cost is fast restoration (spares, logistics, labour) rather than prediction.
shapes: A vertical, asset-specific monitoring company that bundles sensors, models and guaranteed outcomes for one high-value asset class (e.g., rotating equipment, transformers, wind gearboxes, rail). Survivors such as Augury and OEM programmes like Rolls-Royce TotalCare are vertical, while the horizontal platforms (Predix, Uptake, C3) faltered.
An 'act inside the P-F window' company that turns alerts into a kitted job (parts pre-positioned, crew scheduled, outage planned), because value is lost after the alert.
A false-positive and triage layer that scores and verifies alerts across existing monitoring systems to rebuild technicians' trust, a pain point the McKinsey-type critiques name.
A fast-restoration and spares-logistics company for random failures, since 80-90% of failure modes cannot be predicted and the cost lies in the time to restore.
Pooling run-to-failure data across operators (fleet-wide reliability data exchange), which attacks the data scarcity that limits prognostics, though it faces OEM and customer data-sharing resistance.
surprises: The 'famous' predictive-maintenance numbers (10x ROI, 70-75% fewer breakdowns) trace to a 2010 DOE guide drawing on 1990s surveys, and are still recycled by consultancies whose own text cites only problem-side figures.
Random-in-time does not mean undetectable. Nowlan & Heap's 89% non-age-related failures argue for condition monitoring and against fixed overhauls. The real limit is whether a P-F interval exists.
C3.ai, the flagship enterprise-AI predictive-maintenance vendor, still lost ~$289M on $389M revenue in FY2025, and its stock fell from $177 to ~$10.
GE announced and then abandoned a $1.2B standalone spin of Predix. Customers' unwillingness to give data to an OEM-competitor platform was a key reason cited.

Research limitation: the workflow's shared web-search budget was exhausted before this agent ran. Several numbers (Nowlan & Heap percentages, DOE figures, McKinsey, Siemens, Plant Engineering, IoT Analytics) come from prior knowledge, not fresh fetches, and should be verified in a follow-up run.

stances.why: Reliability-centered maintenance and the P-F curve add steps the chain omits. 'Notice' can occur before failure (a potential failure), and a prior strategy step (monitor, replace on schedule, redesign or run to failure) decides what happens. The chain also lacks a feedback loop into design.

OEMs do hoard fleet failure data, which is one reason GE's customers resisted giving data to Predix. But the binding limits on prediction are scarce run-to-failure data and short or absent P-F intervals, not withheld knowledge.
Data scarcity, irreducible uncertainty and the 80-90% of failure modes that are random are not knowledge gaps AI can close; over-alerting erodes trust.

After a decade and billions of dollars in predictive maintenance, credible gains are tens of percent on a minority of critical assets. Headline ROI figures are 1990s or vendor-sourced. Uptake, Predix and C3 show no order-of-magnitude economics.
Not addressed by predictive-maintenance evidence.
The reliability-centered maintenance answer to random failures is on-condition inspection plus redundancy. Inspection stays central, and data mainly re-tunes inspection intervals.

Most plants are still reactive, but aviation built reliability-centered maintenance about 50 years ago. The constraints are physics, economics and integration, not a design for inefficiency, and AI-PdM platforms that tried to 'rebuild' largely failed.

research.q: Reliability-centred maintenance history (Nowlan and Heap 1978 United Airlines study, MSG-3): what it showed about failure patterns and how it changed maintenance cost; implications for "noticing".
research.headline: Nowlan and Heap's 1978 United Airlines study found only about 11% of aircraft components wear out with age; about 89%, including 68% that fail mostly when new, have no wear-out age. Dropping fixed-interval overhauls in favour of on-condition inspection and failure-finding tasks cut maintenance work by one to two orders of magnitude without hurting safety, which makes "noticing potential failures in time" (the P-F interval) the key step. But this 10x+ saving came from eliminating unnecessary work, guided by pooled fleet data and decision logic in a forum shared by airlines, OEMs and the FAA. It did not come from breaking a knowledge monopoly or from cheaper diagnosis or parts sourcing. (Caveat: the search budget was exhausted, so the canonical Nowlan and Heap figures are from domain knowledge and still need checking against DTIC AD-A066579.)
research.bottleneck: The bottleneck is fleet-scale failure and operating data, and the ability to detect potential failures within the P-F window. About 89% of items have no wear-out age, so noticing is the only effective preventive lever. The authority to change a maintenance program is also scarce, because it needs MRB or regulator acceptance. Expert time to run rigorous RCM/FMEA analyses is the scarce layer outside aviation.
research.money_time: Before RCM, cost was dominated by scheduled overhauls and inspections of items that did not wear out (over-maintenance), plus failures that the maintenance itself caused (68% infant mortality). RCM and MSG cut this by one to two orders of magnitude. The remaining spend is detection (on-condition inspection and monitoring at intervals shorter than P-F, plus failure-finding for hidden functions) and unscheduled corrective work after random failures. Diagnosis and parts logistics were not the main cost in this story; the size of the scheduled task list, and how well it was targeted, was.
shapes: 'RCM-in-a-box' for non-aviation asset fleets (grid, wind, robotics fleets, data centres): AI drafts FMEAs and task selection from manuals and work orders, so industries that never had their RCM moment can get the 10x reduction in unnecessary maintenance that aviation achieved 1960-1980.
Detectability and noticing hardware plus software: cheap retrofit sensing that widens the P-F interval for random-failure items. That is the only effective lever for about 89% of components.
Pooled cross-operator failure-data network: the UAL fleet dataset was the scarce asset. A neutral data consortium for an asset class (inverters, batteries, robot actuators) recreates it.
Hidden-failure / failure-finding automation for safety systems (protection relays, fire suppression, security systems), whose failures are not evident until they are demanded.
Regulator-facing evidence tooling: packaging condition-monitoring data so that maintenance program changes (interval escalation) can be accepted faster by MRB or equivalent bodies.
surprises: The best-known 10x+ cut in maintenance cost (DC-8 to 747: about 4M to 66k structural inspection man-hours) came in the 1960s-70s from deciding to do less work, not from better diagnosis or logistics.
68% of aircraft components showed infant mortality: maintenance and repair themselves are a leading cause of failure.
Aviation maintenance knowledge is formally pooled across airlines, OEMs and the regulator through MSG working groups, the opposite of a monopoly at the level of the scheduled program.
Failure curves drift: Backblaze's drive bathtub became a 'hockey stick' within eight years, so noticing models need continuous fleet data.
Cutting maintenance under the RCM label (Disney 1997) produced a safety backlash, so validating any 'efficiency' rebuild is the hard part.
Method limitation: the WebSearch budget was exhausted before this agent ran. The canonical Nowlan and Heap numbers are from domain knowledge and should be checked against DTIC AD-A066579.

stances.why: The chain fits corrective repair. But RCM adds hidden failures that are never noticed without failure-finding tasks, treats run-to-failure as a legitimate optimum, and got its biggest savings by deleting scheduled repairs, not by speeding up the chain.

Pre-RCM inefficiency came from a shared wrong belief (fixed wear-out life), not withheld knowledge. MSG programs are co-developed by airlines, OEMs and the FAA and then published. The scarce input was fleet failure data.
The 1960s-70s knowledge gap was closed by fleet data plus decision logic. AI can cheaply draft RCM/FMEA analyses, but it cannot create the operating data or the regulatory acceptance.

There is precedent for 10x+ cuts (339 to 7 hard-time items; 4M to 66k structural man-hours). But the savings came from eliminating unnecessary work and noticing earlier, not from cheaper diagnosis, parts sourcing or delivery.
RCM and MSG literature does not address bespoke part manufacture.

RCM made on-condition inspection and failure-finding the core of maintenance, with intervals set by P-F, and an MRB/regulator gate approves every program. The Disney backlash shows the risk of cutting inspection.

Aviation maintenance was already fundamentally rebuilt (1960-1980) and is highly data-driven, which contradicts the claim there. But most other sectors never had a rigorous RCM moment and still run time-based or reactive regimes.

research.q: Condition monitoring sensors and industrial IoT (vibration, oil analysis, thermography; Augury, Samsara, Tractian): cost per asset, evidence of avoided failures, who captures value.
research.headline: Condition monitoring hardware is now cheap: AWS Monitron listed about $115 per sensor plus $50 per sensor per year, which is a few hundred dollars per asset. Independent evidence (NIST) shows most of the gain comes from leaving reactive maintenance, while predictive maintenance adds a more modest ~15% downtime reduction over preventive. Value goes to vendors who own diagnosis-with-human-experts and the work-order and parts workflow (Tractian, Augury) or broad operations platforms (Samsara, $2.1B ARR, earned mostly from tracking, utilization and compliance), not to generic AI. Amazon shut down both of its generic machine-monitoring services in 2024-2026.
research.bottleneck: The scarce layer is acting on the data, not collecting it. That means trusted, low-false-alarm diagnosis (vendors still use human analysts), integration into work orders, parts and planning (hence Tractian's CMMS bundle), and the plant workforce and organisational discipline to act on alerts (45.7% of maintenance is still reactive). Generic sensor-plus-ML layers have commoditised and failed (AWS Monitron and Lookout).
research.money_time: Most of the loss is downstream lost output. NIST puts lost sales at $100B of $119B in preventable losses, and Siemens puts an automotive hour at $2.3M. Direct maintenance spend is mostly labour (~37%) and spare parts (~32%). Sensing and diagnosis are a small slice: about $115 per sensor plus $50 a year. Condition monitoring pays by turning unplanned stops into planned ones, so time saved is mainly waiting for parts and crew and the commercial loss of a surprise outage, not cheaper diagnosis.
shapes: A vertical monitor + diagnose + work-order + parts stack for one asset class with a high cost per hour (for example grid transformers, data-center power, wind and solar inverters, compressors). It captures value by owning the post-alert workflow, as Tractian is doing.

An AI reliability-analyst layer that replaces human vibration, oil and thermography analysts on any vendor's sensors, attacking the human-in-the-loop cost behind Augury-style services. Its moat must be a labelled failure corpus, since generic ML commoditised (AWS exit).
Outcome- or uptime-priced monitoring, possibly insurance-linked. Vendor ROI claims are unverified, so pricing on avoided downtime aligns incentives and wins sceptical buyers.
Inspection-automation and compliance-reporting agents for heavy assets, where Samsara shows a 99% cut in report time. This matches C6: inspection evolves rather than disappears.
surprises: Amazon shut down both Monitron (new customers ended Oct 2024) and Lookout for Equipment (discontinued 7 Oct 2026): cheap sensors plus generic ML was not a viable business even for AWS.
Samsara's published equipment ROI is dominated by theft recovery and utilization, not failure prediction, though it is the scaled winner at $2.1B ARR.
The cost per downtime hour rose 113-319% from 2019 to 2023 while downtime hours fell about 30%, so each avoided hour is worth more every year.
NIST: lost sales from maintenance problems ($100B) dwarf the downtime ($18B) and direct repair costs.
In Augury's own 2026 survey, workforce constraints (43%) outrank unplanned downtime (40%) as a top challenge.
Method caveat: the shared web-search budget was exhausted before this agent ran, so all evidence came from direct fetches of known primary URLs.

stances.why: Condition monitoring moves 'notice' ahead of failure so diagnosis, parts and crew can be scheduled in parallel during the P-F interval, which breaks the strictly serial chain. Also, about 58% of downtime is not equipment failure at all (WSJ via Reliable Plant).

The scarce resource is skilled people (Bain: 10% have the right people; Augury: workforce is a top challenge for 43%; vendors still rely on human analysts), not OEM-hidden data. The data is available. The exception is Samsara, which depends on OEM telematics, so the OEM controls that feed.

AWS shut down generic ML monitoring (Monitron 2024, Lookout 2026). The survivors pair AI with human reliability experts and workflow. Data quality (47%) and process (43%) are the main barriers. AI does cut paperwork (99% less report time at Samsara).

Independent data shows predictive over preventive gives only about 8-15% less downtime, and cost per horsepower differs about 2x between strategies. The big gains come from leaving reactive maintenance. Diagnosis is a small share of spend, while labour (37%) and parts (32%) dominate. Claims of 10x or 5-20x ROI are vendor or legacy folklore.
This evidence does not cover part manufacture.

On-condition inspection (RCM, MSG-3) is the foundation of modern maintenance. Sensors amount to continuous inspection, and AI value shows up in inspection reporting. Inspection is evolving rather than disappearing.

Real inefficiency exists: 45.7% of maintenance is reactive, up to 50% of preventive maintenance is unnecessary, and $119B of preventable losses. But it reflects capability, incentive and workforce limits, not deliberate design, and hours lost fell about 30% from 2019 to 2023.

research.q: AI diagnosis evidence in repair: published studies or case results for LLM/ML diagnostic assistants for technicians (automotive, aviation, industrial); measured accuracy and time savings.
research.headline: The shared search budget was used up before this agent's first search, so the evidence base is thin: 4 primary sources were fetched and the rest is flagged as unverified prior knowledge (notes in /home/user/nuketime/research/repair/raw/d01.md). Within that evidence, measured gains from AI diagnosis and knowledge assistants are real but modest (about 14-34% productivity, about 25% less reactive maintenance time, about 26% lower service cost) and go mostly to novices. The one order-of-magnitude result (Delta's cancellations) came from predictive noticing plus logistics, built over years, not from cheaper diagnosis.
research.bottleneck: Access to proprietary diagnostic data, service information, software keys and parts (the FTC's findings), plus scarce skilled technicians whose tacit expertise is retiring. Turning pilots into production (95% of genAI pilots showed no P&L impact) is a further bottleneck. Model reasoning is not the scarce layer; the data, the integration into the workflow, and the authority to sign off are.
research.money_time: The diagnosis evidence suggests that diagnosis and understanding are a material but not dominant share of cost. AI tools trim about 25% of reactive maintenance time and about 26% of service cost. The largest documented gains (Delta, about 100x fewer cancellations) came from earlier noticing via sensor analytics combined with pre-positioned parts and technicians. Downtime, logistics and the lack of skilled hands drive cost more than diagnostic reasoning alone.
shapes: Novice-uplift copilot for scarce technicians (diesel, HVAC, industrial), where NBER shows a 34% gain for novices; it must own proprietary failure-and-fix data to be defensible
Predictive noticing plus parts pre-positioning for asset-heavy fleets, the Delta pattern that produced the only order-of-magnitude outcome
Independent diagnostic data layer that aggregates fault codes and repair outcomes across OEMs, riding right-to-repair rules to break the access monopoly
AI assurance and audit tooling for regulated maintenance (FAA/EASA), certifying when an AI recommendation can be relied on, which fits C6
surprises: Even OEMs' own headline AI maintenance claims are only about 25%, nowhere near 10x
AI makes experts barely better and can make everyone worse on novel problems, which make up the long tail that drives costly OEM field visits
The best-documented 100x repair-related win predates LLMs and came from prediction plus logistics, not diagnosis
Major MROs publish almost no checkable AI outcome data
The search budget was exhausted, so several numbers are unverified prior knowledge and need checking

stances.why: The diagnosis-assistant evidence does not test whether all repair follows one chain.
The NBER and Aquant evidence shows a real, costly gap between novices and experts that AI can partly bridge. The FTC shows much of the 'monopoly' is about access and rights rather than know-how.
Measured gains are 14-34%, experts barely benefit, AI hurts on out-of-frontier (novel) problems, and legal and data access barriers remain. The gap is narrowed, not gone.
No study or vendor claim shows 10x on diagnosis or understanding; figures are about 25%. The one 10x-plus case (Delta) came from predictive noticing plus parts logistics over years.
Not covered by the diagnosis evidence.
The FAA and EASA keep human authority over airworthiness sign-off and are building new AI assurance frameworks.

Access restrictions (FTC) and missing public outcome data suggest structural inefficiency, but incumbents (Siemens, Lufthansa Technik) are adopting AI within existing structures rather than being displaced.

research.q: Medical diagnosis as an analog: diagnostic error rates, cost share of diagnosis in healthcare, what AI diagnostic evidence shows; lessons for machine diagnosis.
research.headline: Medicine shows that diagnostic error stays large (about 5-15% error rates; about 795k US deaths or disabilities a year) even with very little knowledge monopoly, because it comes from missing data, broken workflows and no feedback, not only from missing knowledge. Frontier AI now beats doctors on diagnostic vignettes, but the best trials show diagnostic efficiency gains of about 20-45% (MASAI workload -44%, MAI-DxO test cost -20%), not 10x, and AI given to human experts often adds nothing. Validation and accountability are the binding constraints. Note: the shared web-search budget was used up before this agent ran; findings come from direct fetches of primary sources plus clearly flagged recalled figures.
research.bottleneck: Not knowledge, but three things. First, capturing the right data at the point of noticing (sensor and image quality, records). Second, validated, accountable integration into workflow, since humans underweight AI and vendors over-claim. Third, the absence of a closed feedback loop that tells the diagnostician whether they were right. Liability and certification decide who may act on an AI diagnosis.
research.money_time: In medicine, diagnosis (tests, imaging, cognition) is a small share of direct spend but controls most downstream spend. Errors are costly through wrong or delayed treatment and malpractice, where diagnosis is the largest category of paid claims. The machine counterpart is No-Fault-Found part removals (often 30-50% for avionics LRUs): bad diagnosis inflates the parts-sourcing and logistics steps. The money sits in getting diagnosis right the first time, not in making diagnostic labour cheap.
shapes: AI-alone triage for routine faults with human escalation for the long tail, which is the routing design MASAI and Agarwal et al. support, priced against downtime and No-Fault-Found waste
Independent validation and certification for AI diagnostic models in industrial and aviation maintenance (the Wong et al. role for machines)
A data-capture layer (sensors plus guided capture) at the 'notice' step, since lab-accurate models fail on poor field data
A closed-loop diagnosis-outcome dataset in which repair results automatically label diagnoses, a feedback loop medicine lacks and machines can have cheaply
surprises: GPT-4 alone (92%) beat physicians who were using GPT-4 (76%): adding AI to experts gave almost no gain
Epic's widely deployed sepsis model missed 67% of cases when tested independently
Radiologist demand rose after AI arrived, a Jevons-style effect
Diagnostic error stays around 11% despite medical knowledge being largely open, which weakens the monopoly explanation
The shared web-search budget was used up before this agent ran, so several figures are recalled rather than freshly verified

stances.why: Medicine's canonical diagnostic process (NASEM) is iterative: working diagnoses are revised and often confirmed by response to treatment. The linear chain is a useful simplification, not how it works.

Diagnostic error is about 5-15% in medicine even though knowledge is broadly open. The drivers are missing data, workflow, cognitive load and no feedback loop, so a knowledge gap is only one cause. Proprietary models (Epic Sepsis) do show the harm of closed, unvalidated vendor knowledge.

On knowledge access, yes: AI alone beats physicians (92% vs 74%; 80% vs 20%). In outcomes, no: the AI did not help the humans using it, and deployed models failed independent validation (Epic Sepsis missed 67%; Watson; Google DR).

The best randomised and real-world evidence shows about 20-45% gains on the diagnostic step (MASAI -44% workload, MAI-DxO -20% test cost), not 10x. The big money is in avoiding wrong downstream treatment, not cheaper diagnosis.
Medical diagnosis evidence says nothing about fabricating parts.

Independent validation exposed failures the vendor's own figures hid (Epic Sepsis). Radiologist sign-off, FDA clearance, reimbursement and liability remain binding, and validating AI is itself a new function.

Medicine's inefficiency persists through incentives (fee-for-service, liability, credentialing, no error feedback), not a deliberate design. Rebuilding the incentives matters more than adding intelligence.

research.q: Fault isolation manuals, BITE (built-in test equipment) and fault trees in aircraft and military systems: how good is automated diagnosis already, and why do false removals persist?
research.headline: Automated fault detection in aircraft is mature: BITE (ARINC 604), onboard maintenance systems (ARINC 624), fault forwarding and FIM/TSM procedures are decades old. Isolating the fault to the right part is still weak, because of intermittent faults, wiring, ambiguity built into the manuals, incentives that reward swapping boxes, and bad data. The F-35 case shows that data integrity, contractor-controlled loops, technical data rights and depot and parts capacity dominate cost and time, not the diagnostic reasoning itself.
research.bottleneck: Observability and data integrity, plus who controls the feedback loop. BITE detects faults well, but isolation fails on intermittent and wiring faults that are not measured. Shop findings do not flow back to the line. Records are missing or untrusted (81% of parts arriving without e-records). Technical data rights and AR resolution sit with the OEM or prime contractor. Depot capacity and parts then dominate elapsed time.
research.money_time: In military aviation, time goes to depot repair turnaround (F-35: 172 days on average), parts shortages (about 22% of the time unable to fly in 2017), repair backlogs (10,000+ components) and data or administrative loops (up to 9% of flight hours lost to ALIS data issues at one site). NFF and false removals are a large secondary cost (>$2B/yr in DoD): they inflate spares pools, shop workload and turnaround. The step of working out what is broken is cheap in labour but expensive in its downstream consequences, because wrong isolation multiplies logistics and shop costs.
shapes: NFF / rogue-unit analytics that joins shop teardown findings, BITE logs and serial-number history to re-rank fault isolation steps and flag repeat offenders. It attacks the >$2B/yr DoD NFF cost, and the ROI is measurable in unjustified removals avoided.

A maintenance data-integrity and digital-records layer, sovereign or government-owned, for defence fleets moving off OEM-controlled systems (F-35 services take over sustainment management by Oct 2027). The ALIS lesson is that bad data, not bad logic, grounds aircraft.

Intermittent-fault sensing hardware (in-situ wiring TDR, vibration and thermal loggers on LRUs) that makes invisible faults observable. This is a deeptech wedge, because AI cannot diagnose what is not measured.
Depot throughput and repair-turnaround tools for military components, where the 172-day repair times and 10,000-unit backlogs are.
surprises: The F-35's own diagnostic and logistics system grounded flight-ready jets: 9% of flight hours at one site, because of missing or inaccurate data rather than real faults.
Users ignoring false ALIS alerts creates a safety risk of missing real faults, so more automation without data integrity can make things worse.
AI and model-based diagnosis is a 35-year-old field (DX since 1989) with well-known coverage limits. The new LLM work offers almost no published troubleshooting accuracy data.
The shared web-search budget was exhausted before this agent ran, so the evidence comes from direct fetches of known GAO, Wikipedia and arXiv pages. Items marked BACKGROUND need verification.

stances.why: The chain broadly holds, but in aviation 'diagnose' is really a loop of swap, retest and re-diagnose, and MEL deferral adds a step that separates noticing a fault from repairing it.

A knowledge monopoly exists as data rights and contractor-controlled loops (F-35 technical data, fee-per-AR process). But much NFF comes from physics (intermittent faults) and incentives, not ignorance.

Diagnosis is limited by observability, intermittent faults and data integrity. AI diagnosis has existed since 1989 with known coverage limits, and there is little LLM evidence on troubleshooting accuracy.

F-35 cost and time sit in depot repair (172 days), parts shortages (22% of time), 10,000+ components awaiting repair and data errors. Better isolation can cut NFF costs (>$2B/yr in DoD) substantially, but not 10x across the whole chain.
This evidence does not address bespoke part manufacture.
ALIS alert fatigue and untrusted records show that verification and release-to-service remain critical, and that automated diagnostic systems themselves need assurance and performance measurement.
Misaligned incentives and slow contractor-mediated loops are structural, but much of the apparent inefficiency is deliberate safety tolerance (MEL, redundancy) and physics.

research.q: Remote diagnosis and remote expert/AR support (PTC Vuforia, Microsoft Dynamics Remote Assist, TeamViewer Frontline): measured reduction in truck rolls and expert travel.
research.headline: The measured gains from remote expert/AR support are real but partial. Vendors claim up to about 50% of dispatches avoided and 80-85% remote resolution, but the one named, measured case is a 15% cut in travel cost, and no independent study was found. Microsoft is ending Dynamics 365 Remote Assist and Guides on 2026-12-31, and CareAR has been rebranded as ResolveGrid: AR remote support is becoming a commodity feature inside Teams and AI tools, not an order-of-magnitude shift.
research.bottleneck: Passing knowledge along is no longer scarce: video plus annotation is a free Teams feature and a commodity in TeamViewer. Microsoft's Remote Assist, Guides and HoloLens are being discontinued. What stays scarce: (a) data captured from the asset itself to diagnose without a person on site, (b) skilled hands and tools on site, (c) parts availability, and (d) the authority to sign off and the liability for remote decisions.
research.money_time: The expensive unit in field service is the dispatch, especially a repeat visit or a flown-in specialist. Remote expert and AR tools aim at that second trip: vendors claim 48-50% of dispatches avoided, and the measured named case is a 15% cut in travel cost. They cannot remove the first visit, the hands-on repair, or waiting for parts. Most of the 'AI session' volume is IT and software support, where remote resolution is much easier than with physical machines.
shapes: AI-first remote resolution layer for OEM field service: plug in asset telemetry, the service history and the senior technicians' know-how, then measure dispatches avoided and first-time fix. This is the job left open by Microsoft exiting Remote Assist and CareAR moving to an AI pitch.

Remote witness and inspection platform for regulated assets (energy, aviation MRO, pressure equipment) that produces evidence records the certifying body will accept, building on the remote inspection use cases at SGS and Microsoft.
Avoid building a standalone AR headset or video-call product. It is being commoditised into Teams and TeamViewer, and the flagship (HoloLens/Remote Assist) failed.
Outcome-priced service (pay per truck roll avoided) for operators of distributed machines (EV chargers, solar and storage, robots), where the cost of each dispatch dominates.
surprises: Microsoft is discontinuing both Dynamics 365 Remote Assist and Guides on 2026-12-31, and Remote Assist mobile was already deprecated in March 2025.
CareAR now redirects to ResolveGrid, a rebrand toward 'AI-assisted resolution'.
TeamViewer Frontline's best-known outcomes are in warehouse picking, not repair.
No independent or peer-reviewed measurement of truck-roll reduction was found; every number is vendor-reported. (The search budget was exhausted, so coverage is limited to direct page fetches.)
The one named, measured travel reduction (Cimbali) is only 15%.

stances.why: Remote-assist workflows follow the chain (on site, diagnose with an expert, repair, document), but the steps overlap: diagnosis happens during the repair, and inspection can be done remotely.

The category exists because front-line technicians lack expertise and scarce experts must travel; Microsoft's pitch is 'scale expert knowledge'. The scarce knowledge is often held inside the OEM or the service firm itself, not used against owners.
AI session usage is growing fast (TeamViewer ninefold, 1M+ sessions), but no outcome data shows the gap closed. Products still route to human experts, and the measured gains are partial.

The best vendor claims are about 50% of dispatches avoided, and the named measured case is a 15% cut in travel cost. That is far from 10x, and it reaches only diagnose/understand, not parts sourcing or delivery.
Remote assist evidence says nothing about making parts.
Remote inspection is an explicit use case (Microsoft, SGS on Librestream), and Airbus inspected gearboxes 40% faster. Inspection is changing in form, not going away.

OEMs and service firms adopt efficiency tools on their own, which goes against 'built to be inefficient'. But incumbents absorb the tools (Teams annotation) rather than restructure, and the standalone AR products failed.

research.q: Technical documentation as a bottleneck: cost and quality of maintenance manuals, S1000D/ATA iSpec 2200, documentation errors as cause of maintenance errors (human factors studies).
research.headline: The evidence shows the documentation bottleneck in repair is about who has rights to approved technical data and how good that data is, not raw knowledge. OEM manuals can be wrong or ambiguous, as in Air Midwest 5481. Access is legally restricted by the manufacturer in consumer goods (FTC) or held by the prime contractor in defence (GAO, F-35). And errors happen even when the OEM has full knowledge, as in JAL 123. So AI can speed up finding and understanding a procedure, but on this evidence it does not "close the gap."
research.bottleneck: Rights and authority over approved technical data, and its quality. Who may legally hold and distribute manuals, diagnostics and technical data packages. Whether the OEM procedure is correct and usable for the specific configuration. And the regulatory rule that work must follow approved data, enforced by independent inspection. Raw knowledge is not the bottleneck.
research.money_time: Documentation is a large fixed cost owned by OEMs (authoring, CSDB tooling, revisions, distribution). It costs ongoing technician time in finding, interpreting and working around procedures, and its largest cost is the tail risk of catastrophic errors when procedures are wrong or skipped. In defence, lifecycle sustainment ($1.3T of the F-35's $1.7T) is shaped by who owns the technical data, not by how hard it is to look up. No hard per-step cost split was found.
shapes: AI tooling that checks documentation quality and correctness: it cross-checks OEM procedures against configuration and parts data and flags Air Midwest-type ambiguities into the formal deficiency and change process, rather than replacing approved data.

A point-of-work procedure compliance layer: guided step execution with evidence capture (photos, torque, sign-offs) that makes skipped steps visible. This targets the human factors finding that technicians deviate from procedures, for MROs, depots and energy/robotics field service.

Technical-data rights and conversion infrastructure for defence and government sustainment: specifying, acquiring and converting technical data packages to S1000D. This addresses the GAO F-35 technical data gap.
