AI-native S1000D-grade authoring for new hardware OEMs (robots, batteries, drones, energy assets) generated from CAD and engineering change orders, so structured, certifiable documentation exists from day one.
surprises: The worst single-aircraft accident (JAL 123) came from a repair done by the OEM's own team. Knowledge was not the gap; execution and inspection were.
The post-accident revised Beech 1900D procedure still lacked the stand-alone cable-tension procedure, so OEM documentation errors can persist even after a fatal accident.
The FTC found manufacturers provided no factual support for the claim that authorised repair is safer.
The F-35 shows the documentation monopoly binding a superpower customer, which still lacked the technical data it needed as of 2026.

The WebSearch budget was exhausted before this agent ran, and several human factors statistics (McDonald 34%, Boeing MEDA) could not be re-verified. They are flagged as recalled in research/repair/raw/u01.md.

stances.why: The accident cases fit the stages, but the chain is not linear. The fatal misses happen at notice (Alaska 261 wear checks) and at inspection (JAL 123, Air Midwest QA), and documentation feeds back into every stage.

The FTC (consumer goods) and GAO (F-35) strongly support a documentation and data access monopoly. But aviation accidents show errors with full knowledge (Boeing on JAL 123) or with data available but not used (BA 5390). In airline maintenance the gap is the quality and usability of manuals, not who holds them.

The remaining gaps are legal (IP, data rights, DMCA, diagnostic software locks), about quality (wrong or ambiguous OEM procedures that AI cannot know are wrong), and about authority (work must follow approved data). AI helps navigation but cannot confer legal access or approval.
No direct cost-per-step numbers were found. The F-35 sustainment total shows the stakes, but its cost driver is the data rights structure, not lookup cost.
Outside this question. BA 5390 shows parts identification discipline matters.
In Air Midwest, BA 5390 and JAL 123 the independent inspection or check was the barrier that failed. Approved-data rules make certification the gatekeeper for any AI-generated procedure.

Withheld manuals (FTC) and contractor-held data (GAO) look like rent capture. But aviation's ATA 100, iSpec 2200 and S1000D stack is a deliberate cost-reducing standardisation effort, and much of the apparent inefficiency is redundant safety process.

research.q: Tacit knowledge and the retiring workforce in maintenance (nuclear, utilities, aviation, military): evidence that knowledge loss drives cost/errors; knowledge-capture program results.
research.headline: Losing experienced maintenance staff costs real money: FOGBANK took about 5 years and $92M to recreate, F-35 repair is held back by missing technical data, and 44% of US aviation mechanics are over 60. But in the biggest datasets and the best-known failures, the main drivers are labour and dock capacity, problems found only once a system is opened up, incentives and inspection integrity, not a missing manual. AI so far narrows the novice-expert gap by tens of percent; it does not erase it. (Shared search budget was used up, so this rests on direct fetches of known GAO, NTSB, ATEC, Boeing and NBER pages plus some unverified background.)
research.bottleneck: Experienced, qualified hands and trustworthy verification. The expensive gap is the experience that turns a newly licensed mechanic into someone who can find hidden work and be trusted to sign it off, plus the physical capacity (docks, depots) and data rights to act on it. Text knowledge is the cheaper layer. Embodied and process knowledge, and the inspection record that certifies the work, are the scarce ones.
research.money_time: In large-scale military and nuclear maintenance, time is lost mostly to (1) waiting for capacity (dock slots, depot backlogs: 10,363 submarine idle days), (2) problems discovered only after the system is opened up (4,100+ days of shipyard delay, 36% labour underestimates), (3) skilled labour shortfalls and overtime (4,000+ days; 25-45% overtime), and (4) parts and technical-data gaps (more than 10,000 F-35 components awaiting repair). The biggest single-event costs (Davis-Besse $600M, FOGBANK $92M plus years) came from failures to notice or inspect, and from process knowledge never written down. Not knowing the fix in the abstract was a lesser factor.
shapes: Expert-capture-to-copilot for MRO and nuclear/utility maintenance: wearable or video capture of retiring experts' work, turned into AI guidance for novices. Evidence: novices gain about 34% in the NBER study, 44% of mechanics are over 60, and utility capture programmes have been run as HR exercises without outcome measurement.

Discovery-work prediction for heavy overhauls: predict the unplanned work found at opening using fleet history and sensing, so labour and parts are planned before the outage. GAO attributes 4,100+ days and a 36% labour underestimate to discovery.

Digital inspection and records integrity (tamper-evident, sensor-verified sign-off and removal records). Evidence: the Alaska 1282 removal-record failure, Davis-Besse concealment, and inadequate checks in Alaska 261.

A technical-data reconstruction service for defence and legacy fleets: rebuilding missing technical data packages (scanning, reverse engineering, process characterisation) where the OEM data is missing or locked, as on the F-35. FOGBANK shows this requires physical process experimentation, not just CAD.
Maintenance delay-cause analytics for depots and shipyards, which lacked delay coding until 2019-22.
surprises: FOGBANK failed because the modern process was too clean: knowledge lived in an undocumented impurity, so even full records plus AI would have missed it.
Several iconic maintenance disasters (Alaska 261, Davis-Besse) were not knowledge gaps. Mechanics knew, and incentives or concealment overrode them.
Even the OEM (Boeing, Alaska 1282) failed to pass procedural knowledge to its own workforce, so the 'knowledge monopolist' does not reliably hold the knowledge either.
FAA mechanic certificates hit a record 11,103 in 2025 (+23%), so the shortage is in experience more than headcount.
Rigorous outcome data on decades of nuclear/utility knowledge-capture programmes appear scarce. Capture was rarely tied to maintenance KPIs.

stances.why: The stages appear, but shipyard data show the chain loops: much diagnosis happens only once the system is opened (4,100+ days of delay from unplanned work). It is iterative, not linear.

Knowledge loss is costly (FOGBANK, F-35 technical data, aging mechanics). But in Alaska 261, Davis-Besse and Alaska 1282 the knowledge existed and incentives, execution, records or honesty failed. The F-35 lock-in is contractual data rights as much as know-how.
The best causal study shows +34% for novices in a text-native job, not elimination. Never-written tacit knowledge (the FOGBANK impurity) has no training data. A partial lever, not gone.
In the largest datasets (GAO naval and depot), labour capacity, overtime, docks and discovery work dominate. None of these is in the four steps, and there is no evidence of 10x reductions.
FOGBANK took about 5 years and $92M with full state resources. Davis-Besse needed a salvaged, qualified forging. Process-dependent and qualified parts are not solved.

Davis-Besse (concealed corrosion and inadequate inspections), Alaska 261 (stretched check intervals, bad fixtures) and Alaska 1282 (missing records, weak qualification) all locate the failure in inspection, verification and records. Regulator oversight was itself implicated.

Systems were uninstrumented (no delay codes until 2019-22), capacity-starved and contractually locked. That looks like underinvestment and misaligned incentives more than design for inefficiency, and safety regimes deliberately trade speed for assurance.

research.q: Human factors in maintenance error: share of incidents due to maintenance error (FAA, UK CAA, Boeing MEDA), causes (procedures, knowledge, fatigue); would better knowledge fix them?
research.headline: This could not be fully checked against primary sources this session: the shared search budget was used up and most regulator and Boeing pages refused the fetch, so several figures below are recalled and marked for checking. Maintenance error plays a part in roughly 15-20% of aviation accidents and mishaps (Boeing about 15% of hull losses; USAF about 18%; US Coast Guard about 1 in 5), and roughly 20-30% of engine in-flight shutdowns. Most of these errors are omissions, memory lapses, handover failures and deliberate departures from procedures under time pressure or fatigue, not missing knowledge. The correct information was usually in the manual, so better knowledge alone (including AI) would fix only a minority; job aids, work-state tracking and independent inspection are the levers.
research.bottleneck: The bottleneck is reliable execution and verification of known procedures under time pressure, fatigue, interruptions and shift handovers, together with the barriers of independent inspection, oversight and approved data. Access to knowledge is not the constraint.
research.money_time: The safety-relevant errors concentrate in the repair-execution and reassembly step (omissions about 56%, incorrect installation about 30%) and in shift handovers, not in diagnosis or understanding. Maintenance-caused events are costly: about 20-30% of engine in-flight shutdowns (around US$500k each, recalled) and about half of engine-related delays come from maintenance error.
shapes: AI job aid and electronic task card that tracks step-by-step work state across shifts, flags skipped steps and records part removals. This targets omissions and handovers, the largest error class (BA 5390, Continental 2574, Alaska 1282).
Part verification at the point of fitting, by scanning or vision-matching the fastener or part against the IPC. This targets wrong-part errors like BA 5390.

Inspection and independent-verification tooling, such as vision-based checks that panels are closed and fasteners present, and remote second inspectors. This strengthens the barrier that failed in most accidents (supports C6).
Mining maintenance event data across operators and OEMs, MEDA-style, to surface warnings like the damage history AA191 never shared.
Fatigue- and pressure-aware maintenance scheduling for MROs.
surprises: Even OEM specialist teams made fatal repair errors (JAL 123 by Boeing; the Alaska 1282 door plug at Boeing's factory). The 'knowledge monopoly' holders are not reliably error-free.
About a third of routine tasks depart from the manual, often deliberately because technicians think their method is better, so publishing more knowledge has limited effect.
Lack of knowledge is only 1 of the 12 'Dirty Dozen' causes.

Session limit: no web searches were possible (shared budget used up) and faa.gov, atsb.gov.au, boeing.com and skybrary refused fetches, so several numbers are recalled from literature and need checking against the primary sources.

stances.why: The chain describes the steps, but most errors enter at execution and reassembly and at shift handovers, a step and transition the chain treats as simple.

In landmark accidents the correct knowledge was usually in approved manuals. Errors came from omissions, departures from procedure, time pressure, fatigue, handovers and cost-cutting. The only partial support is information flow between OEM and operator in AA191.
Knowledge-based errors are a minority. Closing the knowledge gap leaves memory lapses, violations and communication failures untouched.
No cost data here. Safety-relevant error sits mostly in the repair step itself, outside the four steps C4 targets, though cheaper part identification would have prevented BA 5390.

Wrong-part and non-standard-method cases (BA 5390, AA191, JAL123) show that bespoke or non-approved parts and methods are where the risk concentrates. Making the part is not the hard part; certifying it is.
In nearly every case the decisive missing barrier was an independent check, inspection or oversight.

Much of the apparent inefficiency, such as duplicate inspections, RII and approved data, is deliberate redundancy that buys safety. Some real waste exists in hard-to-use procedures and paper handovers.

research.q: Has free online knowledge (YouTube repair videos, iFixit guides, forums) measurably increased DIY or independent repair and cut cost? Find data on DIY repair trends and effects.
research.headline: Free online repair knowledge (YouTube, iFixit, forums) has enormous reach. But no study I found shows it causally raised DIY repair rates or cut repair costs at population scale, and in autos DIY's share has kept shrinking while online content exploded. Where independent repair really opened up, the drivers were legal access mandates (information, parts, diagnostics) plus a parts aftermarket. Once knowledge is free, the binding constraints are parts, software pairing, legal restrictions and labour. (Note: the shared web-search budget was used up, so this rests on directly fetched primary pages plus clearly flagged unverified background.)
research.bottleneck: Control of parts and access, not general knowledge: OEM-controlled parts supply and pricing, software part-pairing and diagnostic locks, and legal restrictions (DMCA, EULAs, warranty terms), plus skilled labour time. Free knowledge already flattened the consumer how-to gap without transforming repair economics. The remaining information gap is proprietary machine data and diagnostics access, which is a legal and data-access problem.
research.money_time: Once knowledge is freely available, the evidence points to cost and time concentrating in parts (availability, OEM pricing, software pairing), labour and time, and legal and access barriers, not in diagnosis or understanding. Community repairers fail about half of smartphone repairs and lack quality parts for over 40%. Apple's free manuals did not reduce cost because the OEM kept control of parts pricing and pairing. In autos, independent repair captured 70-75% of the market through legal data mandates and a 15-50% cheaper parts aftermarket, while DIY shrank because of complexity and owners' time cost.
shapes: Parts-access layer: a cross-OEM parts sourcing and compatibility graph plus aftermarket or remanufactured supply, because parts are the binding constraint (>40% unavailable) after knowledge is free

Diagnostics-data access for independents in heavy equipment, EV or industrial settings, modelled on auto OBD-II and the R2R MOU: the leverage is in getting machine data out of OEM lock-in, not in publishing how-to content

Part-pairing and authentication-neutral tooling, or a certification service that lets independent parts and repairs pass OEM software checks and safety sign-off (turns the C6 inspection moat into a product)
Labour amplification for skilled technicians (AI-guided repair for independent shops on complex assets) rather than consumer DIY content, which is already commoditized by YouTube and iFixit
surprises: No causal or even before/after study links free online repair content to higher DIY rates or lower repair costs; the evidence is about reach and usage, not outcomes
Auto DIY share has declined while YouTube auto-repair content exploded; complexity and time cost beat free knowledge (unverified, needs Auto Care Factbook confirmation)
Skilled volunteers at Repair Cafes, with full access to online guides, succeed on only about half of smartphone repairs
iFixit, the knowledge champion, found its partnership with Samsung failed on parts, not information
Apple publishing free official manuals did not lower repair cost versus the Apple Store

stances.why: Nothing here tests whether the chain is universal. Community data only show where failures happen: parts, diagnosis, design.

An information monopoly exists and is legally enforced (DMCA, EULAs; iFixit was founded over a missing manual). But the evidence shows parts, tools, software pairing and legal restrictions are at least as binding as knowledge.

Free YouTube and iFixit content has been widespread for 10+ years, yet community repair success is still ~50%, auto DIY share is shrinking, and 96% of shops turn customers away because of restrictions, not ignorance. AI is incremental over an already-flattened consumer knowledge gap, and for complex assets the key data is proprietary, not online.

No observed order-of-magnitude cost drop from free knowledge. Apple self-repair with free manuals cost about the same as the OEM shop, and the best savings estimates are ~22% of spend, modelled. Parts pricing and labour dominate.

Parts unavailability (>40% of community repair attempts) confirms the need, but there is no evidence on AI or on-demand fabrication meeting it. Software part-pairing would block even a perfect replacement part.

FTC found no empirical evidence that independents are less safe or secure. OEMs use certification and training requirements as a gatekeeping argument (AHAM), so inspection works as both a necessity and a moat.

FTC finds restrictions push consumers into OEM networks and early replacement with scant justification, which supports structural inefficiency. But autos show regulation plus an aftermarket can restructure repair without a ground-up rebuild.

research.q: Tacit vs explicit knowledge in skilled manual work (Polanyi, Collins, studies of technicians e.g. Orr "Talking About Machines" on Xerox reps): what does ethnography say about how repair knowledge actually works?
research.headline: Ethnography finds that repair knowledge is narrative, social, embodied and tied to the particular machine. Diagnosis is sense-making on off-script faults that the manuals never covered, so AI can close the "relational" part of the knowledge gap (documented but hidden or scattered) and give novices large but not 10x gains, while somatic and collective tacit knowledge stays human. Note: the shared search budget was used up before this agent ran, so findings mix pages fetched directly with canonical literature cited from memory (marked as such).
research.bottleneck: The scarce resource is not documents. It is interpretive, embodied judgment on the specific machine in its context, plus outcome-labelled experience (symptom, tried fix, result) that lives in technicians' stories and rarely gets recorded. Apprenticeship, which produces that judgment, is itself threatened by automation.
research.money_time: The ethnographies point to diagnosis of ambiguous, intermittent, context-specific faults as the stage that is hardest to handle with knowledge tools. Orr's reps could spend most of a day on one such fault even with full documentation. Routine, documented faults are cheap. The long tail of off-tree faults, plus the hands-on work, sits beyond what text-based knowledge capture reaches, and that tail is where expert time and repeat visits pile up. The measured gains from knowledge tools (Eureka, GenAI support) are 5-35%, consistent with knowledge being an important but partial share of repair cost.
shapes: An LLM-native successor to Eureka for one vertical's field technicians (wind, solar/BESS inverters, industrial robots, HVAC). It captures war stories, voice notes and fix outcomes, has peers validate them, and serves them in the field. Eureka ($100M) and Brynjolfsson (+34% for novices) show this pays.

A copilot that makes the novice-to-expert curve steeper, plus escalation to remote experts. It complements technicians rather than replacing them, which avoids the ironies of automation and the jagged-frontier risk on hard faults.
A data business recording symptom-to-fix-to-result outcomes, the missing labels that would make tacit diagnostic knowledge learnable. This is the moat that OEM manuals and CMMS records lack.
Bespoke parts only as process-qualified, certified small-batch making, where the value lies in process know-how and qualification, not in AI geometry generation.
surprises: Brynjolfsson et al. found AI slightly lowered quality for the most skilled workers, so the gains are concentrated in novices.
Agents kept part of their AI-learned performance during AI outages, so AI can act as a tacit-knowledge teacher and not just a crutch.

Xerox already ran the 'pool the repair knowledge' experiment in the 1990s. It worked only when technicians authored and peer-validated tips for recognition rather than pay, and it gave percentage savings, not 10x.
The research limit: search budget was used up before this agent ran, so several canonical numbers (Eureka tip count, Dell'Acqua figures) are from memory and should be checked.

stances.why: The stages exist, but Orr shows diagnosis, understanding, repair and customer management happening iteratively and together (try a fix, observe, revise the story). Return to service is negotiated socially, not as a linear chain.

Knowledge really is unevenly spread and lives in communities of practice. Even inside Xerox, field knowledge was non-canonical and invisible to the official system, and pooling it was worth about $100M (Eureka).

AI can close the relational gap and lift novices 34% (Brynjolfsson). Somatic and collective tacit knowledge (Collins, TEA laser), jagged-frontier failures on off-script cases, and the deskilling ironies (Bainbridge, Beane) mean the gap is not gone. It moves.
The best-measured knowledge interventions (Eureka, GenAI support) give gains of single digits to about 35%, not 10x. The costly faults are the ambiguous, contextual ones where AI is weakest.
The TEA laser and Harper cases show that geometry or specifications alone don't give you a working artifact. Process know-how is tacit and embodied, so bespoke part-making stays hard.
Indirect: if outputs carry tacit judgment and AI fails on the jagged frontier, human verification stays essential. The ethnographies say little about formal certification.

The inefficiency comes from a gap between canonical procedure and real practice, not deliberate design. The remedy the literature points to is tools that serve and capture practitioners' knowledge, not a teardown.

research.q: Obsolescence and DMSMS (diminishing manufacturing sources and material shortages) in defence and aerospace: DoD cost estimates, lifetime buys, redesign costs, Rochester Electronics style aftermarket.
research.headline: In defence and aerospace, obsolescence is driven by the mismatch between 30-60-year platforms and chips that are made for only 2-10 years. Its cost sits mainly in lifetime-buy capital, redesign and requalification, and in data rights, not in a knowledge gap about what is broken. The "parts factory for dead suppliers" already exists at scale (Rochester Electronics: about 12 billion die, authorised by over 70 OEMs). Its moat is authorisation and provenance, which AI does not supply. Caveat: the shared search budget was exhausted, so several cost figures come from prior knowledge and were not re-checked here.
research.bottleneck: Assured provenance and qualification are the scarce layer: an authorised, traceable source for a part, or a requalified redesign, plus the legal data rights that decide who may make or repair it. Knowing what is wrong or which part is needed is rarely the binding constraint.
research.money_time: Noticing and diagnosing obsolescence is cheap and already tool-supported (EOL/PCN notices, BOM databases). Cost escalates at the resolution stage. Lifetime buys tie up capital and carry forecasting risk. Emulation and aftermarket cost tens to hundreds of thousands of dollars. Redesign plus requalification and recertification costs hundreds of thousands to millions per case, and it dominates whenever management is reactive. At platform level, F-35 sustainment is about $1.3T of $1.7T, and time is lost in depot repair capacity (over 10,000 components waiting) and missing technical data.
shapes: An AI-accelerated form-fit-function redesign, emulation and requalification engine for obsolete defence and industrial electronics. It attacks the most expensive rung of the DMSMS ladder (redesign plus requalification).

Counterfeit detection and provenance-as-a-service (X-ray, machine-vision, chain-of-custody) for secondary-market parts. GAO's 16/16 bogus result shows that trust, not availability, blocks cheap sourcing.

A qualified-process reverse-engineering and additive foundry for legacy platforms, whose moat is pre-qualified materials and processes plus the airworthiness paperwork pipeline. The RSO experience shows qualification is the gate.
A Rochester-style licensed continuation manufacturer for non-semiconductor obsolete parts (connectors, power supplies, hydraulics). The proven model is OEM licence plus original tooling and data.
A lifetime-buy and refresh-timing decision optimiser that sits on top of incumbent BOM-monitoring data (SiliconExpert, Z2Data). The value is bounded but real, as an inventory-capital optimisation.
surprises: GAO found that 16 of 16 obsolete or rare military parts bought online were not legitimate. Vendors even shipped parts for part numbers that do not exist, usually within two weeks.

The 'AI parts factory for dead suppliers' idea already exists as a 45-year-old business: Rochester Electronics holds about 12 billion die and is authorised by over 70 OEMs. Its moat is authorisation, not fabrication.
The F-35 government sustainment problem is mainly data rights and depot capacity: all 7 GAO recommendations were still open in March 2026, and over 10,000 components were waiting for repair.
Research limits: the shared search budget was exhausted, so several SD-22 and IDA cost figures and the SASC numbers come from prior knowledge and need verification.

stances.why: DMSMS usually starts before any failure, from a PCN or EOL notice and BOM monitoring. It is a predictive supply-side loop, not only a failure-driven repair sequence. The chain still holds for the repair event itself.

There is a monopoly (the F-35 contractor holds the technical data; Rochester holds OEM die and licences). It is legal, contractual and physical (data rights, IP, original silicon), not a gap in cognitive know-how.
NASA, Lockheed and DoD know exactly what part they need and still cannot get a qualified one. AI cannot confer data rights, OEM authorisation or qualified silicon.

AI can cut monitoring, forecasting and reverse-engineering cost. The dominant costs are redesign plus requalification, lifetime-buy capital and depot capacity. Fast, cheap sourcing without provenance raises counterfeit risk: GAO found 16 of 16 parts bogus.

For chips, the dead-supplier parts factory already exists (Rochester, since 1981), and its moat is authorisation and traceability. For AM parts, geometry is easy and qualification is the gate. This may hold for non-critical parts.
Counterfeit prevalence, DFARS authorised-source rules and airworthiness requalification make verification the binding constraint. AI-enabled inspection is a real opportunity.

There is structural mismatch (30-60-year platforms against 2-10-year chips, contractor-controlled sustainment, an F-35 backlog). However, authorised-sourcing rules are deliberate risk control born of counterfeit scandals, not slop.

research.q: Counterfeit and bogus parts: AOG Technics scandal (2023), Senate 2012 counterfeit electronics investigation, FAA SUP program; how authenticity and traceability shape parts sourcing.
research.headline: The evidence shows parts sourcing is held back by trust and provenance, not by knowledge. One man with a home PC forged release certificates for more than 60,000 CFM56 parts over 4.5 years, a GAO sting found every fast-sourced obsolete part was counterfeit, and regulators responded by narrowing sourcing to OEMs and authorized channels. AI lowers the cost of forging documents as much as it lowers the cost of diagnosis, so making authenticity cheap to verify is the opening. Cheaper sourcing alone is not.
research.bottleneck: Cheap, reliable verification of provenance and authenticity at the moment of receipt. Today it rests on paper or PDF release certificates that are easy to forge, a manual check back with the OEM as the only real verifier, broker chains several hands deep with little reporting (271 GIDEP reports vs about 1,800 cases), and slow physical lab authentication. Certification (PMA, production approval) is the second gate, for any non-OEM or bespoke part.
research.money_time: In this domain, cost and delay sit in the sourcing step, specifically in proving a part is genuine and airworthy. That means OEM or authorized-channel premiums (used DC-10 panel at $60 vs more than $1,000 new), traceability paperwork, incoming lab authentication, and the very large cost of finding out afterwards. AOG losses exceeded GBP 39.3m on GBP 6.9m of parts, with global groundings, inspections and engine teardowns. The repair labour itself is not where the money goes. Failed authenticity costs several times the value of the parts, because every affected engine has to be found, inspected and pulled.
shapes: Signed digital airworthiness and release certificates with a verification API that OEMs, MROs and distributors check at receiving. This replaces the 'call Safran' step that caught AOG, and it targets both the paper chain and AI-enabled forgery.

AI-assisted incoming inspection for distributors and MROs: computer vision and ML on X-ray, XRF, acoustic-microscopy and visual images to authenticate electronics and fasteners at scale. This goes after the cost of AS6081/DFARS Tier-3 testing, which is the main drag on sourcing from independent channels.

A provenance graph and anomaly detection over supplier, PO and certificate data, flagging things like invented signatories, nationality mismatches, part numbers that do not exist (as in the GAO sting) and impossible chain-of-custody sequences. This is effectively fraud-detection software for parts brokers and buyers.

An obsolescence (DMSMS) sourcing marketplace that only lists authorized or verified sources, with authentication built in. It sells the speed of a broker without broker risk, aimed at defense and energy operators of legacy systems.

For a bespoke-parts company, the viable shape is a certified PMA/DER-backed or DFARS-compliant manufacturer with digital traceability from birth, not an unregulated 'AI parts factory'. The certification package is the product.
surprises: AOG Technics was essentially one person working from a home office in Surrey with invented employees, yet it got into the supply chains of major US airlines for 4.5 years.
The FAA states that Form 8130-3 is not required for domestic use, so a missing tag does not mean a part is unapproved.
GAO bought parts for part numbers that do not exist, and vendors still shipped them within about two weeks.
DoD did not know about counterfeits in any of the three cases SASC examined in depth.
The policy response to counterfeits was to strengthen OEM and authorized-source preference in law, the opposite direction to opening up the 'knowledge monopoly'.
Generative AI makes the AOG method (altered certificates, fake staff email trails) cheaper, so AI may widen the authenticity gap rather than close it.
Method caveat: the web-search budget was used up before this agent ran, so findings come from direct fetches of known primary URLs. Engine counts for AOG-affected aircraft could not be verified.

stances.why: The chain holds broadly, but it leaves out a sub-step: checking authenticity and provenance between sourcing and repair, which is where AOG and the SASC cases failed. Partnair also shows the notice and diagnose steps failing over 16 flights.

There is a monopoly, but on verification and records (only Safran could say whether a certificate was real), not on repair know-how. Regulators deliberately strengthened it after fatalities and fraud.

Authenticity cannot be known from general knowledge. It needs physical lab tests or OEM records. AI also lowers the cost of forging documents, such as invented staff and altered certificates, which AOG did with just a PC.

Cheaper, faster open-market sourcing is exactly where counterfeits concentrate (GAO: 0 of 16 genuine). The regulatory response, DFARS 252.246-7008, added cost by restricting sources. Cost drops only if verification gets automated.

In aviation and defense, a part made outside approved design and production data is an unapproved part by definition. The legal path is PMA, DER repair or Tier-3 testing, so certification, not fabrication, is the bottleneck.

Every detection relied on inspection or authentication (an OEM back-check, lab testing). The industry kept adding inspection standards (AS5553, AS6081, ASA-100), and the paper-based system shows inspection itself has to modernize.

The paper trust chain is weak: one fraudster ran for 4.5 years, the FAA does not require 8130-3 tags domestically, and GIDEP was barely used. But much of the friction is a fraud defence built deliberately after deaths, so a rebuild has to keep that function.

research.q: Aircraft parts marketplaces and data (ILS, PartsBase, Locatory, Aviall/Boeing distribution): how sourcing works today, search friction, price transparency, broker margins.
research.headline: Finding aircraft parts is already digital and cheap: ILSmart claims 1B+ listings and 180K searches a day, PartsBase 90M+ parts. What still costs money and time is quoting by RFQ, sole-source and certification pricing power (the TransDigm DoD IG audits, the OEM move into distribution) and checking provenance. The knowledge monopoly is real, but it is legal (IP, data rights, FAA approvals), so AI does not close it; traceability and inspection are the binding layer. Caveat: the shared web-search budget was used up before this agent ran, so most evidence comes from direct page fetches, and items marked [M] are background knowledge that was not re-checked.
research.bottleneck: The scarce layers are legal authority to make parts (design data rights plus FAA/EASA approvals) and trusted provenance (an unbroken, unforged trace and release paperwork), along with physical production and shop capacity. Information about where a part is located is already plentiful and cheap.
research.money_time: In aviation, the expensive stages within sourcing are not search. They are: (1) price, set by sole-source and OEM pricing power (TransDigm markups, Boeing's roughly 18% BGS margin); (2) physical availability (engine shop slots, castings, life-limited parts), which IATA links to rising maintenance and leasing costs; and (3) verifying trace and certificates before parts are installed. The RFQ loops on ILSmart and PartsBase add days of quote-chasing, but they are a smaller cost than scarcity and sole-source price. Where alternatives exist, PMA parts save roughly 30-40%, still far short of 10x.
shapes: Provenance and trace verification: AI document forensics on 8130-3 and Form 1, a back-to-birth trace graph, and detection of the same part listed by several brokers, sold to airlines and MROs. This targets the trust bottleneck exposed by AOG Technics.

PMA/DER acceleration: AI-assisted reverse engineering and generation of the compliance packages for ACO and MIDO, to cut the per-part approval cost so low-volume and obsolete parts become worth approving. This is the realistic version of C5.

Procurement agent and price index: automate RFQs across ILSmart, PartsBase and Locatory and normalise condition, trace and lead time. The moat is thin because the incumbents are adding AI themselves, so it is best as a wedge into data.
Tools for defence sustainment and technical data rights, riding DoD's right-to-repair push and the GAO F-35 findings.
surprises: The ILSmart figures imply RFQ value of $5-7B a year against only about $10M sold at auction, so the marketplaces are directories and the transaction still happens off-platform.
Search has been digital for decades, so the 'knowledge gap' at the sourcing step is mostly about trust and legal authority, not about information.
Some of the most extreme pricing (a 9,400% markup on a pin) comes from sole-source IP that buyers know exists but cannot route around legally.

The web-search budget was used up before this agent ran. Several claims (AOG Technics details, Aviall and KLX prices, PMA discount, IATA's ~$11B supply-chain cost) are background knowledge marked [M] in the notes and need verifying. Notes are in /home/user/nuketime/research/repair/raw/p03.md

stances.why: The chain broadly fits, but aviation sourcing is an iterative RFQ loop with a separate trace and paperwork check (8130-3 / Form 1), and return to service needs a certificated sign-off. Those are distinct steps the founder's chain does not show.

A monopoly exists, but in legal form: sole-source IP (the TransDigm audits), withheld technical data rights (GAO on the F-35) and per-part FAA approvals. Owners being uninformed is not the main issue.
AI cannot grant data rights, FAA design and production approval, or trustworthy provenance. Search was already digital: ILSmart reports 180K searches a day.
Search is already cheap. The cost sits in physical scarcity (IATA), sole-source markups and certification. PMA alternatives show savings of roughly 30-40%, not 10x.

A replacement part for a certificated aircraft needs ACO plus MIDO approval for each part number. HEICO shows it can be done, but only part by part and at high fixed cost. A part made without that approval cannot legally be installed.
Forged-certificate fraud (AOG Technics) and broker layering make trace and inspection the scarce layer. Cheaper sourcing raises the value of verification.
Some inefficiency is designed in for rent extraction (sole-source IP, OEMs buying distributors), but much of it is safety regulation working as intended rather than slop.

research.q: Industrial MRO parts distribution (Grainger, Fastenal, MSC, Motion Industries, Applied Industrial): margins, what share of MRO spend is tail/unplanned, procurement friction data.
research.headline: US industrial MRO distributors keep 30-45% gross margin and 8-20% operating margin on mostly commodity parts. The most profitable, Fastenal (45.0% gross, 20.2% operating), earns it by owning the point of use and procurement labour (vending and onsite inventory are 44.7% of its sales), not by owning knowledge. Distributors describe the friction they sell against as tail/unplanned, one-off, small-quantity buying and the 'total cost of procurement', which points to transaction overhead and physical availability, more than a knowledge monopoly, as the bottleneck in this layer.
research.bottleneck: Having the right part physically at the point of use when it is needed, plus the customer's procurement transaction overhead for low-value, high-frequency, unplanned items. Knowing which part to buy matters, but it earns less: Applied's knowledge-led model makes 11% operating margin versus Fastenal's 20% for owning in-plant inventory.
research.money_time: In industrial MRO, about 30-45% of every parts dollar is distributor gross margin (Fastenal 45%, Grainger HTS 42%, MSC 41%, Applied 30%, online Endless Assortment 30%). It pays for breadth (2M-29M SKUs), local availability within hours (hundreds of branches, DCs and vending), and absorbing customers' procurement labour. On top of that, customers carry hidden transaction cost for tail/unplanned buys (duplicated small one-off purchases, POs that can cost more than the item [unverified benchmark]). Money and time go to sourcing, procurement transactions and physical delivery, not to diagnosis.
shapes: AI procurement agent for tail/unplanned MRO spend: turns a free-text or photo need into a matched SKU across distributors and an automatic PO, aimed at cost per PO and duplicate one-off buys (named by both MSC and Fastenal). A partner to distributors, not a replacement.

Part identification and cross-reference engine (nameplate or photo to an interchangeable SKU across 10M+ part catalogues), sold to distributor counter and inside-sales staff or to plant maintenance. This automates Grainger's 'search-and-select'.
Predictive stocking: condition-monitoring data drives replenishment of in-plant vending or VMI so failure parts are pre-positioned. This adds prediction to Fastenal's highest-margin model.
Sell into the GPC Industrial (Motion) spin-off planned for 2027 and roll-ups by Applied and MSC: they need technology to scale technical knowledge across fragmented branch networks.
surprises: The most profitable MRO distributor (Fastenal, 20.2% operating margin) wins on vending and onsite logistics, not technical knowledge; the knowledge-heavy Applied makes 11.1%.
Digital already handles 61-64% of orders or sales at Fastenal and MSC without collapsing margins.
Grainger's online Endless Assortment grows about 8x faster than High-Touch (+15.7% vs +2.0%) at about 12 points lower gross margin, which is what commoditised search looks like.
GPC plans to spin off Motion as a standalone industrial company in Q1 2027.
MRO distributors are also repair shops (Motion services gearboxes, pumps and fluid power; Applied repairs and integrates), which blurs the 'parts vs repair' split.

stances.why: Sourcing and delivery are huge standalone businesses (more than $50B of combined revenue across these five firms), which confirms those stages exist. But distributors' best models (vending, VMI, onsite stores) stock parts ahead of failure, so 'source' and 'deliver' become a continuous stocking problem rather than steps after diagnosis.

Applied, Grainger HTS and MSC explicitly sell technical and search-and-select knowledge. But the parts market is fragmented (5,000-40,000 suppliers per distributor), and the highest-margin firm, Fastenal, earns its money on logistics and procurement labour, not knowledge.

Digital ordering is already 61-64% at Fastenal and MSC, and Grainger's online Endless Assortment grows fast at lower margin, yet the distribution layer persists. Commoditising knowledge pushes margins down; it does not remove the need for physical availability.

Search and procurement transaction cost (one-off buys, cost per PO) is a plausible 10x target. Physical delivery runs on hundreds of branches, DCs and 124k+ vending machines, and Fastenal calls the cost to 'manage, procure, and transport' 'quite meaningful'. That does not drop 10x with AI.
These filings show that the MRO problem is mostly finding and stocking existing standard parts (2M-29M SKUs), not making new ones. Obsolete parts are not addressed.
Distributor filings do not address inspection or certification.

The friction is real and is the incumbents' revenue (30-45% gross margin, 'expensive one-off purchases'). But incumbents have long attacked it with vending, VMI and eProcurement and earn high returns, so they are optimised, not 'slop'. Inefficiency sits on the buyer's side.

research.q: Long-tail spare parts inventory: share of SKUs that rarely move, carrying cost, write-offs in airlines, utilities, militaries, auto OEMs; what spare-parts planning research says.
research.headline: Long-tail spares are a large, chronic cost. In DoD, 22-52% of secondary inventory by value has sat beyond requirements while shortages of other parts ground fleets (F-35 down nearly 30% of the time for parts), and practitioners estimate up to 23% of aftermarket inventory goes obsolete each year. The causes are mostly lumpy, unforecastable demand, deliberate insurance stocking, unreliable lead times, lifetime buys and data rights and qualification, not a know-how gap. Better planning has historically yielded tens of percent, not 10x. (Caveat: the shared web-search budget was used up before this agent started, so the evidence is mostly directly fetched GAO and IATA primary pages plus flagged recalled figures.)
research.bottleneck: Supply-side responsiveness for low-volume, qualified parts. Long and unreliable lead times, single and obsolete sources, depot and repair capacity, and IP, technical-data rights plus qualification and certification force operators to hoard insurance stock. Forecasting knowledge is not the scarce layer, because lumpy demand is intrinsically hard to predict.
research.money_time: In this domain the cost sits in the source-and-deliver stage, as working capital and as downtime. Billions are tied up in stock with no recurring demand (22-52% of DoD secondary inventory by value beyond requirements; up to 23% of aftermarket inventory obsolete per year; airlines paying an estimated ~$4.2B in extra holding cost in 2025, recalled). Meanwhile the parts actually needed are missing or stuck in repair queues: F-35s grounded about 30% of the time for parts, more than 10,000 components in the depot backlog. Time is lost to supplier lead times and depot repair turnaround, not to diagnosis.
shapes: Qualified on-demand manufacturing for obsolete, low-volume parts in regulated sectors (defense, rail, utilities, then aviation PMA): the value is the qualification and data package, not the printer, because GAO finds certification is the gate.
Cross-operator inventory pooling and redistribution marketplace for idle long-tail spares (utilities, airlines, militaries): 20-50% of inventory value sits idle while others face shortages.
Repair turnaround acceleration for rotables and depot backlogs (F-35: more than 10,000 components waiting): shortening the repair pipeline cuts the stock needed (METRIC logic).
Reverse-engineering plus technical-data reconstruction services that break OEM data-rights lock-in for sustainment of out-of-production equipment (FAA ATC systems, legacy military).
surprises: Excess and shortage coexist at near-equal value (Army $3.6B excess vs $3.5B deficit a year).
Most DLA 'excess' ($4.1B of $5.1B) is kept on purpose because disposing of it costs more than keeping it.
76% of FAA ATC systems are unsustainable or potentially unsustainable, citing spare-parts shortages: the obsolete tail is a readiness crisis.
Rising airline inventory carrying cost is a rational hedge against unreliable suppliers, not a planning failure.

Research note: the shared WebSearch budget was used up before this agent started. Several findings (IATA $4.2B, utilities MRO, academic literature) are recalled and flagged unverified in /home/user/nuketime/research/repair/raw/p05.md.

stances.why: The sourcing and delivery stages exist, but in practice parts are pre-positioned before any failure (insurance spares, retention stock, rotable pools). The chain is not linear: inventory decisions are made years before the notice step.

Spare-parts inefficiency stems mostly from demand uncertainty, lead-time unreliability, lifetime buys and requirement changes. Where a monopoly exists (F-35), it is technical-data rights and depot capacity held by the OEM, a legal and IP monopoly rather than a know-how gap.
Planning knowledge (Croston, METRIC) has been mature for decades. Lumpy demand has an irreducible-uncertainty floor, and data rights and qualification are not knowledge problems that AI removes.

Documented planning reforms gave tens-of-percent improvements (on-order excess 12.6% to 5.5%, $710M avoided against an $8B+ excess). Sourcing and delivery costs are dominated by lead times, capacity and insurance stock, not information.

GAO found qualifying materials and certifying parts to be the binding constraint for DoD additive manufacturing. AM complements rather than replaces conventional manufacturing. Plausible only for non-critical parts.
Qualification and certification are the gate for on-demand or alternate-source parts (GAO AM findings), and 700 aircraft were parked for engine inspections.

There is chronic, simultaneous excess and shortage at multi-billion scale (Army $3.6B vs $3.5B), which looks structural. But much of it is rational insurance and policy choice (retention stock costs less than disposal), not stupidity.

research.q: Reverse engineering and second sourcing law: HEICO v Pratt (1998), trade-secret and patent constraints, PMA by test and computation, DLA Source Approval Requests; timelines and costs.
research.headline: US law has allowed reverse engineering and second sourcing for decades: reverse engineering is a "proper means" under the Defend Trade Secrets Act, and Bonito Boats (1989) holds that copying unpatented functional designs is legitimate. HEICO alone holds about 20,000 FAA PMAs (Parts Manufacturer Approvals) and adds 400-550 a year, so the barrier is not knowledge. What holds second sources back is data rights, design-authority approval, the speed of certification queues, and litigation risk: UTC v. HEICO ran 10.5 years and cost over $15M to defend before ending in a licence.
research.bottleneck: Legitimate design authority and certification credit: the right to declare an alternate part airworthy or fit for service. OEM/type-certificate holders, FAA ACOs and DERs, and military engineering support activities hold it. Close behind are contractual technical-data rights. A trusted, regulator-accepted way of producing substantiation evidence is scarcer than engineering knowledge.
research.money_time: In second sourcing, the money and time go to substantiation and approval, not to figuring out the part. The main costs are (1) building the test-and-computation or SAR data package (material and process characterisation, testing, analysis; roughly ~$90k of R&D per new PMA at the most experienced practitioner, my estimate); (2) review queues at the FAA ACO/MIDO or the military engineering activity, rate-limited by regulator resources and applicant track record; (3) DoD per-part economic justification, with screening windows of 12 months to 3-5 years; and (4) legal tail risk: UTC v HEICO ran 1989-2000 with over $15M in defence costs and ended in a licence. Geometry and know-how are the cheap parts.
shapes: An AI-native PMA/DER house, a 'software HEICO': AI-assisted reverse engineering plus automated generation of substantiation packages and compliance matrices, aimed at shrinking the ~$90k-per-part engineering cost and the comment cycles with FAA reviewers. It wins only if it builds an FAA track record, which HEICO says is what speeds approvals.

A DLA SAR / spare-parts-breakout platform: target items coded AMSC C/D/P with rising prices (the DFARS 25%/12-month sole-source price trigger), assemble SAR packages and first-article testing for small manufacturers, and use 10 USC 3243 small-business testing-cost reimbursement.

A qualification-as-a-service lab for advanced manufacturing sources (3D printing): the 2025 10 USC 3243(e) mandate to expedite qualification creates a regulatory opening, because the qualification step is the bottleneck, not printing.

A data-rights intelligence tool for defence and industrial buyers: map which parts lack government data rights and estimate the cost of reverse engineering versus buying data against the 25% savings threshold. GAO says DoD lacks IP valuation expertise.
Avoid: a pure 'AI parts factory' for regulated aerospace. Fabrication capacity without certification credit gets no market access, and the incumbents (HEICO, OEMs) litigate.
surprises: The HEICO/Pratt case was filed in 1989 and settled in March 2000 with a licence. The 1998 event was the insurer's suit over more than $15M in defence costs, so the question's framing of the date is off.

HEICO, the leading second-sourcer, has 'no material patents' and relies on trade secrets. It names FAA bandwidth and its own track record as its moat, so certification is protecting the disruptor as well as the OEMs.
DoD rules explicitly rank reverse engineering last, behind buying sole source from the OEM, and it needs head-of-contracting-activity authorization.
Congress in 2025 (10 USC 3243(e)) ordered a process to expedite qualification of advanced manufacturing sources, which implicitly concedes that qualification, not fabrication, is the choke point.
Lufthansa Technik, an airline MRO, paid about $26M to create competing second sources against the engine OEMs. Buyers fund the disruption.
The search budget ran out before this agent ran, and faa.gov, dla.mil and the DoD IG PDFs were blocked. DLA SAR timelines and FAA PMA cycle times could not be verified.

stances.why: Second sourcing fits the 'source parts' step, but in regulated sectors a separate approval chain (design approval, production/quality approval, first-article test) has to be completed before an alternate part can be sourced at all. The single linear chain misses that layer.

OEM sole sources capture large rents (TransDigm: 90% proprietary sales, ~60% gross margin, DoD IG overpricing findings), and DoD's lack of technical data drives F-35 sustainment problems. The monopoly, though, lies in data rights, design authority and qualification credit, not in knowing how to make the part.

Reverse engineering has been lawful and practised at industrial scale (HEICO: 20,000 PMAs) for decades. The binding limits HEICO itself names are FAA confidence, FAA resources and filing volume, plus litigation risk. AI does not remove any of these.

AI could cut the engineering-data cost per part (roughly ~$90k of R&D per PMA at HEICO). Regulator queues, substantiation testing, quality-system approval, DoD's codified 25% savings hurdle with 12-month to 3-year screening, and decade-long litigation tails are unlikely to fall by 10x.

For regulated parts, making the part is not the bottleneck; qualifying the maker and the part is. DoD treats reverse engineering as a last resort, and Congress only in 2025 required a process to expedite qualification of advanced-manufacturing sources.

Every route requires design approval plus production/quality approval and often first-article testing. HEICO calls the PMA process a rate-limiting barrier to entry, and 10 USC 3243(e) shows policymakers moving to speed up qualification.

Procurement rules codify risk aversion (reverse engineering only as a last resort, per-part economic justification), and OEM aftermarket rents give incumbents reasons to keep things slow. But the system does produce second sources at scale (HEICO holds >50% on some JT8D parts), so it is slow and rent-heavy rather than incapable of change.

research.q: Parts logistics in aviation and service supply chains: AOG courier networks, forward stocking locations, average parts delivery times, cost of expedite; service parts logistics benchmarks.
research.headline: In aviation, getting a part physically delivered is close to solved: couriers, next-flight-out shipments and charters can move a part almost anywhere fast, and the expedite premium is small next to AOG costs of $10k-150k per hour. Time and money are instead lost because parts do not exist or sit in repair queues, because shops lack capacity and labour, and because of certification and traceability gates. Examples are the 250-300-day GTF engine inspections and the 10,000+ F-35 components waiting for repair. (Caveat: the shared search budget was used up before this agent ran, so only known URLs were fetched; items marked RECALL in the notes are unverified.)
research.bottleneck: The scarce layers are: (1) serviceable parts that physically exist, limited by long-lead castings, forgings and life-limited parts, and by rotables stuck in repair queues; (2) MRO shop slots and certified labour; (3) certification, traceability and data rights (PMA, release certificates, OEM technical data). Knowing what is wrong and moving a part quickly are mostly not the constraint.
research.money_time: The stages that dominate in aviation are new-part and rotable availability, repair-shop capacity and labour, and certification/traceability. Physical delivery is not one of them. Engine shop visits and inspections run for months (GTF: 250-300 days), and the F-35 had more than 10,000 components in its repair backlog. Airlines carry an estimated ~$1.4bn a year of excess inventory as a hedge (figure from memory, unverified), against an $11bn+ total supply chain cost hit. Expedite costs (next-flight-out, on-board couriers, charters) are a rounding error next to AOG costs of $10k-150k/hour. So the industry rationally overpays for speed; the waste is in mispositioned or obsolete inventory and in long-lead manufacturing.
shapes: Real-time visibility and pooling marketplace for serviceable rotables and used serviceable material, with verified traceability. This attacks the 'part exists somewhere but nobody can see it' problem plus hedge inventory, and has to have trust built in after the AOG Technics case.
Digital provenance / certificate verification for parts (release certificates, 8130-3/Form 1 authentication). C6 holds, and counterfeit paperwork is a demonstrated failure mode.

Software to raise MRO shop and inspection throughput: scheduling, AI-assisted non-destructive inspection, and repair-development support for PMA/DER repairs. Shop capacity is the binding constraint in engine repair loops.

PMA/repair-development engineering company that uses AI to speed up FAA data packages for out-of-production parts. A fabrication-only 'AI parts factory' would fail the certification gate; this version goes through it.
Predictive inventory placement for forward stocking locations (multi-echelon optimisation) for OEMs and fleets outside aviation. This targets obsolescence (up to 23%/yr) and stockouts together.
surprises: In the GTF crisis the failure mode was fully understood, yet ~350 aircraft at a time were expected on the ground for years. Knowledge was not the bottleneck; inspection and shop capacity were.
Airlines deliberately carry excess spare-parts inventory, estimated at ~$1.4bn a year (figure from memory, unverified), as a hedge. Inefficiency appears as overstock and stockout at once.

GAO says the US military lacks technical data rights to sustain the F-35 itself. This is the clearest case of 'knowledge monopoly', and it is a contractual/IP issue rather than a knowledge gap AI could close.
The whole search budget was gone before this agent ran, so the AOG courier and forward-stocking benchmarks with hard numbers still need a follow-up pass.

stances.why: The steps exist, but aviation runs repair as two coupled loops: a fast swap of a line-replaceable unit from positioned spares, then a slow repair of the failed unit at a shop or depot. Inventory placement decides where in the chain time is spent, so it is not one linear sequence.

OEM control is real, but it is legal and IP control over technical data, repair licences and PMA approvals, as GAO found for the F-35. Diagnostic know-how is not the main gap: in the GTF case the defect was known and aircraft still waited 250-300 days.
The binding constraints are physical (castings, forgings, shop slots, labour) and regulatory (data rights, release certificates). AI does not remove these.

Delivery is already fast, and paying to expedite is rational at AOG costs of $10k-150k/hour. Time and cost sit in parts not existing, repair queues and certification, so a 10x cut on the four middle steps would barely move total downtime. Better visibility into where serviceable spares sit could help sourcing at the margin.
In aviation, any replacement part must pass FAA PMA (or STC) design and production approval. Counterfeit-paperwork cases show that provenance, not fabrication, is the hard part.
Certification and traceability (PMA, release certificates, the AOG Technics case) and inspection throughput (GTF) are gating constraints. Inspection capacity is itself a bottleneck worth modernising.

There are real inefficiencies: ~$1.4bn of hedge inventory, up to 23%/yr obsolescence, 70% of GAO recommendations unimplemented, and military fleets missing readiness goals. But much of the redundancy (spares positioned forward, expensive expedite, certification) is a deliberate response to downtime costs and safety, not dumbness.

research.q: Distributed and on-demand manufacturing of spare parts: Deutsche Bahn, US Navy and Army additive manufacturing at point of need, Maersk, Siemens Mobility; measured lead-time and cost results.
research.headline: On-demand and distributed manufacturing of spare parts cuts lead times sharply (company-reported cuts of 80-95%) for a long tail of obsolete, low-volume, long-lead parts at Deutsche Bahn, Siemens Mobility, Wilhelmsen and the US military. It fails or stalls where certified design data and qualification are missing: Maersk's onboard trial didn't scale, and NAVSEA took months to approve one metal part. The binding constraint is legal access to technical data plus qualification and certification, not the ability to print or to understand the part. (Note: the shared WebSearch budget was used up, so only the DoD AM Strategy and GAO-16-56 were fetched this session. Every other figure comes from memory of training data and needs re-checking.)
research.bottleneck: Legally usable, authoritative technical data (OEM data rights, IP) plus part, material and process qualification and certification. The scarce layer is not printers or understanding; it is the qualified digital twin of the part and the authority to sign it off.
research.money_time: Fabrication is cheap and fast. On-demand AM gains show up in sourcing and delivery (avoiding moulds, minimum orders, air freight to ports, and multi-month or multi-year supplier lead times). For distributed parts, the remaining cost and time sit in three places: (1) obtaining or recreating authoritative design data (reverse engineering, OEM licensing), (2) qualifying material and process, and (3) certifying for safety-relevant use (rail fire norms, class societies, NAVSEA, FAA PMA). For legacy military and rail parts, reverse engineering plus qualification often takes months, longer than the print.
shapes: AI reverse engineering to a qualified technical data package for defence and rail sustainment depots (DMSMS/obsolescence). TDP creation and qualification are the slowest steps, and DoD/Army policy is actively pushing to get the data.
AM qualification and inspection software/hardware (in-situ monitoring, CT, AI analysis) that cuts qualification cost per part. This is the C6 inspection industry that must evolve.

Qualified-part-as-a-service for fleet operators (rail, maritime, energy, defence): licensed digital inventory plus certified print network for long-tail parts. Proven pull at DB, Siemens and Wilhelmsen, but the earlier startups stayed small, so go after the data-rights and certification layer, not printing capacity.
Avoid: generic 'print parts on demand anywhere' marketplaces and onboard desktop printing. Maersk and the digital-inventory startups show weak economics without data rights and certification.
surprises: The DoD strategy itself says business and profit models and IP, not technology, need to change, and floats licensing data instead of buying it.
The OEM, not the independent, is often the main beneficiary: Siemens Mobility's 95% lead-time cut serves its own 30-year full-service contract.
Maersk's highly publicised onboard printing trial quietly didn't scale; shore-based port hubs won.
Even after a decade of DoD AM, GAO and DoD say systematic measured cost and readiness results were lacking.
The shared WebSearch budget was used up before this agent ran, so most figures are recalled from memory and need re-checking.

stances.why: AM sustainment cases do follow notice, source, make, qualify, install. But for on-demand parts there are extra stages the chain leaves out: reverse engineering or acquiring technical data, and material/process qualification. These often dominate the time.
A monopoly exists, but the evidence says it is legal and IP-based (technical data rights, type certificates, OEM files), not cognitive. DoD and the Army explicitly name data rights as the barrier.
AI can speed reverse engineering, but it doesn't grant data rights or certification. The military, with large budgets and urgent need, still takes months to approve single parts.

Order-of-magnitude lead-time cuts (80-95%) are reported, but only for a long tail of obsolete, low-volume, long-lead parts. Studies suggest only a small share of the portfolio qualifies, so system-wide 10x is not supported.

Bespoke printing works for non-critical or long-tail parts, but structural and safety parts are gated by qualification. Maersk onboard printing didn't scale, and per-unit cost is often higher. 'Effectively solved' is overstated.

Every source names qualification and certification as the binding constraint. DoD calls for risk-based qualification and modelling/simulation-based approaches such as the Navy's Quality Made programme, which is an inspection industry evolving.

Incumbents (DB, Siemens Mobility, Siemens Energy, the Navy) adopted on-demand AM themselves and use it to strengthen service contracts. Slowness is largely a deliberate safety and certification design, plus IP economics, not a lack of 'smart'.

research.q: Digital inventory / digital warehouse companies (Spare Parts 3D, Replique, Craitor, 3YOURMIND, Ivaldi, Mighty Buildings? and the failures like Fast Radius, Shapeways bankruptcies): what worked and what killed them?
research.headline: The failures came from economics and capital structure, not from a lack of knowledge. Fast Radius ran at a roughly 7.7% gross margin with a $89M nine-month loss on $20.6M revenue, and its SPAC trust was nearly all redeemed; Shapeways recognized no material software revenue while opex reached $59.9M on $34.5M revenue. The survivors either pivoted to defense point-of-need hardware (Craitor, 3YOURMIND), became process-agnostic contract-manufacturing brokers (Replique), slid toward consulting (Ivaldi), or shrank back to a profitable factory (Shapeways NL relaunch), because the gate is part-data rights, qualification and lumpy low-volume demand, not printing or know-how.
research.bottleneck: Legal access to OEM part technical data (IP and data rights) and the qualification and liability of substitute parts for a specific asset. Behind those sits demand fragmentation: only a small share of catalogues is printable and orders are lumpy, which destroys factory utilisation. It is not knowledge of how to make the part, and it is not printer capability.
research.money_time: In the source and deliver stages, cost and time go mostly into low-utilisation manufacturing of one-off, low-value parts and into qualifying and approving each substitute part. Customer adoption is also slow, with multi-year pilots. Logistics and knowledge are not the big costs. Fast Radius' cost of revenue was 92% of revenue despite the UPS integration. Shapeways' opex was 1.7x revenue. Ivaldi reports about 3-year pilots.
shapes: Point-of-need ruggedised production hardware plus a secure part-data vault for defense and remote operators, who own their data rights and face catastrophic downtime (the Craitor/FieldFab shape, sold via GSA and CRADA)
A qualification and certification-evidence layer for substitute or reverse-engineered parts (data package, test records, approval paperwork), which attacks the C6 gate that all survivors cite
A process-agnostic spares and obsolescence procurement broker with a qualified supplier network across CNC, casting and AM (the Replique shape), not 3D-print-only
Avoid: an asset-heavy 'AI parts factory' financed like software; Fast Radius, Shapeways, Desktop Metal and Markforged show the failure mode
surprises: Shapeways had a healthy 42% gross margin and still died from opex and acquisitions; its profitable Dutch factory was rebought by the founders
Prospective buyers wanted Shapeways' factory or its software, never both, so the integrated digital-inventory thesis was not valued as one thing
Replique, the flagship 'digital warehouse', now sells CNC, casting and forging brokerage
Craitor and 3YOURMIND both converged on US and allied defense as the buyer that actually pays
Markforged was reportedly resold for about $42M about a year after a $116M acquisition
Search budget was exhausted, so evidence relies on SEC filings and company sites; Spare Parts 3D, Deutsche Bahn and Wilhelmsen figures are from memory and unverified

stances.why: Digital-inventory players address only the source and deliver steps. Nothing here tests whether the chain is universal.
The gate is part-data rights and IP plus qualification. That is an ownership monopoly more than a know-how gap. Operators that own their data (Deutsche Bahn, the military) are where adoption works.

AI part-screening (DigiPart, 3YOURMIND Part ID) has existed for years, yet the companies still failed or pivoted. The vendors themselves cite qualification, traceability and data rights as the constraints.

Even with UPS logistics integration, Fast Radius reached only a 7.7% gross margin. The best vendor claims are 'up to' 30% opex and 75% inventory savings on a small printable subset, not 10x across repair.

On-demand parts factories (Fast Radius, Shapeways) went bankrupt, and Desktop Metal and Markforged collapsed in value. Survivors added CNC, casting and forging, and only a small share of spares is printable.
Qualification, certification and traceability are what survivors sell (certified partner networks, Ivaldi training and certification, 3YOURMIND 'qualified part data').

Spares inefficiency is real enough that buyers run pilots. But platform 'rebuilds' died on unit economics and SPAC capital structure, while pivots toward incumbent shapes (contract manufacturer, defense supplier) survive.

research.q: Technician and mechanic shortages across aviation (Boeing/Oliver Wyman forecasts), auto (TechForce), diesel, HVAC, wind, nuclear: numbers and wage trends; is labor the real bottleneck rather than knowledge?
research.headline: There is a real, measured shortage of technicians. TechForce counts 241,842 US technician openings a year against 101,743 graduates across 10 sectors. Oliver Wyman puts North American aviation about 9,100 certificated mechanics short now and about 20,000 short by 2030, and 44% of A&P mechanics are over 60. That shortage is set by hands, training seats, faculty, certification time and pay, not by information. So in most sectors labor, and in aviation parts and capacity too, is the scarcer layer. AI's best role is to raise each technician's output and shorten the time to competence, not to "remove the knowledge gap".
research.bottleneck: Qualified technician-hours: people who are trained, certificated and present at the asset. Their supply is limited by training capacity (faculty, equipment), time to competence, retirements (aviation) and churn driven by pay and conditions (auto, collision, diesel). In aviation, parts and engine shop capacity are an equal co-bottleneck. Knowledge matters mostly as the tacit expertise that makes each technician slow to produce, so cheap AI knowledge helps by shortening time to competence, not by replacing the technician.
research.money_time: Labor-hours from qualified, often certificated technicians, plus waiting for a slot. Next come parts and capacity: in aviation 2023-26, engine shop visits took 100-200+ days, and IATA estimated about $11B in supply-chain costs. Diagnosis and understanding matter mainly because they eat scarce technician hours and depend on tacit skill built over years of on-the-job training. The supply of technicians is limited by school funding and equipment, faculty, regulated training hours, churn (1.14M separations a year across 10 sectors) and pay. Real wages have not risen since 2019.
shapes: AI technician copilot / guided-procedure layer that raises output per tech and lets junior techs do senior-level diagnosis. It attacks the real scarce input, technician-hours.

Remote expert or one-to-many supervision tools (AR plus AI) so one certificated senior tech or inspector oversees several juniors or sites. This fits aviation, wind and nuclear, where sign-off authority is scarce.

Training compression for AMT schools, GWO wind training and diesel/EV programs. The constraint at these schools is faculty and equipment (62% of AMT seats filled), so simulation plus AI tutoring that leverages faculty, aligned to the competency-based FAA Part 147.
Retention and workforce-ops platforms for shops facing 30-60% turnover: pay models, tool financing, career ladders.
Avoid pitches premised on 'the knowledge gap is gone' in sectors where certificated hands or parts bind. Investors who know aviation MRO will push back.
surprises: Aviation's regulated FAA pipeline fills about 80% of demand, versus as little as 9% in unregulated technician sectors. Certification seems to help supply, not just gatekeep.
Real technician wages appear flat from 2019 to 2025 despite the shortage claims, which suggests the shortage is partly at the current wage. The 2019 figures are from memory.
TechForce's own 2022 finding was that auto techs leave less often than average workers. By 2026 its framing had shifted to retention and churn: 1.18M hires vs 1.14M separations.
AMT schools have empty seats (62% load factor) even with a record 11,103 certificates. Funding and faculty limit growth, not demand from students.
Medical equipment (91% gap) and industrial machinery (85%) have far worse gaps than aviation (20%), the sector the founder used as his main example.
Limitation: the shared web-search budget was exhausted, so findings come from direct fetches of BLS, Boeing, ATEC and TechForce, plus clearly labeled memory items.

stances.why: The labor data fits the chain but shows another gating input at the repair step itself: whether a qualified pair of hands and a shop slot are available. That step is often the longest, and the chain under-weights it.

OEM lock-in on platform-specific knowledge is real (wind OEM service agreements, OEM training; FTC auto findings). But workforce reports name headcount, faculty, equipment, pay and churn as the gaps. They do not name missing information.

Most technician skill is tacit, built through years of on-the-job training, and tied to certification. AI cannot supply certificated hands, regulated training hours or physical presence. Industry bodies call these jobs AI-resistant.

AI could shrink diagnosis and understanding time per technician. But labor-hours, parts shortages (engines, castings) and MRO capacity dominate. A 10x cut in four steps would not yield a 10x cheaper repair when hands and parts are the constraint.
Labor data says nothing about bespoke fabrication. Aviation parts shortages imply demand exists, but certification of new parts is the issue.
The FAA-regulated pipeline produces the smallest gap (80% of demand filled), and certification remains central. The inspection and sign-off labor pool is itself aging (44% over 60).

Flat real wages, 1.14M separations a year, flat-rate pay and underfunded schools show structural dysfunction in how the labor system works. They do not show a design aimed at inefficiency. The fix looks like workforce economics, not knowledge.

research.q: Labor vs parts share of repair cost across industries (auto, appliance, aviation, industrial); where does the repair dollar go? Collect concrete breakdowns.
research.headline: Wherever cost data exists, the repair dollar goes to physical parts, to technician hours and, in some domains, to access such as vessels and downtime. No domain shows diagnosis or knowledge as more than a small, bundled slice. Labor is about half the bill in auto repair and dominates appliance and airframe/line work. Parts and OEM-licensed repairs are 75-90% of an airline engine shop visit, and vessels are about 78% of offshore wind OpEx. So a 10x cut in the information steps would move total repair cost by tens of percent at most. The bigger pools are OEM-gated parts prices and technician time.
research.bottleneck: The bottleneck is physical or contractual, never informational, and which one depends on the domain. In aviation it is certified parts supply and the OEM IP and licence control over parts and repairs, which is where the 20-35% margins sit. In auto, appliances and plants it is scarce technician hours and the fixed cost of putting a technician on site. In offshore wind it is heavy-lift access. Knowledge is a small slice that is paid for through the labor hour.
research.money_time: Auto: labor is about 48-57% of the dealer repair dollar ($186/hr; 27.3 labor hours per collision claim), and parts are the rest at retail markup. Severity is rising from vehicle complexity: more parts, scans and calibrations. Aviation: engine shop visits take about half of the $104B MRO spend. In those visits, materials plus OEM-licensed piece-part repairs are 75-90% of direct cost and labor 5-15%. Airframe and line work is about 80% labor. Time is lost waiting for piece parts. Appliances and home systems: the technician visit and labor dominate, with supplier parts about 22% of service cost and about $246 per dispatch. Industrial and mining: labor and materials are roughly even (mining leans to parts), but downtime losses exceed the maintenance budget (1.6x). Offshore wind: vessels are about 78% of OpEx, labor about 4% and inspection about 1%. Diagnosis is never a large standalone bucket. It is billed inside labor or bundled into visit fees and OEM repairs.
shapes: Qualified alternative parts and repairs (PMA and DER development, USM, AI-assisted reverse engineering plus a certification package) for high-materials-share domains such as aviation engines and components and mining rebuilds. It attacks the 60-80% materials share and the 20-35% OEM MRO margins.

Technician-hour multipliers (first-time-fix guidance, correct parts on the first visit, kitting and planning) where labor is about half or more of cost and is the constrained input: auto, collision, appliances, plant crafts. Value is fewer repeat trips and more wrench time.
Access robotics or logistics where access dominates cost (offshore wind vessels are about 78% of OpEx; blades, towers): cut vessel-days, not diagnosis time.

Parts-price transparency and alternative sourcing for auto and collision, where shop gross margin comes from parts, paint and calibration. The pool is large, but shops whose profits depend on it will resist.
surprises: Labor is only 5-15% of an airline engine shop visit, even though engines are the largest MRO segment, so knowledge-heavy labor is a minor share of the biggest aviation repair pool.
In offshore wind, technician labor (about $5/kW-yr) and materials (about $2) are dwarfed by vessels (about $105). The 'labor vs parts' framing misses the main cost entirely.

Collision consolidators earn their gross margin on parts, paint, sublet and calibration markups, while labor margins are falling. Cheaper parts sourcing would squeeze shop profit rather than relieve shop capacity.
Sibling note m01 misread Exhibit 16: non-LLP engine labor is 10-15%, not 5-10%. The 5-10% figure applies to LLP visits.
Diagnosis never appears as its own large cost line in any domain. It is hidden inside labor hours, visit fees or OEM repair prices.

stances.why: Real repair bills are organised as labor, parts, sublet and access, not as these stages. Diagnosis sits inside labor hours and sourcing inside parts markup. Wind adds a dominant access stage, and engines run on planned overhauls rather than notice-and-diagnose.

The OEM rent is real: engine MRO margins of 20-35% vs -5% to 10% on new engines, OEM labor rates 3-5x independents in imaging, and licences barring PMA and USM. But it is collected through parts, licensed repairs and access authorisation, not as a fee for knowledge.
The dollars sit in physical parts, technician hours and vessel or downtime access. Closing an information gap does not change IP- and licence-set parts prices or the hours needed.

No domain shows diagnosis or knowledge as more than a small, bundled share. Engine materials are 60-80% and labor 5-15%. Auto is about half labor, about half parts at retail. A 10x cut in the information steps moves totals by perhaps 10-30% in auto and appliances, and less in aviation.
