Materials are the largest share in engines and mining, so cheaper qualified parts are the biggest lever. But the binding constraints named are certification, licence terms and lessor acceptance, not the ability to make the part.

Inspection is embedded in the main labor content in aviation (disassembly and inspection) and is essential as a gate to return to service. As a separate cost line it can be tiny: statutory inspection is about 1% of UK offshore wind OPEX.

Profit pools are deliberately placed in parts and licensed MRO: razor-and-blade engines, and collision shops' margin from parts, paint and calibration. But much of the cost is physics (labor hours, vessels, high-value consumable parts), and that would survive any rebuild.

research.q: Robotics and automation in repair and maintenance (robotic blade repair, in-situ engine repair robots like GE/Rolls-Royce snake robots, hull cleaning, wind blade robots, DC robots): status and economics.
research.headline: Robots in repair make money mainly by cutting physical access cost, downtime and safety risk (rope access, scaffolds, dry-docks, engine removal) and by gathering dense condition data for inspection, not by closing a knowledge gap. Vendor-claimed gains are about 3-4x on the execution step (Aerones: 4x faster, 10x less idle stay), and the largest outcome so far is the inspection/data company Gecko (Navy IDIQ expanded to $300M), not a wrench-turning robot. Caveat: the web search budget was exhausted, so several aero and funding figures come from background knowledge, are flagged in the notes, and still need checking.
research.bottleneck: Physical access to the asset in service (height, confined space, underwater, inside an engine) together with regulated return-to-service and permits. Data on the asset's real condition is scarcer than know-how. The knowledge itself is not the scarce layer.
research.money_time: In robotically served domains, cost and time sit in physical access and downtime: rope access and weather windows for wind blades, dry-docks and port permits for hulls, engine removal and shop visits for aero (millions of dollars per event), and confined-space access and outages for industrial assets. The execution step plus lost production dominates. Diagnosis and understanding are comparatively cheap once access exists, and the value of inspection robots is that they make condition data cheap enough to gather.
shapes: Access-robot-as-a-service in one high-downtime vertical (Aerones model): priced against downtime days, with wind blades, boiler tubes, tanks or transmission lines as candidates.
Inspection-robot-to-data-platform (Gecko model): robots are the wedge to proprietary condition data, then readiness and forecasting sold to defense and heavy industry, with large IDIQs as the path.

Remote-expert tele-robotics for regulated assets: a robot on site with the expert operating it remotely, removing the fly-the-team-out step in the founder's airliner example. This needs an OEM, MRO or regulator partnership.
Compliance-first hull cleaning with capture and discharge data, timed to the binding IMO biofouling framework (~2029).
surprises: The biggest robotics-in-repair outcome is an inspection and data company (Gecko, $300M Navy IDIQ), not a repair robot.
BladeBUG moved from a repair robot to NDT inspection, so inspection is where robots first make money.
OEM robotics such as Rolls-Royce remote boreblending reinforces the OEM's hold on expertise instead of spreading it.
Hull cleaning robots are gated more by IMO and port environmental rules than by technology.
Search budget was exhausted, so several aero and funding figures are unverified and flagged in /home/user/nuketime/research/repair/raw/r03.md.

stances.why: The robotic cases roughly follow the chain, but notice and diagnose are fused in one inspection pass. Material-removal and additive in-situ repairs (boreblending, coating, LEE filler) skip parts sourcing and delivery. Hull cleaning is recurring maintenance with no diagnose or parts step.

In aero, OEMs build the robots and keep the remote expert in the loop, so tele-robotics extends OEM control of expertise (supports). In wind and industrial work, independents won by owning access hardware and condition data, not by unlocking hidden knowledge (contradicts knowledge as the core gap).

The scarce input is physical access and actual condition data (Gecko's value is sensing), plus weather windows, shop slots and permits. Knowing what to do was not the bottleneck, so AI knowledge alone does not remove these constraints.

Claimed gains are 3-4x on execution and 10x on idle time in one vendor's claim, and they come from access and downtime, not from diagnosis, understanding or parts logistics. No evidence of a combined 10x on the four intermediate steps.
In-situ robotic repair restores material in place instead of making replacement parts. There is no evidence on AI parts factories.

Inspection and NDT is the first robot product that sells (Gecko, BladeBUG's pivot, RR SWARM/INSPECT, GE Sensiworm). Regulators (IMO binding framework by ~2029, aviation return-to-service) shape what robots may do.

Real inefficiency exists (flying specialists out, scaffolds, dry-docks, engine removals), but it comes from physics, safety, regulation and OEM aftermarket incentives. Change is arriving one layer at a time through access robots and data, not a wholesale redesign.

research.q: Repair techniques innovation: cold spray, laser cladding, additive repair of turbine blades, composite repair; how these change repair-vs-replace and who controls approval.
research.headline: This agent ran no web searches: the workflow's shared search budget was already used up, so evidence comes from direct page fetches plus clearly flagged prior knowledge. New repair techniques (cold spray, laser cladding/DED, adaptive blisk repair, additive burner and blade repair, bonded composites) do turn many replace decisions into repairs, which matters because parts are about two thirds of an engine shop visit's cost. But the design authority (usually the OEM) controls who may use them, and inspection and qualification limit what can be repaired, not knowledge.
research.bottleneck: Approval of repairs, and the inspection and qualification evidence behind it. The design authority (usually the OEM) sets the repair limits and repair manuals. Getting a new process (cold spray, laser deposition, bonded composite) approved needs per-part qualification, material data and inspection methods that can verify the result, and some properties, like bond strength, can't be inspected today. Commercial lock-in (OEM flight-hour contracts, lessor return conditions) then limits uptake of approved non-OEM repairs.
research.money_time: In high-value machines the money goes to parts. Engines are the largest MRO block, and parts are roughly 60-70% of a shop visit (prior knowledge, unverified), so the repair-vs-replace decision on hot-section parts dominates cost. Time goes to shop-visit queues, teardown, inspection and waiting for parts: GTF inspections take 250-300 days with about 350 aircraft on the ground. Diagnosis and understanding are comparatively cheap and already digital (borescope, exhaust-temperature trends). A new repair technique saves money only after someone with authority approves the repair limits.
shapes: Repair-qualification-as-a-service: generate the engineering data package for non-OEM (DER) repairs and parts faster (scan, simulation, test plan, in-process monitoring as evidence). The scarce layer is approval evidence, not knowledge.
In-process monitoring plus inspection tools that turn laser-deposition and cold-spray repairs into verifiable, certifiable records; better bond inspection would open larger composite repairs.

Field and expeditionary repair for owner-operators who are their own airworthiness authority (defence, energy utilities, mining, rail): cold-spray and laser-deposition repair cells with digital qualification. The adoption path is fastest there.
Rebuilding parts whose supplier has gone (DMSMS) for non-critical and military parts, where reverse-engineering plus additive manufacturing already shows 10-30x cost cuts.
Avoid a pure 'AI diagnosis' company in aviation or heavy assets: diagnosis is cheap and not where the cost is.
surprises: This agent ran zero web searches because the workflow's 200-call shared search budget was already exhausted; the findings marked prior knowledge need checking.
Non-OEM repair and parts routes (DER repairs, PMA parts) have been legal since the 1960s-80s, yet are a minority of spend. The lock is commercial and liability, not knowledge.
The GTF crisis took 250-300 days per inspection even though the fault was fully understood. Knowledge was not the slow step.
Militaries lead adoption of new repair techniques because owner, operator and approver are the same entity.
Inspection physics (weak bonds can't be detected) directly limits how large a composite repair can be, so better sensors would change repair-vs-replace more than better reasoning would.

stances.why: The chain holds for a single repair event. At the component level there is a separate upstream loop (developing a repair and getting it approved by the design authority) that decides repair-vs-replace before any repair event happens.

OEM control is real (blisk repair limits set by the design authority, right-to-repair cases). But it is enforced through approved data, service agreements, lease return conditions and tools. Non-OEM routes (DER repairs, PMA parts) have been legal for 40-60 years and are still underused for commercial reasons.
What is missing is certified data, qualification evidence, inspection capability and legal authority, not information. AI cannot measure bond strength or sign a release to service.

Cost sits in parts (about 2/3 of a shop visit, prior knowledge) and shop capacity (GTF inspections take 250-300 days). Diagnosis is already cheap (borescope, exhaust-temperature trends). Order-of-magnitude gains (Siemens 44 to 4 weeks) come from repair techniques used by the OEM, not from cheaper diagnosis.

Largely true for non-critical or military-owned parts (SPEE3D, USAF $10k to $300 part, militaries adopting DED and cold spray). Not true for flight-critical or pressure parts: qualification is per part number and per process.

Inspection and qualification are the binding constraint: bond strength can't be inspected, the GTF inspection backlog, repair thresholds tied to what can be verified. Better inspection (and evidence from in-process monitoring) is what would widen repair-vs-replace.

Some inefficiency is commercial lock-in (service agreements, lessor terms, parts pairing). Much of it is the deliberate cost of safety assurance and liability, and it falls fastest where owner, operator and approver are one entity (militaries).

research.q: NDT and inspection industry: market size, inspector shortage, certification (ASNT, NAS410), AI in inspection (borescope AI, eddy current ML, drone inspection); evidence and regulator acceptance.
research.headline: NDT is a roughly $11-18B market. Its binding constraints are person-centric certification (SNT-TC-1A/NAS 410 experience hours, Level 3 sign-off), statistical POD demonstration and the physics of each method, not missing knowledge. AI so far enters as "assisted" defect recognition and drone or robot data capture with a certified human still signing off, so inspection becomes a bigger moat in a world with more AI, not a smaller one. Research was limited: the shared web-search budget was used up, so findings rest on directly fetched pages plus clearly flagged background knowledge.
research.bottleneck: Trust and liability transfer, not knowledge. That means certified humans (scarce because of NAS 410 and SNT-TC-1A experience-hour rules), statistical POD qualification of each method, regulator gates (FAA ADs, Part 108 BVLOS) and the physical access to capture data. AI that does not come with a qualification and sign-off path stays 'assisted' and captures little value.
research.money_time: In aerospace, inspection is a small spend (NDT ~$11-18B globally vs ~$100B aviation MRO), but it gates release. The big costs and delays come after the diagnosis is known: shop capacity, parts and turnaround (GTF: 250-300 day visits, ~350 aircraft grounded, $6-7B mostly compensation). Inspection labour costs are driven by scarce certified Level II/III time and by mandated repeat inspections that ratchet up after accidents.
shapes: Robotic data capture plus AI triage, with an in-house certified Level III network signing off (Gecko Robotics template) for energy, power and defence assets, where access and inspector scarcity are the pain

POD-qualification-as-a-service: a toolkit and specimen library that lets AI NDT methods pass MIL-HDBK-1823A/a90/95 demonstrations quickly, selling to OEMs and MROs. It attacks the acceptance bottleneck directly

Inspector-multiplier software: AI pre-screens borescope, UT and ET data so that one remote Level II/III can review many sites. It fits within the employer-based written-practice system rather than fighting it
BVLOS drone and robot inspection for utilities and pipelines, timed to the FAA Part 108 final rule, where regulation rather than technology has been the gate
Avoid: pure 'AI replaces the inspector' plays in aerospace. Regulators and certification are person-centric, and incumbents (Waygate/Baker Hughes, GE) already ship assisted ADR
surprises: The incumbent NDT OEM (Waygate/Baker Hughes) already ships AI-assisted defect recognition, so AI here is not a greenfield
The most expensive recent aerospace inspection event (P&W GTF, $6-7B) was not a knowledge problem at all. The constraint was shop and parts capacity
Inspection burden ratchets up after accidents (Southwest 1380 led to new UT every 3,000 cycles). AI may increase the number of mandated inspections rather than reduce the role of inspection
Market estimates differ widely ($15B in 2016 vs $11.6B in 2024 from the same firm) because of scope definitions
Search budget was exhausted, so the inspector-shortage numbers could not be verified this session; the shortage is widely asserted but unquantified here

stances.why: The chain roughly holds, but in regulated domains it is a loop. Scheduled or mandated inspection (ADs) is often the 'notice' step, and the same NDT activity closes the loop at release.

OEMs do hold inspection limits and manuals, but the NDT gate is credential and experience-hour based. The costliest aerospace case (GTF, $6-7B) was capacity and parts limited, with full knowledge of the defect.
AI can flag indications, but acceptance needs POD demonstration and a certified human signature. Method physics limits detection: penetrant could not find the 1380 crack whatever the interpretation.
AI borescope and drone capture cut per-inspection time, but end-to-end time is dominated by shop turnaround and parts (250-300 days at GTF), so cheaper diagnosis alone does not deliver 10x.
A bespoke part brings its own qualification and inspection burden (material certs, CT/UT, POD), which adds to the inspection constraint rather than removing it.
Certification is person-centric and acceptance is statistical. ASNT is modernising SNT-TC-1A and running AI and NDE 4.0 work, and drone inspection is gated by FAA Part 108.

Inefficiency is real, but the system is deliberately conservative: inspections are added after each accident. It was built for safety and liability, not to be inefficient, so a rebuild must keep regulators' trust mechanisms.

research.q: Return-to-service sign-off: FAA Part 43/145 and EASA Part-145 rules, A&P/IA and certifying staff, Form 1 / 8130-3; how liability and sign-off structure the repair chain.
research.headline: In aviation, return to service is a legal monopoly held by named certificate holders (14 CFR 43.7; EASA Part-66 certifying staff inside Part-145 organisations). Work must follow the current OEM manual or other approved data (43.13, 145.109), and every part needs a paper passport (8130-3 / Form 1). So the binding constraint is credentialed signatures, approved data and provenance, not raw knowledge. AI can raise how much each signer gets through and improve the checking of records, but on its own it does not remove the knowledge, data or liability gate.
research.bottleneck: The scarce layer is legally accountable signatures plus approved data and provenance. Certificated humans (A&P/IA, EASA Part-66 certifying staff) inside approved organisations are the only ones who can release an aircraft or part. They are bound to OEM or other approved data, they carry personal certificate and liability exposure, and they are aging out faster than they are replaced. Knowledge is necessary but not binding. Approved data, credentials and trusted records are binding.
research.money_time: At the sign-off end of the chain, the time and cost go into three things. (1) Scarce certificated-human time: IA, B1/B2/C and repair station signers, with a projected 20,000 certificated-mechanic deficit in North America by 2030 and 44% of mechanics over 60. (2) Getting approved data: OEM manuals and ICAs that must be current on site, plus engineering approvals for any deviation. (3) Part provenance and records: 8130-3 / Form 1 trace, records review and remediation when trace fails, as when AOG Technics forced engines off wing. Physical work is constrained by the people allowed to do and sign it, and the paperwork that comes with it, not by technical know-how.
shapes: Signer-throughput copilot: AI that drafts 43.9 entries, task cards and Form 337s, and checks the work against ADs, SBs and manuals so each certificated signer releases more aircraft faster with less risk. This targets the real scarcity, licensed signatures.

Digital provenance and forgery detection for 8130-3 / EASA Form 1 and back-to-birth records, with tamper-evident release certificates and records audits across brokers, lessors and insurers. Motivated by AOG Technics and Alaska 1282.

Approved-data factory: an engineering-approval business (DER or DOA-backed) that uses AI to write repair data and push it through FAA/EASA approval. This is the route that turns AI knowledge into legally usable data.
PMA or additive-manufactured replacement parts sold with design and production approval and liability cover included. This is the only workable form of the AI parts factory idea in regulated sectors.
Records review automation for aircraft lease returns and transitions, where records, not physical condition, often set the timeline (background claim, unverified).
surprises: The regulations already separate hands from signature: uncertificated people may do the work under supervision. What is scarce is the right to sign, not who can do the work.
One forger (AOG Technics) got about 60,000 parts with fake paperwork into the CFM56 supply chain over four years, which shows the system trusts paper more than parts.
The Alaska 1282 door plug failure happened inside the OEM, which has all the knowledge, and came from a missing removal record.
GARA's rolling 18-year repose clock means anyone who makes a new replacement part takes on fresh liability. That is a direct headwind for bespoke AI-made parts.

Research limits: the shared web-search budget was used up before this agent ran, and eCFR blocked automated fetches. Findings come from direct fetches of LII, NTSB, GAO, ATEC, Boeing, EASA, ARSA and Wikipedia. Points marked BACKGROUND in /home/user/nuketime/research/repair/raw/i02.md, including the 8130-3 dual-release details and certificate-action and falsification penalties, were not re-verified.

stances.why: The steps are codified (43.9 and 43.11 records, inspection, return to service), but each step produces a legal record, and the record, not the physical act, makes the aircraft legal. The real chain is a chain of signatures attached to tasks. Supervised work and signing off are separate roles.

There is a monopoly, but it is mostly legal: 43.13 makes the current OEM manual the default standard, 145.109 requires OEM data on site, deviations need approved engineering data, and only certificate holders may sign (43.7). It is a data and credential monopoly more than a knowledge gap.
AI knowledge is neither approved data nor a certificate, and a model cannot carry certificate liability. Alaska 1282 shows that full OEM knowledge did not prevent a record and process failure.

Diagnosing and understanding can get cheaper, but in aviation sourcing is a provenance problem (8130-3 / Form 1). Faster, cheaper sourcing without verification raises forgery risk (AOG Technics). The scarce signers stay a fixed cost.

A new part needs production or design approval (PMA, TSO, owner-produced route) and release paperwork. Under GARA-style rules the maker carries fresh liability from installation. Being able to make the part is not the hard part.

Inspection and sign-off is the legally decisive and scarcest layer (IA, Part-66 B1/C), and its workforce is aging (44% over 60). Forgery and record failures (AOG Technics, Alaska 1282) show it urgently needs better tools such as digital provenance and automated record checks.

There is rent at the edges, such as OEM data licensing and outdated curricula (GAO), but the core conservatism is a deliberate safety and accountability design that keeps unapproved-part accidents rare. It is built to make accountability legible, not built to be inefficient.

research.q: Regulatory acceptance of AI and digital evidence in safety-critical maintenance: FAA, EASA AI roadmap, NRC, FDA positions; examples of approved AI inspection use.
research.headline: No major safety regulator (FAA, EASA, NRC, FDA) lets AI sign off a repair or return an asset to service: AI is accepted only as a tool or data, inside qualified processes where a certificated human or organisation stays accountable. That is still true in Oct 2026, with EASA's binding AI rules at the proposal stage (NPA 2025-07) and higher autonomy targeted for about 2035. Approved AI inspection does exist (drone lightning-strike checks, AI-assisted borescope tools, more than 1,000 FDA AI devices), but it was approved through OEM maintenance documents, regulator clearance and qualification of the whole process, not because the knowledge got cheaper. So the binding constraint is qualification evidence and liability, not access to knowledge. (Caveat: the workflow's shared web-search budget was already used up, so only 4 primary sources were fetched in this session; points tagged [BK] in the notes are from background knowledge and need checking.)
research.bottleneck: The scarce layer is approved data and transfer of liability: the right to have AI-produced evidence count, which is held by OEMs (maintenance manuals) and certificated signatories, and checked through process qualification. Cheap knowledge does not remove this; only qualification evidence and someone willing to sign does.
research.money_time: Regulator documents put the time cost of adopting AI in qualification and acceptance, not in diagnosis itself. Examples: OEM acceptance into maintenance documents, EASA learning-assurance evidence, ASME Appendix VIII performance demonstration, FDA clearance. Each takes years per method or product, and every AI output still ends in a human sign-off. Within a single repair, inspection and sign-off are the stages regulators protect most.
shapes: A regulatory-grade evidence and MLOps platform that produces qualification packages for AI inspection tools (EASA learning assurance / NPA 2025-07, FDA PCCP, ASME Appendix VIII): every AI inspection vendor needs this and regulators are just defining it.

AI-assisted inspection (drone, borescope, NDT) sold through OEM or MRO partnerships so the method gets written into OEM maintenance manuals; Donecle and Mainblades show both the path and how slow it is.

A tamper-evident digital maintenance-evidence chain that records where sensor, image and AI outputs came from and attaches them to the human sign-off; electronic records are already legal, so the gap is trust and provenance.
Nuclear and pipeline NDE data-screening AI qualified under performance-demonstration programmes, which has a high regulatory moat but slow sales.
surprises: The NRC's 2025 AI strategy is almost entirely about the regulator's own productivity (document review, inspection planning) and names no approved licensee AI for safety-related maintenance.
EASA's binding aviation AI specs (NPA 2025-07) were still only a proposal in late 2026, while high autonomy is targeted for about 2035.

In aviation the de facto approver of AI inspection is often the aircraft manufacturer, through its maintenance manuals, not the regulator, so the 'knowledge monopoly' turns into an approved-data monopoly.
Digital records and e-signatures have been legal since 2016 (FAA AC 120-78A); the barrier is accountability, not digitisation.
The workflow's search budget was exhausted before this agent ran, so half the findings come from background knowledge and need re-verification.

stances.why: Regulations have the same structure everywhere: inspection or monitoring finds the issue, the work must use approved data, and a qualified human signs the return to service (14 CFR 43, Part-145, ASME XI). The end of C1's chain is written into law.
OEM control is real: AI or drone methods count only once the OEM writes them into its maintenance documents. But that control is over approved data, liability and qualification, not raw know-how.

Regulators accept only frozen, qualified AI as an assistant; learning AI is out of scope for EASA and FAA, and no regulator lets AI sign off. Even if knowledge becomes cheap, approved knowledge still requires qualification evidence that AI does not supply.

Diagnosis and inspection do get faster where AI is accepted (drone lightning-strike checks, borescope AI, radiology AI). But regulatory qualification, OEM acceptance and sign-off costs remain and take years, which makes an order-of-magnitude cut across the whole chain unlikely in regulated assets in the near term.
This research did not cover parts approval (PMA, DER repairs, additive-part qualification). Regulation suggests a new part needs certification, but this research has no direct evidence on that.

Inspection is exactly where regulated AI is landing (drones, borescope, pipeline in-line inspection, FDA imaging), and regulators are building new assurance regimes for it (learning assurance, NPA 2025-07, PCCP, ASME Appendix VIII).

The system is deliberately conservative (EASA's aim is to 'maintain the current level of safety') and slow, with high autonomy around 2035. But regulators are actively adapting through incremental routes, and the framework was built for accountability rather than designed to be inefficient.

research.q: Insurers and boiler/machinery inspection (Hartford Steam Boiler, FM Global, Allianz Engineering, Lloyd's): how insurers drive inspection, repair standards and what they say about failure and repair cost.
research.headline: Insurers created the modern inspection industry (HSB and TÜV in 1866, Lloyd's Register in 1760, FM in 1835) to fill an owner knowledge gap. Today they reinforce OEM knowledge control: they prefer OEMs because "expertise emanates from the OEMs", write OEM manuals into policy conditions, and distrust bespoke or reverse-engineered parts. Their own data puts the cost of large losses in business-interruption downtime and long-lead physical parts, not in diagnosis. Much of the knowledge gap is tacit, proprietary or contested evidence that AI cannot simply erase. Note: the shared search budget was exhausted, so findings rest on directly fetched primary documents (mainly three IMIA insurer-engineer papers, Allianz reports and histories).
research.bottleneck: The scarce layer is trusted qualification and acceptance, not raw knowledge or fabrication. Someone credible (OEM, insurer or class society) must vouch that a part, repair or provider is safe, backed by design data and failure evidence the OEM controls. This sits alongside physical long-lead spares and lost tacit operator knowledge on ageing plant. Insurers say outright that there is no independent organisation to qualify non-OEM parts and providers, and no shared loss register.
research.money_time: For industrial and heavy equipment, insurers locate the dominant cost in business interruption while units are down, then in physical repair or replacement of long-lead, high-value components (turbine blades and rotors, transformers at $12m+, switchgear). Obsolescence and part unavailability 'increase BI costs substantially' (one case: plant down over 4 months). Root-cause analysis can be slow and contested because OEMs control hardware and data. Diagnosis knowledge per se is rarely named as the main cost; the main levers insurers name are spares holding and pooling, maintenance discipline and condition monitoring.
shapes: Independent qualification and certification platform for non-OEM parts and service providers, accepted by engineering insurers (IMIA: 'no independent organisation to assist the Owner'); insurer acceptance is the moat

Insurer-linked shared critical-spares pool or registry for long-lead items (GT rotors, transformers, switchgear), monetised through BI premium reductions; IMIA names the idea and says insurers won't tie up capital themselves
Neutral cross-OEM failure and loss register with root-cause data, sold to insurers, reinsurers and owners (IMIA: no comprehensive turbine loss register exists)

Tacit-knowledge capture for ageing plants (sensors plus AI recording what retiring operators 'hear', plus digitised lost manuals), distributed through machinery-breakdown insurers as a premium-credit product, similar to HSB's IoT credits
Reverse-engineering plus validation-dossier service for obsolete low-to-medium criticality parts, where the deliverable is the qualification evidence insurers accept, not the print itself
surprises: Insurers, the supposed neutral risk party, actively reinforce the OEM knowledge monopoly by writing OEM manuals into policy conditions and preferring OEM service agreements
Under OEM LTSAs, the damaged parts may legally belong to the OEM, so insurers cannot even inspect the failed hardware or recover salvage
Big losses often happen after alarms were noticed and deliberately deferred; the failure is in the decision, not in detection
Insurers themselves call for a public loss register and an independent body to vet non-OEM suppliers, but none exists
In soft insurance markets, a breakdown policy can be cheaper than a maintenance contract, so insurance can subsidise neglect
TÜV and HSB are essentially the same 1866 invention: private insurer-inspectors who replaced state inspection; the inspection industry is an insurance by-product

Workflow-wide search budget was exhausted before this agent ran; findings are from direct fetches of known primary sources, and more searching (FM recommendation-completion stats, HSB claim studies, transformer lead times) is warranted

stances.why: The chain describes corrective repair. But insurers frame value around prevention, obsolescence management and pre-positioned spares. Noticing is often done but not acted on (ignored alarms costing $12m+), and root-cause analysis is a contested negotiation, not a clean step.

Insurers state that expertise 'emanates from the OEMs', prefer OEM LTSAs, and enforce OEM manuals in policy wording. OEMs control parts, data and root-cause analysis, and there is no independent body to qualify alternatives. Nuance: much of the gap is lost tacit knowledge and poor execution (75% of electrical failures are human error), not monopoly.

The missing knowledge is proprietary design data (materials, tolerances), undocumented operator know-how, and failure evidence physically owned by OEMs. None of it is in AI training data. Where knowledge is public (thermography, maintenance rules), failures persist anyway, so knowledge is not the binding constraint.

Sourcing and delivery delays are named as major BI drivers, but they are physical lead-time and capacity limits. Insurer data puts dominant large-loss cost in BI downtime and physical replacement, not in diagnosis or understanding. A 10x cut in information steps would not cut total loss 10x for heavy equipment.

Insurers call bespoke parts expensive, slow and high-risk: no drawings or specs, unavailable materials and processes, cascading-failure risk, and reverse-engineering error sensitivity. Some reverse-engineered parts beat OEM parts, but only with deep testing expertise. Qualification and insurer acceptance, not fabrication, is the gate.

Insurers built inspection and certification (HSB, TÜV, LR, FM) and still underwrite on inspection and compliance. They are moving to IoT and remote monitoring, but outcome data is thin, so evolution is incomplete.

Some structures entrench inefficiency: warranty-voiding, confidential LTSAs, OEM part ownership, no loss register, soft-market moral hazard. But the insurer-inspection system was deliberately built for safety and sharply cut explosion rates. Some 'inefficiency' is the price of assurance and liability.

research.q: Nuclear plant maintenance and commercial-grade dedication (10 CFR 50 App B, Part 21, EPRI CGD guidance): costs, timelines, obsolescence, what makes nuclear repair slow.
research.headline: Nuclear repair is slow and expensive mainly in execution and qualification: the repair work itself, weld requalification, licensing amendments, provenance checks, and replacement power while the unit is offline. Missing diagnostic knowledge is rarely the cause. AI could compress commercial-grade dedication paperwork and obsolete-part procurement, but the large failures (Crystal River, San Onofre, Flamanville, France's stress-corrosion crisis) were diagnosed competently and then blew up in physical repair, requalification and regulatory restart.
research.bottleneck: Accountable qualification capacity: who can produce defensible evidence (tests, NDE, provenance, engineering sign-off) that a part or repair meets safety function, and get the regulator to accept it. Behind that sit scarce certified labour (welders, NDE analysts) and a shrunken Appendix B / N-stamp supplier base.
research.money_time: In nuclear, money and time go to (1) lost generation and replacement power while units are down, which dominates; (2) physical repair execution (weld repair, containment work, heavy-component replacement); (3) qualification and requalification (CGD testing, NDE, new heat-treatment processes, licence amendments, restart hearings). Diagnosis and parts search are comparatively cheap. Sourcing pain shows up as qualification and provenance (dedication paperwork, counterfeit risk, obsolete I&C equivalency), not as not knowing what to buy.
shapes: AI copilot for commercial-grade dedication and equivalency evaluations, paired with an accredited test-lab network: it automates the paperwork-plus-test step that turns commercial parts into safety-related ones
Qualified reverse-engineering and additive-manufacturing service for obsolete parts, where the product is the qualification data package rather than the part
Digital provenance / chain-of-custody for safety-critical parts, anti-counterfeit (the Korea forged-certificate case)
Outage and repair work-package planning intelligence, since Crystal River failed in repair planning rather than diagnosis
AI-assisted NDE analysis (eddy current, ultrasonic testing of welds) to stretch scarce certified analyst capacity, as in the EDF stress-corrosion crisis
surprises: The web search budget was used up before this agent started, so findings came only from directly fetched pages; several background claims are flagged unverified in /home/user/nuketime/research/repair/raw/i05.md
San Onofre: a top OEM's brand-new part failed, and liability was capped at $125m against a $7.57bn claim, so the contract shifted almost all risk to the owner
Davis-Besse's replacement head was cannibalised from a never-finished plant, a sign of how thin the market for unique heavy parts is
At Palisades, custom recovery tooling was built quickly; the delay was the licence amendment
Nuclear already has a mandated fleet-wide defect knowledge-sharing regime (Part 21, EPRI, INPO), which cuts against the knowledge-monopoly framing

stances.why: The stages exist, but nuclear adds mandatory loops (dedication, Part 21 reporting, licence amendments, post-maintenance testing), and diagnosis is sometimes destructive (cutting out pipe in the French crisis). The chain is not linear.

OEM exit and obsolescence created real gaps, and OEMs and dedicators capture value. But EPRI, INPO and Part 21 form a shared knowledge commons, and the costly failures came from execution and culture, not withheld knowledge.
The gating items are physical evidence, accountable sign-off, licensing and certified labour. AI helps with paperwork but does not remove the requirement for testing and approval.

Replacement power, outage-days, repair execution and requalification dominate (EUR18.5bn EBITDA hit, $1.5-3.4bn repair estimates). Diagnosis and sourcing are a small share of these events, so a 10x cut there would only reduce totals by a few percent.

AM parts take years per part family to qualify, and the Korea scandal shows provenance matters more than fabrication capability. Bespoke tooling (the Palisades grapple) is fast, but bespoke safety-related parts are not solved.
Qualification, dedication, NDE and licensing are the binding constraint in nearly every case, and the frameworks are already evolving (RG 1.164, 2015 lab rule, AMT plans).

The conservatism is designed in, and the system responded to market pressure (outages cut from 46 to 34 days). Still, supplier atrophy and slow regulatory pathways (San Onofre, Vogtle) are real structural problems.

research.q: History of the independent automotive aftermarket (NAPA, AutoZone, Haynes/Chilton manuals, Motor manuals): how knowledge and parts monopolies broke and who ended up with the profits.
research.headline: In the US car aftermarket, the parts and knowledge monopolies were broken by distribution networks (NAPA from 1925, then chain roll-ups), by third-party manuals and databases (Chilton, MOTOR, Haynes, ALLDATA, Mitchell 1), and by law (Magnuson-Moss 1975, OBD rules, the Massachusetts 86% ballot in 2012 and the 2014 national agreement). Most of the profit went to the parts retailers with the densest store networks (AutoZone and O'Reilly, each at about 19% operating margin and about $2.4-2.5B net income). It did not go to the knowledge providers: Haynes sold for only GBP 114.5M. Meanwhile carmakers keep rebuilding lock-in at the newest layer: telematics, parts locked to one car, and security gateways.
research.bottleneck: Two layers are scarce. (1) Physical parts availability: having the right part within hours across thousands of locations. That is where the aftermarket's profits went. (2) Carmaker-controlled access and authorisation (telematics data, security gateways, VIN-locked modules, part pairing), defended on safety and cybersecurity grounds and only opened by law or ballot, never by better know-how. Knowledge itself has been commoditized several times over.
research.money_time: In the auto aftermarket, the profit and the operational difficulty sit in parts sourcing and delivery: inventory depth, store density, hub stores, same-day delivery to shops, and credit. The two chains that did this well earn about 19% operating margins and over $2.3B net income each. Advance, at similar scale, earns about 0%. Knowledge (diagnosis and repair procedures) became a commodity. Haynes was worth only GBP 114.5M, and repair databases became add-ons that help sell parts and tools. Labour and diagnostic time remain the shop's cost, but the knowledge needed for diagnosis is cheap. What is restricted is access to carmaker software, telematics and part authorisation.
shapes: Logistics or parts-availability layer for non-auto repair (industrial, energy, robotics fleets): the auto lesson is that the winners owned inventory placement and fast delivery, not information.

Knowledge built into the transaction (like Mitchell or CCC in collision estimating): diagnosis tied to parts ordering, pricing and claims or payment, rather than standalone repair knowledge, which gets commoditized (Haynes).

Authorisation and security-compliant access tooling: secure, auditable third-party access to locked equipment (like NHTSA's short-range compromise), which turns the cybersecurity objection into the product.
Alternative or remanufactured parts with software unlocking (reman control modules, re-pairing), but LKQ shows that alone is a thin-margin roll-up unless paired with an access or IP moat.
Avoid: a pure AI repair-manual or diagnosis product sold on its own; history says it gets absorbed as a free add-on by the parts or tool seller (ALLDATA inside AutoZone, Mitchell 1 inside Snap-on).
surprises: The most famous repair-knowledge brand (Haynes) sold for only GBP 114.5M, while parts retailers earn about $2.5B net income each per year.
AutoZone and O'Reilly both have negative shareholder equity, because their cash generation is so strong that buybacks exceed accumulated equity.
Massachusetts telematics right-to-repair passed with 75% in 2020 and was still tied up in appeal in 2026. NHTSA told carmakers not to comply.
Only 2 of 6,786 FTC auto repair complaints (1996-2006) were relevant to repair-information access, despite shop surveys showing widespread trouble.
Advance Auto Parts became the biggest North American parts provider in 2014 and was running at an operating loss and closing about 700 locations by 2024-25, so scale alone did not win.

stances.why: Aftermarket history does not test whether every repair follows one universal chain. It does show that the parts-availability step is the most valuable part of that chain.

A real gap existed in the electronics era: 59% of shops had trouble getting information and 67% had sent cars back to dealers (2005). But consumer harm barely showed up (2 relevant FTC complaints out of 6,786), and the profit pool always sat in parts and logistics, not in knowledge.

Knowledge was already democratized by Chilton, MOTOR and Haynes, then by ALLDATA and Mitchell 1, and lock-in came back anyway. Carmakers moved control to access and authorisation (telematics, VIN-locked modules, security gateways), and NHTSA backed that on cybersecurity grounds in 2023. AI cannot read data it is not allowed to access.

Cheaper knowledge did make independent repair viable. But the lasting cost and profit centre is getting physical parts to the shop fast: AutoZone and O'Reilly earn ~19% operating margins from store density. That step does not drop 10x with AI.

Alternative parts were solved by salvage, remanufacturing and aftermarket copies at scale (LKQ), not by bespoke manufacturing, and margins are thin. Carmaker software locks (VIN burning, ECU reuse blocks) can stop even a correct physical part from working.

The FTC treats car repair as safe without OEM-run inspection, and states it needs parts, information and training. But safety and cybersecurity arguments (NHTSA 2023) are exactly the tool used to keep access closed, so certification and authorisation is the contested layer.

The independent car aftermarket is a mature, competitive, logistically efficient system worth $516B. Its inefficiencies come from deliberate carmaker lock-in at the newest technology layer, not from an industry structurally built to be inefficient.

research.q: Generic drugs and Hatch-Waxman (1984) as an analog: how knowledge/IP monopolies broke, the role of bioequivalence (verification) as the new gate, who captured value (Teva, Mylan; also price collapse and shortages).
research.headline: Hatch-Waxman broke the drug monopoly by changing what counted as proof. A cheap, standard bioequivalence test against a reference product replaced repeat clinical trials. Generics went from 13% of US prescriptions (1983) to 90% (2024) at 12% of spending. The drug monopoly was legal and regulatory rather than a knowledge gap, though. Incumbents moved their moat into patents and contracts. Value went to payers rather than generic makers (Teva and Mylan ended in losses, consolidation and price-fixing). The price collapse also produced quality fraud and shortages, so verification and paid-for quality became the real bottleneck.
research.bottleneck: Trusted verification of equivalence and of manufacturing quality, at a margin that still pays for quality and redundancy, along with access to the reference product and legal clearance to enter. Knowledge was never the scarce layer. The scarce layers were the right to have a copy accepted as equivalent and the economics of keeping many honest suppliers in business.
research.money_time: In this analog, the expensive steps before reform were proof and legal clearance (repeating efficacy trials, waiting out patents and litigation). Hatch-Waxman cut the cost of that step by more than 100x: a bioequivalence study costing a few million dollars against a $0.8-2.6B NDA, with the ANDA cost from background knowledge. After that, cost and failure moved to manufacturing quality, inspection and data integrity, physical supply resilience (sterile-injectable shortages lasting longer), and the legal fight over market entry (pay-for-delay at $3.5B/yr). The unit price only collapsed (by more than 95%) once about six verified suppliers existed.
shapes: A 'bioequivalence for parts' verification and certification layer: standard equivalence test protocols against a reference part, with tamper-evident provenance, so non-OEM or AI-designed parts can be accepted in aviation, energy and defense. It owns the gate rather than the commodity, which matches the Hatch-Waxman mechanism and the 1989 and Ranbaxy failure modes.
A first-filer alternative source for sole-source or obsolete high-value parts, matching the Paragraph IV / 180-day lesson: margins are strong only until the 4th-6th verified entrant.
Continuous quality and inspection as a service with tamper-evident production records, because self-reported data plus rare audits failed at Ranbaxy and in the 1989 scandal.
Supply-resilience contracts for low-margin critical parts (utilities, militaries, hospitals), the analog of generic sterile-injectable shortages where nobody is paid to keep capacity.

Avoid being a pure commodity cheaper-parts maker: Teva and Mylan show deflation, roll-ups, losses and price-fixing. Durable profit sat at chokepoints such as devices, API exclusivity and complex products.
surprises: The pre-1984 drug monopoly was not a knowledge monopoly. It was enforced by certification rules and patent law, and copying was technically easy.
The verification gate was itself corrupted within five years (the 1989 bribery and brand-substitution scandal) and again at offshore scale (Ranbaxy, a $500M plea).
The biggest generic makers did not capture the value. Teva lost $1.64B in 2024 after its $40.5B roll-up, and both Teva and Mylan turned to price-fixing or chokepoint products like EpiPen.
The success of the price collapse caused chronic shortages of cheap essential drugs, because nobody was paid for quality or redundancy.
Bioequivalence can pass products that are not equivalent in practice (Budeprion XL, reversed in 2012), so equivalence tests need post-market surveillance.

stances.why: The pharma lifecycle does not map directly onto a repair chain. It does show that 'prove equivalence' and 'secure resilient supply' are separate steps from 'make'.
Incumbents did capture value, but the pre-1984 monopoly rested on patents, data rules and Bolar, not on missing knowledge. Copying the molecule was easy, and breaking the monopoly took legislation.

Even with full information, incumbents moved the moat to pay-for-delay ($3.5B/yr), patent listings, denial of access to reference samples and device complexity (EpiPen). A closed knowledge gap does not end the monopoly.

A drop of 10x or more is real (more than 95% off brand with 6+ competitors; 90% of scripts for 12% of spend). It took about 30 years and statute, needed many verified suppliers, and brought shortages and fragility.
Making the copy was the easy part. Proving equivalence and keeping manufacturing honest failed repeatedly (1989 scandal, Ranbaxy, Budeprion, MTRL), and low-volume economics drive producers out.

Bioequivalence became the gate that unlocked the market. It was then corrupted and gamed, and FDA says the market does not reward quality maturity. Verification is both essential and in need of reinvention.

The system was rebuilt by statute and became far more efficient, but the rebuild created new pathologies: shortages, collusion, offshore fraud and consolidation. A rebuild has to price in quality and redundancy.

research.q: Carterfone (1968) and telephone equipment liberalization, and IBM plug-compatible peripherals: how equipment and repair monopolies broke, what happened to prices and to the incumbent.
research.headline: The telephone and IBM equipment monopolies broke mainly because of legal and regulatory acts (Hush-A-Phone 1956, Carterfone 1968, Part 68 registration, Computer II, the IBM consent decree and antitrust settlements) together with published interface standards and neutral certification. Knowledge spreading on its own did not do it. Equipment became cheap commodities and AT&T was eventually broken up, but IBM cut prices, changed interfaces, and later closed the mainframe market again, and most plug-compatible challengers (Telex, Memorex, Amdahl) failed or were absorbed.
research.bottleneck: Permission and certification: the legal right to connect, supply, or service, plus a neutral standard and test regime that replaces the incumbent's safety veto. Interface access (and keeping up with incumbent interface and software changes) comes second. Technical knowledge was not the scarce layer; rivals had it years before the markets opened.
research.money_time: The direct evidence says little about how cost splits across repair stages. In the Bell system the money went to rents: lifetime lease fees bundled with repair, protective coupler rentals and rewiring fees. That was a toll on permission to connect, not the cost of repair work. Liberalization cut equipment cost but shifted repair responsibility and inside-wiring cost to owners. In IBM's world, maintenance and software licensing were the levers of control. In both markets, time was lost waiting on legal and regulatory change: 1956 to 1968 to 1975-77 to 1983-84.
shapes: Neutral, AI-assisted conformity and certification lab for third-party parts or repairs in a regulated domain (aviation PMA parts, grid equipment, EV batteries, industrial robots), playing the role Part 68 registration and third-party certification bodies played in telecom: the certification layer is what opened the market
Standards- and interface-first plug-compatible parts supplier that lands a big institutional anchor buyer (government, fleet, utility), as GSA procurement did for IBM plug-compatibles

Independent third-party maintenance operator for a high-value installed base where the OEM refuses mixed-system service, the Amdahl-maintains-IBM move, ideally backed by regulatory or antitrust tailwinds such as right-to-repair rules
Warning shape: a pure compatible-hardware maker chasing an incumbent's R&D cadence. History says most die or are absorbed unless they control an interface or standard
surprises: The shared web-search budget was used up before this agent ran, so the findings rest on a few direct page fetches plus clearly marked unverified history from memory
The Bell monopoly ran repair well (durable, refurbished, bundled); the inefficiency was rent and slow innovation, not bad repair
After the market opened, owners took on wiring and equipment repair costs and basic service prices rose; many kept paying lease fees above purchase price for decades
IBM refusing to service mixed systems was overcome by a rival entering the maintenance business itself
Opening a market is not permanent: IBM closed mainframes again by 2000 through 64-bit architecture, software licensing and buying the emulator maker PSI

stances.why: These cases are about who may supply, connect and maintain equipment, not the order of repair stages.

Interface knowledge mattered, since plug-compatibles needed IBM's channel interface and IBM changed it. But the binding monopoly was legal and contractual: tariffs, lease-only terms, foreign-attachment bans and refusal to maintain mixed systems.

Rivals had the technical knowledge by 1965-1975, yet the monopolies held until regulators or courts acted. IBM then closed mainframes again through software licensing and architecture changes, so knowledge alone did not dissolve control.
Equipment prices did fall sharply, but because of competition and standards. Incumbent price cuts captured much of the gain, and cheaper often meant replacing rather than cheaper diagnosis or repair.

Building compatible hardware took millions in R&D (Amdahl) and constant tracking of the incumbent's changes. Most compatible makers failed or were absorbed, and the ~$1B cost of keeping pace ended PCM mainframes.

Part 68 registration, and later independent certification, was the mechanism that removed the incumbent's 'network harm' veto. How the certification regime is designed decided whether the market opened.

The structure was built to extract rent (lease-for-life, attachment bans), but Bell repair worked well operationally: equipment was durable and refurbished. Rebuilding took regulation and 15-30 years, not just a better technology.

research.q: Medieval and early-modern craft guilds and knowledge monopolies (Ogilvie, Epstein debate): did guilds hold tacit knowledge or just rents, and how did printed manuals/encyclopaedias erode them?
research.headline: Historians on both sides of the guild debate agree that craft knowledge was real and partly tacit. Epstein says guilds existed to transmit it. Ogilvie says guilds rationed access to it and shared the monopoly gains with rulers. Cheap printed knowledge (books of secrets from 1555, the Encyclopédie in 1751-72) did not end the monopoly; legal abolition did (Turgot 1776, Le Chapelier 1791). So the rent sat in legal privilege and certification plus embodied skill, not in information alone. That is a warning for the claim that AI ends the knowledge gap. (Caveat: the shared WebSearch budget was already used up, so this rests on direct fetches of known sources plus some standard citations that could not be re-checked.)
research.bottleneck: Legal and certification privilege (who may sign off, sell or practise), combined with embodied tacit execution skill. Codified explicit knowledge was not the scarce layer. Printing and encyclopaedias commoditised it without removing the rent.
research.money_time: Historically the expensive, slow parts were gaining the legal right and certified status to practise (7-year apprenticeships, master fees, masterpieces, membership) and acquiring embodied hands-on skill. Information got cheap first (printing from the 1450s, encyclopaedias from the 1750s), yet rents lasted for centuries until states removed the legal privilege.
shapes: Certification and return-to-service layer (a modern guild mark): AI-assisted inspection and sign-off that regulators and insurers accept. Historically, certification was the most durable moat.
Field-technician networks that pair AI knowledge with skilled hands. Mokyr's 'mechanics' were the complement that made codified knowledge pay off.
Shared field-failure and performance data for machines, after Lean's Engine Reporter and collective invention. Openly published data sped up improvement several-fold.
A company that uses regulatory or right-to-repair unlocks (analogous to Turgot and Le Chapelier). Removing legal privilege, not publishing knowledge, is what ended the guilds.
Be cautious with a pure AI-diagnosis or knowledge layer. Like the Encyclopédie, it may be valuable but commoditised, with the rents captured elsewhere.
surprises: Ogilvie, the strongest critic of the guilds, concedes they really did transmit skills. The debate is about access and rents, not whether the knowledge existed.
Guild secrets were mass-printed from 1555 (books of secrets) and in 1751-72 (the Encyclopédie), yet guilds survived until legal abolition in 1791 in France and the 19th century elsewhere.
Encyclopédie subscriptions predict industrial growth but literacy does not. Codified knowledge paid off only where an upper tail of skilled people could absorb it.
The Encyclopédie missed coke-smelted iron, the frontier technology of its day. Codified knowledge lags tacit frontier practice.
Method caveat: the shared web-search budget was used up before this agent ran. Findings marked 'standard citation' in the notes were not re-fetched.

stances.why: The guild literature is about production and training, not the stages of a repair.
Knowledge was real and partly tacit. But the rent was enforced through legal privilege and certification shared with political elites (Ogilvie), and disclosure in print did not break it.

Each earlier fall in information cost (printing, books of secrets, the Encyclopédie) left a tacit residue: Bessemer, Collins, the coke-iron gap. Gains went to places with skilled people who could absorb the knowledge.
Information shocks gave large but slow gains (about 60% faster city growth over a century; several-fold engine gains over decades), not a quick 10x, and they depended on institutions.
Making things hinged on process know-how that specifications did not carry (Bessemer licensees, coke smelting).
Guild quality marks and masterpieces were the inspection layer and the most durable legal moat. Certification outlived secrecy, so who certifies is where the power sits.
Ogilvie: guilds persisted to serve distributional interests. Epstein: they solved a real training hold-up. Both imply that a rebuild needs legal and institutional change, not just a knowledge tool.

research.q: Cuba, the Soviet Union, wartime Britain and other scarcity economies: repair cultures under parts shortages (Cuban almendrones, Soviet DIY repair); what they show about knowledge vs parts constraints.
research.headline: Scarcity economies (Cuba, the USSR, wartime Britain, Russia and Iran under sanctions, Indian jugaad) all had plenty of repair knowledge. Peer networks, state manuals and simple long-lived platforms made it a commons, yet the shortages stayed, because the limits were physical parts, energy and materials, and legal or certification authority. Knowledge was necessary but cheap. Where parts were missing, the workarounds (cannibalising, substituting, grey imports, dropping standards) kept assets running at the expense of safety, efficiency and airworthiness.
research.bottleneck: The physical and legal parts layer: certified, interchangeable parts actually in hand, plus the authority to declare an improvised or substitute repair airworthy or roadworthy. Knowledge spreads fast and cheaply (pamphlets, peers, simple platforms). Parts liquidity, materials and energy, and sign-off from certification do not.
research.money_time: In every scarcity case, time and cost go into sourcing and delivering parts and materials, and into getting authorisation to return the asset to service, not into diagnosis or understanding. Cubans, Soviets and Russians knew what was broken and how to fix it. They spent years and money obtaining or improvising parts (cannibalisation, engine swaps, about €1B in grey imports through third countries), rationing use (Cuban cars driven 800 km/yr instead of 3,000), and leaving assets 'parked' until parts arrived. Wartime Britain's productivity jump came from logistics (transport units, salvage depots, dispersed firms, test flights), not from knowledge.
shapes: Certified parts recovery and teardown network (a modern CRO MPRD / Airspares Ltd): scarcity cases show cannibalised assets become the parts pool, and the value is in grading, tracing and certifying recovered parts.

Cross-platform parts interchange graph and marketplace (what fits what, which substitutes are approved): the Cuban and Soviet repair success came from interchangeability and substitution, and commonality like the Zhiguli's makes markets liquid.
Approval route for non-OEM / reverse-engineered parts (PMA/DER-type, AI-assisted equivalence and test evidence): aviation sanctions show the barrier is approval, not fabrication.
Inspection and test as a service for substituted or improvised repairs: jugaad and Russian aviation show the cost of skipping it; CRO test flights show it scaling.

Distributed repair-capacity orchestration (contract network plus logistics, like the CRO's ~100 firms): the wartime lever was coordinating existing skilled shops and moving assets and parts, not new knowledge.
surprises: The shared WebSearch budget was used up before this agent ran, so the findings rest on direct fetches of reference pages (mostly Wikipedia) plus flagged background knowledge. Primary sources such as Gerasimova & Chuikina 2009, Reuters 2022 and the Finnish 2025 study should be re-verified.

Iran's own deputy minister blamed groundings on lack of parts AND 'technical expertise'. In aviation, expertise means OEM data and authorisations, a legally enforced knowledge monopoly, which is the strongest support for C2 in this sample.
Cuban owners rationed use (driving fell by about 70%) as much as they repaired, so under scarcity demand reduction is a repair strategy.

Russia, an aerospace power, still turned to cannibalisation, grey imports and reportedly to suppressing fault logs within months. Knowledge did nothing to stop safety eroding once certified parts and support were gone.

stances.why: The steps can be seen in every case, but scarcity changes the chain: use gets rationed, assets are 'parked' waiting for parts, one asset is cannibalised to keep others running, and inspection is the step most often quietly skipped (Russian unlogged faults, jugaad). The chain is a useful lens, but it is not a fixed sequence.

In Cuba, the USSR and wartime Britain knowledge was widespread and shared (manuals, classes, magazines), and the inefficiency came from parts, materials and energy. In aviation (Iran, Russia) the 'expertise' lock is OEM data plus certification authority. That is a real monopoly, but it is enforced by law, not by who knows what.

These cases are natural experiments in which knowledge was already close to free (whole populations of skilled improvisers, state how-to manuals), and repair still failed for want of parts, fuel and legal sign-off. Closing the knowledge gap does not remove the binding limits.

Even with deep expertise, Russian aviation needed years, cannibalisation and a black market of about €1B to source and deliver parts. Cuba's Special Period ran into energy and materials limits (oil imports at about 10%). Diagnosis and understanding were cheap; sourcing and delivery stayed expensive and dominated.

Made-to-fit local parts are common in Cuba and in jugaad, but they give lower-spec, less safe substitutes and only work outside certification. In aviation, parts without approval mean grounding and lost airworthiness. Making the part is possible; getting it approved and trusted is not solved.

Every certified field in this sample (CRO test flights, Bermuda's suspension of airworthiness, EU bans, Iranian groundings) shows inspection and certification as the gate. Where it is missing (jugaad, unlogged faults in Russia) the costs are measurable casualties.

Scarcity economies show inefficiency coming from structure (Kornai: shortage is systemic; legal limits in Cuba; sanctions), but the same systems repaired very efficiently under pressure (79,000 CRO aircraft, 60 years of Cuban cars). The CRO precedent suggests rebuilding the organisation and logistics layer, not removing the knowledge layer.

research.q: WWII and military field repair and depot systems (forward repair, cannibalization, Red Ball Express, modern Army battle damage repair): lessons on the cost of diagnosis vs parts vs logistics.
research.headline: Military repair history shows the cost driver depends on the system type. For simple, high-volume equipment (WWII trucks and tanks), diagnosis was nearly free and time went to parts, tires, transport, repair capacity and operator abuse. For complex modern systems (F-35), a real knowledge monopoly exists, but it is enforced through IP and technical-data contracts rather than cognition, and parts shortages and depot capacity still bind even when the knowledge is available. AI therefore attacks one real slice (misdiagnosis, swap-to-diagnose, navigating manuals) but does not dissolve the legal, physical-capacity and certification layers.
research.bottleneck: The scarce layer is the combination of (1) data rights, meaning tech data, part numbers and repair procedures locked up by OEM contracts; (2) repair material and spare parts availability; and (3) physical repair capacity (depots, shipyards, skilled trades). A fourth, often overlooked layer is part pedigree and records, which grounds aircraft even when the part is on the shelf. Diagnosis is a real but secondary cost multiplier: it matters most in complex electronics, where bad diagnosis turns into cannibalization and NFF.
research.money_time: The answer depends on system complexity. For simple, high-volume equipment (WWII trucks and tanks), diagnosis was nearly free. Time and money went to spare parts and consumables (tires), port, transport and repair-facility capacity, and avoidable damage from operator abuse and accidents (about a third of truck replacements, about 40% of tire demand). For complex electronics and software-heavy aircraft, misdiagnosis becomes expensive (swap-to-diagnose cannibalization, NFF >$2B/yr), and access to OEM tech data adds weeks (up to 60 days per request). Even so, the largest single F-35 delay was repair material: 141-day depot cycles driven primarily by lack of material, and NMC-supply at 27%. For heavy industrial assets (submarines, ships), the work is known and depot capacity and skilled workforce dominate (10,363 idle days, $1.5B). Across all three, parts and capacity outweigh diagnosis in time-to-return.
shapes: Diagnostic copilot for complex electromechanical fleets (defense, aviation, energy) that cuts swap-to-diagnose and No Fault Found removals. Evidence: 5.3M cannibalization hours and >$2B/yr DoD NFF show misdiagnosis multiplies parts and labour demand.

Data-rights and tech-data reconstruction tooling: reverse engineering, digitizing legacy manuals, part-number and illustrated-parts-catalog extraction, so organic or independent depots can take workload from OEMs. Evidence: F-35 organic depots were 2x faster than OEMs but blocked by tech data, and 73% of parts still went to OEMs.
Part pedigree and digital records infrastructure (traceability and airworthiness documentation for spares). Evidence: 81% of F-35 spares lacked records, and 9% of flight hours were lost at one site.

Distributed qualified manufacturing for obsolete or diminishing-source parts, with qualification and certification as the product rather than just the printer. Evidence: militaries still default to cannibalization and lifetime buys, and WWII local manufacture hit material limits.

Repair capacity orchestration and scheduling for depots and shipyards (workload allocation across public and private yards, repair-material forecasting). Evidence: 10,363 submarine idle days came from capacity and allocation, not knowledge.
Remote expert and AI field-repair support for coalition or field forces modelled on the Ukraine remote maintenance cells, sold to defense and critical-infrastructure operators (unverified analog).
surprises: Accidents, not mechanical failure, caused about a third of Red Ball Express vehicle replacements, and about 40% of tire demand was operator abuse. Prevention and behaviour outweighed diagnosis.
A Navy study cited by GAO says up to half of Navy cannibalizations were not supply-driven. Some were swap-to-diagnose because mechanics lacked training or test equipment.

F-35 organic military depots repaired parts twice as fast as the OEMs, yet 73% of components still went to the OEMs because of data-rights and activation delays. The knowledge monopoly shows up directly in the numbers.
Missing electronic paperwork, not missing parts, grounded F-35s for 9% of possible flight hours at one site.

The F-35 office deliberately funded spares only to about 15% non-mission-capable-for-supply because a lower rate was unaffordable, so part of the inefficiency is a budget choice rather than ignorance.

Research limitation: the workflow-wide WebSearch budget was exhausted before this agent ran, so findings come from directly fetched GAO and US Army official-history sources. Ukraine and BDAR doctrine points are from memory and unverified.

stances.why: Military doctrine does run assess, recover, diagnose, parts, repair, inspect and return. But it adds recovery and evacuation, and puts prevention and operator care upstream. BDAR deliberately short-circuits the chain (temporary fix now, full repair and inspection later), so it is not a fixed linear sequence.

The F-35 is a textbook case: OEMs and subcontractors hold the tech data and part numbers, military maintainers cannot troubleshoot routine faults, and organic depots are 2x faster once enabled. GAO has documented the DoD IP gap for 30 years. For WWII trucks and Navy shipyards, however, knowledge was not the bottleneck.

The military knowledge monopoly is contractual and IP-based. Subcontractors deliberately withhold drawings and data, and AI cannot infer proprietary tech data it never sees. The gap closes through data rights, not inference. Remote coaching (Ukraine) suggests field-level know-how transfer can be cheap.

Better diagnosis would cut swap-to-diagnose cannibalization (5.3M hours) and NFF (>$2B/yr). But the dominant time sinks are repair material shortages (the primary F-35 depot impediment), depot and shipyard capacity (10,363 sub idle days), and transport and ports. AI will not cut these 10x.

WWII local tire production hit raw-material (carbon black) limits. Militaries still rely on cannibalization and lifetime buys for obsolete parts. Modern additive manufacturing is limited by part qualification and certification (from background knowledge, not verified this session).

81% of F-35 spares arrived without records, and 9% of flight hours at one site were lost to records issues. BDAR requires temporary repairs to be re-inspected. The part's pedigree and certification is a binding layer that needs modernization.

Chronic failure is visible: 4 of 49 aircraft types met goals, 70% of F-35 recommendations are unimplemented, and DoD chose not to buy tech data. But some inefficiency is a chosen trade-off: spares were funded only to 15% NMCS because more was unaffordable, and wartime logistics prioritized the speed of advance.

research.q: Legal and professional services as analog (LegalZoom, TurboTax, travel agents vs real estate agents): when does making knowledge abundant destroy an intermediary and when does licensure keep it?
research.headline: Abundant knowledge has collapsed the price of information but not the price of accountability. Intermediaries died where they mostly sold information and the transaction was low-stakes, unlicensed and fully digital (travel booking, stock trade execution). They survived, often for decades, where they held a licence, a liability-bearing sign-off, a coordination rule or political leverage (real estate agents, tax prep, lawyers, radiologists). For repair, AI will attack diagnosis and "understanding", but the value will move to whoever controls return-to-service sign-off, OEM data and parts channels unless law changes. Caveat: the workflow's shared web-search budget was used up before this agent ran, so the evidence is limited to direct fetches of known pages plus some well-known studies flagged in the notes as not re-verified this session.
research.bottleneck: Accountability and gatekeeping, not knowledge: the licensed or liability-bearing signature, OEM control of data, parts and authorisation (analogous to MLS rules and the Free File non-compete), and incumbents' political organisation. Abundant knowledge kills an intermediary only when (1) no licensed sign-off is required, (2) stakes are low and errors reversible, (3) the whole transaction can be done digitally, and (4) the upstream supplier wants the intermediary gone.
research.money_time: By analogy, the money goes less to producing knowledge (diagnosis, understanding) than to the gated steps: legally required attestation (licence, return-to-service signature), coordination rules that tie the intermediary to the transaction (MLS co-op comp is the analog of OEM authorisation and parts and data access), and distribution defaults. Once knowledge was cheap, the remaining cost in real estate and tax was rent kept by licence, rules and lobbying, not labour spent on knowing things. Expect the same in repair: AI shrinks diagnose and understand time, while sign-off, OEM-gated parts and data, and liability keep the price.
shapes: Be the licensed, liability-bearing entity rather than route around it. Like LegalZoom buying its way into an Arizona ABS law firm, an AI-native repair station (for example an FAA Part 145 certificated shop or a licensed inspection firm) that uses AI internally captures the accountability rent that persists.

Attestation and verification infrastructure: tools that make sign-off auditable, faster and insurable (inspection evidence capture, AI-assisted conformity records), since sign-off is the layer that survives in every analog. Supports C6.
Attack the coordination rule, not just the knowledge: pair the product with right-to-repair policy or antitrust leverage, the way Burnett moved real estate commissions after technology alone had not.

Target domains that meet the kill conditions (unlicensed, low-stakes, fully digital, supplier indifferent or hostile to the intermediary), such as consumer appliance diagnosis and parts matching, where travel-agent-style disintermediation is plausible. Avoid assuming the same dynamics in aviation or nuclear.
surprises: Real estate commissions stayed at about 5-6% for roughly 20 years after listings became fully public. Only a 2023 jury verdict, not technology, started to move them.
In 2019 only 2.7% of taxpayers eligible for Free File used it, despite tax knowledge being fully codified in software. Defaults and dark patterns beat abundant information.
IRS Direct File worked (86% said it raised their trust in the IRS) and was still killed in 2025. A better, free product lost to the incumbents' politics.
LegalZoom's endgame was becoming a licensed law firm owner, not abolishing licensure.
Travel agents did not disappear. About 61,500 remain, with flat projections, concentrated in complex, high-stakes trips.

stances.why: The professional-services analogs do not test a universal repair chain. They only suggest the bottleneck stage differs by domain: transaction or attestation in some, knowledge in others.

Information asymmetry was real in real estate and tax, but making the information public (Zillow, tax law, software) did not remove the rent. Persistent inefficiency came from licensing, coordination rules (MLS co-op comp, the Free File non-compete), defaults and lobbying.
The FTC's DoNotPay action and Mata v. Avianca show AI knowledge is not yet trusted or liability-bearing. Fully public knowledge never dislodged licensed intermediaries by itself.

Travel booking costs collapsed once the whole transaction could go digital and suppliers wanted to cut out agents. Real estate commissions stayed near 6% through 20 years of information abundance until antitrust litigation. Order-of-magnitude drops need the gate to fall, not only knowledge to spread.
No evidence in this analog set on making parts.
In every analog the attestation layer survives and becomes the rent-bearing scarce layer: licensed lawyer and law-firm ownership, licensed broker, radiologist sign-off, Rule 11 verification.

Burnett and the Free File non-compete show inefficiency that incumbents preserved through rules. But fixes came from antitrust and policy, while product-only disruptors tended to be absorbed (LegalZoom became a law firm) or blocked (Direct File was killed).

research.q: Software analog: open source, Stack Overflow, and now AI coding; did abundant software knowledge lower maintenance cost and who captured value (Red Hat, cloud)? Map the analogy to physical repair.
research.headline: Software is the extreme test of the knowledge-monopoly thesis. Free code (about $8.8T in demand-side value), free Q&A, and now AI did not cut maintenance by 10x: developers still spent about 17 of 41 hours a week on maintenance, poor software quality costs the US $2.41T, and AI gains on mature codebases run from -19% to about +18%. Value went to whoever took accountability (Red Hat, $34B), operated the whole lifecycle as a service (AWS, $45.6B operating income in 2025) or owned the data and models, not to the people who produced the knowledge (60% of maintainers are unpaid).
research.bottleneck: Accountability and verification, not knowledge. When knowledge and parts became free in software, the scarce layer became whoever vouches for and takes liability for the working system (Red Hat certification, cloud SLAs, CRA conformity), plus the proprietary field and usage data that AI models need. In physical repair that means certification authority, part qualification and pedigree, liability, and failure-data ownership.
research.money_time: In software, where parts (libraries) and delivery are essentially free and knowledge is abundant, cost and time concentrate in understanding system-specific context in large legacy codebases, integration and dependency upkeep, and verification and stability. About 42% of developer time goes to maintenance and $1.52T is held as tech debt. AI speeds up writing and fixing code but pushes cost into review, debugging 'almost right' output and stability. The lesson for physical repair: once diagnosis knowledge is cheap, the dominant costs become system-specific context, part qualification and pedigree, and inspection/return-to-service sign-off, plus the parts and logistics costs that software never had.
shapes: Red Hat for physical repair: a certified-repair and assurance layer that guarantees the outcome on top of commoditized AI diagnostics and open parts data. This is where software value moved once knowledge was free.

Cloud/managed-operations analog: uptime-as-a-service or power-by-the-hour for fleets of machines (robots, energy assets, industrial equipment), absorbing the whole notice-to-return chain. Cloud captured the most value by making maintenance someone else's problem.

Provenance and attestation infrastructure for parts and repairs (the analog of SBOMs, signed builds and supply-chain security): digital pedigree, AI-assisted inspection and conformity evidence. This is the C6 bottleneck, and it grows as AI and distributed manufacturing spread.

A failure-data moat company: aggregate proprietary field-failure and repair-outcome data across OEMs and operators, because AI diagnostics are only as good as the data. The Stack Overflow lesson is that data owners capture value when the public commons erodes.
Avoid a pure 'AI knowledge assistant for technicians' as the whole company. The software analog suggests it commoditizes fast, gives modest gains for experts, and loses value to model vendors.
