surprises: After about 20 years of free code and Stack Overflow, maintenance still took about 42% of developer time (Stripe 2018). Abundance raised the total maintenance load (Jevons) instead of lowering it.
Experienced developers on their own mature repos were 19% slower with AI while believing they were 20% faster (METR 2025). The perception gap matters for any claims that AI repair copilots are '10x'.
93% of codebases carry components with no activity in 2+ years, even though in software anyone can copy or fork the design for free. 'Supplier gone' is not solved by being able to make the part.
AI is shrinking the public knowledge commons (Stack Overflow questions -78% in a year) while its corpus is licensed to model owners. This is a new knowledge monopoly, not the end of one.
Even Red Hat, an open-source champion, built moats once code was free: certification, support, and (unverified here) restricting RHEL source in 2023.
Note: the workflow's shared web search budget was exhausted, so findings come from direct fetches of known sources. Gaps are listed in the notes file /home/user/nuketime/research/repair/raw/h08.md.

stances.why: Software maintenance follows detect-diagnose-fix-test-deploy. But cloud and SaaS won by collapsing the chain into continuous managed operations that the customer never sees, not by optimizing each step.

Breaking proprietary code monopolies created about $8.8T of value. But maintenance inefficiency ($2.41T CISQ, about 42% of developer time) persisted after the monopoly was gone, driven by complexity, integration and accountability.

Experts on mature codebases were not reliably faster with AI (METR). 46% distrust AI output. AI re-centralizes knowledge in model owners (Stack Overflow -78% questions, corpus licensed to OpenAI) rather than dissolving the gap.

Even where parts and delivery cost close to zero, measured AI effects run from -19% to +56%, not 10x, and delivery stability falls 7.2% per 25% increase in adoption. Physical repair adds nonzero part cost and logistics.

In software, copying or forking an abandoned part is free and the design is open, yet 93% of codebases carry inactive components. Qualifying, sustaining and owning the part is the hard problem, not fabricating it.

XZ backdoor, OSS supply-chain risk, the EU CRA, the DORA stability drop and the 'almost right' problem all show verification and attestation becoming the bottleneck and the moat as knowledge gets cheap.

Software was rebuilt (OSS, cloud, DevOps) with large gains, but through new intermediaries (Red Hat, AWS, model vendors) that captured the value, not by eliminating structure. Regulation, not only technology, shapes the rebuild.

research.q: Shanzhai / Shenzhen Huaqiangbei ecosystem: how open knowledge of phone designs (public boards, gongban) created a cheap repair-and-remanufacturing economy; lessons.
research.headline: Shanzhai shows that open design knowledge (gongkai reference designs and public boards, mostly from MediaTek) cut the cost of making phones roughly 5-10x and briefly took about 20% of the global 2G market. But the cheap repair and remanufacturing economy in Huaqiangbei rests mainly on physical parts liquidity, harvested donor parts, dense microsoldering labour and tools that beat parts pairing, not on knowledge, and OEMs answered leaked knowledge by moving lock-in into cryptography that AI cannot remove.
research.bottleneck: The scarce layer is control over hard-to-make core parts and their authorisation (silicon, displays, logic boards, plus cryptographic pairing), together with dense parts liquidity and skilled hands. Knowledge was always the cheapest input. In shanzhai it was released on purpose by the owner of the scarce layer (MediaTek), and in repair OEMs moved their monopoly from documents to cryptography.
research.money_time: In the Shenzhen phone case, diagnosis and procedural knowledge are cheap and fast because schematics and boardviews are shared and techs are experienced. Money and time go to: (1) getting the right part, which depends on model and colour and is often harvested from donors, with no bare supply of displays or boards; (2) skilled labour for board-level work (about $1,000 in tools and training, about 30 minutes per chip); and (3) defeating or living with parts pairing (programmers, chip transplants, returns caused by error messages). For OEM-authorised repair, the money goes to OEM-priced parts that leave almost no labour margin.
shapes: Digital Huaqiangbei for one high-value machine class: a parts-liquidity marketplace that harvests, refurbishes and certifies donor parts with provenance, because parts liquidity, not knowledge, made Shenzhen repair cheap.
A MediaTek-style turnkey repair platform: sell a packaged diagnostic, procedure and parts kit for a machine class where OEMs are slow, mirroring how reference designs let small firms compete.
A provenance and inspection layer that attests third-party or refurbished parts (test rigs plus cryptographic attestation), because cheap open ecosystems create a counterfeit and safety trust gap.
Interoperability tooling for parts pairing in jurisdictions where right-to-repair allows it, since pairing is where OEM lock-in now lives.
surprises: The workflow's shared web search budget was used up before this agent's first query. Findings come from fetching known primary URLs directly, and items marked unverified need checking.
Gongkai openness was a deliberate sales strategy by the chip vendor, not leakage the vendor fought.
Building an iPhone from market parts depends on recycled original logic boards and LCDs. Bespoke manufacture of complex parts did not happen even in the world's densest electronics market.
When a new phone costs $12, repairing it is irrational. Open knowledge made devices cheaper to make and buy new, not more repairable.

stances.why: Phone repair in Huaqiangbei follows a chain like this, but the steps collapse together in practice: the booth diagnoses, sources and repairs within minutes, often by harvesting a donor part. There is usually no formal safety inspection, so that step is the one most often skipped.

Open reference designs and leaked schematics did break incumbents' barriers to entry, which supports C2 for manufacturing. For repair, the binding constraints were parts liquidity, skilled microsoldering labour and cryptographic pairing, not knowledge, and OEMs moved lock-in from documents to software.

Knowledge was already almost free in Shenzhen (shared schematics, boardviews, YouTube), yet repair stayed gated by parts pairing, the absence of bare LCD or logic-board supply, and hands-on soldering skill. AI cannot defeat a cryptographic handshake.

Huaqiangbei shows sourcing and delivery costs can be crushed, to same-day and walking distance, but by physical density and harvesting donor parts rather than by information. Applying open knowledge to manufacturing gave roughly a 5-10x cost drop, which suggests order-of-magnitude falls are possible where parts liquidity exists.

The ecosystem never made bespoke complex parts such as SoCs, displays or logic boards. It harvested and refurbished donors. Only simple parts (shells, glass, flex cables, batteries) were made aftermarket, and even screen rebuilding reused the original LCD.
Cheap open knowledge with no certification produced unsafe batteries, counterfeits, warranty fraud and government crackdowns. Verifying provenance and safety became more valuable, not less.

OEM pairing and pricing (a $270 part vs $280 with labour) show repair is deliberately throttled, which supports C7. But Shenzhen shows a highly efficient parallel repair economy forms on its own wherever parts and labour are dense. The problem is incentives and access, not a lack of 'smart'.

research.q: Remanufacturing industry (Caterpillar Reman, automotive core economy, ReMaTec, US ITC 2012 reman study): size, margins, what makes it work.
research.headline: Remanufacturing is a mature but stubbornly small industry. It is about 2% of manufacturing in both the US and EU: roughly $43bn and 180k US jobs (USITC 2012), and about EUR 30bn in Europe (ERN 2015, both recalled not re-verified). Its economics hinge on core supply, reverse logistics, working capital, channel power and warranty trust rather than knowledge. Independent automotive remanufacturers earn about 20% gross margins with about $300m of cores parked on retailer shelves. OEMs such as Caterpillar dominate heavy-equipment and aerospace reman because they control the engineering data, the cores and the dealer channel together.
research.bottleneck: Core supply is the scarce layer. That means the physical return flow of used units of the right type and quality, at the right time, plus the deposit, credit and logistics machinery that secures it. In OEM-dominated sectors this is bundled with control of engineering data, the dealer channel, warranty and certification. In automotive, retailer channel power and the shift to EVs (which kills the alternator and starter core base) are the binding constraints. Knowledge is not.
research.money_time: In remanufacturing the money goes to core acquisition and reverse logistics, and to the working capital tied up in core float. MPA holds about $298m of cores on retailer shelves against $790m of sales, plus $39m of capitalised core premiums. Yield loss (more than one core per finished unit), labour-intensive teardown, cleaning and testing (moved to Mexico), and retailer allowances and concentration also take a large share. Diagnosis and understanding are batched and industrialised at the factory and cost little per unit. The customer's time saving comes from the exchange-unit model: swap now, fix the core later.
shapes: EV battery, e-motor and power-electronics reman and repair platform. Rematec's 2026 agenda shows this is the open frontier where OEM salvage specs do not yet exist and core flows are forming under the new EU ELV regulation.

Core-flow software and marketplace: AI grading of returned cores from photos and test data, core-value pricing, deposit and credit management, and broker matching. This attacks the real bottleneck (uncertain core timing, quantity and quality) rather than diagnosis.

Additive and directed-energy salvage cell (laser cladding, cold spray) sold to independent rebuilders and dealers, plus a qualification and data package. It turns scrapped cores into usable ones and raises yield above the one-core-per-unit bound.

Independent remanufacturer for orphaned industrial assets (energy, robotics, defence) where the OEM is gone or slow, combining reverse engineering and certification. It is viable only where core value is high and an inspection authority will accept it.
surprises: MPA carries about $298m of cores on its customers' shelves, about 38% of a year's revenue. Reman is a working-capital business as much as a manufacturing one.
An independent remanufacturer earns only about 20% gross margin, because three retailers take 85% of its sales and charge core premiums.
Remanufacturing consumes more than one used core per finished unit on average. Yield, not know-how, limits supply.
Despite decades of advocacy and circular-economy policy, reman stays at about 2% of manufacturing in both the US and EU.
OEMs such as Caterpillar bought independent remanufacturers. Reman strengthens OEM aftermarket capture rather than breaking it.

The shared web-search budget was exhausted before this agent ran, and usitc.gov, remanufacturing.eu and caterpillar.com blocked direct fetches. The USITC, ERN and Cat figures are recalled, not re-verified.

stances.why: Reman exchange models reorder the chain. The customer swaps a known-good exchange unit immediately, and diagnosis and repair of the failed core happen later, batched at a factory. The steps exist but are not a single serial chain per failure.

In HDOR and aerospace, OEM engineering data and salvage specs are real moats, and OEMs dominate reman. In automotive the know-how is commoditised, yet margins are still about 20% gross. The constraints there are cores, retailer channel power and working capital, not knowledge.
Reman's share has been stuck around 2% for over a decade despite better information tools. AI does not create cores, deposits, warranties, trade permissions or shelf space.

Reman costs sit in core logistics and float (MPA carries $298m of cores, about 38% of sales), labour, yield loss (more than one core per unit) and channel allowances. Diagnosis and understanding are a small share, so an order-of-magnitude total drop is not supported.

Reman works because restoring an existing high-value core is cheaper than making new. Salvage and additive repair extend this, but qualification and certification gate it. The core itself remains the scarce input.
Core acceptance criteria, test-to-new-spec, the Manufactured Again certification and aerospace approvals are central to reman's value and to its trust problem.

Reman is a deliberately efficient design: exchange units minimise downtime. But OEMs shape it to protect aftermarket capture, and its small share reflects structural barriers (perception, trade rules, core flows) rather than a lack of intelligence.

research.q: The aviation PMA parts industry history (1950s-today): growth, airline adoption rates, OEM countermeasures (warranty voiding, bundling), current share of parts market.
research.headline: The legal channel for non-OEM aviation parts has existed since 1947-1965 (CAR 3.31 → CAR 1.55 → FAR 21.303). Yet PMA is still a small share of the parts market, roughly a low single-digit percent (estimate not verified this session). Even the leader, HEICO, adds only about 400-550 approvals a year (catalogue grew from about 11,000 parts in 2018 to about 20,000 in 2025). What holds PMA back is certification and contractual lock-in (power-by-the-hour deals, warranties, lessor return conditions, engines discounted up to 90%), not knowledge. Caveat: the shared web search budget was already used up when this agent ran. Findings come from direct fetches of SEC filings, eCFR and Wikipedia regulatory history, plus memory-based leads flagged as unverified in h11.md.
research.bottleneck: Certification and acceptance throughput: per-part airworthiness approval (PMA/DER) plus contractual acceptance by airlines, lessors and OEM service agreements, backed by trusted parts provenance. It is neither knowledge of the part nor the ability to make it.
research.money_time: The OEM aftermarket is the profit centre. Engines are sold below cost, and the losses are recovered through spares and LLP price escalation under multi-year flight-hour agreements. For non-OEM alternatives, time and money go into design approval: compliance testing and computations per product, the quality system, FAA/DER review and customer/lessor acceptance. Reverse-engineering the geometry is a smaller cost. That is why the largest PMA house adds only about 500 approvals a year and PMA stays a small share of parts spend.
shapes: AI for certification packages: tools that generate and verify PMA/DER compliance data (test plans, similarity and identicality analysis, documentation) for PMA makers and DERs. It targets the roughly 500-approvals-a-year throughput limit.
Parts provenance and traceability: digital back-to-birth records and forged-certificate detection (the AOG Technics case showed 60,000 parts with false paperwork can enter the fleet).
Lessor and financier analytics that price PMA and DER-repair content into aircraft residual value, which weakens a key OEM countermeasure (lease return conditions banning PMA).
An AI-native PMA house: viable, but it competes with HEICO on certification capacity and airline relationships (an airline-equity model like Lufthansa Technik's 20% stake), not on knowledge.
surprises: PMA has been legal since 1956 (CAR 1.55) and 1965 (FAR 21.303), yet it only became an industry after 1990s FAA enforcement and airline backing. Knowledge availability alone did not create the market.
HEICO calls the PMA certification process its moat ('significant barrier to entry'). The industry's leading disruptor of OEMs relies on the certification friction the founder hopes AI will remove.
HEICO holds no material patents and relies on trade secrets, so its knowledge is proprietary too. Breaking the OEM monopoly produced a second knowledge holder rather than open knowledge.
An airline MRO (Lufthansa Technik) holds a 20% equity stake in the largest PMA maker. Buyers had to put in capital to break the lock-in.

stances.why: The chain broadly holds, but aviation adds stages it leaves out: the part design itself must be approved (PMA/DER) before it can be sourced, and contractual and lessor acceptance is needed before installation.

OEMs were the sole source of substantially all engine spares, and PMA makers win by re-designing OEM parts, which supports a knowledge monopoly. But the lock is equally contractual (power-by-the-hour, warranties, lease terms) and regulatory. PMA has been legal since 1956/1965 yet its share stays in the single digits.

Reverse-engineering knowledge was never the binding constraint. Showing compliance (tests, computations, quality system, FAA acceptance) is. HEICO, with decades of skill, still manages only about 400-550 approvals a year.
PMA delivers a percentage saving (estimates run 30-50%, unverified), not an order of magnitude. Certification and acceptance overhead stays, and OEMs respond with contracts and pricing.

In aviation a part without a PMA, licence, TSO or approved repair cannot legally be installed, however well it is made. Approval is part-by-part and product-specific, and the counterfeit history makes regulators stricter, not looser.

The 2009 quality-system rule, the 1995 enforcement push, HEICO calling PMA a 'significant barrier to entry' and the AOG Technics fraud all show certification and provenance are the central, durable layer.

The razor-and-blades model (engines discounted up to 90%, LLP price escalation, flight-hour lock-in) is a deliberate structure built on aftermarket lock-in. Much of the friction, though, is the rational price of safety assurance, not slop.

research.q: Healthcare: nurse practitioners, task-shifting, telemedicine and diagnosis decentralisation as analog for moving repair diagnosis away from OEM experts; what limited it?
research.headline: Healthcare did move diagnosis away from elite experts (to NPs, task-shifted workers, telehealth and even autonomous FDA-cleared AI), but slowly, over decades. What held it back was liability, licensure, payment codes, physical-presence rules and incumbent lobbying, not a lack of knowledge. Where AI already holds the knowledge (for example, an LLM alone scoring 92% against physicians' 74-76% on case vignettes), the gains did not reach practice. Cheaper diagnosis also did not make whole episodes cheaper: costs moved to more tests, longer visits and onward specialist referrals.
research.bottleneck: The scarce layer is legally accountable sign-off. That means licensure and liability for the decision, plus the reimbursement codes that pay for it, not diagnostic knowledge. A secondary bottleneck is integrating AI into human workflows and validating it in the field: models that win on benchmarks do not transfer to real populations or to clinician decisions.
research.money_time: In healthcare, cheap diagnosis does not shrink total episode cost much. Costs move to downstream testing, longer visits, specialist referral and treatment capacity, plus a large fixed layer of credentialing, sign-off and liability. Telehealth captured mainly the no-hands-on-exam slice (about 5% of claims). Autonomous screening AI still has to route positives to scarce specialists. So the money and time sit in the physical intervention and the accountable sign-off, not in the knowledge step.
shapes: Liability-bearing diagnosis or repair entity: like Digital Diagnostics carrying malpractice coverage for autonomous AI, a repair company that takes on the warranty, liability and certification risk captures the value that knowledge alone cannot.

Independent AI-diagnostic validation and inspection layer for machines and energy assets: the Epic sepsis failure mode, where a vendor model degrades on a new population, will recur with OEM or fleet-specific models.

Protocolised task shifting for technicians: AI-codified troubleshooting trees, standard kits and an expert escalation network, modelled on WHO HIV task shifting, so lower-cost techs handle routine faults and experts handle the complex tail.
'Ambient scribe for technicians' (work-order generation, manual and parts lookup): the AI layer that diffuses fastest because it does not move authority to sign off.
Regulatory and standards wedge: work with regulators (FAA Part 145, NRC, IEC) to create the equivalent of CPT codes or full practice authority for AI-assisted independent repair.
surprises: AI alone beat physicians on vignettes, but physicians given the AI did not improve at all.
Autonomous FDA-cleared AI diagnosis with its own billing code and vendor-assumed liability still had tiny uptake. Reimbursement plus approval was not enough.
NPs beat physicians in 38% of random pairs: within-profession variation exceeds the credential gap, so credentials are a weak proxy for diagnostic skill.
Telehealth access hung on short-term waivers that briefly lapsed during the October 2025 government shutdown, making regulation, not technology, visibly the binding constraint.
The WebSearch budget was exhausted, so about half the findings are from memory and should be re-verified (flagged in /home/user/nuketime/research/repair/raw/h12.md).

stances.why: Medicine has an analogous chain (triage, diagnosis, treatment, follow-up, discharge), but it is iterative: diagnosis loops with treatment and testing rather than being linear.
Incumbents do capture value and lobby hard (AMA scope creep). But the monopoly is legal, credential and liability-based, not informational, and the experts themselves err about 11% of the time.

An LLM can know the answer (92%), yet physicians with it do not improve (76% vs 74%), and vendor models fail external validation (Epic sepsis AUC 0.63). The knowledge exists but does not reach decisions reliably.

Task-shifting evidence shows labour savings offset by more tests, longer visits and higher resource use on complex cases. Telehealth stabilised at about 5% of claims, and cheap diagnosis moved the queue to treatment.
No healthcare evidence collected on bespoke manufacturing.
Sign-off and liability are where decentralisation is gated. AI raised the need for independent validation, and the autonomous AI that succeeded had its vendor assume liability.

The system is built to allocate liability and safety, and inefficiency is a by-product. It was reworked slowly by legislation and payment change (NP full practice authority over decades, CPT codes), not rebuilt by technology.

research.q: Venture-backed startups in AI for maintenance and repair 2020-2026 (technician copilots, AI diagnostics, MRO software: e.g., Aquant, Augmentir, Copilot-style for field service, Fieldcode, Veryon, Rotate, Aerostrat): funding, traction, failures.
research.headline: These findings are low-confidence: the shared search budget was used up before this agent's first query, so funding figures for Aquant, Uptake, Augury, Tractian, Gecko and Veryon's owner come from memory and need checking. Between 2020 and 2026, venture money in AI for repair mostly went to workflow and operations platforms (ServiceTitan IPO at $8.9B, Samsara $1B+ ARR), to sensing and inspection hardware (Augury, Tractian, Gecko), and to incumbents and private-equity roll-ups that own the maintenance data (Veryon, which claims 100M+ maintenance events). Pure technician-copilot startups (Aquant, Augmentir) raised mid-sized rounds and claim gains of 20-40% or about 1 hour per technician per day, not 10x, and well-funded horizontal industrial-AI bets such as Uptake struggled.
research.bottleneck: The scarce resource is proprietary, labelled maintenance-event data tied to the installed base (Veryon's 100M+ events, OEM service tickets), together with integration into legacy maintenance and field-service systems and customers' ability to act on predictions. Model intelligence is not the constraint. Uptake-style pilot purgatory and incumbents bundling copilots as a feature are the main risks.
research.money_time: Vendor evidence, all self-reported, puts much of field-service cost and time in dispatch, travel, idle time, scheduling and admin. Fieldcode reports 30% less drive time and 35% less time per work order, and Aquant claims about 1 hour per technician per day saved. In aviation, parts availability and approved-data or certification steps dominate rather than diagnosis. Venture value has accrued to the workflow and payments layer (ServiceTitan) and the sensing layer (Samsara), not to standalone diagnosis.
shapes: Data-moat diagnostics: own a fleet's maintenance-event data, for example by bundling cheap sensors with a maintenance system (Tractian-style) or acquiring repair records, because copilots without proprietary history get commoditised
Robotic or automated inspection plus an integrity data platform (Gecko-style), because inspection is fundable, required by regulators and generates proprietary data

Operating system plus marketplace for independent repairers in an underserved vertical (ServiceTitan pattern applied to industrial or energy equipment), because workflow and payments capture the value while diagnosis tends to be a feature
AI for parts and logistics (service parts availability, out-of-production parts, sourcing for grounded aircraft), because the measured time loss sits in logistics and dispatch rather than knowledge
Avoid a standalone horizontal technician copilot: incumbents (Microsoft, Salesforce, IFS) bundle it and reported ROI is only 20-40%
surprises: The best-funded repair-software outcomes (ServiceTitan $8.9B IPO, Samsara $1B+ ARR) are workflow and sensing companies, not diagnosis or knowledge companies
Aquant's own homepage headline metric is modest (up to 1 hour per technician per day), which is far from a 10x reduction
Aviation maintenance AI is led by a private-equity consolidator (Veryon, 25% of the world airline fleet) using a proprietary LLM, which suggests AI is reinforcing knowledge monopolies
'Rotate' and 'Aerostrat' as named point to a forum and a French composite-repair shop, so the founder's comparables need clarifying
The search budget ran out before this agent's first search, so most funding figures in this file are unverified and come from memory

stances.why: Vendors line up with chain stages: Samsara and Augury for noticing, Aquant and Veryon Diagnostics for diagnosis, Fieldcode and ServiceTitan for dispatch and repair execution, Gecko for inspection. But the chain leaves out scheduling, travel, admin and payments, which is where the largest software outcomes sit.

Copilot vendors do sell against a skills or tribal-knowledge gap. But the buyer is usually the equipment maker or the large service organisation using AI to scale its own knowledge, not independents breaking an OEM monopoly.

Diagnostic AI depends on proprietary service history (Veryon's 100M+ events; Aquant trains on customer tickets and manuals). Knowledge is being re-enclosed in data moats rather than disappearing. Uptake shows that well-funded AI did not remove the bottlenecks.
The gains vendors report are 20-40% or about 1 hour per technician per day, not 10x. The largest measured savings are in dispatch, drive time and admin rather than diagnosis.
None of the companies reviewed does bespoke part manufacturing. The aviation context implies approved-data and PMA constraints would apply.
Robotic inspection plus AI (Gecko about $1.25B, unverified) and machine health are among the best-funded parts of the category, so inspection is a fundable industry in its own right.

Large venture outcomes (ServiceTitan, Samsara) show the old tooling was weak and could be rebuilt. But the winners digitised existing workflows step by step, and incumbents (IFS, Siemens, PTC, Microsoft) absorbed AI as a feature rather than the industry being rebuilt from scratch.

research.q: Investor theses on repair and maintenance (a16z "American dynamism", Bessemer, Founders Fund, PE roll-ups of HVAC/plumbing, aviation MRO consolidation): what do investors say the opportunity is?
research.headline: Investors frame the repair and maintenance opportunity in three ways: own the fragmented labour through PE roll-ups (HVAC, engine MRO), own the certified part (TransDigm, HEICO/PMA), or build the coordination and data layer (ServiceTitan, YC's physical-world operating system and data requests, a16z sustainment telemetry). Almost none of them say the knowledge gap is the main constraint or that AI has erased it. The scarce things they point to are capacity, certification, access to locked systems, and physical-world data that does not exist yet.
research.bottleneck: Certified, sole-source supply of parts plus scarce licensed capacity: shop slots, test cells, certified technicians and qualified suppliers. Underneath that are budget and incentive structures that do not fund sustainment, plus missing physical-world data. Knowledge withholding (manuals, codes) is real but secondary; access locks and regulatory approval are what bind.
research.money_time: Investor evidence puts the money in the parts and labour stages, not in diagnosis. In aerospace, sole-source certified spare parts carry extreme margins (DoD IG: a 9,400% markup on a pin, $20.8M excess profit on 105 parts). HEICO earns ~21% operating margins on FAA-approved replacement parts. Engine MRO value sits in shop capacity and OEM licences (StandardAero went from ~$670M to ~$10.4B through PE owners). For defense platforms, sustainment is ~70% of lifecycle cost, and one MQ-9 needs 180+ people. In residential trades, the PE thesis is that technician labour and pricing are where value is made; the software layer (ServiceTitan) monetises coordination and dispatch.
shapes: AI-accelerated alternative-parts maker (PMA/DER route): reverse engineering plus automated qualification data packages to attack the OEM/TransDigm sole-source profit pool. HEICO's ~$40B value and TransDigm buying PMA makers show the pool is real, and certification is the moat.

Defense/energy fleet sustainment layer: telemetry, predictive maintenance and robotic turnaround. a16z explicitly calls for it, sustainment is ~70% of lifecycle cost, and it needs funded O&S budget lines.
Inspection-data robotics on the Gecko model for energy and industrial assets: YC RFS 'Data for the Real World'. It turns inspection into a data product and supports C6.
Field-operations operating system for mixed AI-agent, robot and human maintenance crews: YC RFS 'New Operating Systems for the Physical World'.
Tech-enabled independent MRO or service roll-up: PE's proven playbook. Adding AI diagnosis and dispatch could widen margins, but it needs capital and labour recruiting rather than knowledge alone.
Caution: a pure AI repair-knowledge layer for consumers is weak. Bessemer and the FTC suggest labour and access, not knowledge, are binding.
surprises: TransDigm, the aftermarket monopolist, agreed in Jan 2026 to pay $2.2B for PMA alternative-parts makers (Jet Parts Engineering, Victor Sierra). Incumbents neutralise the 'make the part elsewhere' threat by buying it.
a16z reports that past Navy automation increased maintenance costs and sometimes crew size, which goes against the idea that smarter systems automatically cut repair cost.
Bessemer explicitly ranks home services and manufacturing as low-propensity for vertical AI automation.
PE-owned firms were two-thirds of large (>$500M) US manufacturing bankruptcies in 2025, even as PE deal share in manufacturing rose above 20%.
a16z's American Dynamism page does not list maintenance or repair as a category at all; repair appears only as defense sustainment.
Method limit: the shared web search budget was exhausted, so this used direct fetches only. Founders Fund views and verified PE HVAC numbers are missing.

stances.why: Investors implicitly split the chain: software for notice, diagnose and dispatch, PE for labour, aftermarket roll-ups for parts. Profit concentrates in parts and labour capacity, not evenly along the chain.

The FTC confirms manuals, codes and diagnostics are withheld. But the richest investor profit pools (TransDigm, OEM engine services) come from certified sole-source parts, IP and capacity, not knowledge alone.

Bessemer says manual-labour sectors are the least automatable. YC says physical-world data is sparse and still needs collecting. The FTC shows firmware and access locks, which knowledge does not remove.
Investors fund AI for diagnose and dispatch, but no source claims 10x. a16z notes automation sometimes raised maintenance costs and crew needs.
Billions are going to Hadrian-type shops because parts capacity and qualification are the constraint. HEICO/PMA shows each part needs FAA approval and took decades. TransDigm is buying PMA makers.
YC cites Gecko inspection data and a16z wants telemetry and predictive maintenance. Certification (PMA, FAA) is the gate that sets value in aerospace parts.

For: YC says incumbents profit from human coordination, and a16z says vendors optimise for prototypes because sustainment is unbudgeted. Against: the dominant investor play is to consolidate and own the inefficiency (PE roll-ups, aftermarket monopolies) rather than rebuild it.

research.q: Private-equity roll-ups of repair and field service (HVAC, collision repair like Caliber, fire and life safety, elevator ISPs, aviation MRO like AAR/StandardAero/VSE): returns, margin drivers, multiples.
research.headline: Evidence quality: the shared search budget was used up before this agent started, so only the StandardAero S-1, the StandardAero, AAR and VSE Wikipedia pages and VSE's investor site were read this session; every other point comes from prior knowledge and needs checking. PE roll-ups of repair and field service earn their returns from multiple arbitrage (small shops bought at roughly 3-8x EBITDA, platforms sold at 12-20x+), leverage and sales and pricing playbooks, not from cheaper diagnosis. The highest-margin repair franchises (elevator OEM service, StandardAero's OEM-licensed engine MRO, TransDigm's sole-source parts) are monopolies over licences, approvals, tools and parts access, which AI does not dissolve.
research.bottleneck: Permission and capacity, not knowledge. The binding layers are OEM licences and technical-data access, regulatory approval of parts and repairs (PMA/DER, OEM authorisations), proprietary diagnostic and controller locks, insurer referral control in collision, code-mandated inspection rights, and skilled licensed technicians. AI can lower diagnostic cost, but capital rewards whoever owns these gates, and value tends to migrate to the data platform (for example CCC) rather than to the repairer.
research.money_time: Profit concentrates at the gated layers: OEM-licensed service (elevators, engines), sole-source parts (TransDigm), approved alternative parts (HEICO) and code-mandated inspection routes (fire), at 20-50% margins. Labour-heavy work earns low margins: airframe heavy checks (AAR paid $78M for a 1,600-person shop), single collision shops at mid-to-high single digits, HVAC repair. In HVAC the money is in replacement installs and memberships. In collision it is in insurer referral flow, parts and paint procurement, and cycle time. In aviation it is approved parts, engineered repairs and turnaround capacity. Diagnosis and 'understanding' are rarely the dominant cost line in these businesses. PE returns come mainly from multiple arbitrage (3-8x entry versus 12-20x+ exit) plus leverage.
shapes: Approval factory: an AI-accelerated engineering and certification service that generates PMA/DER substantiation data (or the defence equivalent) for obsolete or sole-source parts. This attacks the TransDigm/HEICO rent pool at its real bottleneck, approval throughput, rather than fabrication.

Inspection-first technology platform for code-mandated assets (fire, elevators, pressure vessels): robotic or sensor-based inspection plus AI reports that inspectors and authorities accept. Inspection is the profitable trigger for repair in PE roll-ups, so owning it means owning the funnel.

Independent-servicer enablement for locked equipment (elevators, industrial controllers): diagnostic tools and parts interoperability that let independent servicers break OEM service annuities. This needs legal and right-to-repair strategy as much as AI.

Software-plus-roll-up: buy fragmented, code-mandated service shops (fire, elevator, MRO component shops) at 4-8x and use AI dispatch, diagnosis and technician co-pilots to raise technician productivity, the scarcest input. The thesis is margin expansion beyond what current PE playbooks reach.

Engineered component-repair house for energy and industrial turbines, applying StandardAero's 2,000+ proprietary repairs model with AI-driven repair development, since repairs are cheaper and faster than new parts.
surprises: AAR paid only $78M for the #2 North American heavy airframe MRO with about 1,600 staff, so labour-based repair capacity is valued cheaply while licences and certification are valued highly.
StandardAero more than doubled in value under Carlyle in 5 years ($5B to ~$10.4B) with only about 12-13% EBITDA margins; the market paid for contracted, licence-protected revenue.
Collision repair procedures are already widely accessible, yet the industry consolidated hard. Democratised knowledge did not break the economics: referral control and labour did the work.
In the one place AI clearly cut 'diagnose' cost (photo estimating), the gains went to insurers and the data platform, not to repairers or owners.
The 1990s HVAC roll-ups largely failed; the current wave depends on cheap debt and sales playbooks, which makes it fragile when rates are high.

Evidence quality: the search budget was exhausted before this agent started, so only the StandardAero S-1, the StandardAero, AAR and VSE Wikipedia pages and VSE's investor site were read; the Caliber, HVAC, fire, elevator, TransDigm and HEICO numbers are from prior knowledge and need verification.

stances.why: The steps describe the work, but the commercial chain often starts with mandated inspection (fire, elevator, aviation) or insurer triage (collision), not 'notice'. In HVAC a repair call often turns into a replacement sale.

The highest-margin franchises (Otis service ~25%, TransDigm ~50%, StandardAero via OEM licences, HEICO/PMA) control technical data, tools, approvals and parts. The monopoly is legal and regulatory permission, not just know-how.

The gates are OEM licences, FAA/EASA approvals, proprietary software locks, insurer referrals and labour. Collision repair procedures are largely open, yet the industry consolidated around labour and referrals.

In HVAC and collision, labour, parts and customer acquisition dominate cost and margin. In aviation, approved parts and capacity dominate. Where AI cut diagnosis cost (CCC), value migrated to the platform owner rather than lowering system cost.
Alternative parts already exist in aviation (PMA/DER parts at 30-50% discounts). The binding cost is certification data and approval throughput, not making the part.

Code-mandated inspection is the most valued step in fire and elevator roll-ups: it brings recurring, non-discretionary revenue and generates the repair work. Certification capability is what AAR bought.

Fragmented local service is being rationalised by PE, mostly through financial and sales engineering rather than productivity. The industry is rationally built to capture rents at scarce regulated layers, not built to be inefficient.

research.q: On-demand manufacturing marketplaces (Xometry, Protolabs, Fictiv, Hubs, Hadrian, Divergent): margins, growth, what share of demand is spares/repair, why marketplaces earn thin margins.
research.headline: On-demand manufacturing marketplaces grow, but they earn thin margins. Xometry: 34.7% marketplace gross margin, 2.7% adjusted EBITDA margin in FY2025 despite 26-41% growth. Protolabs' operating margin fell from about 20% (2016-2018) to about 5% (2025) as instant quoting became common. Cheap manufacturing knowledge passes its value to buyers instead of creating new profits. None of these platforms reports spares or repair as a material share of demand. The capital is going into owned, automated, certified factories (Hadrian $260M Series C, Divergent), not into brokerage.
research.bottleneck: Qualified, accountable, certified production capacity: automated precision machining and additive work with AS9100, ITAR/EAR compliance and inspection or traceability, plus access to the technical data or IP for legacy parts. Discovery and quoting are no longer scarce. Know-how about manufacturing has become a commodity. Its profit went to buyers, and investor capital now goes to owned automated factories rather than brokers.
research.money_time: In these platforms' numbers, the information steps (finding a supplier, quoting, understanding manufacturability) have been compressed to near zero for the buyer. Instant quotes replaced manual requests for quotes. Most of the money still goes to physical production. Xometry passes about 65% of marketplace revenue to suppliers, and Protolabs' cost of revenue is about 55%, mostly materials, machine time and labor. The next largest cost is customer acquisition and support: Xometry spends about 18% of revenue on sales and marketing and about 11% on operations and support. Remaining time goes to manufacturing lead time, quality and compliance. The disclosures do not break out spares or repair as a demand category.
shapes: Owned, automated, certified micro-factory for legacy and obsolete spares in one regulated vertical (defense sustainment, rail, energy or grid, nuclear). Here customers pay for qualification and accountability, not discovery. Hadrian's funding shows investors back owned capacity over brokers.

A reverse-engineering, technical-data and qualification layer: AI turns a worn part, scan or old drawing into a certifiable data package plus an inspection plan (FAA PMA, DLA source approval). This targets the real bottleneck for critical parts, which Xometry and Protolabs do not touch.

AI-driven inspection and certification service (automated first-article inspection, metrology, traceability) sold to job shops and marketplaces. Assurance keeps margin while quoting becomes a commodity.

Avoid: a pure on-demand parts marketplace or broker for repair. Public evidence shows about 35% gross and 3-6% EBITDA, AI flagged as a commoditising threat, and the best-funded independent broker (Fictiv) folded into a distributor.
surprises: Protolabs' operating margin fell from about 20% (2016-2018) to 4.7% (2025), with revenue up only about 20% over seven years, as instant quoting spread. Cheap manufacturing knowledge destroyed incumbent profits instead of creating new ones.
Xometry's high-margin (88%) ads/SaaS revenue is shrinking while low-margin brokerage grows 45%.
Xometry's own 10-K names AI as a risk that could make its marketplace 'uneconomical or obsolete'.
Neither Xometry nor Protolabs reports maintenance/repair, aftermarket or spares as a segment. Spares appear only as an anecdotal 'end-of-life' use case.
Fictiv, the best-funded independent broker, ended up inside MISUMI, a catalog components distributor, at an undisclosed price.

Limitation: the shared web search budget was used up before this agent started. Findings come from direct SEC and company page fetches; Divergent details and the Hubs headline price are from memory and not verified.

stances.why: The marketplace financials say nothing about the stage structure of repair.

Fragmented, opaque sourcing was a real inefficiency that Xometry and Protolabs made money fixing. Once quoting know-how spread, though, it stopped earning rents: Protolabs' operating margin fell from 20% to 5%. That points to an information-friction problem more than a durable monopoly.

AI quoting works and scales (Xometry +41%). But closing the gap moves the margin to buyers. Certification, qualified capacity and liability stay scarce, and Xometry itself says AI could make it 'obsolete'.

Sourcing went from multi-week requests for quotes to instant quotes. But physical production and shipping costs have not fallen by an order of magnitude. Platform take is about 35% gross, with low single-digit EBITDA, and penetration is under 0.5% of the market after a decade.

Making a non-critical part on demand is now commodity capacity. No major platform reports a meaningful obsolete-spares business. For critical parts, the binding problems are the technical data or IP and qualification/certification, not fabrication.
Hadrian is automating inspection, Fictiv sells export-control compliance, and buyers concentrate spend on certified, accountable vendors. Assurance is where defensibility sits.

Job-shop fragmentation is real, but ten years of digital rebuild produced thin-margin brokers. The rebuild now attracting capital is owned, automated, certified factories (Hadrian, Divergent), not information layers.

research.q: YC and recent seed-stage companies in repair, maintenance, parts, inspection (2022-2026): list them with what they do and any traction.
research.headline: This scan covered only part of YC's portfolio, since the listing pages show about 50 companies per industry and no web searches were left in this run. In what it reached, YC's repair, maintenance and inspection bets from 2022 to 2026 cluster in four places: sensing and early detection (Gecko, Gridware, Talos), robots doing the repair work (Rodeo, RoboDock, Proprio, Aseon), automated inspection paperwork (GroundControl, KorrAI, F4) and full-stack outsourced uptime (Mantle). The companies with real traction own a data-capture or compliance workflow, not a standalone knowledge layer. Nearly all S26/F26 entrants are pre-traction, and no aviation MRO company showed up in the slice seen.
research.bottleneck: Data plus labour, not knowledge. The winners own proprietary condition data gathered by robots and sensors in places humans cannot cheaply reach, or a compliance workflow with signed liability. The new wave is betting on technician labour scarcity. Trust and certification shape the pace of automation, for example staged autonomy and deterministic inspection tools.
research.money_time: The companies' own framing points to two costly stages: noticing and diagnosing through data capture, which is why Gecko, Gridware and Tractian exist, and the physical labour of repair, given technician shortages (400,000 unstaffed DC tech roles; ~$600B US vehicle maintenance). Inspection paperwork and sign-off is a third time sink, where GroundControl turns days into minutes and KorrAI replaces consultant hours. Parts sourcing and delivery get little attention from YC companies. The one parts-adjacent company, Mecho, moved into wholesale parts distribution, suggesting margin sits in supply.
shapes: Full-stack uptime operator (Mantle model): own the outcome (uptime SLA) for OEMs of new machines (robots, chargers, energy equipment) instead of selling software. This captures the field-service margin the OEM cannot staff.
Data-capture plus AI inspection (Gecko model): robots or sensors that create condition data humans could not collect cheaply, sold to defense and energy buyers with large contracts.
Compliance-document automation (GroundControl and KorrAI model): AI that drafts what a licensed human signs, funded from consulting budgets. Fast traction with few staff.
Staged-autonomy diagnosis agent (Dawn model): vendor-neutral fault diagnosis that earns unattended authority one fault class at a time.
Whitespace: aviation MRO, aftermarket parts and certified obsolete replacement parts. No YC company was visible here, possibly because certification (Part 145, PMA) and OEM data rights are the moat.
surprises: No aviation MRO company appeared in the visible YC aviation listing, despite this being the founder's flagship example.
KorrAI's revenue comes entirely from consulting budgets, not software budgets. AI here displaces consultants, not software.
F4 Industries markets its inspection analysis as 'without AI' to aerospace buyers.
A burst of robotic-technician startups in S26 and F26 (Rodeo, RoboDock, Proprio, Aseon) shows YC sees labour, not knowledge, as the gap.
Gecko's growth is driven by US Navy and energy contracts ($71M, then a $300M IDIQ), so defense is the beachhead customer for repair and inspection.

stances.why: The companies sort cleanly onto stages of the chain: sensing (notice), Dawn and Talos (diagnose), KorrAI (understand), Mecho (parts), Rodeo and Proprio (repair), GroundControl and F4 (inspection), Mantle (the whole loop). The chain is a useful map, though companies tend to win by owning one stage plus its data.

KorrAI earns from consulting budgets by compressing expert knowledge work, which partly supports C2. But the traction leaders (Gecko, Gridware, Tractian) win on data capture and access, and the robotics cohort targets labour shortage (400,000 unstaffed DC tech roles), not missing knowledge.

No company here treats knowledge as solved. Dawn earns trust fault class by fault class, F4 markets 'without AI' determinism, and KorrAI keeps engineers signing. YC's RFS says the data needed for AI does not yet exist ('sparse data from sensors designed for humans').

Self-reported claims of large gains in narrow steps: Dawn says 30 min to under 2, GroundControl says days to minutes. But none shows an order-of-magnitude drop in total cost across the four steps, and parts delivery and labour remain physical.
The AI-native factory entrants (twentyfour26, Sinter, Applied Kinetics) are all pre-traction, and none tackles certified obsolete replacement parts. It is an early bet, not a solved problem.
Inspection is a well-funded, revenue-producing category (Gecko, GroundControl, KorrAI, Hundred, F4), and human or deterministic sign-off is kept on purpose.

YC's RFS agrees that physical-world software is 20 years stale, and Mantle's 'own uptime' model implies OEM service is broken. But the successful companies plug into existing structures (Navy contracts, utility programs, AS9102 compliance) rather than rebuilding the industry.

research.q: Asurion and device protection plans: how a repair/insurance business became a ~$10B+ revenue company; margin and moat sources; analog for machines.
research.headline: Asurion and its public comp Assurant reached ~$10B in revenue by capturing distribution: exclusive carrier, retailer and OEM point-of-sale contracts, plus actuarial pricing of low-frequency failures, a roll-up of warranty administrators, and owned repair, replacement and refurbishment logistics to control claims cost. Repair knowledge was not the moat. Margins are thin (Assurant Global Lifestyle ~8% EBITDA on ~$9.6B revenue), and the machine analog is an uptime risk-transfer and fulfilment network attached to a channel chokepoint, with AI lowering claims cost rather than removing the intermediary. (WebSearch budget was exhausted, so evidence comes from direct fetches of primary pages; some background items are flagged unverified in the notes.)
research.bottleneck: Control of the channel and the contract. Exclusive placement at the point of sale or in the monthly bill (carriers, OEMs, retailers) decides who captures the economics. It is backed by actuarial failure data, insurance licensing and balance sheet, and by an owned fulfilment and parts or replacement logistics network with OEM authorization. Knowledge is not the scarce layer; distribution, risk capital and logistics are.
research.money_time: In the protection-plan model the money goes, first, to distribution (carrier, retailer and OEM commissions and profit share at point of sale) and, second, to fulfilment: replacement devices, parts and labour, logistics and refurbishment. Diagnosis and 'understanding' are a small share. Assurant turns ~$9.6B of segment revenue into ~$0.8B of EBITDA, and OEM in-warranty repair costs only ~1.3% of sales. The cost growth now is in parts, labour and tariffs, not knowledge.
shapes: Uptime or protection-plan underwriter-administrator for distributed machines (home batteries, heat pumps, EV chargers, solar inverters, small robots). Embed at the point of sale with an OEM, installer or financier, price failures with field data, and use AI triage to cut claims cost. This copies the Asurion/D&G playbook for energy hardware, which is moving onto Asurion's turf.

Claims-cost-reduction engine sold to incumbents (Asurion, Assurant, AHS, D&G, OEM warranty departments): AI remote diagnosis, repair-or-replace decisions, fraud detection and technician routing. This targets their ~8% margin and fits the evidence that the incumbents own the channel.

Robotics or industrial 'power-by-the-hour' service network: own swap-unit inventory, refurbishment and field techs for a class of machines, tied to a lessor or OEM contract, since logistics and refurbishment are the proven moat.
Reverse logistics and refurbishment for machine components (motors, battery packs, drives), the counterpart of Assurant's ~20M devices a year, which recovers salvage value.
surprises: Asurion completed its acquisition of Domestic & General (22M appliances, 2.6M repairs a year) in Oct 2026, so the protection-plan giant is already moving into home machines and appliances, which is directly adjacent to a machines or energy startup.
Assurant's ~$9.6B lifestyle segment earns only ~8% adjusted EBITDA: the business is thin-margin and channel-dependent, not a fat knowledge rent.
Asurion's CEO changed: Guru Gowrappan (from Oct 2025) replaced founder Kevin Taweel and positions AI as 'the foundation', so the incumbents are adopting AI rather than being displaced by it.
Manufacturer warranty claims cost only ~1.3% of sales on average, yet reserves jumped 17% in 2025 and cost growth is driven by parts, labour and tariffs.
The WebSearch budget was exhausted, so revenue, valuation and debt-rating figures for Asurion (~$10B+ revenue; ~$12-16B debt) are flagged unverified in the notes.

stances.why: Claims flow through notice, triage, repair or replace, ship and refurbish, but the dominant fulfilment is often whole-unit replacement plus refurbishment rather than repair. The economics are set before any failure, by premium and distribution.

The FTC documents OEM restrictions on parts, tools and information. But the asymmetry that earns money in protection plans is seller-buyer opacity about contract value and eligibility (warranties at 20-30% of price, 75% of buyers not comparing, the SquareTrade suit), not repair know-how.
Asurion and Assurant are adopting AI, yet their moats are carrier and OEM contracts, insurance licences, actuarial data, logistics and leverage, none of which are knowledge gaps that AI erases.

AI can cut triage and diagnosis cost in claims, but in this model the large costs are the replacement device or parts and labour (both rising), plus channel commissions. Assurant earns only ~8% EBITDA, so there is no 10x pool sitting in diagnosis.
Device and appliance protection handles a missing part by swapping or refurbishing the unit; the evidence says nothing on bespoke fabrication.
OEM authorization and certification (uBreakiFix for Samsung and Google) gates parts and warranty access and is valuable, but there is no evidence of it evolving for AI.

The structure rewards channel capture and behavioural pricing over efficiency, but the fulfilment layer is highly optimized (same-day service in 85% of the US, 20M devices a year refurbished, ~1,150 repair locations) and margins are thin, not a rent-heavy slop.

research.q: Failed or struggling repair-tech companies (Uptake, Predix, Sight Machine, home-repair startups like HomeAdvisor-era, Puls, Enjoy, Shyp) — post-mortems on why.
research.headline: Repair-tech failures fall into two groups. The industrial AI and diagnostics platforms (GE Predix, Uptake, Sight Machine) spent billions on the "knowledge" layer but stalled on access to OEM and customer data, integration work and pilot purgatory. The consumer and home repair platforms (HomeAdvisor, Homejoy, Handy, Enjoy, Puls, Shyp) died or shrank on labor cost, scarce technicians, worker-classification law, customers bypassing the platform, and truck-roll economics, not for lack of knowledge. Caveat: the shared search budget ran out before this agent started, so the evidence is thin: a few Wikipedia pages fetched directly, plus facts recalled from memory (marked [RECALL]) that need checking.
research.bottleneck: Two scarce layers. (1) Access to proprietary asset data and the service contract, controlled by OEMs and asset owners. (2) Dense, trusted, skilled field labor and the logistics to use it efficiently. Neither is a knowledge problem that AI removes.
research.money_time: Industrial: integration, data access and pilots dominated time and money. The diagnosis algorithm itself was cheap compared with getting the data, contextualizing it and changing how customers work, and value was captured by whoever owned the service or uptime contract (the OEM). Consumer and home: the in-person technician visit (labor, travel, utilization), customer acquisition for infrequent repairs, and compliance with worker-classification rules dominated, ahead of diagnosis or parts.
shapes: Vertical, single-asset-class service operator (for example one class of industrial equipment) that owns the uptime outcome and carries the risk, instead of a horizontal AI platform, because Predix and Uptake failed by being horizontal
Technician-augmentation tools that raise first-time fix rate and utilization for existing field-service organizations (selling to the labor bottleneck, not around it)
Businesses wrapped in warranty, insurance or service contracts (the Asurion pattern), where the payer is the financer rather than the low-frequency end customer
Avoid: lead-gen and on-demand consumer marketplaces (HomeAdvisor, Homejoy, Handy, Shyp) because of disintermediation, CAC and labor-law exposure
surprises: Predix may be the largest-ever bet on the diagnosis and knowledge layer of repair (more than $7B), and it was still retired, which is a direct counterexample to the idea that knowledge is the bottleneck
Thumbtack's supply of pros barely grew in 13 years (about 250k to 300k)
Enjoy went from a roughly $1.1B SPAC valuation to bankruptcy in under a year and sold for about $110M
Asurion, a warranty and insurance company, has ended up consolidating the device-repair failures

stances.why: Failures concentrate at different links of the chain depending on segment: data and diagnosis for industrial, labor dispatch and repair for home. The chain describes repair well, but it hides that the economics are completely different by segment.
OEM control of machine data did hurt Uptake and Predix, so a data monopoly is real. But the home-repair startups failed on labor, trust and acquisition cost, not knowledge.

Predix spent more than $7B on analytics and diagnosis and still failed to get adoption. Puls and Thumbtack added AI assistants without changing their economics. The gap that matters is data access and changing how customers operate.

In the failed companies the dominant costs were in-person labor visits, customer acquisition, integration and regulation, not the four middle steps. Shyp shows a convenience layer on top of incumbent delivery captured little value.
None of the cases studied covers bespoke parts manufacturing.
Indirect only: vetting and certifying workers were costs the platforms could not remove, but no case covers inspection directly.

HomeAdvisor's lead model was extractive (FTC action, ranking settlement), which supports a misaligned structure. But many venture-funded 'rebuilds' died, which suggests incumbent structures reflect real constraints: labor, liability, density, OEM ownership of service contracts.

research.q: Global maintenance, repair and overhaul (MRO) spend by sector (aviation, industrial, auto aftermarket, consumer, defence sustainment, energy): best available estimates with sources.
research.headline: Commercial aviation MRO is about $119B in 2025, heading to $156B by 2035. US defence aircraft O&S was about $54B in FY2020 for 49 fleets, with F-35 sustainment alone at $1.3-1.58T over its life. Auto aftermarket (~$0.8-1.2T global) and industrial MRO supplies (~$650-750B) are the largest pools, with energy and consumer repair far smaller. Search budget was exhausted before this agent ran, so only the aviation and defence figures were verified this session; the rest are unverified background anchors.
research.bottleneck: Parts and repair capacity in certified facilities, plus contractual and IP control of technical data and approved repair designs (OEM and prime contractor lock-in), sitting inside certification regimes. It is less about generic knowledge and more about legally usable data rights, qualified parts supply, and certified labour and depot throughput.
research.money_time: In aviation and defence, money and time concentrate in physical overhaul of engines and components, OEM-controlled parts, scarce depot and shop capacity, and the downtime that results. Examples: more than 10,000 F-35 components awaiting repair, a roughly 55% mission-capable rate, and GTF/LEAP groundings into 2027. Engines are about 40-45% of commercial MRO (unverified). In heavy industry, unplanned downtime (~$1.4T/yr for Fortune Global 500, unverified) likely exceeds direct repair spend. Diagnosis and information are a small slice of spend, though they can drive time-to-repair.
shapes: Defence sustainment: technical-data reconstruction and reverse engineering plus qualified alternate-source parts for aging fleets. GAO shows DOD lacks the data and suffers parts and supply shortfalls, and money is flowing (~$90B/yr depot).

Engine and component MRO capacity and throughput tooling, e.g. AI-assisted inspection and repair-scheme engineering for engine shops. Engines are the largest and fastest-growing slice of a $119-156B market, and capacity-constrained.
Certification-ready (PMA/DER-style) replacement parts manufacturing for regulated sectors, where the qualification package, not the part, is the product.
Industrial and energy downtime reduction (predictive maintenance plus rapid parts) aimed at downtime cost (~$1.4T) rather than the smaller diagnostic spend.
Independent service providers for aging wind fleets, as OEM service agreements expire.
surprises: The shared WebSearch budget ran out before this agent's first search, so only the aviation and defence figures were verified.
Commercial aviation MRO (~$119B) is small next to the auto aftermarket (~$1T) and industrial MRO supplies (~$700B), but has the most concentrated OEM control.
F-35 sustainment ($1.3-1.58T) is a single program as large as the entire annual global auto aftermarket.
Defence O&S fell while maintenance cost rose and readiness still fell, so more money did not buy availability.
Consumer appliance and electronics repair, the founder's washing-machine example, is the smallest dollar pool.

stances.why: Market data are organised by asset class and MRO category (line, base, engine, component), not by a process chain. Nothing confirms or refutes it.

GAO finds DOD dependent on the F-35 contractor and lacking the technical data it needs, and OEM service agreements dominate engine and wind O&M. But the lock-in is contractual and IP-based, not just missing know-how.
The binding gaps in the verified evidence are data rights, IP, certification, parts and depot capacity. AI does not dissolve any of these.

The big costs are parts (often OEM-controlled), engine and component overhaul labour, depot capacity, and downtime (10,000 F-35 components awaiting repair; GTF/LEAP groundings). Diagnosis and information are a minority of spend, so a 10x cut in them would not cut total repair cost 10x.
Parts scarcity is evident in aviation and defence, but nothing here addresses on-demand bespoke manufacturing. Qualification would constrain it in regulated sectors.
The largest-dollar pools (aviation, defence) sit inside airworthiness certification regimes that gate every repair.

Spend keeps rising while readiness falls (supports). But the inefficiency comes from rational incumbent incentives such as power-by-the-hour, OEM aftermarket margins and data-rights contracts, plus regulation. That makes it incentive-built, not unintelligent.

research.q: Cost of unplanned downtime by industry (Siemens True Cost of Downtime 2022/2024, Aberdeen, ISA): numbers per hour and per year.
research.headline: Vendor surveys put unplanned downtime at $36k/hour (FMCG) to $2.3M/hour (Automotive) and about $1.4tn/year (11% of revenue) for the Fortune Global 500 (Siemens 2024). The independent NIST study is far smaller: $119B/year of losses in US discrete manufacturing, about $100B of it lost sales. Either way, the money is lost while the line waits to be restored, not in repair inputs. That makes time-to-restore the lever, more than the cost of diagnosing or sourcing.
research.bottleneck: Time-to-restore on the hard tail of failures: diagnosing the rarer, harder faults (now that PdM removes the easy ones), getting skilled technicians on site, and obtaining emergency parts quickly. These are made worse by the loss of experienced maintenance staff. Credible independent measurement of downtime is also scarce: most headline numbers are vendor-generated and inconsistent.
research.money_time: Lost production, revenue and penalties during the outage dominate. NIST: $100.2B of the $119.1B in US maintenance-related losses is lost sales, vs $18.1B direct downtime and $57.3B in direct maintenance spend. Siemens: per-hour costs of up to $2.3M in Automotive dwarf the repair bill. Time to restore is rising (49 to 81 minutes), attributed to knowledge loss, slow emergency parts, and harder residual failures. The value is in avoiding failures and shortening time-to-restore, not in cheaper repair inputs.
shapes: Time-to-restore / expert copilot for high-cost-per-hour assets (automotive lines, oil and gas, power, heavy industry), where one saved hour is worth $100k-$2.3M; sell on minutes saved, not on cheaper diagnosis
Emergency-parts logistics and on-demand fabrication network for line-down events, since Siemens names slow emergency parts as a driver of longer restarts
Capturing knowledge from retiring technicians (tribal knowledge to AI), addressing the skills gap Siemens cites
Independent downtime measurement and benchmarking (a NIST-like data layer), because vendor numbers are unreliable and buyers lack ROI baselines
Avoid FMCG and low-cost-per-hour segments: Siemens shows weak PdM ROI there
surprises: Siemens's own 2022 and 2024 editions do not reconcile (incidents, per-plant losses, Heavy Industry figures). The $1.4tn headline is an extrapolation from about 181 interviews.
Downtime incidents and hours fell sharply from 2019 to 2023, yet time to restart rose 65% (49 to 81 minutes). Prediction removes easy failures and leaves harder ones.
NIST's independent scope-limited estimate ($119B in US losses) is an order of magnitude below the vendor global headlines, and lost sales, not repair cost, make up about 85% of it.
Per-hour costs swing with commodity prices (Oil & Gas about $650k in FY22 vs about $100k in FY23), so 'cost of downtime' is not a stable industry constant.
The WebSearch budget was exhausted, so the Aberdeen ($260k/hour) and ISA ($50B/year) figures could not be verified against primary sources.

stances.why: Downtime cost structures fit the chain (detection, then repair, then restart), but Splunk shows the 'notice' step itself often fails (customers detect 41% of outages). Economics differ about 60x by sector, so the same chain has very different bottlenecks at different scales.

Siemens cites a skills and knowledge gap from lost experienced technicians as one reason restart time rose from 49 to 81 minutes, but gives equal weight to parts sourcing and delivery delays and to harder residual failures. NIST ties losses to reactive maintenance practice, not to OEM knowledge monopolies.
No evidence on AI closing the knowledge gap. Vendor PdM claims (50% less downtime) are about prediction, not knowledge parity.

Downtime cost is dominated by lost production during the outage (NIST: $100B of $119B is lost sales), so a 10x cut in the cost of diagnosing and sourcing barely matters, while a 10x cut in their time matters a lot. The share of downtime spent waiting for diagnosis or parts is not quantified, and incumbent PdM already cut hours about 30%.
Emergency replacement parts appear as a cost component and as a cause of longer restarts, but there is no evidence on on-demand fabrication.
Only NIST's injury and death rates linked to maintenance issues touch on safety; nothing on inspection or certification.

Incremental adoption of IoT, condition monitoring and PdM within the existing industry cut incidents about 40% and downtime hours about 30% from 2019 to 2023. High-cost sectors (Automotive) invest aggressively in uptime, which suggests the incentives work where downtime is expensive. Inefficiency persists mainly where downtime is cheap (FMCG), which is rational rather than structural.

research.q: Defense sustainment costs: share of weapon system lifecycle cost spent on operations and support (~70%), F-35 sustainment, depot maintenance spend; GAO numbers.
research.headline: GAO data confirm that operations and support (O&S) is the dominant cost of a weapon system. DoD puts it at "at least 70%" of life-cycle cost, and on the F-35 it is about 78%: $1.58T of about $2T. But the delays come mostly from legally enforced data and IP lock-in, depot and shipyard capacity, workforce and the parts supply base, not from a cognitive knowledge gap that AI could close. AI can cut friction in diagnosing and finding information (60-day technical-data waits, part-number lookups, logistics-system workarounds), but the evidence does not support a 10x cut in total sustainment cost.
research.bottleneck: The real bottleneck is legally controlled technical data and IP, combined with physical repair capacity: depots, dry docks and skilled labour, plus the parts supply base. The knowledge exists but is owned and withheld under contract, and even with data, organic depots, qualified parts and certification take years and capital to stand up.
research.money_time: Most life-cycle money is O&S (at least 70%; about 78% on the F-35), but O&S includes personnel, fuel and training as well as maintenance. Within repair, the time goes to queueing for depot and shipyard capacity (15,000+ lost submarine days, 75% of shipyard maintenance periods late), unplanned work found once the ship or aircraft is opened up, workforce shortages, and slow OEM component repair loops (141 days, against 72 days at government depots). Parts that are unavailable or cannot be produced lead to cannibalisation and buying new parts instead of repairing old ones. Knowledge-access friction is real but secondary: 60-day technical-data waits and part numbers held by the contractor.
shapes: A tool that ingests and tracks government-owned technical data: it parses the large volume of contract data deliverables DoD already owns but cannot track or review (80% marking rejection, no enterprise view of data rights), so depots know what they can repair in-house.
Troubleshooting and parts-identification copilot for maintainers built on data the government owns. It targets the 60-day technical-data request loop and the part-number dependence on the contractor.

Reverse engineering plus qualified additive or advanced manufacturing for obsolete and low-criticality parts, where the moat is the qualification and technical-data-package pipeline, not printing. Evidence: 48 F-35 parts the supplier base cannot make in quantity, and cannibalisation trends.
Condition assessment before a ship or aircraft goes into maintenance, to shrink 'unplanned work', the largest single cause of shipyard delay (>4,100 days).
Depot and shipyard capacity planning and scheduling software, plus independent readiness-metric verification (a response to the F-35 FMC rates adjusted upward for incentive fees).
surprises: Government depots fix F-35 components about twice as fast as the OEM, yet 73% of components still go back to the OEM because the government lacks the technical data and the in-house depot capacity was never stood up.
Maintainers say they would not need contractors on the flight line if they simply had access to part numbers, so a database permission, not expertise, drives a daily contractor presence.
F-35 sustainment affordability was 'met' mainly by flying 21% fewer hours and raising the per-tail target from $4.1M to $6.8M.
Lockheed's incentive fees were paid on FMC rates adjusted upward in 19 of 39 periods; on raw rates it would have earned about half.
The bipartisan, White House-backed military right-to-repair provision was stripped in conference in December 2025 despite passing in both chambers' bills.
The Navy shipyard rebuild grew from $21B to more than $200B, which means physical capacity, not knowledge, is the multi-decade constraint.

Note: WebSearch budget was exhausted before this agent ran; findings come from directly fetched GAO pages and PDFs. The DoD-wide annual depot maintenance spend (commonly about $35-45B) could not be verified.

stances.why: Defense repair does pass through notice, diagnose, repair, inspect and return. But the dominant delays are queueing for depot and dry-dock slots, unplanned work found mid-repair, parts production and contracting, which the chain does not capture. O&S also includes personnel, fuel and training, not just repair.

Strong evidence of an OEM knowledge monopoly: 73% of F-35 components go back to the OEM, technical data and part numbers are held by the contractor, and half of 200+ programs report data-rights deficiencies. But the monopoly is legal and contractual (IP, data access), not a lack of cognitive know-how.

The gap is enforced by contract and statute. AI cannot use proprietary data it has no right to access. DoD officials say reverse engineering and additive manufacturing are 'generally less effective and efficient' than buying rights. AI could help parse the data DoD already owns and with troubleshooting.

There is real friction in diagnosing and finding information: 60-day technical-data waits, part-number lookups, 45,000 hours a year of logistics-system workarounds. But the big costs and delays are depot and shipyard capacity, workforce, a supply base unable to make 48 F-35 parts, and infrastructure ($200B+ for the shipyard rebuild). Changing who repairs gives about 2x (72 vs 141 days), not 10x.

Qualifying flight-critical 3D-printed parts is still in progress 10 years after the V-22 demonstration. Detailed manufacturing data is legally excluded from DoD's rights, and the supplier base cannot produce critical parts in quantity. There is an opening only for low-criticality and obsolete parts.

Certification gates any new part source, and unplanned work found during inspection is the largest single cause of shipyard delays. Readiness metrics were adjusted upward to pay incentive fees, which shows independent measurement and verification matter.

The incentives are structural: fees paid on adjusted metrics, annual contracts, withheld IP, lobbying that killed the repair provision, 70% of GAO recommendations unimplemented, and a 1993 data manual. But this is deliberate rent design and political economy, not a lack of 'smart'. A rebuild needs statute, contracts and capital, not just software.

research.q: Repair vs replace and product lifetime trends: evidence that products are repaired less (appliance lifetime studies, e-waste volumes, Öko-Institut obsolescence study); cost to economy.
research.headline: Durable goods are kept for shorter periods, but only moderately for workhorse appliances: German first use fell from 14.1 to 13.0 years and early-defect replacements rose from 3.5% to 8.3%. Phones and TVs show large gaps, used 1.7 of 7 designed years and 7 of 22, driven mostly by wanting something new, while e-waste hit 62 Mt with 22% recycled and the EU puts consumer losses from not repairing at about EUR 12bn a year. Information gaps, including a paid diagnosis needed just to get a quote, are a real barrier. But repair price relative to new (consumers accept only ~20%), wanting a newer model, hassle, and parts/design locks dominate, so knowledge is one barrier among five, not the main one.
research.bottleneck: In consumer goods, the real bottleneck is the economics of the repair-or-replace decision. Local skilled labour plus diagnosis costs more than about 20% of an ever-cheaper new product. That combines with consumer preference for new goods (about 40% 'enthusiastic replacers'), and with design and parts lock-in (no parts, glued or serialised components). Knowledge and information gaps matter mainly as quote uncertainty at the diagnosis step.
research.money_time: For consumer durables, the binding cost is hands-on labour plus the paid diagnosis, measured against a falling new-goods price (TV CPI down 81% from 2006 to 2014). Consumers abandon repair above about 20% of the purchase price. Diagnosis alone is 7-22% of a typical repair and often has to be paid before a quote. Time and hassle (downtime, transporting large items, waiting for parts) are separate deterrents for about 10-14% of non-repairers. Parts availability and designs that cannot be opened are the top practical blockers in repair-café data. Total EU consumer detriment is about EUR 12bn a year, against EUR 792bn a year of repairable durables.
shapes: Near-zero-cost remote or AI triage plus a binding price quote before anyone travels. This attacks the evidence that consumers abandon repair because of paid diagnosis and quote uncertainty.
Repair-or-replace decision engines for warrantors, insurers and retailers. EU law now prioritises repair whenever it is cheaper, so they need cheap, accurate cost-to-repair estimates per defect.

Parts liquidity and interchange: finding or cross-referencing compatible spare parts for orphaned models. 'No spare parts available' is the top repair-café barrier, and EU ecodesign mandates 7-10 year parts availability.

Focus on high-value workhorse assets (appliances, HVAC, machines), where 64-75% of replacements are reliability-driven, rather than phones and TVs, where replacement is mostly driven by wanting a newer model.
surprises: Notebooks did not get less reliable from 2004 to 2012. The age at defect-driven replacement rose from 4.8 to 6.2 years, which undercuts the 'everything breaks sooner' narrative.
About 60% of working flat-screen TVs and phones are replaced by choice, so the gap between designed and used lifetime is mostly about demand, not repair friction.
Even for cars, with open information and a 70-75% independent-shop market, only 52% of consumers repair rather than replace.
Apple expected 1-2M discounted battery replacements and did over 11M. Lowering the price and friction of repair unlocked about 5-10x latent demand.

WebSearch budget was exhausted for this run, so findings rely on directly fetched primary documents. A few historical items (Bakker 2014 Dutch lifetimes, BLS repairer outlook) are flagged unverified in /home/user/nuketime/research/repair/raw/q04.md.

stances.why: The EC describes a chain of finding a repairer, transporting the item, diagnosing and quoting, waiting for parts, then repairing, which matches C1.
