It also shows a decisive repair-or-replace-or-abandon gate (price vs ~20% of new, preference for new) that C1 leaves out. Many failures never enter the chain.

The FTC finds scant justification for OEMs restricting manuals, diagnostics and parts, which supports the access-monopoly form. EU surveys rank information as one barrier among several, behind price, preference for new and hassle. Cars, where information is open (70-75% use independents), still see only 52% repair.
Most consumer replacement, about 60% of phones and TVs, happens while the device still works, or is economic (labour vs cheap new goods). Closing the knowledge gap leaves these drivers untouched.

Paid diagnosis (7-22% of repair cost) and quote uncertainty make consumers abandon repair, so cheap AI diagnosis and quoting matters. But labour, downtime and parts availability set the ~20% price threshold, and those sit outside the four steps.
There is strong evidence of demand ('no spare parts available' is a top barrier) but no evidence that bespoke or on-demand fabrication solves it at consumer price points.
Trust in repair quality scores 8.2/10 as a decision factor, but the consumer-goods evidence says little about formal inspection.

There are structural anti-repair incentives: universal EULA restrictions, turnover-driven business models, advertising linked to fewer TV technicians. But much of the decline is rational Baumol economics plus consumer preference, not just how the industry is built.

research.q: Steelman: arguments that OEM control of repair is efficient (safety, liability, quality, warranty, security, investment recovery); find the best academic and industry evidence.
research.headline: The strongest case for OEM-controlled repair is not that independent repair is unsafe. When the FTC (2021) and FDA (2018) asked manufacturers for data, they found 'scant evidence' and could tie only 3 of 4,301 device adverse-event reports to servicing. Instead, the case rests on incentive alignment (outcome contracts like power-by-the-hour raise reliability), recovering investment through lifecycle pricing (opening repair can lead OEMs to raise prices or cut durability), parts provenance in safety-critical domains, and security of remote command access. Those are levers made of locks, certification and pricing, not knowledge, so they survive even if AI closes the knowledge gap. (Method caveat: the shared web-search budget was already used up when this agent ran, so findings come from directly fetched primary documents plus some flagged background literature not re-verified this session.)
research.bottleneck: Trust and accountability infrastructure: certified parts provenance, authentication and parts pairing, and assigning legal liability (emissions, airworthiness, vehicle safety), plus who bears outcome risk. These are what OEMs actually defend once the knowledge argument collapses under scrutiny, and they don't go away when information becomes free.
research.money_time: The steelman evidence says little directly about which stage costs most. It suggests that in high-value assets (aero engines) cost is driven by unplanned downtime and reliability, which OEM outcome contracts attack through design feedback and fleet data, more than by diagnosis labour. In consumer and appliance repair, the contested costs are access to parts, diagnostics and authentication. OEMs couldn't show that these restrictions bought any safety benefit.
shapes: Parts provenance and certification layer (digital chain of custody and authenticity verification for parts, AI-assisted documentation checks), because counterfeit parts are the best-evidenced safety risk and the AOG Technics fraud got past paper certificates

Independent outcome-based maintenance provider that offers power-by-the-hour uptime contracts across brands, because performance-based contracting is the one efficiency gain from OEM control that has empirical support (Guajardo et al. 2012)
Secure scoped-access broker for diagnostics and telematics (short-range, credentialed, audited sessions) that meets NHTSA-style security concerns while giving independents data parity

Liability and insurance-backed certification network for independent repairers (warranty-grade traceability, repair records) that answers the OEM reputation and liability objection with data the OEMs never supplied
surprises: Even in medical devices, the FDA could link only 3 of 4,301 adverse-event reports to servicing, and manufacturers gave the FTC essentially one anecdote despite a formal call for data.
The most rigorous pro-OEM academic results are about incentives and pricing (outcome contracts; strategic re-pricing under right-to-repair laws), not about safety or knowledge.
Aviation, the most safety-critical domain, already allows non-OEM repair stations and parts under certification. The safety function is separable from OEM ownership.
AHAM says over 87% of its 20,000 authorised appliance servicers are local independents, recasting the 'monopoly' as a certification gate.

stances.why: The steelman literature doesn't test the stage chain. It implicitly adds stages the chain omits: authentication/pairing (software locks), certification of parts provenance, and accountability for liability.

The FTC found the knowledge gap is largely manufactured (manuals, diagnostics and parts withheld) and that OEM justifications lack evidence, which supports C2. But the strongest OEM levers are not knowledge: emissions and airworthiness liability, remote-access security, parts provenance, and lifecycle pricing.

AI can spread repair information, but the OEM's remaining levers are cryptographic parts pairing, regulatory certification, legal liability and strategic re-pricing (Jin et al. 2023). Knowledge diffusion doesn't remove these.

Diagnosis and information costs could fall, but the Jin/Yang/Zhu model shows OEMs re-price or redesign in response, so savings can be captured or offset upstream. For airliners, outcome contracts already internalise much of the diagnosis cost.

Counterfeit and unapproved parts are the best-evidenced catastrophic risk (Partnair 394, AOG Technics). In safety-critical domains a part is worthless without certified pedigree, so making it is not the bottleneck. Certifying it is.

Aviation shows safety can come from regulator certification (Part 145 repair stations, PMA parts, release certificates) rather than OEM exclusivity. Provenance and inspection are the defensible core, and the parts-fraud cases show that layer needs to improve.

Performance-based contracting evidence shows time-and-materials repair gives perverse incentives, which supports the 'not built for smart' diagnosis. But the evidence-backed fix is often OEM-led outcome contracts (power-by-the-hour), not dismantling OEM roles. In a few domains (aviation, autos) the system already has working independent channels.

research.q: Steelman: why AI will NOT close the repair knowledge gap: tacit/embodied skills, liability, verification, data access, the "last mile" of physical work (Moravec), evidence of AI limits in physical domains.
research.headline: The strongest case against C3: AI mostly closes the codified, text-based part of the repair gap (it lifts novices about 34% in a text domain), while the binding gates are physical, legal and liability-based. Those gates are tacit and tactile skill (robot dexterity is 10+ years from field-grade reliability), software and permission locks (Deere Service ADVISOR, parts pairing), licensed human signoff that requires 18 to 30 months of hands-on work, and verification of fluent but wrong output. Note: the shared WebSearch budget was already used up, so all findings come from directly fetched primary URLs, plus a few flagged background items that were not re-fetched.
research.bottleneck: Permission and embodied execution, not information. The scarce layers are: (1) the legal right to act, meaning licensed signoff, OEM software unlocks and approved design data; (2) skilled hands with tacit, tactile skill, which is short by hundreds of thousands of technicians and which robots cannot replace before about 2030-2040; (3) trusted verification that someone will bear liability for; (4) proprietary service data that AI cannot access.
research.money_time: The evidence points to physical labor and execution plus parts supply as the dominant costs, not diagnosis. Aviation needs 728k new technicians over 20 years, and the $104B MRO market is constrained by labor and raw-material shortages and OEMs at capacity. Software and permission-gated steps (dealer-only tools, parts pairing) add delay and price markup. Certification and qualification add long fixed lead times for new parts. Diagnosis and understanding are the steps where AI demonstrably helps, mainly by speeding up novices, but they are a minority of end-to-end time on complex assets.
shapes: AI copilot for licensed technicians, not owners: compress novice-to-competent time (the 34% novice effect) amid the 728k technician shortage, sold to MROs and dealers who already hold data access and signoff rights

Verification and inspection tooling: sensor- and vision-based proof-of-work and digital signoff records (lessons from the Alaska 1282 parts-removal failure) that lets regulators and insurers trust AI-assisted repairs

Data-access play riding right-to-repair rulings (FTC v. Deere, state laws): aggregate the newly mandated manuals and diagnostic software into a machine-readable repair corpus, which is the gate AI actually needs opened
Qualified bespoke-part service for obsolete parts that bundles the certification dossier (PMA, material and process qualification), since paperwork rather than printing is the moat
Tactile and force data infrastructure for repair robotics: collect force and touch demonstrations of repair tasks, the missing modality Brooks identifies
surprises: The FTC found scant evidence for OEM safety and liability justifications, so the liability leg of the steelman is weaker than expected: much of the gap is a manufactured permission monopoly rather than a real knowledge gap.
Real AI usage data shows repair is the least-used skill category of all, even though the knowledge is supposedly freely available.
Alaska 1282: the OEM with complete knowledge still failed at the reinstall-and-verify step, which suggests knowledge is not the main failure mode.
Brooks: deployed robot hands have shown essentially no improvement in 40 years despite the lab demos.
Tool limitation: the shared web-search budget was used up before this agent started, so findings rely on directly fetched known URLs, and a few items are flagged as unverified background.

stances.why: The chain is a reasonable taxonomy, but the evidence shows permission and authorization steps (software unlock, licensed signoff, approved design data) that sit outside it and often gate the repair. Alaska 1282 also shows reassembly verification as a distinct failure point.

The FTC and Deere evidence supports OEM capture, but what is withheld is mostly access (software tools, pairing, data, signoff rights) rather than knowledge as such. Tacit skill shortage (728k technicians) is a separate gap from information asymmetry.

AI lifts novices 34% in text tasks but barely moves experts. Repair is the least-used skill domain in real AI usage. Manual work is rated unexposed. Tactile and dexterous skill is 10+ years from robotic reliability. Proprietary manuals and telemetry are not in training data. Certification requires human hours.

Diagnosis and understanding of codified faults could fall sharply. Sourcing and delivery are bound by OEM capacity and raw-material shortages. Labor, execution and certification lie outside the four steps, so even a 10x cut there gives far less than 10x end to end.

Fabrication is not the bottleneck for regulated assets. Approved design data, material and process qualification, and part-level test and inspection (PMA, NASA-STD-6030) take years and cannot be skipped by AI design. Background evidence only; not re-fetched.

Licensed signoff is legally required (14 CFR 65.77). Alaska 1282 shows verification failing even with full OEM knowledge. AI output is fluent and sometimes wrong outside its frontier, which raises the value of independent verification. EASA guidance covers only Level 1-2 AI.

The FTC finds repair restrictions mostly unjustified, which supports an inefficiency built by design. But much friction (certification, experience requirements, qualification) is deliberate safety design, not slop.

research.q: Is the bottleneck actually capital, inventory and logistics rather than knowledge? Find evidence where knowledge is free but repair is still slow (e.g., open designs, military with full data rights).
research.headline: Mostly yes. Where the repairer already holds full knowledge (P&W on its own GTF engines, Navy public shipyards on Navy-owned submarine designs, utilities replacing transformers, legacy military fleets, cars after data-access deals), repair is still slow, often by months to years. The elapsed time goes into shop and dock capacity, long-lead certified parts and materials, skilled labour and funding approval, not diagnosis. Knowledge is still a real constraint in some places: contractor-held technical data (F-35), front-line skills (Navy sailors), and owners not analysing data they already have.
research.bottleneck: Physical throughput capacity plus certified long-lead parts inventory: dry docks, engine shop slots, transformer factories, circuit-card and forging supply, and the skilled technicians to use them. The gating mechanism is the qualification and certification needed to add any of these. Knowledge is a secondary bottleneck: legal data rights on new platforms, front-line skill transfer, and owners failing to use their own maintenance data.
research.money_time: In heavy assets (aircraft engines, submarines, grid transformers, military aircraft), elapsed time is dominated by waiting for capacity (dock or shop slots, test cells), long-lead certified parts and materials (turbine disks, circuit cards, GOES steel), skilled labour, and funding or contract approval. Diagnosis takes hours to days against months to years for the rest. In cars, where repair information is largely open, cycle time is driven by parts count, ADAS calibration and technician labour. Money goes to sustainment overall (F-35: $1.3tn of $1.7tn life-cycle cost), customer compensation for groundings (GTF: ~80% of $6-7bn) and capital overruns (dry docks).
shapes: Pooled rotables and spares exchange or inventory-as-a-service for long-lead critical parts (engines, large transformers, CCAs): converts multi-year lead times into days for members; evidence shows inventory, not knowledge, sets repair time.

AI capacity and throughput orchestration for scarce repair assets (docks, shop slots, technicians), with growth-work prediction so parts are pre-staged before a unit is opened. This targets the queue and late discovered work that GAO identifies as the main delay drivers.

Qualification-first replacement parts: reverse engineering plus additive or CNC sold with a certification evidence package for obsolete or out-of-business-supplier parts in defence and energy. The moat is test and qualification data, not fabrication (A-10 lesson).

Distributed or modular repair capacity (mobile test cells, modular transformer repair or refurbishment, regional engine module shops) to add physical capacity faster than greenfield yards or factories.

AI job aids and maintenance-data analytics for organisations that already own their data but lack skilled hands or analysis (Navy sailor-led maintenance, intermediate maintenance periods). This is the one place the knowledge-gap thesis holds up well.
surprises: The shared web-search budget was exhausted before this agent started, so findings come only from direct fetches of known primary URLs. Wind, rail, appliance and Russia-sanctions analogs are missing and need a follow-up run.
The biggest single surface-ship repair delay driver GAO found was funding approval (26-189 days), not parts or knowledge.

Knowledge decay inside the data owner (A-10: 80% of the workforce cut, data 'could no longer be trusted'; Navy not analysing its own maintenance data) is a different problem from an OEM monopoly and arguably more AI-addressable.
The FTC treats parts gatekeeping as part of the same restriction bundle as manuals and diagnostics. In consumer goods, cheap diagnosis is useless if the part is withheld or serialised.
GTF compensation (~80% of $6-7bn) shows that downtime, not repair labour, is where the money goes in aviation.

stances.why: The chain is a usable skeleton, but GAO evidence adds steps it leaves out that often dominate elapsed time: funding and contract approval (26-189 days), queueing for scarce slots (Boise idle >2 years) and growth work discovered mid-repair. Repair is iterative, not linear.

Real for F-35 contractor-held technical data and for front-line skills (75% of Navy XOs say sailors struggle to complete repairs). Weak where the knowledge holder is the repairer and repair is still slow: GTF engines, public-yard submarines, transformers, cars.

Remaining knowledge gaps are legal (data rights AI cannot read), tacit and hands-on, or caused by data that is missing or untrusted (A-10). In none of the cases studied would knowledge alone have cleared the delay.

Sourcing and delivery in heavy assets are bound by factories and certification: 19-34 month CCAs, 80-210 week transformers, 250-300 day engine shop visits. Diagnosis is a small share of time and cost, so a 10x combined drop is implausible there.

The A-10 rewing (supplier gone) took a prime contractor, ~5 years and $1.72bn because of fatigue testing and qualification. CCAs, castings and electrical steel depend on fabs and material supply, not design knowledge.
Qualification and testing gate replacement parts (A-10 test wing failure). Regulator-mandated inspections drive GTF/LEAP groundings. Certification evidence is the moat for any bespoke-parts play.

Real structural inefficiency exists: funding rules, fragmented lessons learned, the Navy not analysing its own data, and the FTC's 'scant evidence' for restrictions. But much of the delay is underinvestment in capacity and spares (dry docks, transformer factories), not an industry designed to fail.

research.q: Cases where full technical data rights or open designs existed (e.g., government-owned designs, open-source hardware, older aircraft with public manuals) — did repair become cheap? What remained expensive?
research.headline: Where repair knowledge was fully available (government-held data on Navy ships and the KC-135, the 2012-2014 auto right-to-repair rules, the DC-3's public manuals, open-source hardware), repair did not get cheap, apart from low-stakes, commodity-part, uncertified products like RepRap printers, Framework laptops and Fairphones. What stayed expensive: shipyard, depot and labour capacity; certification and an accountable design authority; low-volume physical parts lost to obsolescence; diagnosis and calibration that need special equipment; and funding and contracting processes. Missing data (F-35) really does cripple repair, so knowledge is necessary but nowhere near sufficient.
research.bottleneck: Accountable engineering authority plus physical capacity. Someone legally responsible must approve the repair or part (TC, STC, PMA holder, depot engineering). There must be the dock, depot or skilled hands to do the work. And low-volume certified parts must exist. Knowledge is a gating input only when it is withheld. Once available, the bottleneck shifts to certification, capacity and parts.
research.money_time: Once the data is in hand, the cost and time go to physical work and authority. In order: (1) capacity and skilled labour hours, meaning dock and depot slots and teardown and rework (Navy $1.8B backlog, auto labour hours up from 23.0 to 27.3 per claim); (2) low-volume parts supply lost to obsolescence and vanished manufacturers (KC-135 $4.24B O&S, A-10 wings $1.72B, Iran, Cuba); (3) qualification and certification of any non-OEM part or repair (PMA, STC, TC); (4) scope discovered only after opening and equipment-based diagnosis and calibration (Navy unquantified work, 56% of ADAS calibrations found late on supplements); (5) funding and contracting process (26-189 days). Diagnosis and 'understanding' are a minority of cost in mature, data-rich fleets. They become dominant only where data is withheld (F-35).
shapes: Certified engineering-authority-as-a-service for orphaned or out-of-production equipment: become the TC, STC or PMA holder or a DER-style repair approver, using AI to speed up the substantiation package (stress, materials, test plans). This attacks the actual scarce layer that the Concorde, A-10 and PMA cases show.

Qualification-accelerated legacy part remanufacturing for defense and aviation, focused on high-impact non-flight-critical parts first (the Travis-type cases), with digital-thread and first-article inspection automation. The economics work where the AOG or downtime cost is high and the qualification burden is bounded.

Pre-teardown scoping and inspection tech (NDI, sensor fusion, AI damage assessment) to shrink 'unquantified work' and late supplements. Navy growth work and ADAS calibration supplements show that scope uncertainty drives schedule more than knowledge does.
Depot and shipyard throughput or capacity tools (scheduling, robotics for corrosion and coating removal) rather than knowledge tools, since capacity and labour hours dominate in data-rich fleets.
Avoid: a pure 'AI repair knowledge' layer for mature, data-available fleets. Auto right-to-repair shows information access alone did not lower costs.
surprises: Auto repair costs kept rising after independent shops won dealer-equivalent information access in 2014. The cost moved to labour hours and to equipment-based ADAS calibration.
The most expensive aircraft to sustain in the DoD sample (KC-135, about $4.24B a year) is one of the oldest and best understood.
Concorde was grounded not for lack of knowledge but because Airbus surrendered the type certificate. Authority is the monopoly.
Iran, a state with strong incentives and engineering capacity, could not reverse-engineer its way around sanctions at fleet scale.
Navy repair delays hinge partly on fiscal-year funding approval rules (26-189 days), a purely institutional bottleneck.
Fully repairable-by-design hardware (Fairphone) makes repair cheap for owners but leaves the maker thin-margin, because years of spare-parts inventory are expensive to hold.
Process limitation: the workflow's shared WebSearch budget ran out before this agent ran. Findings come from direct fetches, and items marked unverified need checking.

stances.why: The steps exist in every case, but the Navy evidence shows loops: scope is only found after teardown ('unquantified work'), and funding approval sits between steps for 26-189 days. Repair is iterative, not a linear chain.

The F-35 shows a missing data package really cripples sustainment. But wherever knowledge was fully available (Navy, KC-135, DC-3, auto after the 2014 MOU), most of the cost remained. Knowledge is necessary, not sufficient.

Even full human-readable knowledge (government data, public manuals, open CAD, mandated information access) did not close the gap. The binding constraints were capacity, certification authority, parts and equipment, none of which AI supplies.

Auto repair costs rose after information access (+$1,285 since 2020, more labour hours per claim). The best documented gains from breaking a parts or knowledge monopoly are about 30-40% (PMA, unverified), not 10x. Calibration and diagnosis now depend on equipment.

Replacing a supplier that is gone took about $1.7B and roughly a decade for A-10 wings. Iran and Cuba show reverse engineering and improvisation without certification gives grounded fleets or low-utilisation survival. It is feasible only for non-critical parts.

When Airbus surrendered Concorde's type certificate, the fleet was grounded despite intact design knowledge. PMA and STC regimes and the A-10 data-trust problem show that accountable design authority and qualification are the scarce layer.

Institutional inefficiency is real (Navy fiscal-year funding approvals, F-35 contractor reliance, lessors refusing PMA parts). But much of the cost is physical: fatigue, corrosion, teardown hours, low-volume parts. That is not just bad design of the industry.

research.q: Where has repair already been made highly efficient (hyperscale data centres, Toyota TPM, Southwest/Ryanair maintenance, F1 pit crews, US Navy nuclear)? What were the enablers, and were they knowledge?
research.headline: Repair became highly efficient where the owner-operator controlled the design and ran a standardised fleet: hyperscalers, Southwest and Ryanair, Toyota, F1 and Naval Reactors. The main enablers were standardisation, design for service and modular swap units (LRUs), redundancy, spares placed in advance and drilled organisational discipline, with knowledge playing a real but secondary role. Knowledge mattered as data owned by the operator (Meta: only 3 of 419 interruptions needed manual intervention) and as tacit, certified human skill (Rickover, TPM). It did not mainly come from closing a gap in access to information.
research.bottleneck: Variety and fragmentation of the installed base, plus physical capacity. Efficient repair needs a standardised, instrumented, modular fleet under one owner who controls the design, data and spares. Most assets lack that, and AI on its own does not create standardisation, redundancy, spares placed in advance or certified skilled labour.
research.money_time: In the efficient regimes, the time left in the critical path is the physical swap: F1 tyres, GPU or drive swaps, line LRU changes. Diagnosis was automated or pre-empted, and parts were already in place. The money goes into designing for serviceability, redundancy, spares inventory, training and certification. Where efficiency breaks down (Navy shipyards, unverified here; Southwest 2022), the time is lost in capacity, scheduling and logistics, not in diagnosis or understanding.
shapes: A hyperscaler-style maintenance OS for fragmented fleets of standard energy and robotics assets (solar and wind, BESS, EV chargers, telecom sites, robot fleets): telemetry, automated fault isolation down to the swappable module, and spares positioned in advance. This copies Meta's automated diagnosis and the LRU model.
A cross-operator spares pool and positioning network for one asset type, giving small owners Southwest's single-type economics.
A design-for-service / LRU engineering platform sold to new hardware OEMs (robots, eVTOL, grid storage) as lower lifetime opex, the OCP and F1 single-wheel-nut lesson.
RCM/MSG-3-style inspection and certification programmes plus tooling for new asset classes (drones, eVTOL, humanoids, grid batteries), where C6 holds and regulators need structured evidence.
surprises: Meta handled 416 of 419 unexpected Llama 3 training interruptions with automation, but hardware still failed about every 3 hours. Efficiency came from tolerating failure, not from preventing it.
The most efficient 'repair' at hyperscale is often no repair at all: Natick's early failures were simply taken offline.
Even Ryanair, at its scale, needed a 2026 deal with CFM to bring engine maintenance in-house, so the OEM gate is real.
The airline industry's order-of-magnitude knowledge gain in maintenance (RCM/MSG) happened in 1978 and was then written into regulation.
Southwest's worst operational failure was crew-scheduling software, not maintenance.

Search budget note: the shared WebSearch quota was exhausted before this agent ran, so the findings rely on direct fetches of known pages. Some figures (Nowlan & Heap 89%, OCP technician ratios, GAO submarine backlog) are flagged as unverified.

stances.why: The most efficient regimes collapse or reorder the chain: F1 and MSG hard-time replace on schedule, Natick and hyperscalers fail in place without repairing, and LRU practice swaps first and diagnoses later at the depot. The gain comes from restructuring the chain, not from speeding up each step.

OEM control is real: Ryanair needed a CFM agreement, and hyperscalers built OCP to escape OEM lock-in. But efficient systems also concentrate deep knowledge on purpose (depots, Naval Reactors), and the big failures found (Southwest's scheduling meltdown) were not knowledge gaps.

The crucial knowledge in the Navy, TPM and F1 is tacit, rehearsed and certified. Google's SMART study shows that even fleet data predicts individual failures poorly. Meta's near-free diagnosis needed telemetry the owner built on a uniform fleet.

Order-of-magnitude gains exist (RCM labour-hours, Meta's 3 of 419 manual interventions, OCP technicians per server). But they came from design, standardisation and data within controlled uniform fleets, and parts delivery was solved by stocking spares in advance, not by AI. They may not transfer to long-tail heterogeneous assets.
No efficient regime relies on bespoke parts. All rely on the opposite: standard interchangeable LRUs, a single fleet type and spares stocked in advance.

Every high-consequence regime builds inspection and certification into the system: MSG-3 programmes, Rickover's sign-off on crew competence, return-to-service rules. RCM gains were locked in through regulator-approved programmes.

Where one owner controlled design and scale (hyperscalers, Ryanair, Toyota, the Navy), repair was rebuilt and became very efficient, so the inefficiency is not built into the industry itself. It sits in fragmented, heterogeneous, small-scale ownership.

research.q: Gas turbine and power plant repair: OEM vs independent service providers (PSM, EthosEnergy, Sulzer, MD&A), hot-section repair, LTSA economics, outage durations and what drives them.
research.headline: Gas turbine servicing is a real but time-limited OEM knowledge monopoly. The EC found GE held over 60-70% of servicing on its own mature frames and over 90% on the 9FA, with independents entering only after 8-16 years. But the lock is enforced as much by warranties, lender and insurer requirements, 12-20 year LTSAs, IP and redesign costs, superalloy casting capacity and proven fleet hours as by missing information, so AI alone does not dissolve it. Outage time and cost go mainly to hot-section parts and their lead times, plus fixed physical steps. Diagnosis is not the main cost: in planned outages it is largely pre-computed from counted hours and starts.
research.bottleneck: The scarce layer is qualified, trusted hot-section hardware and the right to use it: superalloy single-crystal castings and coatings from a few casting houses with pricing power; repair processes and parts with proven fleet hours; and the risk-transfer wrapper (OEM warranty, lender and insurer acceptance, 12-20 year LTSAs) that decides whose parts and repairs may go into a machine. Proprietary fleet operating data is the other moat, and it scales with installed base. Knowledge matters, but it is bundled with capital, qualification and liability, which is why ISPs with the know-how still do not enter.
research.money_time: Money goes mainly to hot-section hardware (new or repaired nozzles, buckets, shrouds and combustion liners, replaced after about 3-4 HGP inspections, and rotors) and to lost generation margin during outages. Labour and diagnosis are secondary. Gas Power services make up about 66% of GE Vernova Power revenue, and growth there came from parts volume and price. Time goes to parts availability and lead time (GE: a 2-5 day combustion inspection becomes weeks without on-site spares), fixed physical steps (4-24 hours of cooldown, disassembly, shop repair, recoating, 2-8 hours on turning gear), and specialist technical direction. For planned outages, diagnosis is largely pre-computed from counted hours and starts. Operating profile (trips at 8-10x, starts, fuel) sets how often outages happen. The largest lever is avoiding outages altogether by extending intervals through better parts (PSM's 7F packages: 32k+ hours versus 24k), not by making diagnosis cheaper.
shapes: Cross-owner fleet-data pool and condition-based life-extension engine that independent owners and ISPs can use to justify interval extensions to insurers and lenders. It replicates Calpine's scale advantage for mid-sized fleets, and attacks the OEM's data moat rather than 'knowledge' generally.

Qualification and evidence layer for non-OEM parts and repairs: digital traceability, automated borescope and NDE records, and statistical reliability files packaged so insurers and lenders accept them. This targets C6, which is the actual gate.

Rotable-pool and parts-logistics marketplace for mature frames (pooled exchange sets of HGP parts and rotors across owners), taking parts off the outage critical path. This is where time goes, per GE's own spares warning and EthosEnergy's lead-time pitch.

AI copilot for outage execution and field technicians (procedures, checklists, change-order tracking, escalation). This addresses user complaints on the 7F field-service quality gap, but it is a modest wedge that OEMs are also building (GE Field Vision).

Qualified additive-manufacturing and repair cell for long-tail or orphaned frames' combustion and non-rotating parts. This is a partial version of C5, scoped to where AM is proven, not first-stage blades.
surprises: The shared WebSearch budget was used up before this agent ran, so evidence comes from directly fetched primary documents (EC decision, GE manual and 10-K, Calpine and Howmet 10-Ks, CCJ). Some background figures in the notes are flagged UNVERIFIED.
EthosEnergy told the EC it 'could certainly develop 9FA capability' but would not, because GE had locked the market through LTSAs. The barrier was the addressable market, not knowledge.
Only about 26% of GE's roughly 7,000 gas turbines (1,800 units) are under LTSAs, so a large transactional aftermarket exists for older frames.
Calpine ran much of its own major maintenance across about 26 GW with a 2.3% forced outage factor, showing insourcing works at fleet scale.
GE's own manual says outage time blows out because owners lack spares, not because problems go undiagnosed.
AI-style remote diagnostics already exist in this domain and are run by the OEM, which may reinforce its knowledge monopoly rather than dissolve it.
The EC forced divestment of PSM, the main independent service provider, as a merger remedy. Regulators treat ISPs as the main source of competition in servicing.

stances.why: Forced outages follow the founder's chain. Planned gas turbine maintenance does not: it starts with counted hours and starts (24k hours/1,200 starts for HGP inspection), which set inspections years ahead and trigger parts pre-purchase. Diagnosis is largely pre-computed and then confirmed by borescope. Fleet-level rotable pools and parts planning sit outside any single repair event.

The EC found OEMs hold over 60-100% of servicing on their own frames and that know-how is proprietary until 8-16 years of maturity. GE ties warranties to its approved repairs. But the lock is also enforced by warranties, lenders, insurers, LTSA terms and capital barriers, so knowledge is only part of the moat.

EthosEnergy said it could develop 9FA capability but had no addressable market. The barriers are casting and tooling capex, IP redesign cost, proven fleet hours and risk transfer. The OEM already runs AI-like remote diagnostics on proprietary fleet data, so AI may widen its lead. Calpine closed the gap through fleet scale, not information access.

Parts sourcing and lead time does drive outage time (GE: 2-5 days becomes weeks without spares). But the cost is hot-section hardware, superalloy castings from a price-setting oligopoly, plus lost generation. Diagnosis and understanding are a small share of planned-outage cost. An order-of-magnitude cut in those steps would barely move the total. Reducing outage count by extending intervals (PSM: 24k to 32k hours) is the bigger lever.

Hot-section parts are cooled, coated superalloy castings. Competitors told the EC that reverse engineering and tooling investment is 'huge' and that customers will not buy parts until they are 'proven'. Howmet and similar casting houses have pricing power and capacity limits. Additive manufacturing helps for some combustion and repair parts, not for first-stage blades at fleet scale.

Warranty, lender and insurer requirements and 'approved repair' rules decide who may repair, and acceptance of reverse-engineered parts depends on provenance and insurance. Qualification and certification, not knowledge, is what lets an independent part or repair be used. That layer would need to evolve (for example, data-backed qualification) before AI-derived repairs could count.

The structure does favour OEM annuities: services are 66% of GE Power revenue, prices are rising, and 12-20 year LTSAs foreclose entry. But much of it is rational risk transfer that buyers choose and price competitively at purchase. Efficient alternatives exist (Calpine's 2.3% forced outage factor in-house; PSM interval extensions). It is concentrated rather than structurally 'built to be inefficient'.

research.q: Transformer and grid equipment repair: transformer lead times (2-4 years), repair vs replace, field repair, utility spares sharing programs (STEP, SpareConnect, Grid Assurance).
research.headline: For large power transformers, the 2-4 year outage is not caused by a knowledge gap. Factories, materials (GOES electrical steel, copper, bushings), designs that differ unit to unit, and heavy-haul logistics cause it: lead times went from about 50 weeks in 2021 to about 120 weeks in 2024, and 80-210 weeks for large units. Diagnosis takes hours to days. The 10x restoration gains seen so far came from standardized modular hardware and pooled, pre-positioned spares (RecX energized in under a week; STEP and Grid Assurance), not from better information. So AI helps at the margins (diagnosis, matching spares) but cannot reach the dominant cost.
research.bottleneck: Physical manufacturing capacity and materials: GOES electrical steel, copper, bushings and tap changers, skilled winding labour, and high-voltage test bays, with about 80% of supply imported. Two further constraints compound it: almost no standardization, so spares cannot be interchanged (more than 20 voltage ratios plus varied impedances and bushings), and heavy-haul logistics. Knowledge (OEM design data, secret spare locations, a thinning expert workforce) matters only at the margins.
research.money_time: Almost all of the time goes to sourcing and delivering a replacement: 80-210 weeks of manufacturing lead time (about 120 weeks average in 2024), then weeks of heavy-haul logistics (about 30 Schnabel cars in North America, route permits), then install and commissioning (about 1 week in the best case). Diagnosis takes hours to days, using dissolved gas analysis, electrical tests or visible damage. The money is the unit itself ($2-10M, up 60-80% since 2020), the cost of operating the system without it (congestion, redispatch, reliability risk), and the insurance cost of holding pooled spares.
shapes: Standardized modular recovery transformer or spares-as-a-service business (RecX, Wattstock, Grid Assurance). It is capital heavy, but it is the only approach with demonstrated 10x restoration speed.

Confidential multi-utility spare registry plus an electrical and mechanical compatibility-matching engine. It would improve on SpareConnect's contact list and could use privacy-preserving matching to overcome the security secrecy around spare locations.

AI condition monitoring and fleet risk ranking (dissolved gas analysis, bushings, partial discharge) for an old fleet (38-40 years average age) with a 0.5% per year failure rate, turning emergency replacements into planned ones.

Field rewind and refurbishment with digital design reconstruction (scanning, reverse-engineered winding designs) for units whose OEM is gone or slow. This is the closest real analogue to an 'AI parts factory', but it is limited by labour and test bays.
Automation of transformer manufacturing (core stacking, winding) and alternative core materials (amorphous steel) to attack the true capacity bottleneck. This is deep tech and capital intensive.
surprises: STEP, the main US sharing program, only obliges members to share after a terrorist attack plus a Presidential declaration. Ordinary failures fall to voluntary SpareConnect, which is just a contact list.
DOE rejected a federal transformer reserve mainly because of non-standardization: it would need more than 100 units to cover the variety of designs.
The demonstrated order-of-magnitude speedup (RecX: under 1 week against years) came from a standardized hardware design, not from information.
The 2-4 year lead time is cyclical. Lead times were 5-16 months in 2010 and also spiked to 18-24 months in earlier booms, so it is a capacity cycle, not a permanent structure.
Utilities' fallback plan is to move a working transformer out of a less critical substation, which is cannibalization rather than repair.

stances.why: Restoration does follow a source, deliver, install and commission sequence. But the grid often skips diagnosing and understanding by substituting a spare or a transformer taken from a less critical substation, and its redundancy can hide a failure entirely (Metcalf). Prevention and monitoring are steps the chain does not include.

The binding constraints are physical: GOES, copper, bushings, factory slots, test bays, Schnabel cars and winders. There are real information frictions (secret spare locations, SpareConnect being only a contact list, OEM design data needed for rewinds, a thinning workforce), but they are secondary.
AI could help diagnostics and spare compatibility matching, but it cannot create manufacturing capacity, materials or heavy-haul logistics, which make up most of a 2-4 year outage.

Diagnosis takes hours to days. Sourcing and delivery take 80-210 weeks of factory backlog plus heavy haul. The 10x restoration gains seen so far came from standard modular hardware and pre-positioned pooled spares (RecX under 1 week), not from cheaper information.

The scarce parts are cores, windings and bushings, which need specialized metallurgy and high-voltage factory acceptance testing. The industry and regulators are converging on de-bespoking (standard designs, interchangeable spares) rather than on-demand bespoke manufacturing.

Factory acceptance testing, commissioning tests and NERC CIP-014 security assessments are essential gates. DOE notes overseas test witnessing is costly, which leaves room for remote or AI-assisted inspection.

Real structural inefficiencies exist: bespoke specs per utility, about 80% import dependence, boom-bust capacity cycles, and STEP's terrorism-only trigger. But much of this reflects rational reliability, security and regulatory choices, and DOE explicitly chose incremental industry pooling over a rebuild.

research.q: Nuclear plant component repair and outages: refuelling outage durations, emergent repairs, obsolete I&C, EPRI data; what drives cost.
research.headline: In nuclear, repair time and cost are dominated by downtime (about $1M a day per GW unit), labour (operations is about 60% of generating cost) and regulator-acceptable qualification and inspection, not by missing diagnostic knowledge or parts logistics. The worst repair disasters (San Onofre, Crystal River) came from OEM or contractor design and execution errors and ended those plants. Note: this agent had no web search budget left, so several numbers are background knowledge flagged as unverified in the notes file.
research.bottleneck: Qualified evidence and qualified people. First, regulator-acceptable proof that a part, repair or software meets the design basis (Appendix B QA, ASME code, commercial grade dedication, digital common-cause-failure analysis). Second, certified NDE technicians and welders, and inspection methods able to size defects without destructive cut-outs. Third, scarce heavy-forging capacity. Knowledge as information is not the constraint.
research.money_time: Downtime is the main cost: lost generation of about $0.7-1.5M a day per GW unit, plus replacement power (EDF bought €29B in 2022). Next is labour: operations is about 60% of generating cost, and 1,000-2,000 contractors arrive per outage. Then emergent discovery work found during inspection on the critical path, and engineering disposition and regulatory paperwork (50.59, ASME XI, relief requests, dedication). Rare catastrophic component repairs ($0.6-3.4B) have ended plants. Parts and shipping costs are minor, except for large forgings, where years of lead time are the problem.
shapes: AI-assisted NDE analysis (eddy current, UT, phased array) to cut critical-path inspection days and give confident crack sizing; it hits the time-dominant step and inspection is the bottleneck

Qualification and dedication-as-a-service: AI-built, Appendix-B-compliant evidence dossiers for reverse-engineered or additively manufactured obsolete parts, where the dossier rather than the part is the product, because qualification costs more than fabrication
Drop-in replacements for obsolete analog I&C (FPGA or analog-equivalent) with a pre-built licensing basis that avoids software common-cause failure, since licensing risk stalls digital upgrades
Outage critical-path and emergent-work prediction from operating-experience and plant data, because each outage day is worth about $1M
Provenance and anti-counterfeit tracking for safety-related parts, given the Korea 2012-13 and Le Creusot 2016 scandals
surprises: The two most expensive repairs (SONGS, Crystal River) were caused by the OEM or contractor, the supposed knowledge holders, and liability caps left owners carrying almost all of the cost ($125M recovered against $7.57B claimed).
Davis-Besse's replacement reactor head came from a mothballed, never-finished plant, so salvage beat new manufacture.
The US fleet cut outage durations roughly 3x and raised capacity factor from about 60% to about 93% without any rebuild of the industry, purely through operational discipline.

This agent had no search budget left (the shared 200-search limit was used up), so several key numbers (NEI cost per MWh, outage day counts, the additive-manufacturing installs) are unverified background and need confirming.

stances.why: Nuclear follows the chain explicitly. However, noticing is mostly scheduled inspection, and engineering disposition, regulatory screening and qualification sit between understanding and sourcing; these are often the longest steps.

OEMs do hold design-basis and I&C knowledge, but the costliest failures (SONGS, Crystal River) were OEM or contractor errors. The industry already pools knowledge through EPRI, INPO and owners' groups. What is scarce is qualified, legally accountable knowledge and certified people.

The binding constraints are NRC-acceptable QA evidence (Appendix B, ASME), software common-cause-failure licensing, certified welders and NDE staff, and forging capacity. AI does not remove any of these.

Cost is dominated by downtime (about $1M a day per unit), labour (about 60% of generating cost) and compliance. The 30-35% cost cut since 2012 came from process and organisation; a 10x gain in diagnosis and logistics would move totals modestly.

Additive manufacturing works for small parts, but qualification and dedication take years and cost more than fabrication. Large forgings remain scarce and are solved by salvage (Midland head). Counterfeiting history raises the burden on new supply routes.
Inspection sets outage critical paths. EDF 2022 showed weak NDE crack sizing forcing destructive cut-outs, and better NDE and online monitoring is where the leverage is.

Some inefficiency is deliberate (defence-in-depth) and some is regulatory ossification (the digital I&C stalemate). But the fleet roughly tripled its outage efficiency through incremental discipline without a rebuild.

research.q: Oil and gas / process industry rotating equipment repair (pumps, compressors; API standards; repair shops; turnaround costs): structure and inefficiencies.
research.headline: In oil and gas rotating equipment, the knowledge monopoly is real but narrow: it holds for engineered compressors and turbines, and pump OEMs say themselves that common API standards keep the standard-pump aftermarket competitive. Cost is set by lost production per hour, scarce craft labour in turnarounds, lead times on engineered parts, and legally required qualification and inspection, not by diagnosis or know-how, so a 10x drop in the "knowledge" steps would not give a 10x gain. (Note: the shared web-search budget was used up before this agent started. These findings come from directly fetched primary documents: SEC 10-Ks, OSHA, CSB, a Siemens study and Sulzer's pages. Practitioner background is flagged as not re-verified.)
research.bottleneck: Four constraints matter more than missing information: (1) qualified craft capacity in turnaround windows; (2) lead time on engineered, material-certified parts; (3) qualification and certification of non-OEM parts and repairs under PSM (j)(6) and insurer rules; (4) organisational discipline, meaning deferred inspection and poor installation and operating practice.
research.money_time: Lost production dominates: O&G per-hour downtime cost tracks the oil price, and per-plant losses run to tens to hundreds of millions of dollars a year. Within planned work, turnarounds are the largest maintenance cost. Their cost and critical path are set by contractor craft labour in compressed windows, emergent scope found when equipment is opened, and long-lead engineered parts (rotors, impellers, dry gas seals, compressor bundles). Diagnosis is a small share and is already being automated by condition monitoring. OEMs earn about half their revenue on the aftermarket, through proximity, speed and long-term service agreements.
shapes: OEM-agnostic, AI-assisted reverse-engineering plus qualification house for obsolete or long-lead rotating-equipment parts, selling a certified PSM-compliant data package with the part. It targets the qualification bottleneck that Sulzer-type shops serve slowly.

Turnaround scope-prediction software that forecasts discovery work before equipment is opened, using inspection and condition-monitoring history, so long-lead parts are pre-ordered and emergent scope shrinks. It attacks the real turnaround cost driver.

Tacit-expertise capture and copilot for rotating-equipment reliability engineers (aimed at the aging-workforce risk OEMs disclose), letting owner-operators cut LTSA dependence on non-critical machines.
Mechanical-integrity and inspection platform (possibly robotic) that makes inspection deferrals auditable and speeds RAGAGEP inspection inside PSM, in line with the CSB Chevron recommendations.
surprises: Flowserve's 10-K itself says common API standards make the standard-pump aftermarket competitive. The OEM's lock-in is limited to engineered and custom equipment plus physical proximity.
Downtime hours at large plants fell from 39 to 27 per month (2019-2023) through monitoring, before generative AI. Notice and diagnose were already being compressed.
Catastrophic refinery failures (Chevron Richmond) stemmed from deferred and denied inspection work on a known damage mechanism, a governance failure rather than a knowledge gap.
OSHA puts the legal burden of part suitability on the plant owner, which is a direct regulatory brake on any 'AI parts factory'.
The OEM worries about knowledge loss too: Flowserve lists replacing retiring workers' expertise as a risk factor.

stances.why: The steps exist, but process plants batch repairs into planned turnarounds where sourcing comes months before 'noticing' on opening equipment. Condition monitoring and LTSAs merge or reorder the steps. A usable rubric, but not a fixed sequence.

Real for engineered compressors and turbines and custom pumps (OEM cites customized designs; LTSAs over 10 years). Not true for standard API pumps, where the OEM says common standards keep the aftermarket competitive. Major failures came from deferred inspection, not missing knowledge.

Codified knowledge (API standards, reliability practice) was never the binding gap. Tacit craft skill, liability, and the owner's legal duty to assure part suitability remain. AI helps mostly with capturing retiring expertise and with diagnosis, which is already being automated.

Cost is dominated by lost production per hour and by turnaround craft labour, discovery scope and long-lead parts. Diagnosis and understanding are a small slice, and parts delivery is limited by metallurgy and machining lead time, not information.
Reverse engineering with scanning and AM is already commercial (Sulzer and independents). What limits it is material certification, testing and OSHA (j)(6)(iii) suitability, not part design.
OSHA PSM mandates RAGAGEP inspection and testing, documentation and pre-startup review. CSB cases show deferred inspection as a root cause, and regulators push changes back into API standards.

OEMs deliberately build aftermarket capture (QRC expansion, LTSAs, 53% aftermarket). But much of the apparent inefficiency is deliberate safety redundancy, and downtime hours fell about 30% in four years, which points to improvement rather than structural rigidity.

research.q: Robotics and automation equipment repair in factories (FANUC, ABB robot service, PLC obsolescence like Allen-Bradley/Siemens S5): how plants keep legacy automation alive.
research.headline: Plants keep legacy automation such as S5, PLC-5 and old FANUC/ABB robots running through OEM lifetime-support and remanufacturing programs, a gray market of surplus and board-repair houses, and deferred migration. A downtime hour costs $39k to over $2m, so the value is in time-to-restore, not in the information. Note: the shared web-search budget was already used up, so only 5 fetched primary sources are verified; about half the findings come from my prior knowledge and are flagged unverified. The binding constraints are physical scarcity of discontinued electronics, tacit plant-specific knowledge such as uncommented code and retired staff, and safety/GxP revalidation, not an information monopoly that AI simply removes.
research.bottleneck: Two things are scarce. One is physical supply of discontinued electronics (boards, CPUs, servo amps) together with validated test benches. The other is the tacit, site-specific knowledge of how a given line's code and wiring work, plus the authority to recertify safety functions after a change. Information about generic OEM products is not the scarce layer.
research.money_time: Downtime dominates: $39k to over $2m per hour (Siemens 2022), against parts that often cost hundreds to thousands of dollars. The time goes to diagnosis on undocumented legacy systems, finding a working obsolete part (gray-market search, shipping, testing) and, for migrations, re-engineering non-portable code plus safety/GxP revalidation. When parts are gone, migration and revalidation, not the repair itself, become the largest cost.
shapes: AI-assisted legacy-code understanding and migration: read uncommented S5/PLC-5/SLC ladder logic, document it and auto-translate it to modern platforms with test harnesses. This attacks the tacit-knowledge and re-engineering cost.

An obsolescence-risk and spares-twin platform: inventory a plant's automation base against OEM lifecycle notices and gray-market stock, and predict which failures will strand the line. It turns reactive sourcing into planned buying.

A component-level electronics repair and reverse-engineering network with automated board test (AI-assisted fault isolation on boards, form-fit-function clones). Electronics scarcity is the real C5 gap.
Vendor-neutral condition monitoring and diagnostics for mixed-brand robot and PLC fleets, as an alternative to OEM-locked ZDT and Senseye.
Retrofit-with-validation as a service: package the migration together with the safety/GxP revalidation evidence, since revalidation dominates cost (C6).
Legacy-OT security wrappers for unauthenticated legacy PLCs (Stuxnet-class risk), relevant for a security-tech founder.
surprises: The shared web-search budget was already used up when this agent started, so no new searches ran. Only 5 primary sources were fetched and verified; the other findings come from prior knowledge, are flagged in /home/user/nuketime/research/repair/raw/e05.md, and should be checked in a follow-up run.
FANUC openly promises lifetime parts support. The OEM model is to monetize longevity, not to abandon customers, which weakens 'built to be inefficient'.
Obsolescence in automation is announced years in advance. The failure is deferred migration (capex, downtime windows, revalidation), not lack of warning.
The knowledge gap is mostly tacit and plant-specific (uncommented code, retired staff) rather than OEM-held secrets.
AI diagnostics in this domain are already owned by OEMs (FANUC ZDT, Siemens Senseye, ABB Ability), so AI is concentrating control rather than dispersing it.

stances.why: The chain broadly holds, but in factories detection is increasingly automated, and when parts are discontinued the chain branches into migration/retrofit (re-engineering plus revalidation) rather than 'source part'.

OEM concentration is real (FANUC holds 65% of CNC, plus proprietary tools and cables), but much of the pain is tacit plant-specific knowledge (uncommented code, retired staff) and physical parts scarcity, not an OEM secret.
AI cannot make discontinued ICs exist, extract code from air-gapped old hardware or sign off safety functions. Existing AI diagnostics (ZDT, Senseye) are OEM-owned and entrench OEM control.

With downtime at $39k to over $2m/hr, faster diagnosis and parts search are very valuable and could shrink a lot. Sourcing and delivering obsolete parts is bounded by global used stock and logistics, not information.

Mechanical parts can be machined or printed, but the binding constraint is obsolete electronics and firmware (ASICs, servo amps, CPU cards), which cannot be printed. Board-level repair or cloning is slow and legally fraught.
Safety and GxP revalidation often dominate migration cost and explain why plants prefer like-for-like used parts.

The system is fragmented and slow, but OEMs publish phase-outs years ahead, FANUC promises lifetime parts, and a functioning secondary market exists. Much of the inefficiency is a rational deferral of capex and revalidation, built around OEM lock-in.

research.q: Security tech and critical infrastructure equipment repair (SCADA/ICS spares, legacy control systems, secure supply chain requirements): constraints on who can repair.
research.headline: In security-sensitive critical infrastructure, who may repair is limited mainly by regulated trust, not by missing knowledge: vetted vendors, proof of where parts and software came from (provenance), controlled remote access, and nuclear quality rules. For the heaviest assets the binding limit is physical manufacturing capacity measured in months to years, so AI shrinking the knowledge gap only moves a small part of cost and time, and cheap sourcing of obsolete parts makes counterfeit risk worse. (The shared web-search budget was used up before this agent ran, so the evidence comes from fetching known primary sources directly, plus clearly marked prior-knowledge items.)
research.bottleneck: Trust and qualification: proving a part, a piece of firmware, a technician or a maintenance tool is authentic, uncompromised and allowed to touch the system (CIP-013, DFARS counterfeit rules, NRC dedication, IEC 62443-2-4). For the largest assets, physical manufacturing capacity (electrical steel, winding, testing) is the second bottleneck. Knowledge is not the scarce layer.
research.money_time: Heavy grid assets: manufacturing lead time dominates (transformers 18-24+ months historically, about 2-4 years since 2022; generators more than a year), then transport, commissioning and testing. ICS electronics: buying authenticated obsolete spares, and engineering effort to migrate and re-validate off end-of-life controllers. Cyber incidents: recovery and return to service, plus manual-operation readiness (Colonial: 6 days). Diagnosis and 'understanding' are a small share, though detection ('notice') is chronically under-instrumented.
shapes: Provenance and authentication for obsolete ICS and electronic spares (testing plus chain-of-custody certificates): it turns the counterfeit risk GAO documented into a trusted supply that DFARS and CIP-013 buyers can use

AI-accelerated commercial-grade dedication and qualification packages for nuclear and utility spares, including reverse-engineered and additively manufactured parts: it attacks the certification step where the time actually goes

Vetted maintenance-access platform: AI-guided field technicians on verified-clean engineering workstations, with CIP-013 and IEC 62443-2-4 evidence generated automatically, since maintainers are the attack vector (Stuxnet)

Legacy controller emulation and migration (PLC-5/S5-era drop-ins with automatic logic translation and validation): installed base is huge, OEM support is ending, and CISA is pushing operators off end-of-life devices
OT visibility and detection for small utilities and water systems: only about 30% of OT networks have visibility, so 'notice' and 'diagnose' lack data, not knowledge
surprises: GAO received 'genuine' quotes even for part numbers that do not exist: fast obsolete-parts sourcing is the counterfeit channel itself
NERC CIP-013 names switching vendors as a risk event, so regulation actively discourages opening up who can repair
Colonial's 6-day outage came mostly from a lack of manual restart planning, not from damage to equipment
A cyber command can destroy a generator in about 3 minutes, while replacing it takes more than a year: a gap of about five orders of magnitude between breaking and fixing

stances.why: The chain holds broadly, but critical infrastructure adds stages it leaves out: vetting and authorising the repairer, checking where parts and software came from (CIP-013 R1.2.5), and making sure maintenance tools are clean (Stuxnet). 'Notice' is weak because only about 30% of OT networks have visibility.

OEMs do hold proprietary tools and firmware. But the main limit on who can repair is regulated trust (CIP-013, DFARS, NRC Part 21, IEC 62443-2-4), adopted for real security reasons shown by Stuxnet and Volt Typhoon, not mainly a knowledge gap.

Knowledge is not the binding constraint. Diagnosis lacks data, and AI-guided repair by unvetted parties widens the attack surface. Partial exception: AI could fix basic-hygiene capacity gaps at small utilities (the Unitronics case).
For transformers and generators, the months-to-years delay is in manufacturing, not diagnosis or sourcing. Fast, cheap sourcing of obsolete parts is the counterfeit vector (GAO: 16 of 16 bogus).

Electrical steel, 400-ton custom transformers and safety-qualified nuclear parts are limited by material supply and qualification. The niche that is real: qualified reverse engineering, additive manufacturing of mechanical spares, and emulation of obsolete electronics, with certification attached.
Provenance checks, commercial-grade dedication, software integrity checks and return-to-service validation (Colonial's manual restart gap) are central bottlenecks and growing needs.
Much of the friction is a deliberate security and safety perimeter. Some is real dysfunction: transformer capacity shortfall, underfunded rip-and-replace, orphaned legacy PLCs.

research.q: Battery energy storage and solar O&M: inverter failure rates and repair, BESS augmentation and repair, warranty disputes; what is inefficient?
research.headline: This could not be fully checked this session: the shared search budget was used up, so only some findings were confirmed by fetching the page and the rest come from memory of named sources. The evidence still points one way. In solar and battery storage operations, detecting and diagnosing faults is already cheap and largely automated, yet losses kept rising. The time and money go to truck rolls and technicians, manufacturer return-and-replace cycles, part lead times, control of firmware and data, safety approval, and warranties that become worthless when the company behind them goes bankrupt (SunPower, Fimer, Powin). In battery storage, failures come mostly from system integration and controls spread across many parties, and inspection and regulators set how long a site takes to return to service. Not knowledge.
research.bottleneck: The scarce layer is permission and access, not knowledge. That means certified integration (fire codes, safety standards, fire-authority approval), access to manufacturer firmware, commissioning software and monitoring data, and a solvent party standing behind warranties and long-term service contracts. Field labour and spares inventory for 10-15 year power electronics that outlive their manufacturers sit just behind that.
research.money_time: Lost revenue comes mainly from corrective-repair downtime, especially inverters, which cause about 43% of tickets and 36% of lost energy in the SunEdison data. That downtime goes to truck rolls to remote sites, scarce qualified high-voltage technicians, manufacturer warranty replacement cycles and spare-part lead times; during the 2021-23 supply crunch these ran to many months, and more than a year for transformers. For battery storage, the time after an incident is dominated by investigation, fire-authority approval, re-certification and community politics: Elkhorn was out about 3 months, Moss Landing Phase 1 about 5 months in 2022, and cleanup after 2025 was expected to take more than a year. Long-term cost is dominated by adding batteries as capacity fades and by the replacement cycle of inverters and battery power-conversion units, which last 10-15 years inside 30-40 year assets. Diagnosis is a small and falling cost.
shapes: An independent repair, refurbishment and pooled-spares network for inverters from many manufacturers, serving orphaned fleets (Fimer/ABB, SunPower, SolarEdge storage, Powin). It could be sold as a 'warranty of last resort' to owners and insurers, because bankruptcies keep wiping out warranties.

Battery-storage service-contract takeover and capacity-addition-as-a-service, bundled with the safety re-certification and fire-authority approval package, because battery augmentation is an integration and certification problem and integrators fail.

Warranty-claim automation: assemble the evidence from site monitoring data, file the claim and recover labour costs. AI genuinely helps with documentation and adjudication, and disputes centre on labour exclusions and burden of proof.

Third-party battery-storage inspection, commissioning and post-incident investigation tools for fire authorities and insurers, because inspection sets the return-to-service timeline and manufacturers' self-certification is not trusted.
surprises: Solar losses from equipment faults roughly doubled (2019-2023) even as AI and drone detection spread, so detection is not the constraint.
Only about 11% of battery-storage failures are in the cells; most are in controls and the rest of the system, an integration problem spread across many parties.
The real 'supplier gone' cases (Fimer, Satcon, SunPower, Powin) were solved with circuit-board repair, refurbished spares and service takeovers, not custom fabrication.
The battery-storage failure rate per GW fell about 97% in five years (from memory), which undercuts the claim that the industry is built to be inefficient.
This was a research gap: the shared search budget was used up, so many figures come from memory and should be checked before use.

stances.why: The chain broadly fits. But battery storage adds steps outside it: post-incident investigation, fire-authority re-approval and community politics, plus planned capacity additions, which are repair before anything fails. The steps loop and overlap rather than running in a line.

Manufacturers do control firmware, warranty replacements and monitoring data, and require warranty claims to go through the original installer. But battery failures come from integration spread across many parties. The gap is access, coordination and money behind the warranty, not a monopoly on know-how.
Detection is already automated by drones, control-system data and AI analytics, yet solar losses roughly doubled. Firmware access, field labour, spares and certification are not knowledge problems.

Diagnosis is already cheap. Sourcing could improve through pooled and refurbished spares. But most downtime comes from technicians, lead times, warranty replacement cycles and regulators, so a 10x drop is not supported.

Orphaned inverters get circuit-board repair, refurbished spares or a new-model replacement, not custom-made parts. Battery cells are mass-produced; the hard part is certified integration into the system.

Fire codes and safety standards, fire authorities, insurers and third-party factory audits set the timeline. At Moss Landing the time to return to service and the rule changes after the fire dwarfed the time to diagnose.

The inefficiencies come from misaligned contracts (warranty labour exclusions, service-contract lock-in), fragmentation and bankruptcies, not deliberate design. Battery failure rates fell about 97% as the industry learned.

research.q: Space and satellite servicing (Northrop MEV, in-orbit servicing) and launch vehicle refurbishment (SpaceX reuse): what made repair possible where it was not, and the economics.
research.headline: In space, repair became possible where it had not been through access hardware and design for serviceability, not through closing a knowledge gap. Falcon 9 cut refurbishment to under about 10% of new-build cost (per Musk) by redesigning the asset for reuse, and MEV bypassed the failing subsystem with a docking "jetpack". Where assets were not designed for service, attempts were expensive or were cancelled (Shuttle at about $1.5B per flight, NASA's OSAM-1 cancelled after about $2B). Inspection and certification set the economics throughout. Caveat: the shared search budget was used up before this agent ran, so findings come from fetching known pages directly, and a few numbers are unverified leads.
research.bottleneck: Physical access plus design for serviceability, meaning standard interfaces, and trusted inspection and certification that lets customers and insurers accept a reused or serviced asset. Knowledge was not the bottleneck.
research.money_time: Satellite servicing: almost all the cost is in getting to the asset (launch, rendezvous and proximity operations, docking/capture hardware, a dedicated servicer vehicle) and in qualification, with timelines of about a decade from concept to service. Diagnosis and parts are minor. Launch reuse: once recovery is solved, the recurring cost is inspection, refurbishment and requalification. The Shuttle (engines pulled and requalified every flight, standing army) versus Falcon 9 Block 5 (designed for minimal inspection) comparison shows that design for cheap inspection is the lever.
shapes: Standard serviceability interfaces (docking plates, refuelling ports) sold into new builds, the Astroscale/Orbit Fab model: the evidence shows that prepared clients make servicing economic
Inspection and certification-as-a-service for reused and serviced hardware (automated post-flight inspection, health data, insurer-grade attestation): inspection cost and trust gated reuse adoption
Design for reuse and fast refurbishment tooling for reusable vehicles and engines: the Shuttle versus Falcon gap was refurbishment and inspection cost
Mass-produced standardised 'jetpack' life-extension pods (MEP-like) rather than bespoke repair: standardisation beat custom repair
Autonomous rendezvous, proximity and inspection software for servicers: helps the access step, which dominates cost
surprises: The most successful satellite 'repair' (MEV) involves no diagnosis or repair at all. It bypasses the depleted function by docking a propulsion module onto the satellite.
NASA cancelled a $2B mission to refuel an unprepared satellite, signalling that retrofit repair of legacy assets is not worth it.
The Shuttle was fully reusable yet roughly 25x over its per-flight cost projection, and its engines are now thrown away on SLS: reuse without cheap inspection destroys value.
The first commercial partner for the GEO robotic servicer (Maxar) quit because its own satellite orders dried up: demand-side economics, not technology, stalled servicing.
Even with servicing available, Intelsat 33e ended as an uninsured total loss.

stances.why: The chain works as a skeleton, but space adds a dominant access/reachability stage. MEV skips diagnosis and repair entirely by bypassing the failed function. Falcon refurbishment is scheduled inspection, not reactive diagnosis. Most satellite failures stop at 'notice' and end in write-off.

The barriers were physical access, the lack of designed-in interfaces, capital and qualification, not knowledge. There are minor knowledge gaps (Solar Max undocumented grommet), but no breakthrough came from freeing up information.

None of the enabling breakthroughs (propulsive landing, MEV docking) were knowledge-gap closures. AI-type autonomy helps rendezvous but does not remove the delta-v, hardware or certification constraints.

Falcon got roughly 10x on refurbish versus new (company claim), but by redesigning the asset, not by cheaper diagnosis. In orbit, 'deliver' (launch plus rendezvous, $200k/kg for GEO fuel) dominates and has not fallen 10x.
Flight hardware is gated by qualification and reachability, not fabrication. The servicing industry is converging on standardised pods and ports, not bespoke parts.

Inspection and certification set reuse economics: the SES risk premium, certification steps from 10 to 40 flights, static-fire checks, Shuttle engine requalification, the Hubble test failure, and ADRAS-J inspecting before capture.

The replace-and-insure model was rational when access was impossible. Launch was rebuilt by a vertically integrated new entrant, which supports the 'incumbents won't rebuild' view. Satellite servicing remains tiny (2 MEVs, 1 MRV), and NASA's $2B OSAM-1 was cancelled.

research.q: Trucking and fleet maintenance (Class 8 trucks, telematics, Decisiv, Fleetio, dealer vs independent, downtime cost per day): inefficiencies and data.
research.headline: In Class 8 trucking, the cost of a repair is mostly days out of service, worth about $1,500 in lost revenue per truck-day, rather than the repair bill. Those days go mainly to queueing, approvals, parts waits for certified electronic and emissions parts, and a 52% diesel technician shortfall; lack of knowledge is a smaller factor. Information access was formally opened years ago and telematics already automates noticing and pre-diagnosis, so AI's opening is coordination and technician productivity, not closing a knowledge monopoly.
research.bottleneck: Three layers bind: (1) diesel technician labour, with a 52% supply gap; (2) coordination and authorization latency across fleet, dealer, OEM and warranty; (3) availability of certified electronic and emissions parts, made worse by emissions derate rules. Knowledge access is secondary because it was formally opened in about 2015-2018, though it remains costly and fragmented.
research.money_time: Time goes to days out of service, dominated by waiting for a bay and triage, authorization and warranty approval, and back-ordered parts rather than wrench time. Decisiv says coordination alone saves 1-3.4 days per event. Money goes mainly to lost revenue of about $1,500 per truck-day, which outweighs most repair invoices; direct repair and maintenance is about $0.20/mile, roughly 9% of cost per mile (unverified this run).
shapes: An AI triage and pre-staging layer that turns a telematics fault code into a confirmed diagnosis, parts list, pre-ordered parts and a booked bay before the truck arrives. It targets days out of service, the dominant cost.
A multi-OEM diagnostic copilot for independent and in-house fleet technicians. It multiplies scarce techs' output and narrows the dealer advantage.
Repair-authorization and audit AI for fleets that catches unnecessary repairs and speeds approvals (Fleetio's Auto-Chlor case avoided $280K+ a year).
Mobile and roadside emissions-fault service built around the 2025 EPA derate changes.
Avoid a general AI parts factory for Class 8. The binding parts are certified electronics, so only a niche in legacy mechanical parts for older or vocational fleets is plausible.
surprises: Decisiv claims about 60% of North American commercial vehicles run through its platform. The coordination layer is already consolidated, and it alone claims a 33% downtime cut without any diagnosis AI.
Heavy-truck right to repair was largely settled by an industry MOU around 2015, yet downtime remains high. That weakens the knowledge-monopoly explanation for trucking.
A major downtime generator was a regulator-designed feature: DEF/SCR derates. The regulator, not AI, is the one rolling it back.

WebSearch budget was exhausted before this agent ran; several numbers (ATRI R&M per mile, the 2015 MOU, the EPA 2025 guidance, the $448-760/day range) come from prior knowledge and should be verified.

stances.why: The chain broadly holds, but trucking adds triage/bay queueing, authorization (POs, warranty claims) and towing. Remote diagnostics also reorder and parallelize the steps: parts are ordered before the truck arrives.

Formal information access is largely open (2015 CV MOU; FTC finds weak justifications). Downtime is driven more by coordination latency, technician scarcity and parts availability. Knowledge still matters through fragmented, costly OEM tools and shop-fleet asymmetry (over-repair).

Telematics and OEM remote diagnostics automated noticing and pre-diagnosis years ago, yet dwell persists. Electrification and new emissions rules keep creating fresh knowledge gaps. AI gains so far are anecdotal (minutes saved per day).

Most lost time is in the middle steps (waiting for parts and approvals), so cutting them is valuable when measured in downtime days. But repair and maintenance is only about 9% of cost per mile, and hands-on labour (52% tech gap) sits outside the four steps.
Delay-driving Class 8 parts are certified emissions and electronic components with firmware. On-demand fabrication only fits niche legacy mechanical parts.
Emissions certification and anti-tamper derate rules, plus FMCSA inspections, shape repair downtime. EPA is already revising rules to cut repair-induced downtime.

Real structural inefficiencies exist: derate design, warranty steering to dealers, per-OEM tool silos, phone and fax approvals. But a large incumbent coordination layer (Decisiv, Fleetio, OEM uptime centres) already exists, so change is more likely incremental than a ground-up rebuild.

research.q: Marine commercial shipping repair (shipyards, class societies DNV/ABS/Lloyd's Register, engine makers MAN/Wärtsilä service): how classification and OEMs structure repair.
research.headline: In commercial shipping, repair is run by a class oligopoly and two OEM engine-design duopolies. Class (IACS members cover more than 90% of cargo tonnage) is the legal gate woven through every repair.
