OEMs keep design data and service letters and earn their margin from lifelong parts and service agreements. The scarce layers are the authority to sign off, OEM design data, docks and skilled hands, and off-hire time. Knowledge as such is not scarce, and OEMs and class are themselves deploying AI and remote surveys, which may deepen lock-in rather than erase it. CAVEAT: the turn's shared WebSearch budget was used up before this agent ran, so only direct page fetches were possible. Many figures are tagged [BK] (background knowledge, not re-verified) in the notes file.
research.bottleneck: The scarce layers are, first, the legally accountable sign-off held by a class oligopoly that flag states and insurers rely on. Second, OEM-held design data, service letters and control software, which gate part qualification and third-party repair. Third, physical capacity: dock slots, skilled yard trades and seafarer officers, and getting parts and people to a moving ship. Knowledge itself is widely held and already being digitised by the incumbents.
research.money_time: Time dominates: off-hire days. Routine drydocks take about 2-4 weeks, and yard bills run from hundreds of thousands to several million dollars [BK]. Charter income is lost at tens of thousands of dollars per day. For unplanned breakdowns, the time goes to deviating to port, waiting for a flown-in OEM engineer and waiting for long-lead parts (liners, turbocharger cartridges, crankshafts). Diagnosis itself is a small share. The OEM margin pool is lifelong genuine parts and service agreements. Class cost is small in dollars, but its scheduling and attendance gate the timeline.
shapes: Independent, OEM-agnostic condition-monitoring and evidence layer that produces survey-grade data class accepts for remote surveys and survey-interval extensions. It targets the evolving inspection gate and sells against off-hire days.

Qualification-first digital inventory for long-tail and out-of-production marine spares (reverse engineering plus AM/CNC plus a class approval pipeline per part number), starting with non-critical parts for orphaned older engines. The bottleneck is qualification and IP, not printing.
OT cyber repair and patch attestation for ships under IACS UR E26/E27: a new class-regulated repair category in security tech.

Breakdown-response orchestration that compresses unplanned repair (remote diagnosis, pre-positioned parts, nearest qualified independent technician, scope pre-agreed with class), because the waiting loop, not the diagnosis, is the cost.
surprises: In the Prestige case, the class society already had fatigue evidence from the sister ships. The failure was in incentives and follow-through, not in knowledge, which runs against the knowledge-gap thesis.

Engine OEMs already split knowledge from making: MAN designs while licensees build. The licensing model resembles a 'design central, factory distributed' structure, and the OEM still captures the aftermarket.
More than 90% of Wärtsilä service-agreement customers renew. Owners appear to pay willingly for OEM-bundled predictability, so they are not obviously trapped by ignorance.
Some inefficiency is deliberate policy (the 50% US duty on foreign repairs) and some is deliberate rigidity (the anti-class-hopping agreement), which AI does not dissolve.
Cyber patching of engine controls is now a class requirement and an OEM service line, creating a new 'repair' category.

stances.why: The chain holds as a logical skeleton, especially for unplanned damage. But most marine repair is calendar-batched into class survey and drydock windows. Class is woven through the repair (scope approval, attendance, part certification) rather than sitting only at the end.

Real monopoly pockets exist: OEM design data and service letters, engine control software, and class sign-off authority. But owners, ship managers and independent yards hold deep expertise. The major disasters (Prestige, Erika) happened despite the knowledge being available, through incentive failures.

OEMs (Wärtsilä Expert Insight, Everllence CEON) and class (remote surveys) are the ones deploying AI and remote diagnosis on proprietary fleet data, which may deepen lock-in. Liability, sign-off and IP are not knowledge gaps that AI removes.

Diagnosis can get much cheaper. But off-hire days, yard labour and steel, dock slots, part lead times and delivery to a moving ship dominate costs. A 10x cut across the four steps would not be a 10x cut in total cost, except possibly for unplanned breakdowns where waiting dominates.
Class AM frameworks exist and non-critical spares are being printed. Critical parts need per-part qualification and class approval, and OEM drawings and IP block access. Far from solved.
Class remains the legal gate (flag RO role, insurance, port entry) and is already evolving: remote surveys, drones and ROVs (Rec 42), AM approvals, cyber UR E26/E27.

There are adverse structures (owner pays the inspector, class-hopping, the 50% Jones Act repair duty, OEM aftermarket rents). But much apparent inefficiency is deliberate redundancy and liability management, and the system adapts incrementally. Targeted layer rebuilds fit the evidence better than a wholesale rebuild.

research.q: Software locks and parts pairing as a tool of repair control across industries (serialised parts, encrypted ECUs, licensed diagnostic software): catalogue them and their economic effect.
research.headline: Software locks such as parts pairing, VIN burning, dealer-only diagnostic tools, signed firmware and geo-fenced "time bombs" are used across phones, cars, tractors, trains, printers, food equipment, medical devices and servers to keep the profitable repair aftermarket with the OEM. The FTC found "scant evidence" for the safety and security reasons given and documented 2.5-4x price gaps and extreme markups. The scarce layer they protect is cryptographic and legal authorisation, not knowledge, so AI-driven knowledge alone does not dissolve it; legal mandates (the FTC–Deere case, Oregon, the EU 2024/1799 directive, DMCA exemptions) are what open it. Note: the shared web-search budget was used up, so this rests on direct fetches of primary and secondary pages plus a few leads from background knowledge, which the notes mark as unverified.
research.bottleneck: Cryptographic and legal authorisation: who holds the signing keys, the pairing tool, the type certificate or design data rights, and whether DMCA §1201, EULAs and warranties allow anyone else to use them. Knowledge and fabrication are secondary. Regulation (the FTC–Deere settlement, Oregon's pairing ban, EU 2024/1799, DMCA exemptions) is the main lever that moves this layer.
research.money_time: In locked domains the money goes to monopoly-priced OEM parts and labour: 2.5-4x OEM service rates in medical, a 9,400% markup on aerospace parts, dealer-only Deere repairs, and repairs making up about 25% of Taylor's revenue. The time goes to waiting for the one authorised technician or tool: Deere harvest delays, 4-hour OEM minimums in medical, Newag trains stranded at a competitor's depot, broken McDonald's machines. The pairing, calibration and authorisation step after the physical fix is often the gate. Diagnosis knowledge is rarely the dominant cost once a skilled independent can get in.
shapes: OEM-agnostic authorisation and attestation clearinghouse, like AutoAuth generalised to ag, medical, rail, energy and robotics. It turns new legal mandates into logged, auditable access to pairing and calibration for independents, while keeping anti-theft and cyber goals intact.
Compliance and repairability-by-design tooling for OEMs facing EU 2024/1799 and Oregon/Colorado laws, replacing pairing locks with secure but open part authentication.

Independent diagnostic and pairing platforms for newly opened verticals (Deere equipment after the settlements, commercial food equipment after the 2024 DMCA exemption, medical devices), sold to independent service organisations.

Firmware and protocol audit services for fleet buyers (rail operators, hospitals, utilities), modelled on the Newag researchers, that find hidden repair locks before procurement and enforce contract terms.
Caution: pure 'AI knowledge' or 'AI parts factory' plays fail where parts are serial-authenticated or certification-gated. Pair them with the authorisation and certification layer.
surprises: The web-search budget was used up before this agent began, so the evidence comes from direct fetches. Some background-knowledge leads (Tesla Toolbox pricing, the PIRG hospital survey, IATA engine-aftermarket complaints) are flagged as unverified in the notes.
Newag's trains contained deliberate geo-fenced sabotage of competitor workshops, which is stronger evidence of intent than most consumer-electronics cases.
Once regulation forces access, the lock can collapse into a cheap subscription: car secure-gateway access via AutoAuth costs $5-17.50 a month.
The FTC accepted that VIN burning may have real anti-theft benefits, but said they 'could likely be achieved without imposing a substantial burden on independent repair'.

Wikipedia (fetched 2026-10-20) reports that Deere settled both the class action ($99M) and the FTC case in 2026, including opening 'previously software-locked' component pairing. These are unverified primary facts that need docket confirmation.

stances.why: Locks add a step the chain leaves out, 'authorise / pair / calibrate with an OEM key', between repair and return to service. It is a control gate, not a natural repair stage, but it is now often where the delay happens.

OEMs do capture the aftermarket (Deere's 100% share, Taylor's repairs at ~25% of sales, the 2.5-4x medical premium). But the binding constraint is authorisation (crypto keys, dealer-only tools, DMCA §1201, licences), not knowledge. Independents and hackers (Kytch, the Newag researchers) often fully understood the systems and were still blocked.

AI can explain fault codes but cannot sign firmware, produce a paired serial or make circumvention legal. Encrypted ECUs, signed firmware and serial pairing are built to defeat exactly the 'more knowledge' route.

The excess cost sits in monopoly rents on authorisation and parts and in downtime waiting for the authorised technician, not in the cost of cognition. Big cuts have come from legal mandates (the auto MOU, the Deere settlements, DMCA exemptions), not from cheaper diagnosis.

A perfectly made replacement part is still rejected if it lacks the OEM chip or paired serial (HP cartridges, Apple parts, VIN burning, Newag serial checks). In aerospace the barrier is design approval and data rights. Fabrication is not the bottleneck for locked parts.

OEMs justify locks as safety and cybersecurity (Newag's 'safety system', NHTSA's telematics hacking concern, AHAM certification). Opening repair needs a credible neutral attestation and inspection layer to replace the OEM gate, and the FDA's 2018 safety finding suggests such a layer is feasible.

The system is inefficient by design for rent extraction: the FTC found scant evidence for the justifications, Newag sabotaged competitor depots, and TransDigm earns a ~47% margin. It is 'built smart' for the OEM, not 'not built for smart'. Autos and appliances show partial opening through MOUs and authorised networks without a full rebuild.

research.q: Warranty and liability as repair control: how warranty terms, Magnuson-Moss, insurance and product liability push repair to authorised channels; evidence of effect.
research.headline: Warranty, liability and insurance do push repair toward authorised channels. The pressure works mostly through consumer belief, software authorisation and contracts, not through any data showing independent repair is unsafe. The FTC found "scant evidence" for OEMs' liability and safety justifications, and 45 of 50 warranties studied appeared to violate the Magnuson-Moss anti-tying rule. The real lock is authority (tools that unlock software, signatures on return to service, acceptance by lessors and insurers), not knowledge, so AI alone does not dissolve it. Caveat: the shared web-search budget was already used up when this agent started, so several findings come from prior knowledge and are flagged as not re-verified this session.
research.bottleneck: Authority and trust, not knowledge. That means the right to unlock and complete a repair (software authorisation, parts pairing), the right to have it count (warranty causation, lessor and insurer acceptance of parts, signature on return to service), and a defensible allocation of liability backed by an auditable repair record. OEMs keep these layers with contracts and code, and regulators find their safety and liability justifications largely unsupported by data.
research.money_time:
Warranty and liability control shows up most in the diagnose and complete steps.
- **Diagnose:** warranty causation disputes, and OEM bulletins that blame aftermarket parts without analysis.
- **Authorise and complete:** dealer-only software such as Deere's Service ADVISOR, ECU flashing and parts pairing. This creates downtime because farmers must wait for dealers at harvest.
- **Parts margins:** the economic prize is aftermarket parts margin. Deere's ag segment had $7.0B operating profit on $26.8B in sales in FY2023, and engine OEMs earn most of their profit in the aftermarket.
- **When the locks lapse:** after the warranty period about 70-75% of auto repair moves to independents, so the warranty window is where authorised channels capture value.
- **Liability costs** land on repairers (a ~$42M verdict), pushing them to OEM procedures and certification overhead.
shapes: Independent repair attestation and liability layer: an auditable, sensor- and photo-verified repair record plus procedure-compliance proof that insurers, lessors and warrantors accept. It replaces the 'only our network is accountable' justification.

Repair-backed warranty or insurance product for B2B machines (energy assets, robots, ag or industrial equipment) that underwrites independent repair. It flips the warranty lever, in the spirit of the EU's +1-year guarantee for repair.
Causation and diagnostic arbitration tool that settles warranty denial disputes (aftermarket part vs. OEM defect) with evidence. This is valuable because the MMWA turns on causation.

Compliance and enablement for the right-to-repair regulation wave (EU 2024/1799 transposed by July 2026, state ag and electronics laws, FTC v. Deere remedies): helping OEMs publish tools, information and parts while managing security and liability.
Certified alternative-parts qualification service (PMA-like) that makes non-OEM or bespoke parts acceptable to insurers and lessors. Manufacturing alone is not the bottleneck; acceptance is.
surprises: The FTC asked manufacturers for liability data and got none, so the liability argument rests on assertion.

The strongest real liability force falls on independent repairers (the ~$42M body-shop verdict), not on OEMs. It pushes toward OEM procedures, which are information, rather than toward OEM channels as such.
Insurers often push AWAY from OEM parts (Direct Repair Programs, aftermarket parts), so insurance is not a uniform OEM ally.
The MMWA does not cover B2B equipment at all, so the founder's target sectors (energy, machines, aviation) are controlled by contract and software rather than warranty law.
The EU is turning warranty into a pro-repair lever, adding one year of legal guarantee when a consumer chooses repair.

Research limitation: the shared web-search budget was already used up when this agent started. Several findings (the John Eagle verdict, the FDA 2018 report, insurer practice, aviation lessor barriers, the 2022 FTC orders) come from prior knowledge and are flagged as not re-verified in research/repair/raw/z02.md.

stances.why: The warranty and liability evidence adds steps the chain misses. Authorisation and unlocking (software pairing, dealer tools), warranty-causation adjudication, and liability allocation and documentation sit between 'repair' and 'return to service'. The chain is incomplete rather than wrong.

OEMs capture repair, but the FTC and Deere record shows exclusivity enforced by legal and technical locks (warranty tying, software tools, parts pairing, contracts), not only by know-how. It is an authority monopoly more than a knowledge monopoly. Independents do well once the locks lapse (70-75% share after warranty).

AI can supply information, but it cannot grant Service ADVISOR access, change lessor or insurer acceptance, sign a return to service, or shift tort liability. The John Eagle verdict shows that liability enforces procedure fidelity, and any AI-generated procedure would carry that liability.

Diagnosis costs could fall, but diagnosis is also where warranty causation is contested (TSBs blaming aftermarket parts). Sourcing is constrained by lessor and insurer acceptance of non-OEM parts. These cost layers are legal and contractual, so a 10x drop needs regulatory change as well as AI.

Bespoke or alternative parts face acceptance barriers: PMA versus lessor and OEM agreements, insurer and OEM fights over non-OEM parts, and parts pairing that rejects non-serialised parts. Making a part is not the same as having it accepted and allowed.

Liability and insurance arguments hinge on a trusted record and attestation of repair (AHAM: records 'assist in insurance claims'). The FDA could not conclude either way for lack of data. Independent, auditable inspection and certification is the scarce trust layer that would replace OEM-channel justifications.

The inefficiency is real and partly deliberate (the FTC found steering and a lack of justification), but it is built for rent capture through legal design, not 'not built for smart'. Regulators (FTC enforcement, Deere suit, EU directive, state laws) are already dismantling it piecemeal. That is a regulatory tailwind, not a need for a total rebuild.

research.q: Dealer and authorised service networks economics (car dealers earn most profit from service and parts; ag and construction dealers): why do networks persist and what share of OEM profit flows through them?
research.headline: Across autos, heavy trucks and ag/construction, parts and service are only about 10-35% of dealer revenue but about 40-64% of dealer gross profit. On the OEM side, parts can be about two-thirds of profit: PACCAR made $1.67B pretax on parts versus $0.87B on trucks in 2025. Dealer networks persist mainly because law, contracts, dealer-only diagnostic tools, warranty flows and parts capture lock repair to them, not mainly because of know-how. So AI that closes the knowledge gap alone will not dissolve them.
research.bottleneck: The scarce layer is authorised access, not knowledge. It consists of dealer-only diagnostic and calibration software, proprietary parts distribution, near-total dealer parts capture, warranty tying, and state franchise statutes protecting dealer territories. All of this sits on top of a physical constraint of local technician capacity and parts inventory. Aftermarket absorption (above 100% at Rush) is what keeps dealers alive, so they and the OEMs will defend these chokepoints.
research.money_time: The money is in parts and labor, not in diagnosis as a separate line. US auto dealer fixed ops were $93.4B in parts and $75.8B in labor in 2025, at a $186/hour customer rate. Diagnosis and 'understanding' are billed inside labor hours. Parts carry the margin: about 31% gross at ag dealers, about 24% pretax at PACCAR, and 'massive' at Deere per the FTC. Service labor carries 50-60% gross margin at dealers. OEMs pay about $32B a year of warranty work into US auto dealers. Time losses come from dealer capacity and travel: a 30-60 mile service radius, field-call charges, owners 'often unable to obtain timely dealer service' (FTC v. Deere), and a technician constraint of 16 technicians per store and 278k nationwide.
shapes: Diagnostic and service-tool layer for independents in heavy equipment and ag, the 'Snap-on/Bosch for Deere-class machines' play. It rides any FTC v. Deere settlement or state R2R law that forces tool and data access, since the market opens as the legal locks fall.

AI technician co-pilot sold TO dealers and OEMs, not against them. Dealers are technician-constrained (16 techs per store, $186/hr) and live or die on absorption ratio, so throughput gains are bought immediately and channel conflict is avoided.

Multi-brand independent field-service network for mixed fleets (trucks, ag, construction, energy assets), competing on response time against the 30-60 mile dealer radius and on 'often unable to obtain timely dealer service', using remote diagnosis to dispatch the right part the first time.

Aftermarket and remanufactured parts platform for out-of-warranty installed bases, attacking the 24-31% parts margins. This needs IP-clean parts and a certification story to counter the OEM safety narrative, because legal capture rather than manufacturability is the barrier.

Telematics and data-access intermediary for owners, in the spirit of the Massachusetts telematics law and the EU block exemption. Whoever controls machine data decides where repair goes, so an owner-controlled data layer redirects the profit pool.
surprises: PACCAR's parts segment made nearly twice the pretax profit of its truck segment in 2025 ($1,668M vs $871M) on about a third of the revenue. Aftermarket is the OEM's real business in a down cycle.
Rush's 130.7% absorption ratio means the truck dealer's aftermarket alone covers all overhead.
About 25% of Lithia's aftersales and about $32B of US dealer fixed ops are OEM-paid warranty, so the OEM directly funds the network's service P&L, which ties dealers to OEMs further.
Dealers wholesale $24.5B a year of OEM parts to independent shops, so independents are partly customers of the network rather than pure competitors.

Even with 63% of gross profit from parts and service, Titan Machinery ran an operating loss. Ag dealer economics are thin, which weakens the 'fat rent' story for ag dealers specifically, though not for the OEM.
Deere disclosed in its Dec 2025 10-K that it is in preliminary settlement discussions with the FTC, so forced tool access may arrive soon.

stances.why: Dealer financials do not test a universal repair chain. They only show that triggers and payers vary: warranty (OEM-paid), internal reconditioning and customer-pay repair orders take different paths.

The OEM and dealer capture is real and large (Deere dealer-only tool, near-total dealer parts capture, FTC findings). But it is enforced mainly through software and tool authorisation, contracts, warranty and franchise law, not through knowledge scarcity. Dealers also wholesale $24.5B of OEM parts to independents, so independents are not shut out everywhere.

The binding constraints in dealer networks are tool authorisation (Service ADVISOR), proprietary parts, warranty tying and state franchise statutes. AI-generated knowledge does not unlock these. The Deere case shows owners often know how to fix the machine but cannot get the software to do it.

Diagnosis and understanding are bundled into $130-200/hour labor, and parts carry 30% gross margins at dealers and about 24% pretax at the OEM. These rents are compressible. But physical parts ($93B of $165B dealer fixed ops), technician time and a 30-60 mile service radius do not fall 10x from information alone.

OEM parts are 'proprietary'. Dealer agreements push OEM parts, and warranty and IP protections defend them. The barrier is legal and commercial capture, which an AI parts factory does not remove. No evidence here shows bespoke manufacture displacing OEM parts.

Authorised repair and warranty requirements act as a de facto certification layer that OEMs use to keep work in the network. Inspection persists, but often as a steering mechanism; the FTC found scant evidence for the safety justifications.

The system is structurally designed to monetise the installed base. Equipment is sold at 4-7% margins and profit is recovered through aftermarket parts and service (40-65% of dealer gross profit, about two-thirds of PACCAR pretax), protected by franchise law and software locks. It is inefficient for owners but rational for OEMs and dealers, so a rebuild faces entrenched opposition.

research.q: Standardisation and modularity as repair enablers (line replaceable units, Open Compute, modular phones like Fairphone/Framework, MIL-STD parts): evidence that modularity cut repair cost.
research.headline: Modularity and standardisation do cut repair cost and especially downtime: field-level swaps return the asset to service while the failed unit is fixed offline, and Fairphone-style user-swappable parts are roughly 2-4x cheaper per repair. But the cost doesn't disappear. It moves into spares inventory, logistics and fault isolation, and adoption is held back by incentives, certification and physical penalties far more than by a knowledge gap.
research.bottleneck: Control and standardisation of the interface (who owns the spec, data rights, parts serialisation), accurate fault isolation down to the replaceable unit, and certification/qualification of any module that isn't the original. Repair-procedure knowledge is mostly not the scarce layer where modularity exists; incentives (replacement revenue, prime-contractor lock-in) and qualification are.
research.money_time: With modular/LRU architectures, time at the asset collapses to fault isolation plus a swap, so downtime (often the dominant cost for airliners, servers and industrial assets) falls most. The money then sits in (a) rotable spares inventory and logistics needed to make swaps instant, (b) depot repair of pulled units, and (c) waste from poor fault isolation: no-fault-found removals cost DoD more than $2bn a year. In consumer devices the part price dominates once labour is near zero (Fairphone modules EUR20-115), and the remaining friction is part availability, delivery time, serialisation and firmware support, which is why the EU now mandates 5-day parts delivery and 1-day information access.
shapes: Fault-isolation / no-fault-found reduction software for LRU-based fleets (defence, avionics, rail, wind, data centres): there is a clear dollar pool (>$2bn/yr at DoD alone), and it turns built-in-test and maintenance logs into the right swap decision.

Modular open systems tooling (interface spec generation, conformance testing, metrics) for defence, drone and robotics programmes: GAO found DoD lacked both the expertise and the metrics, while NDAAs mandate MOSA.
Rotables/spares-pool optimisation for modular energy, robotics and drone fleets: modularity moves cost into inventory, so predictive placement of LRUs is the lever.

Design-for-repair modular platforms for new hardware categories (swappable actuator, battery or inverter modules with open interfaces), copying the LRU and Framework playbook where no incumbent lock-in exists yet.
Independent conformance/certification labs for third-party modules: the inspection layer a modular aftermarket needs, since self-reported repair scores and per-configuration certification are gaps.
surprises: Fairphone's modularity overhead is only 2.3% of production carbon but 17.2% of mineral-resource depletion, because of gold-plated connectors.
After 12 years and 10/10 repair scores, Fairphone shipped about 145k phones in 2025 (around 0.01% of the global market) with near-zero EBITDA.
Framework's main pain points are firmware/BIOS updates and shipping delays, not mechanical repair.
Interchangeable parts cost more than hand-made ones for decades before savings appeared (around 1853).
Aviation is partly moving away from many federated LRUs toward integrated modular avionics, trading LRU count for certification complexity.
Research limitation: the shared web-search budget was exhausted, so findings come from direct fetches of known sources; the DTIC LRU cost study returned 403.

stances.why: The steps exist, but modularity forks the chain: at the point of use it becomes notice, isolate to module, swap from stock, test, and the full diagnose/repair chain runs later and offline at the depot. It is not one linear sequence at system level.

The EU rule treats information access as one barrier among several (parts, 5-day delivery, fasteners, serialisation). GAO and Ara show the lock-in comes from incentives, interface ownership and data rights as much as from knowledge.

In the past the knowledge gap was closed by standards embedded in interfaces (gauges, ARINC trays, screws), not by information. The remaining hard problems are firmware, certification, pairing and physical penalties, which AI does not remove.

Modular part-level repair is 2-4x cheaper for phones and cuts downtime sharply in aviation and data centres. But the cost moves to rotable inventory and logistics, and NFF (>$2bn/yr at DoD) shows diagnosis stays expensive. Nothing here shows an order-of-magnitude drop across all four steps.
FCC per-configuration certification, DO-254/297 qualification of every module, and connector/interface qualification mean a bespoke part is not a drop-in without requalification.
Certification is the gating constraint for modular avionics, and self-reported repairability scores show a verification gap that needs an independent inspection layer.

Incentives do keep systems closed (carriers and OEMs profit from replacement, slow MOSA adoption at DoD). But wherever the owner bears the downtime cost (airlines with LRUs, hyperscalers), repair is highly optimised. The industry is misaligned rather than built to be inefficient everywhere.

research.q: Information asymmetry in repair markets (credence goods literature: Dulleck & Kerschbamer, auto repair fraud studies, Taylor 1995): how much overcharging comes from diagnosis opacity?
research.headline: Diagnosis opacity is real but accounts for a modest share of repair overcharging. Audits find strict billing fraud at only 4.5-6% of garages and about 2% of total charges, plus 5-15% price premiums charged to visibly uninformed customers. The large multiples come from elsewhere: third-party payment (+80% when an insurer pays) and OEM control of tools, software and parts (2-4x hourly-rate gaps). The literature also finds that the institution that fixes credence-goods fraud is liability (a guaranteed fix), not transparency.
research.bottleneck: Incentives, not information. The same party diagnoses and repairs, there is no liability for outcomes, the customer cannot verify the work afterwards, and a third party often pays. On top of this sits OEM control of diagnostic software and parts. Knowledge asymmetry lets these extract value, but the lab evidence shows that transparency alone barely helps while outcome liability (a guaranteed fix) is what drives efficiency.
research.money_time: In consumer auto repair audits, outright billing fraud is low single digits (about 2% of charges). Price discrimination against visibly uninformed customers adds roughly 5-15%. Over- and under-treatment, driven by both incompetence and incentives, is 'pervasive': about 15% of even easy faults are missed, and about 28% of dentists overtreated a healthy patient (unverified). This is probably the largest share, but it is poorly measured. The biggest multiples sit in payer structure (+80% when insured) and in OEM-locked access to tools, software and parts ($500-600/h OEM vs $150-250/h independent; OEM parts 15-50% dearer). The diagnosis step is where fraud originates, but the money is extracted in treatment and parts.
shapes: Guaranteed-outcome or fixed-price repair (pay only if fixed), underwritten by AI diagnosis accurate enough to price the risk. Liability is the institution the lab evidence (DKS 2011) shows works.

Independent AI diagnosis and audit sold to third-party payers (insurers, fleets, lessors, MRO buyers), because insurance coverage inflates bills by more than 80%. Customer-requested monitoring is shown to cut overcharging and undertreatment.
Competence copilot for technicians. Missed faults (about 15% of easy ones) and undertreatment are as costly as fraud, and low competence predicts fraud.
Access-layer plays (diagnostic software and data interoperability, remanufactured or alternative parts) aimed at the 2-4x OEM gaps, dependent on right-to-repair law and DMCA 1201 exemptions.
Inspection designed for independence (the inspector is not chosen or paid by the inspected party), with AI evidence capture, since Hubbard shows inspection chosen by the customer drifts lenient.
Caution: a consumer 'AI tells you what's wrong' app attacks the smallest slice (about 2% fraud, 5-15% quote discrimination).
surprises: Strict billing fraud in audited garages is low (4.5% of German corporate garages; 6% of US visits; 2% of charges), while 74% of consumers fear being cheated.
Insurance coverage (+80%) drives overcharging more than customer ignorance (+15pp in the taxi study).
In the lab, transparency (verifiability) barely helps; outcome liability is what matters.
Shops that cheat are the same ones that miss faults: incompetence and fraud go together.
Separating diagnosis from treatment cut overtreatment but raised undertreatment.
Reputation fails to discipline mechanics, yet it pushes inspectors toward leniency.

The shared web-search budget was exhausted before this agent could search. The findings come from direct fetches of primary pages, and two items (Gottschalk et al. dentists; the DOT 53% estimate) are from memory and unverified.

stances.why: The credence-goods model treats repair as diagnosis then treatment and says the fraud comes from one seller doing both. It does not test a universal multi-stage chain.

Information asymmetry is the defining feature, and uninformed customers are exploited (taxis +15pp; quote premiums for uninformed callers). But strict fraud is small (2-6%). The large rents come from OEM control of tools, software and parts (FTC, 2-4x gaps) and from payer moral hazard (+80% when insured), which are not knowledge gaps.

AI can cut price opacity and make second opinions cheap, which reduces fraud. But the customer still cannot verify what was done inside the machine, verifiability barely helped in the lab without liability, experts adapt, and insurance-driven overcharging is untouched by customer knowledge.

The measured information-rent share of repair bills is about 2-15%. Only OEM access-locked segments show 2-4x gaps. Nothing in the credence-goods literature supports a 10x drop from better information alone.
Only indirect: the FTC shows alternative parts are 15-50% cheaper but are blocked by OEM software and legal locks, not just by slow manufacturing.

Hubbard shows inspectors chosen by the inspected party drift lenient, and lab work shows the design of monitoring matters. Inspection is essential, its incentive design (who pays the inspector) is the crux, and cheap AI audits on demand fit the evidence.

The inefficiency is a rational equilibrium of bad institutions: bundled diagnosis and repair, unverifiability, short-term contracts, third-party payers and access restrictions. The fixes the literature points to are institutional (liability, guarantees, competition) as much as technological.

research.q: Repair as a share of GDP and productivity: economic studies on maintenance spending, capital depreciation and the maintenance economy (e.g., Jo Guldi, "Maintainers" movement Vinsel & Russell); what do they argue?
research.headline: Repair is large and stable: in Canadian business data it has run at 23-28% of capex for 20 years (about 3% of GDP for business repair alone), and its main costs are scarce, rising-price labour and downtime, not missing knowledge. Maintenance scholars (Vinsel & Russell, Edgerton, ASCE) blame under-maintenance on funding, incentives, low status and accounting invisibility, and even predictive-maintenance boosters claim cost cuts of 5-40%, not 10x.
research.bottleneck: Skilled maintenance labour and its stagnant productivity (the Baumol wedge), combined with institutional under-funding of upkeep: capital budgets favour new builds and maintenance is invisible as an expense line. Information access is not the main bottleneck. The costliest symptom is downtime driven by time-to-restore.
research.money_time: Business repair is about a quarter of capex (Canada: C$95B against C$369B in 2024, about 3% of GDP for business repair alone, and possibly about 6% including all maintenance per McGrattan-Schmitz, unverified). It approaches capex in heavy mobile equipment (mining, 74%). Within repair, skilled labour is the dominant and fastest-inflating cost (US vehicle repair CPI +61% vs +33% since 2019). The largest economic loss is downtime (about $1.4T a year, 11% of Global 500 revenue). Downtime is driven by time-to-restore, meaning waiting for parts, technicians and approvals, more than by diagnosis cost.
shapes: Technician-productivity AI (field copilots that let junior techs do senior work). It attacks the labour scarcity and Baumol price rise, which is where the evidence says the cost is.
Downtime-minimisation services for high cost-per-hour assets (auto plants at $2.3M/hr, heavy industry, mining). Examples: predictive spares positioning, guaranteed time-to-restore contracts.
Heavy mobile equipment and mining maintenance as a beachhead, because repair spend nearly equals equipment capex there (74% in Canada).

Asset-condition and maintenance-liability registries for municipalities and utilities. They make deferred maintenance visible and financeable, addressing the Vinsel/Russell/ASCE failure mode, which is about governance and money rather than knowledge.
surprises: Canadian manufacturing machinery repair spending fell 31% in nominal terms from 2006 to 2024 while machinery capex rose 53%. Repair intensity in factories is declining, not exploding.
Repair as a share of capex has been remarkably stable for 20 years (23-28%) in Canada, the rare country that measures it.
Downtime hours per plant are falling (39 to 27 a month since 2019) while cost per hour has doubled. The value of speed is rising.
The leading maintenance scholars (Vinsel & Russell) would read a 'rebuild repair with AI' pitch as the innovation-speak they critique. Their fix is funding and status for maintainers.

The WebSearch budget was exhausted before this agent ran. Findings rely on direct fetches of primary data plus flagged unverified leads (notably McGrattan & Schmitz 1999, and Guldi's work, which could not be fetched).

stances.why: No source disputes a generic chain. But much maintenance is scheduled or condition-based replacement that skips the notice and diagnose steps, and the economic value sits in downtime and time-to-restore rather than in a linear chain.

The repair price premium and technician scarcity fit specialists capturing rents. But the maintenance literature attributes under-maintenance to funding, incentives, status and accounting invisibility, and Edgerton's evidence shows repair knowledge diffuses where lock-in is weak.
The binding constraints are skilled labour (569k openings a year, rising wages) and tacit, embodied skill, not information access. Repair price inflation through 2026 shows no sign of collapse.

Even digital-maintenance boosters claim 5-10% cost cuts (Deloitte) up to 40% (Siemens' own claim). Most cost is labour, parts and downtime. In Canadian data repair is a stable 23-28% of capex, with no sign of 10x compressibility.
The macro maintenance literature does not address bespoke part fabrication.
Inspection-led regimes (ASCE, DoD) are implicit, but there is no direct evidence on how inspection must evolve for AI.

Scholars agree on structural under-investment in upkeep (innovation bias, capital budgets favouring new builds). But they call for revaluing maintainers and funding upkeep rather than a tech rebuild, and Canadian repair intensity is stable, even falling in manufacturing.

research.q: Design for maintainability and its absence: studies on how much of lifecycle repair cost is locked in at design; examples where redesign cut maintenance (e.g., LEAP vs CFM56, A350 vs older).
research.headline: Most lifecycle repair cost is set at design and contract time. Sustainment is about 76% of the F-35's $1.7T lifecycle cost, and GAO says cuts get harder as programs mature, though the precise "70% committed at design" figure is folklore. Redesigns aimed at efficiency usually raise maintenance cost and lower durability in their first generation (LEAP support was priced about 64% above the CFM56; the GTF engine's problems cost $6-7B). Maintenance falls through later step-by-step fixes, material changes and modules that can be swapped on the aircraft, and better knowledge alone does not achieve it.
research.bottleneck: Durability and maintainability set at design, plus physical capacity to repair (shop slots, life-limited parts, specialist tooling) and certified traceability of parts. In defense, technical data rights fixed in the acquisition contract also gate repair. Knowledge of what is wrong is rarely the bottleneck.
research.money_time: Over a life cycle, operating and sustainment cost dominates: about 76% of the F-35's lifecycle cost. Within it, the money goes to physical shop work, life-limited parts (about $3.5-4M per CFM56 engine) and replacing hot-section parts. The time goes to queues for shop slots and parts: 250-300 day geared-turbofan inspections and 10,000+ F-35 parts awaiting repair. Diagnosis and understanding are a small share. Design and contract choices (durability margins, modules that can be swapped on the aircraft, rights to technical data) set most of these costs before service begins.
shapes: Tools that model maintainability and lifecycle cost at the design stage for hardware and robotics OEMs: costs get locked in early, so that is where the value is
Software to improve shop throughput and capacity for engine and component repair shops, since queues dominate time
Traceability and certification infrastructure for parts (digital records of origin, approval-ready paperwork for made or repaired parts), as AOG Technics shows the gap
Durability analytics that link fleet operating conditions (dust, heat) to retrofit decisions, as with the LEAP durability kit
Help for defense buyers to specify and value technical data rights at contract time
surprises: Next-generation engines cost more to maintain, not less: LEAP-1A support was priced about 64% above the CFM56, and the geared turbofan was a durability disaster costing $6-7B
The '70% of cost committed at design' figure is weakly sourced folklore, though its direction holds
Measurable maintenance savings came from step-by-step tech-insertion programs (CFM56-7 15% cheaper to maintain than the -3), not from clean-sheet designs
The F-35 'knowledge monopoly' is a contractual artifact (technical data never purchased), not a gap in know-how
The web search budget was used up for this run, so several aviation details (A350 check intervals, LEAP durability kit) come from prior knowledge and were not checked this session

stances.why: The chain describes field repair, but it leaves out design, which sets most cost before any failure, and the shop-capacity queue, which dominated the geared-turbofan crisis.

Information gating is real (F-35 data rights, EU access rules), but it is legal and contractual and was created at design and contract time. Much of the cost is physical: durability, life-limited parts, shop slots.
AI cannot create approved repair data or data rights, and it cannot make hot-section parts more durable. The F-35 and engine cases are not bottlenecked on knowing what is wrong.

The big costs in engines are shop work and parts. Diagnosis by borescope and temperature trend is cheap. The 250-300 day geared-turbofan inspections are a capacity problem, so a 10x cut in the four intermediate steps would barely move total cost.

Provenance and certification bind (AOG Technics). Flight-critical hot-section parts with ceramic-composite coatings and powder metallurgy are among the hardest parts to make and qualify. The powder-metal contamination crisis was itself a manufacturing-quality failure.
The geared-turbofan recall, the A350 paint dispute, the 787 inspections and AOG Technics all show inspection and certification as the gate. New designs create new inspection needs.

Inefficiency is largely designed in and hard to remove later (GAO), which supports 'built to be inefficient'. But it comes from deliberate trade-offs (fuel efficiency over durability) and aftermarket business models, not from a lack of smarts. The place to fix it is design and contracts.

research.q: Digital twins and maintenance records (aircraft back-to-birth traceability, blockchain parts tracking, Skywise, Boeing AnalytX): do digital records reduce repair cost and who owns them?
research.headline: Digital maintenance records and twins do cut specific repair costs: they lower no-fault-found removals, let parts be staged before an aircraft lands, reduce technical cancellations, speed lease transitions and resist forged certificates like AOG Technics. The benchmarks point to 10-40% savings in specific categories, not an order of magnitude. Operators legally own their maintenance records, but OEMs (Skywise, AnalytX, power-by-the-hour engine contracts) control the sensor data, analytics, manuals and repair approvals, so the 'knowledge monopoly' has moved into a data plus certification plus IP monopoly rather than disappearing. CAVEAT: the shared web-search budget was used up and direct fetches failed (404/403/empty), so every finding is from model prior knowledge and none was re-verified this session.
research.bottleneck: Trusted, machine-readable, transferable provenance and certification: serial-level part and aircraft history that a regulator, lessor or buyer will accept, plus access to the OEM-controlled sensor and repair data behind it. The scarce asset is not knowledge but authenticated data rights and certification authority.
research.money_time: In aviation, money goes mostly to material and engine shop visits, priced by OEM IP and certification (engines ~40% of MRO spend, recall). Time is lost in diagnosis (no-fault-found removals, ~30-50% of line-replaceable-unit removals), in waiting for parts while an aircraft is grounded, and in records reconciliation during lease transitions and parts trading. Digital records attack time and waste (staging parts before arrival, fewer no-fault-found removals, faster audits). They affect price only indirectly, by making used serviceable material (USM) and PMA (non-OEM approved) parts tradeable through trusted provenance.
shapes: Records digitisation plus AI provenance layer: turn paper and scanned PDF trace packs into verified, back-to-birth-complete digital records for lessors and MROs. Lease transitions and used-parts sales are blocked by records, not knowledge. (Check incumbents such as FLYdocs, Bluetail and ProvenAir, recalled names to verify.)

Native issuer of digital release certificates (ATA Spec 2000 Ch.16) with physical anchoring (part marking or fingerprinting), so certificates cannot be forged the way AOG Technics forged paper ones and blockchain could not prevent.
OEM-independent component digital twin for no-fault-found reduction: serial-level fault histories across operators. Diagnosis waste is measurable and OEM platforms are siloed.

Data-rights connector for energy and robotics fleets that uses the EU Data Act and right-to-repair rules to give independent repairers access to OEM machine data. That access gap is the real knowledge monopoly outside aviation.
surprises: The value of an aircraft part can depend more on its paperwork than its metal: an LLP without back-to-birth records is near-scrap.
Blockchain parts tracking mostly stalled because a ledger cannot stop forgery at the point of entry; the value came from marketplaces and standards.
Operators legally own the records, yet OEM data platforms (Skywise) became the new moat by owning the analytics and cross-fleet insight.
Regulators accepted electronic records and certificates years ago (AC 120-78A, 2016), so regulation is not what is holding back digitisation.
Research note: the shared web search budget was used up, so no finding in this report was verified this session.

stances.why: OEM health monitoring (AHM, Skywise) is built around the notice, diagnose and source-parts steps, which fits the chain. But records and provenance are a cross-cutting layer that runs through every stage and through asset transfer, not a step in a linear chain.

OEMs control fleet data platforms, engine sensor data under power-by-the-hour contracts, manuals and repair approvals. The Deere and Massachusetts telematics fights show the gap is often an enforced access gap rather than missing know-how.
The gap that matters is access to proprietary serial-level data, certification and trusted provenance. AI cannot synthesise those, and AOG Technics shows the binding problem is trust, not knowledge.

Hard benchmarks show 10-40% savings in specific categories (predictive maintenance, no-fault-found, avoided cancellations). The main aviation cost drivers (engine shop visits, OEM-priced material) are not reduced 10x by better records.

Back-to-birth requirements mean a part without certified provenance is worth near zero even when it is physically perfect. A newly made bespoke part needs PMA/DER approval and traceability before it can be installed.

Forged certificates and the oracle limits of blockchain show certification and physical inspection are the binding trust layer. Digital e-certificates (Spec 2000 Ch.16) are how that layer is evolving.

Fragmented paper records, failed blockchain pilots and OEM data lock-in point to structural inefficiency. But the regulatory permission for digital records already exists, so this looks more like incentives and business model (OEM aftermarket margins) than an industry 'built to be inefficient'.

research.q: Cannibalisation and pooling (airline component pools like Lufthansa Technik TCS, AFI KLM, military cannibalisation rates): how sharing spares cuts cost; why not universal?
research.headline: Sharing spares does cut cost: pooling needs much less safety stock, and cannibalisation keeps fleets flying. But GAO data show military cannibalisation costing about 5.3M extra labour hours over FY1996-2000, and the F-35 global pool failing (aircraft unable to fly about 30% of the time for lack of parts, 188-day repair turnaround, 44% of a deployment package incompatible). Pooling breaks on repair throughput, configuration and traceability data, correlated demand, allocation governance and who controls the pool, not on knowledge alone. That is why it is not universal.
research.bottleneck: Repair-loop throughput (depot and shop capacity and turnaround) and qualified part supply, plus control of the pool: configuration and traceability data, allocation rules across owners, and OEM ownership of technical data. Knowledge gaps matter at the edge (swap-to-diagnose, missing test equipment) but are not the main constraint.
research.money_time: Time and money pile up in the repair loop for broken rotables and in parts production, not in diagnosis. F-35 repair turnaround was about 188 days against a 60-90 day objective, the backlog grew from 4,300 (2018) to more than 10,000 (2023), and aircraft could not fly about 30% of the time for lack of parts. Cannibalisation converts parts shortages into labour (about 7.2 extra hours per action, 5.3M hours over 5 years) and into hidden reliability costs. In commercial aviation the money is rotable inventory capital plus AOG downtime. Pooling attacks the capital term; proximity and pre-agreed exchange terms attack the downtime term.
shapes: Neutral, configuration-aware rotable pool and exchange for fleets without TCS-style pools (wind, rail, mining, data-centre power, defence drones): pooling's square-root inventory savings are proven in airlines, but the governance and traceability layer is missing elsewhere

Swap-to-diagnose reducer: AI-guided troubleshooting plus portable or automated test equipment for military and fleet maintainers. GAO quantifies up to half of Navy cannibalisations as non-supply-driven, with millions of wasted hours
Rotable repair-loop accelerator (automated test stations, high-throughput component repair) because turnaround time, not knowledge, sets pool size and readiness

Qualified re-manufacture for diminishing-manufacturing-sources parts with certification and traceability built in, selling to defence and legacy fleets that currently rely on donor hulks and lifetime buys
surprises: Up to half of Navy cannibalisations are not caused by missing stock: they happen because it is faster than walking across base, or to diagnose faults without test equipment or training

The largest shared spares pool in defence (F-35, run by the OEM) performed badly: about 30% of the time unable to fly for lack of parts, cannibalisation at more than 6x target, 44% of a deployment kit incompatible, and thousands of parts missing from the registry
Pooling across sovereign owners created a governance problem: there is no mechanism to give priority units more parts without breaking program rules
DoD called 5.3M cannibalisation hours 'negligible', and all of GAO's 2001 recommendations were closed without being implemented
WebSearch budget was exhausted before this agent ran, so the evidence comes from direct fetches of GAO primary sources and commercial pooling figures are thin

stances.why: The stages exist but the chain is not linear. Cannibalisation merges sourcing into diagnosis (swap-to-diagnose), and sourcing from a donor creates a new repair loop on that aircraft.

The Navy IG blames some cannibalisation on poor training, outdated manuals and missing test equipment, and the F-35 lacks government-held technical data. But the dominant drivers are parts supply, repair capacity and readiness incentives.

The F-35 data gap is about IP and contracts, repair turnaround (188 days, 10,000-part backlog) is physical capacity, test equipment is hardware, and cannibalisation incentives are organisational. AI does not remove any of these.

Pooling shows sourcing cost can fall sharply through sharing. But the F-35 pool shows gains vanish when repair throughput, configuration data and allocation governance fail. The binding cost is downtime in the repair loop, not information.

Replacement makers for obsolete parts (F-14 transmitter, F-35 canopy coating, EA-6B antenna) brought delays and QA failures. Institutions prefer donor hulks and lifetime buys because qualification is the hard part.
Used and cannibalised parts carry life and traceability risk, pools depend on certification paperwork and accountability registries, and QA caught a failing antenna from a new contractor.

Inertia is real: 2001 GAO recommendations were never implemented and 70% of F-35 recommendations are open. But cannibalisation is a rational response to readiness incentives and shortages, so this is an incentive and ownership design problem, not 'not smart'.

research.q: Time decomposition of a repair event: find any studies that split total downtime into detection, diagnosis, waiting for parts, waiting for technician, repair, test/inspection (any industry: e.g., military ALDT/MLDT logistics delay time, mean logistics delay).
research.headline: Military reliability engineering has split downtime into active repair, logistics delay and administrative delay (MDT = Mct + MLDT + MADT) for decades. Where the split is measured, waiting for parts, waiting on approvals and funding, and missing physical capacity take far more time than diagnosis or hands-on repair. GAO's F-35 report also shows a knowledge monopoly that is real but contractual: OEMs hold the technical data and withhold it, which AI cannot fix by itself.
research.bottleneck: Availability of parts and repair material, set by spares-inventory economics and OEM control of the supply chain, combined with legal control of technical data (data rights, part numbers). Physical repair capacity and skilled labor come after that. Knowledge is a bottleneck mainly where it is contractually withheld. Better reasoning alone does not unlock it; it needs access to the data plus authority to repair or make the part.
research.money_time: In every domain with measured data, total downtime is dominated by waiting rather than working. The order is: (1) waiting for parts or repair material (F-35 NMCS about 27% of all aircraft time, depot cycle 141 days, wind turbine major-component failures about 95% of downtime); (2) administrative, approval and funding delay (Navy 26-189 days for funding approval, truck authorization workflows); (3) physical capacity and labor (dry docks, skilled trades, cranes, vessels: 33,700 extra Navy ship-days). Diagnosis matters a lot in avionics and electronics (30-50% NFF false removals feed the parts pipeline) and wherever OEMs withhold technical data (60+ day request loops). Active wrench time and final test are usually the smallest buckets.
shapes: An AI diagnostics / NFF-reduction layer for avionics and industrial electronics. It targets the 30-50% false-removal rate that wastes parts-pipeline capacity, has a measurable ROI, and can sell to MROs and defense depots.

Organic repair / reverse-engineering plus qualified additive or CNC remanufacture for long-lead or obsolete defense and energy parts. GAO shows 95-week buy vs 4-week repair, and the DoD is actively pushing right-to-repair and IP strategy for F-35-like fleets.

Repair workflow / MADT-killer software that routes approvals, estimates and funding decisions, as in the Decisiv truck model. It attacks the administrative bucket, which is large and needs no new physics.

A technical-data reconstruction service for sustainment (AI-assisted creation of repair manuals and data packages from teardown and inspection). It speaks directly to the F-35 depot finding that manuals are too vague to learn from.

Predictive spares positioning for heavy assets such as wind or ships. Since the downtime tail is long-lead parts plus lift logistics, pre-positioning based on failure prediction moves the dominant bucket.
surprises: The founder's chain is not new. The DoD has formally decomposed downtime as MDT = active repair + MLDT + MADT since at least the MIL-HDBK-472 era, and the RAND Velocity Management work cut Army order-ship time by about 60% using exactly this segment-by-segment framing, without AI.
F-35 spares are deliberately funded to tolerate 15% NMCS because lower is 'not affordable'. Part of the parts-waiting inefficiency is a chosen cost trade-off, not ignorance.
The F-35 knowledge monopoly runs even between OEM tiers: a subcontractor refused to share data partly to keep it away from the prime contractor.
Navy delays are dominated by capacity, labor and funding approval (26-189 days), not diagnosis.

Method caveat: the shared WebSearch budget was exhausted, so several findings (wind turbine 25/95, NFF 30-50%, RAND 22->8 days, MIL-HDBK splits) are from memory and need verification. Notes are in /home/user/nuketime/research/repair/raw/z10.md

stances.why: The chain matches the long-standing DoD/MIL-HDBK decomposition (detection/latent time, active repair broken into isolation through checkout, MLDT, MADT) and the SEMI E10 states. It leaves out administrative, approval and funding delay as a stage, though, and that is one of the biggest buckets (Navy funding approval 26-189 days; truck authorization).

The F-35 is a textbook case. The OEM controls the technical data, tech-data requests take 60+ days, contractors are needed for 'routine troubleshooting', and depots cannot learn the repairs. The monopoly is contractual (data rights), not a lack of general know-how.

Where the knowledge is proprietary and withheld, as with F-35 technical data and part numbers, AI has nothing to ground on. NFF rates also show diagnosis is limited by observability and intermittent faults, not only by expertise.

Documented step-changes are 2.5-3x (Army order-ship time, F/A-18 generator) and up to 24x for a single part (gearbox). Total downtime is floored by parts inventory economics (F-35 spares funded only to 15% NMCS), physical capacity and heavy-lift logistics, so a 10x drop across the whole event is not supported.

Organic repair or remanufacture instead of OEM new-buy collapses time (95 weeks to 4 weeks). But F-35 depot delays came from lack of repair material and data rights, which an AI factory needs too. The evidence gives no sign that bespoke making is solved.
The standards treat checkout and qualification as distinct states, but no source here measured inspection's share of downtime or how AI is changing it.

The inefficiency is real and persistent: 75% of Navy maintenance periods ran late, and most aircraft types miss mission-capable goals. Much of it, however, is a deliberate cost trade-off (spares budgets) or a capacity and labor shortage, not a structure that is 'not built for smart'.

verdicts.text: Every repair at any scale follows one chain: notice, diagnose, understand, source parts, deliver parts, repair, safety inspection, return to service.
verdicts.one_line: Of the 98 agents that took a stance, 92 say mixed, 5 support and 1 contradicts. All eight steps show up in nearly every domain, so the chain works as a checklist of tasks. It fails as a description of one linear, universal process: most money and elapsed time sit in loops, gates and pre-positioning that the chain leaves out (authorization or approval, queueing for capacity, repair-or-replace decisions, scheduled replacement, and swap-now-repair-later).
supporting_evidence: Regulation writes the tail of the chain into law. Inspection or monitoring finds the issue, work must use approved data, and a qualified person signs the return to service: 14 CFR 43.9/43.11, EASA Part-145, ASME XI (i03, i02).
The DoD/MIL-HDBK maintainability breakdown matches C1: detection or latent time, active repair split into isolation through checkout, MLDT and MADT. SEMI E10 equipment states map the same way (z10).
Apple Self Service Repair runs the chain directly: manual, order part, repair, System Configuration, return the old part (s02).

Startups sort cleanly onto the stages: sensing for notice, Dawn/Talos for diagnose, KorrAI for understand, Mecho for parts, Rodeo/Proprio for repair, GroundControl/F4 for inspection (x05). Software vendors do the same: Samsara/Augury, Aquant/Veryon, ServiceTitan, Gecko (x01).
Sourcing and delivery are large standalone businesses: more than $50B combined revenue across five MRO and parts distributors (p04).

Nuclear repair follows the chain explicitly, with engineering disposition and qualification inserted between understand and source (e03). The EC repair impact assessment describes: find repairer, transport, diagnose and quote, wait for parts, repair (q04).
Even skeptical agents agree the steps exist: no agent among the 98 disputes that each stage occurs in its domain (v07, z06).
contradicting_evidence: Approval and funding gates the chain omits often dominate elapsed time. Navy surface-ship funding approval takes 26-189 days (GAO via k03, k04, z10). Insurer prior authorization comes before parts can be ordered (s07). Insurer supplements turn up 56% of collision calibrations (s04, s05). OEM software pairing, unlock and emissions re-enablement (Deere: v01, v04; z01; z02).

Queueing for scarce capacity, not any chain step, drives delay. USS Boise sat idle pierside for more than 2 years waiting for a shipyard slot. Navy subs logged 10,363 days of idle time and maintenance delay in FY2008-2018 at more than $1.5B cost. 191 of 414 sub maintenance periods ran late, adding 2,525 days (GAO, k03/m11). Engine shop visits went from a 30-60 day norm to more than 300 days in some cases (m01, z07).

Repair is a loop, not a line. Industry first-time fix is about 77% (top 88%, bottom 60%), and each failed first visit triggers about 2.5 more visits and about 20 days to resolve (Aquant benchmarks, discover.aquant.ai/field-service-benchmark-report; m06). No-fault-found is 14% to over 40% of airline unscheduled LRU removals and 30-70% of returned appliances, costing DoD more than $2B a year (m04; Scott et al. 2022 PMC9502349; Wikipedia NFF citing Aerospace America 2015). Growth work found only after opening a system loops back to diagnosis (u02, k04, m11).

Most of the dollars run on schedules, not on noticing a fault. Gas turbine hot-gas-path inspection is set at 24,000 hours or 1,200 starts, and major inspection at 48,000 hours or 2,400 starts, years ahead (GE GER-3620 via e01). Engines are about 50% of MRO spend and Oliver Wyman calls them 'highly predictable' scheduled events (m01). Rail heavy overhauls run every 8-12 years (m12), elevators run on PM contracts (m10), mining on component-life change-outs (m13).

Efficient regimes restructure the chain instead of speeding up its steps. Microsoft Natick and hyperscalers fail in place or swap to spare capacity in minutes and batch or skip diagnosis (m14, k05). LRU and reman exchange models swap first and diagnose at a depot later (l01, h10, z04). The MEL lets aircraft fly with deferred defects (m02, m03). RCM got its biggest savings by deleting scheduled repairs and treating run-to-failure as a legitimate choice (n02; Nowlan & Heap 1978).

Many failures never enter the chain at all. Only about 10% of broken phones are repaired, and 39.5% of EU consumers are 'enthusiastic replacers' (v02). A decisive repair-or-replace gate sits at roughly 20% of the new price (q04, s01, x06).

The 'notice' step itself often fails. Customers are the first to detect downtime in 41% of cases (Splunk/Cisco 2024, q02). 57% (Downey & Proctor 2002) to 72% (Mowris 2004) of HVAC systems are mis-charged and running degraded unnoticed (s03). Only about 30% of OT networks have visibility (e06). About 58% of industrial unplanned downtime is not equipment failure at all (WSJ via Reliable Plant, n03).

Value and cost cluster at specific links, not evenly along the chain. Lost production dominates breakdown cost: NIST puts $100B of a $119B loss in lost sales, against $57.3B in direct maintenance (q02, NIST AMS 100-34). Downtime economics differ by about 60x across sectors (q02). Customer acquisition is about 49% of Angi revenue (s06). Profit concentrates in parts and labor capacity (x02); engine OEMs take about 47% of the aerospace profit pool (AlixPartners via m01).
best_analogs: Medicine's diagnostic process (NASEM, d02/h12): triage, diagnose, treat, follow up, discharge is the textbook chain, but in practice working diagnoses are revised and confirmed by response to treatment. That supports the chain as a vocabulary while showing linearity is a simplification.

Software operations (h08): detect, diagnose, fix, test, deploy. Cloud and SaaS won by collapsing the chain into continuous managed operations the customer never sees, not by optimizing each step. Expect repair winners to restructure the chain rather than speed its links.

Reliability-centered maintenance (Nowlan & Heap 1978; n01, n02, n03): the P-F curve moves 'notice' ahead of failure, and a strategy step (monitor, hard-time, redesign, run to failure) comes before any repair event. The biggest savings came from deleting unnecessary repairs.

Hyperscale data centers and Microsoft Natick (m14, k05): with redundancy, the repair chain drops off the critical path (fail-in-place, swap to spare capacity in minutes). The efficient regime is to decouple restoring service from repair.

LRU, rotable and reman exchange (l01, h10, z04, m13): two coupled loops, a fast swap at the point of use from pre-positioned stock and a slow batched depot repair. Inventory placement, decided years before the notice step, determines where the time goes.
Formula 1 and MSG hard-time (k05): replace on schedule before failure, with no notice or diagnose step.
Military BDAR (h06): deliberately short-circuits the chain, a temporary fix now with full repair and inspection later, much like aviation MEL deferral (m02, m03).
verdicts.refined_claim: Every repair touches a common set of functions: detect, diagnose/understand, decide (repair, replace, defer or abandon), authorize, source/deliver parts, execute, verify/certify, return to service. Two things change by domain. The first is how these functions are arranged: serially for unplanned corrective work on single assets (appliances, collision, forced outages, line maintenance), and as loops or parallel and pre-positioned flows for most high-value assets (scheduled or interval-driven overhauls, swap-now-repair-later rotables, fail-in-place redundancy, MEL deferral). The second is which steps are skipped altogether. Elapsed time and cost concentrate less in the knowledge steps than in steps the original chain leaves out. Those steps are the repair-or-replace and deferral decision, authorization and funding gates (OEM software unlock, insurer or payer approval, approved repair data, 26-189 day funding approvals), queueing for scarce capacity (shop slots, dry docks, vessels, qualified technicians), and diagnostic iteration (first-time fix around 77%, NFF 14-60%). The chain is useful for mapping where a given industry's bottleneck sits. Treated as one fixed sequence, it misses where most of the value is, and the most efficient regimes win by restructuring it rather than by making each step cheaper.

verdicts.text: Much of the inefficiency in repair comes from a knowledge monopoly / knowledge gap: owners and independent repairers lack the knowledge to fill the gaps, so OEMs and specialists capture it.
verdicts.one_line: There is a repair monopoly, and it is well documented, but it is mostly a monopoly over access and authority (data rights, software keys, approvals, parts, contracts), not over what people know. Opening up the knowledge is necessary but nowhere near enough: where the knowledge was already open, most of the inefficiency stayed.
supporting_evidence: Tally of all 114 agents: 24 support, 84 mixed, 6 contradict. Almost every supporting and mixed agent (about 100 of 114) agrees that OEMs or specialists capture repair value. About 90 of them say the capture is enforced legally, contractually or cryptographically, rather than by what independents can understand.

Medical devices: 91.8% of biomedical technicians had been denied service information for critical equipment (ventilators, defibrillators, imaging). OEM labour rates run 3-5x those of independents. FDA and ECRI found independents repair safely. [v06, v09, r02]

Agriculture: in the Deere class action, plaintiffs' expert estimated an overcharge of $190M-$387M over about 8 years (the case settled for $99M), and there was an FTC consent order. PIRG found no manual for 48% of covered products and no parts for 44%. Internal Deere documents describe a deliberate dealer-only gate on reprogramming, calibration and the DTAC knowledge base ('Control the Wrench'). [v03, v04, z01]

Autos: 84% of independent shops call data access their top business issue (Auto Care/Hanover, n=407, 2024), and 63% have difficulty with routine repairs daily or weekly. About 51% send cars to dealers, an estimated $3.1B a year. [v05]

F-35: 73% of components go back to the OEM, even though government depots repair about twice as fast once enabled. Depot repair is 12 years behind schedule, with 141-day repair times. Technical-data requests take 60+ days. Half of 200+ DoD programs report data-rights deficiencies. GAO has documented this for about 30 years. [q03, h06, z10, p06]

Aero engines: OEMs hold 63% of engine MRO (about 79% with JVs) and earn 20-35% MRO margins, versus -5% to 10% on new engines. They do it by controlling manuals, repair instructions, test equipment and licences. Where the rules opened up (CFM56), about 40 shops compete. [m01, r02]

Sole-source rents: TransDigm has about 90% proprietary sales, about 60% gross margin and DoD IG overpricing findings. Siemens Energy has more than 90% service share on its own fleet. The EC found OEMs service 60-100% of their own gas-turbine frames, with know-how proprietary for 8-16 years. [p06, o01, e01, x03]

Real know-how gaps inside firms: Xerox's Eureka pooled about 25,000 field tips and is estimated to have saved about $100M (Brown & Duguid). Top versus bottom technicians: 75% vs 59% first-time fix. Spread between top and bottom service organisations: 28 points on first-time fix. Generative AI in customer support lifts novices most (NBER). [u05, m06, s03, d01]
contradicting_evidence: Community repair data: missing information accounts for only 12% of failed repairs. No spare parts 25%, parts too expensive 18%, design that cannot be opened 16%; parts and design together are about 59%. [v07]

Autos after the 2013-2014 MOU opened service information: about 70-75% of owners use independent shops once the warranty expires, yet only about 52% of broken items get repaired. Before the MOU, the FTC received 6,786 auto parts and repair complaints (1996-May 2006), of which only 2 were relevant. The profit pool sat in parts and logistics. [z02, q04, h01, k04]

Repair is often slow even when the knowledge is complete. On the Pratt GTF, the defect was known, yet aircraft waited 250-300 days, about 700 aircraft were parked, and the cost was $6-7B; the limits were capacity and parts. The Navy owns its shipyards and largely its technical data, and delays persist anyway. For transformers, the binding constraints are GOES steel, copper, bushings, factory slots and Schnabel cars. [l01, i01, m02, m11, e02]

Major accidents (Alaska 261, Davis-Besse, JAL 123, Aloha 243, BA 5390, Prestige) happened with the correct knowledge already in approved manuals. The failures were in execution, incentives, records, time pressure and cost-cutting. [u02, u03, m03, e10]

No-fault-found rates are just as high inside OEM and depot shops that hold all the knowledge; the causes are physical intermittent faults and gaps in the test environment. In medicine, diagnostic error is about 5-15% even though the knowledge is open. [m04, d02, d03]

Home services: incumbents earn from aggregation, lead brokerage and route density, not from proprietary knowledge. Active Pros at Angi fell 19%; Sears calls per technician fell 26%. AHAM says 87% of 20,000 appliance servicers are local independents. Consumers cite cost and quality (77%, Eurobarometer), not lack of knowledge. [s06, s01, x07]

Shutting rivals out did not depend on ignorance. Rivals who were shut out already had the know-how: Kodak's ISOs, Kytch, the Newag researchers, HEICO's reverse engineering. PMA parts have been legal since 1956/1965 yet hold a single-digit share. DER repairs have been legal for 40-60 years and are underused for commercial reasons. [v08, z01, o05, h11, r04]

When the information friction was removed, the rent disappeared rather than shifting to whoever removed it: Protolabs' operating margin fell from 20% to 5% as quoting know-how spread. Publishing the information did not end incumbent rents in real estate or tax; licensing, coordination rules and defaults kept them. [x04, h07]
best_analogs: Pre-1984 generic drugs (Hatch-Waxman/Bolar) [h02]: copying the molecule was easy. The monopoly was patents plus data-exclusivity rules, and only legislation broke it. Lesson: the gate is the right to rely on someone else's approval data, not the know-how.

IBM plug-compatibles and the foreign-attachment era [h03]: interface knowledge mattered, but the binding locks were lease-only terms, tariffs and refusal to maintain mixed systems. Lesson: the incumbent moves the lock to contracts and interfaces.

Kodak (1992) and Deere [v08, v04]: competitors fully understood the machines and were blocked through parts and software authorisation. Lesson: antitrust and right-to-repair law, not AI, opened these markets.

The 2014 auto MOU and the Massachusetts right-to-repair law [s04, z02, k04]: information was opened, independents won 70-75% of post-warranty work, and the lock moved to telematics, security gateways and part serialisation. This is the cleanest natural experiment: knowledge opened, most costs remained, and the monopoly moved to the next layer.

Xerox Eureka [u05]: the real knowledge gap is tacit and sits inside service organisations. Pooling it was worth about $100M, a single-digit to roughly 35% gain, not 10x. This is the best precedent for AI copilots, and the value went to the incumbent.

Smartphone repair [h09, s02]: leaked schematics and iFixit guides made the knowledge public, and the lock moved to cryptographic parts pairing and serialised parts. This directly confirms the sibling thread's thesis that the monopoly moves to the next scarce layer.
Medieval guilds [h04]: the knowledge was partly tacit, but the rent came from legal privilege and certification. Printing the knowledge did not break the guilds.

F-35 versus organic depots [h06, q03]: the one case where withheld technical data is the binding constraint. When depots get the data, they repair about 2x faster. This is the strongest pure-knowledge case, and it is still contractual: DoD did not buy the data rights.
verdicts.refined_claim: A large, measurable share of repair rent (OEM engine MRO margins of 20-35%, 3-5x medical labour premiums, the $190-387M estimated Deere overcharge, TransDigm-style sole-source pricing) comes from OEMs controlling the right to repair, not from owners lacking understanding. The levers are technical-data rights, design authority and approved data, software and calibration keys, parts pairing and sole-source parts, and warranty, lease, LTSA and insurance terms. A genuine know-how gap exists in two narrower places. The first is tacit expert-versus-novice skill inside service organisations (a 16-28 point spread in first-time fix), where AI copilots give gains of roughly 10-35%, mostly to incumbents. The second is a few true data blackouts (F-35, orphaned or obsolete equipment), where missing documentation really cripples sustainment. Across most categories, information is not the dominant cost: it explains only 12% of community repair failures, and repair stays slow where everyone knows the fix (GTF, Navy yards, transformers) because parts, capacity, physical diagnosis and incentives bind. AI therefore largely removes the cognitive part of the gap, but it does not remove the access and authority monopoly. That monopoly moves to approvals and certification, test evidence, cryptographic authorisation and scarce capacity, so the leveller keeps little value unless it also holds approvals or capacity (as PMA/DER houses like HEICO do).

verdicts.text: With AI, that knowledge gap is essentially gone.
verdicts.one_line: 110 of 114 agents contradict C3 and 4 are mixed (d02, d04, n02, x04); none support it. AI makes codified, public repair knowledge cheap: diagnostic accuracy is high on public vignettes and error codes, and novices gain 14-34%. But the gaps that actually hold up repair are rights, cryptographic locks, certification, missing sensor data, tacit skill and physical capacity. In every natural experiment where knowledge was already close to free, repair stayed gated, and the AI tools that work today are re-enclosing knowledge inside proprietary data moats.
supporting_evidence: [d02/h12] AI alone has the knowledge on clinical vignettes. GPT-4 alone scored 92%, against 74-76% for physicians (Goh et al., JAMA Netw Open 2024, https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamanetworkopen/fullarticle/2825395). MAI-DxO scored about 80% (85.5% at max setting), against about 20% for generalist physicians (arXiv 2506.22405). This is the strongest evidence that the cost of accessing knowledge has collapsed.
