[v06] An LLM support platform for biomedical technicians in low- and middle-income countries reached 100% precision on error-code interpretation and 80% accuracy on corrective actions for a Philips HDI 5000 ultrasound (arXiv 2601.16967, Jan 2026). It is a single-device proof of concept.

[d01/k02/u05] In Brynjolfsson, Li & Raymond (NBER w31161, 5,179 support agents), AI raised issues resolved per hour by 14% on average and by 34% for novices. AI really does compress the time a novice needs to reach competence.
[k05] Meta's GPU fleet needed manual intervention in only 3 of 419 failures. When the owner instruments the fleet, diagnosis can become close to free.

[h01] There was a real information gap historically: in a 2005 Tarrance Group survey, 59% of auto shops had trouble getting repair information or tools and 67% had been forced to send cars back to dealers.

[m06/s03] Vendors say AI gets about '80% of the way' and cuts escalations ('we used to escalate two out of three'). [n03] Samsara reports 99% less time spent on reports. AI is clearly cheapening triage and paperwork.

[d04] AI remote-support usage is growing fast: TeamViewer usage up about ninefold, more than 1M sessions. Vendors claim 81-82% first-time fix and 48-50% fewer dispatches, but these figures come from unnamed customers and are self-reported.
contradicting_evidence: [v07] In the Open Repair Alliance/Restart data (208,491 attempts, Oct 2024), lack of information accounts for only about 12% of failed repairs, while parts and design account for about 59%. Only 53% of products were fixed, even with free YouTube and iFixit.

[u04] 96% of independent repair shops surveyed by iFixit/repair.org have turned customers away because of restrictions (parts, tools, software pairing), not lack of know-how. Community repair succeeds only about 50% of the time after more than 10 years of free online content.
[m06] First-time fix has held at about 75% for over a decade despite a decade of field-service software. The top 20% of technicians reach 75% and the bottom 20% reach 59%.

[s03] Bluon's own benchmark: generic AI with web search scored 11% on replacement parts and 12% on procurement (Bluon claims 95% and 90%) and 59% on OEM part numbers. The value sits in a proprietary graph built from 18M+ jobs, not in general AI.

[h08] In the METR RCT (July 2025), experienced developers working on mature repos were 19% slower with AI (https://metr.org/blog/2025-07-10-early-2025-ai-experienced-os-dev-study/). 46% of Stack Overflow survey respondents distrust AI accuracy. Stack Overflow questions fell 78% (Dec 2024 to Dec 2025) and its corpus was licensed to OpenAI. Knowledge is re-centralising in model owners rather than dissolving.

[d02/h12] Physicians given GPT-4 did not improve (76% vs 74%). The Epic Sepsis Model scored AUC 0.63 on external validation, against 0.76-0.83 internally, and missed 67% of cases. Having the knowledge does not mean it reaches decisions reliably.

[x07] GE spent more than $7B on Predix analytics and diagnosis and did not get adoption; the name was retired in 2022. [n03] AWS closed Monitron to new customers (Oct 2024) and discontinued Lookout for Equipment (7 Oct 2026). Data quality (47%) and process (43%) are the main barriers.

[m04] Smarter built-in test has historically added no-fault-found removals (F/A-18E/F: about 85k wasted man-hours). Systems are often specified to around 70% false alarms (Ungar 2014). AI cannot recover a 50 ns intermittent that was never measured. [k05/m14] Google 2007: SMART-only models are 'unlikely to be useful for predicting individual drive failures', and 36-56% of disk failures show no SMART signal.

[p06/h11] HEICO has about 20,000 PMAs, no material patents and decades of reverse-engineering skill, yet adds only about 400-550 approvals a year and wins only a minority share at roughly 30-40% off OEM price. The limits it names are FAA throughput, airline and lessor acceptance, and litigation risk, not knowledge.

[v03/v04/z01/s02/h09] Cryptographic pairing, signed firmware (Deere payload files, Service ADVISOR), VIN-locked modules and Activation Lock opened only through statute, settlement or FTC order (the Deere 2026 order and $99M settlement), not through information. In Shenzhen, where schematics are near-free, repair is still gated by the cryptographic handshake.

[q03/v10/l02] DoD officials say reverse engineering and additive manufacturing are 'generally less effective and efficient' than buying the data rights (GAO). [p01/z09] F-35 repair turnaround is 188 days with a 10,000-part backlog, which is physical capacity, not diagnosis.

[o02/m10/m13/e10/e05] OEMs are the ones deploying AI: about a third of OEMs run AI in guided troubleshooting and use it to add 3-4 points of EBIT on parts pricing. Otis has 1.1M connected units and KONE more than 40% of its base. Wärtsilä Expert Insight and Everllence CEON run on proprietary fleet data. AI tends to deepen lock-in.

[i01/i02/i03/m03] No regulator lets AI sign off. EASA and FAA accept only frozen, qualified AI as an assistant. Acceptance requires probability-of-detection (POD) demonstration and personal certificate liability. Penetrant could not detect the 1380 crack however it was interpreted. [p02] AI also lowers the cost of forging certificates, as in the AOG Technics case.

[z06/s04/r01] The binding constraint is skilled labour: about 569k openings a year, rising wages, and 18-24 month apprenticeships for tacit skill. [k02] In real-world AI usage, repair is among the least-used skill domains.
best_analogs: Auto repair manuals (h01): Chilton, MOTOR and Haynes, then ALLDATA and Mitchell 1, democratised knowledge. OEMs moved control to access and authorisation (telematics, security gateways), and NHTSA backed that on cybersecurity grounds in 2023. Lesson: when knowledge is levelled, the lock moves to authorisation.

Generic drugs (h02): the full formula is public by law, yet incumbents kept rents through pay-for-delay (about $3.5B a year), patent listings, denial of reference samples and device complexity (EpiPen). Lesson: once knowledge is free, the moat becomes approval, evidence and supply.

Software after open source, Stack Overflow and AI coding (h08): code and diagnostic Q&A are close to free, yet maintenance still takes about 40% of developer time. Value went to whoever certifies (Red Hat), operates (cloud) or owns the data and model (OpenAI licensing Stack Overflow). Lesson: the leveller rarely keeps the value.

Medicine (d02/h12): AI beats physicians on vignettes, but outcomes do not improve and deployed models fail external validation. Lesson: there is a gap between having knowledge and acting on it, and validation becomes the scarce layer.

IBM/AT&T unbundling (h03): rivals had the technical knowledge by 1965-75, but the monopolies held until regulators or courts acted, and IBM re-closed through licensing. Lesson: legal action, not knowledge, opens access.

HEICO PMA (p06/h11): an industrial-scale reverse-engineering house that already has the knowledge and is limited by about 400-550 approvals a year. Lesson: certification throughput is the rate limiter. This is consistent with the prior-thread hypothesis that value moves to an approvals and test-evidence layer.

Meta and Google hyperscale fleets (k05/m14): diagnosis became nearly free, but only because the owner built uniform telemetry on its own fleet. Lesson: AI diagnosis works where the data exists and is owned. That points to an instrumented 'maintenance OS', not general LLM knowledge.

Pre-modern technology transfer (h04): printing and the Encyclopédie left a tacit residue (Bessemer, Collins, the coke-iron gap). Lesson: the gains went to places with skilled people who could absorb the knowledge.
verdicts.refined_claim: AI sharply lowers the cost of codified, publicly available repair knowledge: interpreting fault codes, navigating manuals, triage, cross-referencing where curated data exists, and paperwork. It narrows the novice-expert gap by roughly 14-34%, which matters given the technician shortage. It does not remove the knowledge monopoly, because most of what binds is not cognitive. The binding constraints are: (1) legal rights to proprietary design data, telemetry and software; (2) cryptographic and authorisation locks; (3) certification, approved data and liable sign-off; (4) missing or untrustworthy sensor data, where the fault was never measured; (5) tacit, embodied skill; and (6) physical parts, tooling and shop capacity. Where AI diagnosis works at scale, it runs on proprietary fleet data, mostly held by OEMs. So the likely near-term effect is that knowledge rents shift toward owners of data and approvals (OEMs, curated-data vendors, certification and test-evidence houses), not a collapse of the gap. The claim holds only for consumer and legacy assets that are documented and unlocked, and even there the gap shrinks rather than disappears.

verdicts.text: The combined cost of four intermediate steps (diagnosing, understanding, sourcing parts, delivering parts) can drop by an order of magnitude, making all repair, from washing machines to airliners, far more efficient.
verdicts.one_line: Of 113 agents that took a stance, 0 support C4, 61 contradict it and 52 call it mixed. The four information steps are a small share of repair cost. Labour, physical parts, capacity and downtime are the large shares. Where repair did get 10x cheaper, the causes were competition among verified suppliers, legal mandates, fleet scale, redesign or pre-positioned spares, not cheaper knowledge. Taken literally ("combined cost of the four steps drops 10x, so all repair gets far more efficient"), the claim is mostly contradicted. Measured in elapsed time to restore an asset, it holds in narrow cases.
supporting_evidence: A 10x price drop in one gated step has happened. Deere's customer diagnostic tool cost $3,160 per machine in year one ($2,560 to renew). Under regulatory and antitrust pressure it fell to $195 per machine per year, about 16x. But this was regulation, not AI, and it covers only one input. [v04, Deere antitrust litigation, agrisk.umd.edu and farmdocdaily.illinois.edu]

Downtime, not repair price, is most of the loss, so cutting the time spent in the middle steps matters more than cutting their cost. US PIRG estimates farmers lose about $3B a year to downtime against $1.2B in excess repair cost (about 70/30; advocacy modelling). NIST puts $100B of a $119B manufacturing downtime loss in lost sales. [v01, pirg.org; q02, NIST]

Rents that could be competed away are large. DoD IG found TransDigm margins of 17% to 4,451% on 46 of 47 sampled parts ($16.1M excess profit), and more than 75% of TransDigm sales are sole-source. [v08/q03, DODIG-2019-060, DODIG-2022-043]

Generic drugs show a 10x+ unit-price drop once there are enough verified competitors: more than 95% below brand with 6 or more generics, and generics are 90% of prescriptions for 12% of spend. [h02, FDA/IQVIA, from recall]

Hyperscalers repair servers in-house for about 0.75% of capex a year, against 5-15% for OEM on-site contracts (about 2x that for 4-hour response). That is roughly a 10x gap. [m14, Barroso et al., Datacenter as a Computer]

Individual cases show 100x drops: 460 hours to 4 hours, and 11 months to 30 minutes, in no-fault-found and fault isolation. No-fault-found is 30-60% of repair actions. [m04, Warwick thesis Jones 2008; DTIC a134449]

Opening up design knowledge cut device making cost about 5-10x in Shenzhen ($12 phone vs $60-100 equivalents). Huaqiangbei's physical density of parts made sourcing same-day and walking distance. [h09, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huaqiangbei, strangeparts.com]
The best field-service operators spend $688 per service event against $5,706 for the worst, about 8x. So order-of-magnitude spreads exist between organisations. [m06, Aquant benchmark reports]
Estimate time and quote turnaround can fall more than 10x (days to minutes). Dawn (30 min to under 2) and GroundControl (days to minutes) claim 10x+ on narrow steps. [s05; x05, company claims]
contradicting_evidence: Aero engines are the biggest-ticket repair. In a non-LLP shop visit, materials are about 60%, piece-part repairs 20-30% and labour 5-10%. Life-limited parts can reach about 80% of a visit. 80% of MROs name piece-part availability as the top cause of longer turnaround times. Cutting diagnosis tenfold barely moves the total. [m01, IATA MCX FY2024 report, iata.org; o01; o03]

The GTF recall covered about 3,000 engines, with shop visits of 250-300 days, about 350 aircraft on the ground through 2026, and a $6-7B cost (about 80% customer compensation). The causes were shop capacity and parts, not diagnosis. [o03, m03, z07, r04, i01]

Offshore wind (NREL Cost of Wind Energy Review 2024): vessels are about 78% of OpEx and 93% of maintenance cost. Technician labour is about 4% of OpEx and materials about 1.5%. 'Delivering parts' here means heavy-lift vessels. [m08, osti.gov/biblio/2479271]

Consumer goods: a display repair is 42% of a new phone's price, and diagnosis is 7-22% of common repair costs. The EU's strongest measures raise repair take-up only 13-15%, and the EUR 176.5bn saving comes from buying fewer new goods. [v02, EU Council impact assessment ST-7767-2023; q04]

Information access has not lowered auto repair costs. Total repair cost is up $1,285 since 2020, and labour hours per claim rose from 23.0 (2013) to 27.3 (2024). Scans appear on 86% of estimates, calibration averages about $547 per claim, and 56.3% of calibrations are found only after teardown. [k04, s04, s05, CCC/AAA newsroom.aaa.com]
Audits put the information-rent share of repair bills at about 2-15%. Only OEM access-locked segments show 2-4x gaps. [z05, credence-goods literature, ideas.repec.org]

Field service: about $246 per dispatch, mostly on-site labour plus parts (Frontdoor/AHS 10-K). Aquant, which sells this outcome, models recoverable waste for a median organisation at low teens up to 26%. [s06, sec.gov; s03, m06]

After a decade of investment, predictive maintenance shows credible gains of tens of percent on a minority of critical assets. Predictive over preventive gives about 8-15% less downtime. Claims of 10x ROI trace to 1990s studies or vendors. [n01, n03, m07 (12-40% lower maintenance cost), z06 (Deloitte 5-10%)]

F-35 component repair averages 141 days. Service depots took 72 days, so changing who repairs gives about 2x, not 10x. 10,000+ components are awaiting repair, and the supply base cannot make 48 parts. [q03, d03, GAO-25-107468, GAO-23-105341]

Grid transformers: sourcing and delivery means 80-210 weeks of factory backlog plus heavy haul. RecX's recovery in under a week came from standard modular hardware and pre-positioned spares. [e02, DOE LPT study, energy.gov; k03]

Cheaper, faster sourcing is how counterfeits get in. GAO found 16 of 16 obsolete or rare military parts bought online were bogus, and the regulatory response (DFARS 252.246-7008) added cost. [p01, p02, e06, gao.gov/products/gao-12-375]

Additive and on-demand parts: Fast Radius reached only a 7.7% gross margin even with UPS integration. Vendors claim savings 'up to' 30% on a small printable subset. Xometry-type platforms are under 0.5% of the market after a decade. [l03, x04]

When AI cut the cost of estimating (CCC), the value went to the platform owner, not to lower system cost. Even with near-zero parts and delivery costs, as in software, measured AI effects run from -19% to +56%. [x03, h08, DORA 2024]

Change takes a long time even when the economics are clear. Real estate commissions stayed near 6% through 20 years of abundant information, until antitrust litigation. Generics needed about 30 years and a statute. [h07, h02]
best_analogs: Generic drugs (Hatch-Waxman): a 10x+ price drop came from 6 or more verified, interchangeable suppliers plus a statutory approval path (an ANDA-like route), not from knowing the molecule. It brought fragility and shortages. For repair, this points to PMA/DER-style approval as the lever, at about 30-50% off price today. [h02, h11, p03]

Hyperscale data centres: about 10x cheaper repair (0.75% vs 5-15% of capex a year). The causes were redundancy that turns urgent failures into batched work, homogeneous fleets and owned spares. It works for fleets, not one-off assets. [m14, k05]

MSG-2/RCM in aviation: hard-time items fell from 339 (DC-8) to 7 (DC-10), and structural man-hours fell from 4M to 66k. The 10x gain came from removing unnecessary work through shared analysis, not from cheaper diagnosis. [n02]

Travel agents vs real estate agents: costs collapsed only where the whole transaction could go digital and suppliers wanted to bypass the gatekeeper. Where the gate was legal or contractual, it held until litigation. [h07]
Shenzhen Huaqiangbei: sourcing became same-day through physical parts density and donor-part harvesting. That is liquidity, not information. [h09]
Auto aftermarket (AutoZone/O'Reilly, about 19% operating margins): once knowledge became cheap, the lasting profit centre was fast physical delivery through store density. [h01]
Deere right to repair: the tool price fell 16x through settlement and regulation. The labour premium (about 30-45%) and downtime remained. [v04, z01]
RecX transformer and Grid Assurance: restoration fell from years to under a week because of standardisation and pooled spares placed in advance. [e02]

Russian aviation under sanctions and Cuba's Special Period: deep expertise was there and diagnosis was cheap, but sourcing and delivery stayed binding (about a €1B black market, cannibalisation). [h05]
verdicts.refined_claim: AI can cut the cost and time of diagnosing and understanding by large factors for codified, repeatable faults. Narrow cases show 10-100x, for example no-fault-found isolation, estimating and part identification. But these steps are typically about 5-25% of a repair bill: 7-22% for consumer goods, about 5-10% for aero engines, about 5% for offshore wind. So the total repair cost falls roughly 10-30%, not 10x. Sourcing and delivery are limited by physical inventory, factory lead times, certification and provenance, not by the cost of information. Making sourcing fast and cheap without automated verification raises counterfeit risk. The large economic prize is elapsed downtime, which is often 70%+ of the loss. Downtime falls by an order of magnitude only when cheaper information is combined with non-information levers: verified competing suppliers or approvals (generics, PMA, about 30-50% off and up to 95% with many suppliers), pooled or pre-positioned spares, fleet-scale redundancy and batching, modular redesign, and legal removal of authorisation gates. Expect 10x outcomes in uniform fleets, long-tail obsolete parts and gate-locked segments, and gains of tens of percent across most repair. Absent these complements, much of the value is likely to accrue to whoever controls the next scarce layer (approvals, physical stock, capacity, platforms) rather than become system-wide efficiency.

verdicts.text: Bespoke making of a specialised part (when the supplier is gone, out of business or too slow) is effectively solved: an AI parts factory can make it.
verdicts.one_line: Of 83 agents with a stance, 74 contradict C5, 9 are mixed and none support it. Physically making a part is already cheap and routine. The slow, costly steps are certification, provenance, data rights, software pairing and material or process qualification, and none of them is solved. On-demand making works only for non-critical, obsolete, low-volume parts, and businesses built only on that have mostly failed.
supporting_evidence: [l02] Deutsche Bahn's printed spares. Recalled from company data, not re-verified this session. DB has printed 100,000+ parts across about 1,000+ part types since about 2015 and cut lead times from months to days or weeks (claims of up to about 90% time reduction). Its fleets run 30+ years and many original suppliers are gone. This is the strongest real case for C5, but it is mostly low-criticality parts, and DB owns or negotiates the part data.

[l02] Other on-demand programmes, all company-reported: Siemens Mobility up to about 95% lead-time reduction, Wilhelmsen about 80-90%, Siemens Energy burner-tip repair from weeks to days (about 90%). The gains are in the sourcing and delivery steps, for the long tail of parts.

[k04, r04] Travis AFB 3D-printed a C-5 lavatory/galley part for about $300 against a $10,000+ quote from the original supplier (widely reported, 2018-19). The USAF Rapid Sustainment Office and Tinker's reverse-engineering groups report large savings per part on legacy aircraft parts.

[r04] Cold spray repairs military parts 'in minutes': an Army Black Hawk component, and Navy adoption across global operations (USNI, 12 Sep 2023; standard MIL-STD-3021). It turned magnesium gearbox housings that had been scrapped into repairable parts, so restoring a part can stand in for buying a new one.

[o05] Making the part is the cheap step. TransDigm's half-inch drive pin carried a markup of about 9,400% (Wikipedia). The price is rent, not manufacturing cost, so there is a layer that competitors can contest.

[o02] Daimler Trucks prints parts where suppliers lack tooling or lead times are long. Consultants describe 15-20x the SKU count and 23% obsolescence, which is real long-tail demand, though printing only chips at it.

[z10] Repairing or remanufacturing a part in the military's own depots instead of buying new from the OEM cut lead time from 95 weeks to 4 weeks, which shows the size of the prize when the gate can be passed.

[x03, m05] Alternative aviation parts already sell at a discount: PMA parts at roughly 30-40% below OEM and used serviceable parts at 30-50%+ below OEM list (trade press: Aviation Week, ICF, Oliver Wyman).
contradicting_evidence: Tally across 83 agents with a stance: 74 contradict (89%), 9 are mixed (v07, o02, m09, m10, m12, r02, r04, s01, z10) and 0 support. Every mixed stance says certification, qualification or electronics, not the ability to fabricate, is the binding step.

[m05, x02] HEICO holds about 20,000 FAA PMA approvals built over decades and adds about 400-550 a year, including through acquisitions. Approval comes part by part, and FAA capacity sets the pace. TransDigm is buying PMA makers.

[k03, k04] The A-10 rewing, a case where the original supplier was gone: Boeing's new-wing programme cost about $1.72bn for up to 242 wings. The option was chosen in 2006 and first flights came in Nov 2011. Fatigue testing (a test wing failed early) and qualified production drove the cost. A 2003 review said the legacy data 'could no longer be trusted' (Wikipedia, citing USAF and GAO).

[u02] FOGBANK: recreating a lost process took about 5 years and about $92M ($23M + $69M), and deliveries were about 2 years late, even with full state resources. Tacit process knowledge was not in the specifications. Davis-Besse needed a salvaged, qualified forging.

[l03] On-demand parts factories failed. Fast Radius had a 7.7% gross margin and an $89M nine-month loss on $20.6M revenue. Shapeways filed Chapter 7 on 2 Jul 2024 after $59.9M of operating expenses against $14.5M gross profit (SEC 8-K). Desktop Metal fell from a $1.5B valuation to a $135-183M sale and filed Chapter 11 in Jul 2025. Markforged sold for $116M and then for about $42M (Wikipedia).

[l02, l03] Only about 5-10% of spare-parts catalogues are technically and economically printable (Roland Berger and Deloitte-type estimates, recalled). Maersk's onboard printing trial (2016-17) did not scale.

[q03, v10, p05] Qualification of flight-critical 3D-printed parts is still under way about a decade after the V-22 demonstration. GAO names material qualification and part certification as the binding constraint for DoD additive manufacturing.

[p01] A factory for parts whose maker is gone already exists. Rochester Electronics has worked since 1981, holds about 12 billion die and is authorised by 70+ OEMs. Its moat is that authorisation plus traceability, not fabrication. GAO-12-375: 16 of 16 test buys of parts from unvetted sources were bogus.

[z01, v03, v05, s02, h01] Software pairing blocks even a part that is physically perfect: VIN-burned modules, Apple parts pairing, HP cartridge chips, Newag serial checks. Design patents on collision parts also block substitutes.

[k01, z07, z08, l01] Provenance is the scarce asset. AOG Technics forged paperwork, and Partnair 394 crashed because of counterfeit parts. A part without back-to-birth traceability is worth near zero.

[m08, m14, e02, e05, e06, s02] The parts that matter most cannot be made bespoke: wind main bearings and 100 m composite blades, transformer electrical steel and windings, GPUs and HBM, OLED panels and SoCs, and obsolete ASICs and firmware. They need fabs, certified forging or high-voltage factory testing.

[i04, h02, u05] Insurers call bespoke reverse-engineered parts expensive, slow and high-risk. In generic drugs, proving equivalence and keeping manufacturing honest failed repeatedly (the 1989 generic-drug scandal, Ranbaxy, Budeprion). The TEA laser case shows a specification alone does not give a working artifact.
best_analogs: HEICO and PMA (aviation): reverse-engineering parts has been routine since the 1990s, yet about 20,000 approvals took decades at about 500 a year. The lesson: the value accrues to whoever owns the approval pipeline, and throughput is set by the regulator. That points to 'PMA/DER-as-a-service', with AI cutting the cost of each approval, rather than 'AI factory'.

Rochester Electronics: the parts maker for dead suppliers has existed since 1981. Its moat is OEM authorisation (70+ OEMs) and traceability. The lesson: licensed continuation manufacturing beats unlicensed bespoke making.
Generic drugs (h02): copying is easy, while bioequivalence evidence and manufacturing integrity are the hard, scandal-prone parts. Generics end up at a discount to the original, not 10x cheaper.
Deutsche Bahn's printed spares: works because the operator owns the data and accepts the risk on non-critical parts. The lesson is that the buyer, not a startup, captures the value.

Fast Radius and Shapeways: on-demand factories with job-shop economics and lumpy long-tail demand went bankrupt. The survivors added CNC, casting and forging, or became spare-parts managers for B2B buyers.
A-10 rewing and FOGBANK: when a supplier or process is gone for a critical part, the cost is billions or tens of millions of dollars and 5-10 years, driven by testing and requalification, not design.

Remanufacturing (Cat Reman, LKQ salvage, iPhone donor-harvest repair): the industry answered 'no supplier' by restoring existing cores and harvesting genuine parts, not by making new ones. The scarce input is the qualified core.

Mainframe plug-compatible makers (Amdahl, h03): building compatible hardware was possible but cost about $1B to keep pace, and most makers failed or were absorbed. The incumbent can move the interface.
verdicts.refined_claim: AI-assisted reverse engineering plus on-demand making (AM, CNC, cold spray) has already made it cheap and fast to produce non-critical, low-volume, obsolete mechanical parts. Where the operator owns the design data or the original maker is gone and the risk is acceptable (rail interiors, cabin parts, tooling, military-owned legacy parts), lead times fall from months to days and costs fall sharply. But this is roughly 5-10% of a typical spares catalogue. For safety-critical, certified, software-paired, or fab- or forging-dependent parts, being able to make the part is not the bottleneck. Approved design data, material and process qualification, production approval, traceable provenance, OEM data rights and pairing are the bottleneck, and they cost per part number on regulatory clocks (HEICO: about 500 approvals a year; A-10 wings: about $1.7bn and 5+ years). So the opportunity is not an 'AI parts factory' but an AI-accelerated qualification and approval pipeline (PMA, DER, class or rail approval, OEM licensing) attached to a process-agnostic, pre-qualified supply network. This is the HEICO and Rochester model with lower cost per approval, capturing generic-style discounts of about 30-50% rather than 10x.

verdicts.text: Inspection / certification remains essential and is itself an industry that must evolve for AI.
verdicts.one_line: Of 108 agents with a stance, 95 support the claim, 12 are mixed and 1 contradicts. Inspection and certification is the gate that decides when an asset returns to service in every regulated, high-consequence sector, and cheaper knowledge and parts make it more valuable. Two caveats: in consumer repair it often works as a pretextual moat rather than a safety need, and evidence that it is specifically evolving "for AI" is real but early (EASA NPA 2025-07, ASNT NDE 4.0, Gecko) rather than proven.
supporting_evidence: Tally: 95 of 108 stances support (88%), 12 mixed (11%), 1 contradicts (v07). Support is close to unanimous in aviation, defence, nuclear, energy, medical, rail and maritime agents (m, k, e, i, p, l, u, n sets).

AOG Technics (UK, 2019-2023) supplied about 60,000 CFM56 parts with forged airworthiness certificates. Cheaper or broker-sourced parts raise the value of provenance checks (p03, m05, h11, i02, k01, z08).

81% of F-35 spares arrived without electronic records, and about 9% of flight hours at one site were lost to records issues. Pedigree and certification is a binding layer that needs modernising (h06, d03; DOT&E F-35 reports).

The licensed inspection and sign-off workforce is aging: 44% are over 60 (up 3 points on the 2025 report), with more than 39,000 retirements expected within 10 years (r01, i02). There is a 24-27% technician gap, and new hires take 2-3 years to become productive (m01).
About 700 aircraft (2% of the fleet) were parked specifically for engine inspections during the GTF powder-metal recall, so inspection throughput is itself the bottleneck (p05, l01, r04, k03).
When Airbus surrendered Concorde's type certificate the fleet was grounded, even though the design knowledge was intact. Accountable certification, not knowledge, is the scarce layer (k04).
Fatal accidents (Aloha 243, JAL 123, Alaska 261, BA 5390, Alaska 1282, Davis-Besse) each trace to a failed independent inspection, check interval or records barrier (u01, u02, u03, m03, k02).

EDF's 2022 stress-corrosion crisis: NDE could not reliably size the cracks, which forced destructive pipe cut-outs and about €29B of replacement-power purchases. Better NDE would have been the leverage (e03).

Regimes are already evolving for AI. EASA's learning-assurance concept and NPA 2025-07 (DS.AI) is the first binding-track AI specification. ASNT is 'modernizing employer-based NDT qualification under SNT-TC-1A' and running NDE 4.0 and AI work. Others: FAA Part 108 BVLOS NPRM (Aug 2025), the FDA PCCP, PHMSA acceptance of ML-analysed ILI data under API 1163, class remote surveys and IACS Rec 42 (i01, i03, e10, d01).

Investors treat inspection as a category: Gecko Robotics reached a valuation of about $1.25B in 2025 (unverified), and NDT services are about $10-11B in 2025, rising to $18-20B by 2035 (6-8% CAGR). Robotic inspection is the first robot product that sells (x01, x05, r03, i01).

Fire and elevator roll-ups value code-mandated inspection most, because it is recurring and non-discretionary and generates the repair work. Europe's elevator big four raised EBIT 56% in 2008-09 while industrial earnings fell 37% (x03, o02, m10).

Hubbard (2002, J. Law & Econ 45(2)) found that inspectors chosen by the inspected party drift lenient: consumers return 30% more to stations that pass them. So inspection's incentive design is the crux (z05).

Analog: Hatch-Waxman opened generic drugs by changing what counted as proof (ANDA plus bioequivalence, 90% CI within 80-125%). The verification gate was then gamed (Vitarine and Par tested Mylan's product in place of their own, and FDA reviewers took bribes), showing verification is both essential and needs reinvention (h02).

In AI-adjacent fields, independent validation exposed failures the vendor's own figures hid (Epic Sepsis), and the autonomous AI that succeeded had its vendor assume liability (d02, h12). The 'almost right' problem and the XZ backdoor show verification becoming the bottleneck as knowledge gets cheap (h08).
contradicting_evidence: FTC, Nixing the Fix: 'there is scant evidence to support manufacturers' justifications for repair restrictions'. The FTC found no study comparing authorized and independent repair quality, and treats car repair as safe without OEM-run inspection. Outside regulated sectors, inspection and safety claims look largely pretextual (v07, u04, h01, s02).

As a cost line, inspection can be tiny: statutory inspection is about 1% of UK offshore wind OPEX. It decides timing, not cost, which weakens any 'inspection is a big industry to rebuild' reading in some sectors (r02, m08).

In consumer repair, formal safety inspection is largely absent beyond permits and licensing. Authorized networks and warranty rules act as a steering mechanism that keeps work in the network (s06, z03, x06, v01). France's repairability index is self-declared and unverified (v02).

Several agents found no direct data on certification actually evolving for AI (v01, v02, m06, m07, x06, u05). The 'must evolve' half rests mostly on early regulatory drafts and startup funding, not on outcome data. EASA guidance covers only Level 1-2 AI and frozen models (k02, i03).

Inspection anchors incumbent lock-in rather than disrupting it. Elevators are the most entrenched OEM aftermarket because inspection is mandated (o02), and Intuitive's approval process was called 'illusory' (v08). An 'evolving' inspection layer may get captured by OEMs, not by challengers.

Evidence that verification is underbuilt is weak and vendor-sourced: ServicePower reports that 25% of assets fail within 3 months of a preventive maintenance visit (m06). Insurer outcome data on IoT-based inspection is thin (i04).
best_analogs: FCC Part 68 / Carterfone (h03): the AT&T monopoly broke through a published standard plus a neutral registration and certification regime that replaced the incumbent's 'network harm' veto, not through knowledge diffusion. Lesson: how the certification regime is designed decides whether the market opens.

Hatch-Waxman bioequivalence (h02): a cheaper, accepted proof unlocked generics at a fraction of brand price. The gate was then gamed, and FDA says the market does not reward quality maturity. Lesson: 'bioequivalence for parts' is the lever, and the verifier's integrity and incentives must be designed in.

FAA PMA / DER / Part 145 (o01, p06, h11, k01): HEICO calls PMA 'a significant barrier to entry'. Regulator certification, not OEM exclusivity, delivers safety, and whoever holds approvals captures the rent, consistent with the prior HEICO hypothesis.
Concorde type-certificate surrender (k04): knowledge alone cannot keep a fleet flying without an accountable certificate holder. This is directly relevant to orphan-parts plays.
Medieval guild marks and masterpieces (h04), and licensed sign-off in law, brokerage and radiology (h07): the attestation layer outlived secrecy and became the rent-bearing layer.
Hubbard emissions inspection (z05): who pays the inspector determines leniency, an incentive-design warning for any AI or third-party inspection business.

RCM / MSG-3 (n01-n03, k05): data and sensors re-tuned inspection intervals and made inspection continuous and on-condition, and the gains were locked in through regulator-approved programmes. This is the historical template for how AI will change inspection.
Hyperscaler fleet health (m14): automated, continuous return-to-service gating (Fleetscanner, Ripple, Hardware Sentinel) shows the end-state where inspection is in-production, not a one-off sign-off.
verdicts.refined_claim: In regulated, high-consequence assets (aviation, defence, nuclear, energy, medical, rail, maritime, pressure equipment, elevators and fire systems), inspection, qualification and certified sign-off is the gate that decides return-to-service timing. It is legally human-signed and capacity-constrained by an aging certified workforce, and it becomes more valuable as AI and cheaper sourcing drive down the cost of diagnosis, knowledge and parts, because provenance and equivalence risk rise (AOG Technics, F-35 records). It is often a small share of cost (about 1% of wind OPEX) but dominates time and liability. Inspection is changing from periodic, paper-based checks to continuous, sensor-based and robot-captured evidence with digital provenance, and regulators are starting to build AI assurance (EASA learning assurance and NPA 2025-07, ASNT NDE 4.0, PCCP, Part 108). But this is early and outcome data is thin. In consumer repair the claim is weaker: OEM certification mostly acts as a pretextual moat (FTC 'scant evidence'), and the opportunity there is a neutral, incentive-aligned attestation layer that replaces the OEM gate, not more inspection. Whoever designs and runs the equivalence and verification gate (a 'Part 68 or bioequivalence for parts') is positioned to capture value. Neutral verifiers do not capture it automatically, because inspection mandates have so far entrenched incumbents (elevators, PMA holders).

verdicts.text: The repair industry is structurally built to be inefficient (not built for smart) and needs to be fundamentally rebuilt.
verdicts.one_line: Agents split about 7 supports, 4 contradicts and about 103 mixed. The evidence strongly backs "repair is deliberately structured to capture aftermarket rent at specific choke points". It rejects "not built for smart / slop", and it rejects "needs a ground-up rebuild" as the way change actually happens.
supporting_evidence: Equipment is sold cheaply so the service tail can be monetised: Otis 2025 New Equipment margin was 4.8% against Service at 25.1%, and TKE gets about 65% of sales from service and modernisation with adjusted EBIT up from 11.1% to 14.8%. Elevator maintenance cartels had effects lasting decades, and the CJEU Kone C-557/12 'umbrella pricing' ruling followed [m10].

Deere internal documents (FTC/states complaint, para 54): the customer diagnostic tool cost $3,160 for the first year and $2,560 to renew. An employee wrote that it 'will be cost prohibitive for nearly all customers but then we can't be accused of not making it available' and that 'this does not deteriorate the service business at dealerships'. Strategy phrases include 'Control the Wrench' and 'Capture the Service' [v04; ftc.gov DeereCoREDACTEDComplaint].

FTC, 'Nixing the Fix' (2021): there is 'scant evidence' to justify repair restrictions, and they steer consumers to OEM networks and to early replacement. It is the most-cited source across the corpus, appearing in about 14 files [v02, s01, s02, u04, k02; ftc.gov/reports/nixing-fix].

Aerospace aftermarket: IATA/Oliver Wyman (Oct 2025) calls the model 'unbalanced', with OEMs aiming to generate profit in the aftermarket. Licensed MROs are contractually barred from using PMA, DER repairs and USM, OE discounts run up to 80-90%, and supply-chain costs to airlines exceeded $11bn in 2025 [m01, o01, h11].

Sole-source rent: TransDigm's operating margin is about 47% on $8.83B FY2025 revenue. DoD found a 9,400% markup on one pin, and the 2021 DoD IG found $20.8M of excess profit on 105 parts [z01, o05, v10].
Medical imaging: service is about one third of GE HealthCare revenue at about 52% gross margin, against 37% on products. ISOs charge 20-40% less [v06].

Trucks and heavy equipment: aftermarket parts and service are 40-65% of dealer gross profit and about two thirds of PACCAR pretax income, protected by franchise law and software locks [z03]. Auto dealer fixed operations are about 50% of dealer gross profit [v05].

Defence sustainment fails chronically: only 4 of 49 aircraft types met mission-capable goals in most of FY2011-2021 (2 of 49 in FY2021), about 70% of GAO F-35 recommendations are unimplemented, and lobbying killed the FY26 repair and data-rights reform [h06, q03, v10].

Structural friction blocks diffusion even of proven fixes: the Ogden IFDIS tester saved about $62M, but an OSD memo was needed to spread it. Split line and shop budgets also distort repair decisions [m04].
Data-centre urgent service on the OEM vendor model costs 7-30x more than batched repair, and vendor datasheets understated field failure rates by 3-30x [m14].
contradicting_evidence: Execution gaps inside the same structure dwarf the structural ones. First-time fix is 77% on average and 88% for top performers, and cost per service event is $688 for leaders against $5,706 for the bottom quintile (8x). Best-in-class plants reach under 10% reactive maintenance and 2-3% of replacement asset value, using methods known for decades [m06, m07].

Mature industries already improved a lot without a rebuild. US nuclear outages fell from about 100 to about 30 days and capacity factor rose from about 60% to about 93% [e03]. Industrial downtime hours fell about 30% and incidents about 40% from 2019 to 2023 through incremental IoT and PdM adoption (vendor data) [q02, n03]. A targeted Navy plan cut active idle time by about 90%, from 1,518 to 166 days [m11].

Fab tool service is highly optimised: about 10,000 ASML field staff, uptime-linked contracts, and 95% of 30-year-old tools still running. Service margins are not monopoly-high: Applied AGS gross margin is 33.4% against 54.2% on systems, and ASML service is about 50.9% against about 53.5% on systems [m09].

The independent auto aftermarket is a $516B competitive, logistically efficient system with a 70-75% independent share for ICE vehicles. The FTC treats autos as the model of self-regulated open repair [h01, v01, s04].

Under fixed-price power-by-the-hour contracts, OEMs gain from durability. Rolls-Royce targets more than a 100% time-on-wing improvement by end-2027 and stopped selling loss-making OE engines [o01, k01]. Outcome contracts measurably improve reliability [o03].

Much apparent waste is deliberate safety and liability redundancy written after accidents: MEL, RII, duplicate inspections, approved data, and authorised sourcing after counterfeit scandals. Aviation achieves 98.9% dispatch reliability [m01, m03, u03, i01, i02, p01, p02].

Physics and capacity dominate cost in many sectors. Materials are about 60% of a narrowbody engine overhaul and labour only 5-10% [o01]. Offshore wind is constrained by vessels, cranes, weather and the Jones Act, with OEMs losing billions [m08]. Dry docks and transformer factories are further limits [k03, e02].

Where one owner controls design and fleet scale (hyperscalers, Ryanair, Toyota, the Navy, Calpine with a 2.3% forced-outage factor in-house), repair was rebuilt and became very efficient. So the inefficiency is not inherent to repair; it sits in fragmented ownership [k05, m14, e01].

Tech-first 'rebuilds' mostly failed: Homejoy shut down, Handy sold for about the capital it raised, Angi Services posted -$52M Adjusted EBITDA, AI-PdM platforms and standalone AR largely failed, and SPAC-funded spares platforms died. The winners digitised incumbent workflows: ServiceTitan ($961M revenue, $82B GTV) and Samsara [s06, n01, d04, l03, x01, x04].

Remedies are coming piecemeal through law and contract rather than teardown: EU 2024/1799, Oregon, NY and MN state laws, the FTC suit against Deere, and the IATA-CFM deal. Regulators chose incremental fixes on purpose [v01, v02, z02, m05].
best_analogs: Bell System (lease-for-life, attachment bans) [h03]: the structure existed to extract rent, yet repair was operationally excellent. Opening it took Carterfone, divestiture and 15-30 years. The lesson is that rent structure and operational inefficiency are different things, and the fix is legal.

Hatch-Waxman generics [h02]: a statutory rebuild produced large efficiency gains, but also shortages, collusion, offshore quality fraud and consolidation. Any rebuild has to price in redundancy and quality assurance.
Auto aftermarket and the right-to-repair MOU [h01, v01]: an access mandate plus an independent channel restructured repair without a ground-up rebuild. This is the template for other sectors.

Software (OSS, cloud, DevOps) [h08]: a real rebuild delivered large gains, but new intermediaries (Red Hat, AWS) captured the value. The rebuild moved the chokepoint rather than removing it, which matches the sibling-thread hypothesis.

Hyperscaler data-centre repair and RCM in aviation from 1960 to 1980 [m14, n02, k05]: genuine end-to-end rebuilds happened where one owner controlled asset design and fleet scale, and they worked by designing around expected failure.
Guilds (Ogilvie vs Epstein) [h04]: these institutions persisted both to protect insiders and to solve a real training hold-up. Removing them needs institutional change, not just a knowledge tool.

Legal and tax services (LegalZoom, Free File, Direct File) [h07]: inefficiency preserved by incumbent rules was absorbed or blocked when product-only disruptors attacked it. Fixes came through antitrust and policy.

Shenzhen and the Cuban car fleet [h09, h05]: where parts and labour are dense, or pressure is high, efficient repair economies form on their own. The binding constraint is access and incentives, not intelligence.
Rolls-Royce TotalCare and power-by-the-hour [o01, k01]: changing the payment structure flips OEM incentives toward durability. Contract redesign is the cheaper rebuild.
verdicts.refined_claim: Repair is not 'built to be inefficient' or 'not built for smart'. In many durable-goods sectors it is deliberately and rationally built to capture installed-base rent: OE is sold at about 0-7% margin and the aftermarket earns 25-50%+ operating margin. The rent is protected by control of a few choke points: design data and approvals, diagnostic software, licence terms that bar PMA, DER and USM, franchise law, long-term service agreements and sole-source certification. That makes repair costly and slow for owners, by tens of percent (ISO discounts of 20-40%, generic and PMA parts at 30-70% of OEM price) and in delay, but usually not by 10x on cost. A large separate share of the observed waste is execution (an 8x spread between top and bottom performers within the same structure), deliberate safety redundancy, and physical capacity limits that no rebuild removes. Wholesale industry rebuilds have occurred only where one owner controls asset design and fleet scale (hyperscalers, the RCM era in aviation). Elsewhere change comes layer by layer through access mandates and antitrust, outcome-based contracts, independent second-source and parts houses (HEICO, FTAI), and workflow software that incumbents absorb. The actionable version: target specific rent-protected chokepoints (orphaned or sole-source parts, approval evidence, diagnostic data) and expect the chokepoint and its margin to migrate rather than disappear.

costMd:
# Where repair time and money go, by stage and industry

**Legend.** Each figure carries the ids of the research notes it comes from. `[E]` marks my own estimate or inference. `[U]` marks a figure the agent recalled from memory and could not re-verify, because the shared search budget ran out for most agents.

**Stage keys.**
- N = notice
- Dx = diagnose
- U = understand (procedure, repair data)
- S = source parts. **S-search** is finding and buying the part. **S-exist** is the part's existence, price and certification.
- Dl = deliver parts
- L = repair labour
- I = inspect and sign off
- Non-chain = OEM margin, inventory, downtime

**The distinction that drives the whole answer.** "Sourcing" mixes two things.
- **S-search** (finding, quoting, ordering) is an information and transaction cost. A 10x knowledge gain can cut it.
- **S-exist** (the part exists, is certified, and has a price set by OEM rent or manufacturing capacity) is where most parts money and parts waiting time sits. A 10x knowledge gain does not touch it.

Most of the "parts" share below is S-exist.

---

## 1. Decomposition by industry

### Commercial aviation (MRO about $104-119B a year: m01, q01)

| Stage | Money | Time | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mix of spend | Engines about 52% of MRO; components about 18%; airframe and line about 30% | — | m01 |
| Engine shop visit: materials and OEM piece-part repairs (S-exist) | **75-95% of direct cost**. Life-limited parts can be 50-60% of a life-limited-part visit | Piece-part availability is the top cause of longer turnaround (80% of survey respondents). Visits run 100-300+ days against a 30-60 day norm | m01, r02, o01, o03 |
| Engine labour (L, with Dx/U bundled in) | 10-15% on non-life-limited visits; 5-10% on life-limited visits (r02 corrects m01) | — | r02 |
| Airframe and line (L) | About 80% labour | Dispatch reliability is already 98.86% | r02, m01 |
| Dx (no-fault-found) | 30-60% of avionics removals turn out to have no fault. Historically about $22k per event (ATA 1995); about $20M a year for a 200-aircraft airline | NFF inflates spares pools and shop queues | m04, d03 |
| Aircraft on ground (outstation) | $10k-150k per hour (a 2008 Boeing figure, never audited) | Parts wait **50-70%** of an outstation AOG `[E]`; **over 90%** of an engine grounding `[E]` | m02 |
| U (repair outside the structural repair manual: OEM, DER or DOA disposition) | Small | Hours to days for an AOG; weeks to months for a permanent fix | m03 |
| Dl (couriers, next flight out) | Small next to the cost of AOG | Close to solved | l01 |
| I and records | NDT is roughly $11-18B globally | Gate on release. Records and trace problems (AOG Technics) | i01, i02, p02 |
| Non-chain | OEMs take 47% of the aero profit pool. Engine MRO margin 20-35%, against -5% to 10% on new engines. About $11B of supply-chain cost in 2025 `[U]`: $2.6B extra leases and $1.4B extra spares | ~350 aircraft (GTF) and ~700 aircraft parked for engine work | o01, m01, m05, l01 |

**Verdict: aviation.** Dx and U together are **at most about 5-15%** of engine cost. The NFF waste in avionics is the main exception. Time is S-exist plus shop capacity.

### Automotive (light-duty aftermarket about $414B: v05)

| Stage | Money | Time | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| L | 48-57% of the dealer repair dollar at $186/hr; 27.3 labour hours per collision claim, and rising | Technician gap of about 20.8k a year | r02, s04, z03 |

## 2. Do the four intermediate steps dominate?

**No, with three bounded exceptions.**

1. **Money.** In no domain is Dx plus U a large standalone cost line. They are billed inside labour or visit fees (r02).
   - S-search and Dl are small everywhere: aviation delivery is close to solved, auto parts arrive same day, and aircraft-parts search is cheap and digital (l01, p03, h01).
   - The big money sits in four places:
     - S-exist: OEM and certified part price, and life-limited parts (aviation 75-95%, phones).
     - Labour and truck rolls (auto, appliances, trades about 50%+).
     - Access: vessels and cranes (offshore wind 78%).
     - Non-chain downtime. This often exceeds the repair bill by 1.6x (NIST) to 2.5x (ag) to orders of magnitude (fabs, auto plants, transformers).
2. **Time.** Measured splits put waiting, not working, at the top: parts existence and lead time, capacity (docks, shops, cranes), approvals and funding, then labour (z10, m11, k03). The long poles are certified parts and capacity. Knowledge is not one of them.
   - GTF: the fault was fully understood, yet repairs took 250-300 days.
   - Navy: the service is its own OEM and shows the same delays.
   - Transformers: diagnosis takes hours; replacement takes 2-4 years.
3. **Exceptions where the four steps do dominate.**
   - **(a) Electronics and avionics NFF.** Misdiagnosis generates the parts and shop flow: 30-60% of removals, over $2B a year at DoD.
   - **(b) Dealer-locked equipment (ag, trucks, medical).** Dx and authorisation are the long pole; about 70% of ag harm is downtime waiting for the dealer. But the lock is cryptographic and legal permission, not knowledge. It is being opened by the FTC Deere order, which cut the tool price about 16x (v04), not by AI.
   - **(c) Consumer goods.** Paid diagnosis and quote uncertainty (7-22% of cost) suppress demand rather than inflating the cost of repairs that happen.

**Smaller exceptions where knowledge itself binds:**
- Tacit and plant-specific knowledge (legacy PLC code, retiring experts): e05, u02.
- Unplanned "new work" discovered when a system is opened: Navy 4,100+ days, 36% labour underestimates (m11, u02).
- Diagnosis that is wrong at scale: HVAC mis-charge, per NIST (s03).

## 3. Ceiling if Dx, U, S-search and Dl got 10x cheaper

The savings ceiling is about 0.9 × the share those four steps hold today.

| Domain | Share of direct cost held by the 4 steps today `[E]` | Ceiling on direct-cost saving | Downtime and time effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| Aviation engines | About 5-15% (inside labour) | **About 5-13%** | Small. Parts and shop slots bind |
| Avionics / defence electronics | About 30-50% via NFF knock-on effects | **About 25-40%** of component repair spend | Meaningful: fewer removals means smaller pools |
| Auto (mechanical and collision) | About 5-15% | **About 5-12%**, plus trust | Cuts supplements and late calibrations |
| Appliances and home service | About 15-30% (Dx plus repeat truck rolls) | **About 10-25%** (matches the vendor 10-26%) | Fewer second visits |
| Field service and HVAC | About 25-35% (failed visits, unneeded rolls) | **About 15-26%** | MTTR 4.5 days could fall materially |
| Industrial plants | About 20-30% of labour time (planning, search, Dx) | **About 10-25%** of maintenance cost | Restore time on the hard tail; worth the most per hour |
| Ag and trucks (if authorisation counts as "Dx") | Up to about 70% of total harm | **About 30-60%** of harm, but only with legal access | Large. Not achievable by knowledge alone |
| Medical devices | About 20-40% (access-driven) | **About 20-40%**, requires opened access | Moderate |
| Offshore wind | About 5% or less | **Under 5%** | Negligible. Vessels and weather bind |
| Transformers, nuclear, shipyards | Hours to days against months to years | **Under 5%** | Negligible. Capacity and qualification bind |
| Consumer phones | About 5-10% (screen and battery Dx is trivial) | **Under 10%** | — |

**Bottom line.**
- **Realistic ceiling on total repair cost: about 10-25% in labour-heavy field service, about 5-15% in parts- and access-heavy domains, and about 25-40% only in diagnosis-heavy electronics and access-locked niches.**
- That is consistent with every measured intervention:
  - AI copilots: 14-34% gains, concentrated in novices (d01, u05).
  - Remote and AR support: about 15% (d04).
  - Medical diagnosis AI: 20-45% (d02).
  - Collision costs rose 63% even after estimating was automated (s05).
- An order-of-magnitude system-wide gain is not available from cheaper knowledge. The documented roughly 10x cases came from other levers:
  - **Eliminating unnecessary work.** RCM/MSG cut structural inspection from about 4M to 66k man-hours (n02 `[U]`).
  - **Redundancy and batching.** Hyperscalers went from 5-15% of equipment value to 0.75% (m14).
  - **Standardised pre-positioned spares.** RecX restored a transformer in under a week against years (e02).
  - **Prediction plus logistics.** Delta cut cancellations about 100x, before LLMs (d01).
  - **Legal opening of access.** Deere tool price fell 16x (v04).
- The value released by cheaper knowledge also tends to go elsewhere:
  - **To buyers**: Protolabs' operating margin fell from about 20% to 5% (x04).
  - **To whoever holds sign-off, data or the parts channel**: h01, h07, h08.

*Built from the research summaries [v01–z10] and the notes in `/home/user/nuketime/research/repair/raw/*.md`. ## Bottom line

In every case examined, the monopoly that broke was **not mainly a knowledge monopoly**. Challengers almost always already knew how to do the work:
- Kodak's independent service organisations were cheaper and sometimes better than Kodak [v08].
- Plug-compatible makers had IBM-grade engineering [h03].
- HEICO held about 20,000 PMA approvals with "no material patents" [p06, h11].
- Generic drug chemistry was easy to copy [h02].
- Guild secrets were in print from 1555 [h04].

What held each monopoly together was **permission**: the legal right to connect, install, sign or sell; a cryptographic key; an accepted standard of proof. Each one broke when a **regulator, court or standards body changed what counted as acceptable proof or access**. Once it broke, the rent did not disappear. It **moved to the next scarce layer**: verification, distribution density, physical capacity, liability-bearing sign-off, or proprietary outcome data. ## Cross-case regularities

**1. What broke it.** In about 15 of the 18 cases, the trigger was a change in **law, standard of proof or certification**: Hatch-Waxman bioequivalence, Part 68 registration, PMA rules, the Massachusetts ballot and MOU, the FTC v Deere order, Turgot and Le Chapelier, Burnett. Technology and knowledge diffusion came first by years or centuries without breaking anything: printing before the guilds fell, public listings before real estate commissions moved, free tax software before Free File uptake, YouTube before DIY auto repair (DIY share actually shrank) [h04, h07, u04].

The exceptions are where the *owner of the scarce layer chose* to release knowledge (MediaTek with shanzhai), and where the transaction was unlicensed, low-stakes and fully digital (travel booking) [h09, h07].

**2. How long it took.** Without a legal shock, decades to centuries: PMA about 35 years, Carterfone about 28, guilds about 236 after print, real estate commissions about 20 after listings went public. Once law moved, months to a few years: Deere tool price −16x in months, ANDA filings straight after 1984, about 2 years from the Massachusetts ballot to the MOU.

But **mandates without enforcement stall**. The 2020 Massachusetts telematics vote is still in litigation six years on. No state attorney general has enforced an electronics repair law. Military right-to-repair was stripped in conference in December 2025 [v03, v05, v10].

**3. What happened to prices.** Prices fell in proportion to the **number of verified, accepted entrants**, not to how widely the knowledge spread:
- One certified alternative takes off roughly 30–40% (PMA, recalled), or roughly 15–50% for auto aftermarket parts.
- About six verified generic suppliers take off more than 95% [h02].
- Total system cost often **rose** while unit prices fell. Collision severity was +63% with open repair data [s05]. Software maintenance load grew [h08]. Telecom owners took on wiring costs [h03].
- Cheaper access released latent demand. Apple's $29 battery programme did 11M+ replacements against 1–2M expected [s02, q04].

**4. The new scarce layer.** It was always one of five:
- **(a) Verification and certification throughput**: bioequivalence, FAA approvals, Part 68 labs, commercial-grade dedication.
- **(b) Cryptographic and legal authorisation**: pairing, keys, return-to-service signatures.
- **(c) Physical liquidity and density**: parts within hours, cores, rotables, route density, technician hands.
- **(d) Physical capacity**: castings, test cells, docks, shop slots.
- **(e) Proprietary outcome data and telemetry.**

The same move shows up inside AI-era incumbents. OEMs are the leading deployers of AI and telemetry in elevators, mining, fab tools and gas turbines [m10, m13, m09, e01].

**5. Who captured value.** Not the knowledge producer: Haynes, Stack Overflow, Red Hat's upstream maintainers, the Encyclopédie, Predix's $7B+ bet [x07]. The value went to whoever owned the adjacent layer:
- **Distribution density**: AutoZone, O'Reilly, Fastenal (20% operating margin on vending and onsite stock vs Applied's 11% on technical knowledge) [p04].
- **Payers**: generics, collision insurers.
- **Accountability or certification holders**: HEICO, Red Hat, licensed agents.
- **Operated-lifecycle providers**: AWS, Rolls-Royce TotalCare, which repriced its risk transfer [o03].
- **Acquiring incumbents**: IBM buying PSI, TransDigm's $2.2B PMA purchase, Caterpillar buying remanufacturers, Asurion absorbing uBreakiFix and Domestic & General [x06].

## Test of the sibling-thread hypothesis

*"Knowledge levels → monopoly moves to approvals, test evidence, installed fleets and scarce factories; the leveller rarely keeps value; hardware goes generic at 30–70% of OEM price; best shape is an orphan-parts house growing toward 'HEICO for everything'."*

- **Monopoly migrates, leveller doesn't keep value: strongly supported** across all 18 cases.
- **"30–70% of OEM price": partly supported.** It holds for single-entrant certified domains: PMA at about 60–70% of OEM price, medical independents 20–40% cheaper. It is wrong as a general law. Price depends on entrant count. Where certification throughput is high and the product is a commodity, prices go to about 5% of brand (generics). Where throughput is rationed (about 500 approvals a year), they stay near 60–70%. The "physics clock" is really a **certification-throughput clock** plus capacity.
- **Orphan-parts house: supported, with three amendments.**
  1. Independents win **late in the lifecycle**: FTAI on 25-year-old engines; CFM56 overhauls spread across about 40 shops with the OEM doing about a third; gas-turbine independents entering after 8–16 years; Rochester Electronics at about 12B die under licence from 70+ OEMs [m05, m01, e01, p01].
  2. The moat is **approval track record plus feedstock plus records**, not fabrication. Every "parts factory" that skipped certification failed or shrank (Fast Radius, Shapeways, Maersk onboard printing) [l02, l03].
  3. **Expect to be bought, not to stay independent**: TransDigm bought PMA makers [x02]. HEICO's ~23% margin is real but is about half of TransDigm's, so certified competition narrows the rent without removing it [o05].
- **Not supported: "AI erases the knowledge gap, so the industry rebuilds."** In the cost data, knowledge or diagnosis is 5–15% of engine shop-visit cost [m01, r02], about 12% of community repair failures [v07], and a 10–26% recoverable slice in field service [m06, s03]. The only measured 10x gains came from removing unnecessary work (RCM [n02]), standardised hardware (RecX transformers [e02]), redundancy (hyperscalers [m14]), or prediction plus logistics (Delta [d01]). None came from cheaper knowledge.

## Laws: who wins when AI makes repair knowledge abundant

**Law 1. Knowledge is never the last lock.** When know-how commoditises, rent moves to the **permission layer**: the right to install, sign, pair or connect. The winner is whoever holds or manufactures that permission. Examples: guilds → certification [h04]; Lexmark patents → chips [v08]; manuals → cryptographic pairing [v03, s02]; F-35 data rights [q03]. *Prediction:* AI-native **approved-data and sign-off organisations** (DER/DOA houses, Part 145 stations, accredited dedication labs) capture more than AI diagnosis vendors.

**Law 2. Monopolies fall when the standard of proof changes, not when knowledge spreads.** The time constant is decades without a legal or standards shock and months with one. Examples: Hatch-Waxman [h02], Part 68 [h03], Massachusetts/MOU [h01], FTC v Deere's 16x tool-price cut [v04]. *Prediction:* the biggest AI-era value event in repair is a regulator accepting an **AI-generated equivalence or qualification package**, the "bioequivalence for parts" (EASA NPA 2025-07, 10 USC 3243(e) expedited qualification [i03, p06]). Whoever writes that test protocol, and is first to pass it, gets the first-filer rent.

**Law 3. The leveller doesn't keep the value; the adjacent layer does.** The knowledge producer is absorbed as a free add-on by whoever owns distribution, payment or accountability. Examples: Haynes vs AutoZone [h01]; ALLDATA inside AutoZone and Mitchell 1 inside Snap-on [h01]; Stack Overflow vs model owners [h08]; Tractable via Mitchell [s05]; Protolabs and Xometry margins passing to buyers [x04]. *Prediction:* standalone AI repair copilots get bundled by OEMs, field-service platforms and parts sellers. Durable profit goes to whoever owns **parts liquidity, payment or claims, or the liability wrapper**.

**Law 4. Price falls with the number of verified entrants, and certification throughput sets that number.** One accepted alternative gives about a 30–40% discount; about six give more than 95% [h02, h11, o05]. Unverified abundance gives counterfeits, not lower prices: GAO's sting found 16/16 bad parts, and AOG Technics put 60,000 forged parts into the fleet [p01, p02]. *Prediction:* AI-assisted substantiation that multiplies approvals per year (HEICO manages about 500) is worth more than any fabrication capability. The first two or three entrants per part family earn the margin.

**Law 5. Abundance creates a trust deficit, and verification becomes the scarce layer, which is then attacked.** Examples: the 1989 generics scandal and Ranbaxy [h02]; AOG Technics [p02]; AI lowering forgery cost [p02, p03]; policy tightening toward authorised-source preference after counterfeit scandals [p02]. *Prediction:* winners include **signed digital release certificates, provenance graphs and independent inspection that is not chosen or paid by the inspected party** [z05, z08, i02]. Inspection grows in a world with more AI; it does not shrink [i01].

**Law 6. Incumbents re-lock at the next layer and buy the breakers.** Examples: IBM/PSI [h03]; TransDigm's $2.2B PMA purchase [x02]; Caterpillar buying remanufacturers [h10]; Asurion consolidating [x06, x07]; OEMs owning the AI telemetry [m09, m10, m13, e01]; medical OEMs pricing cloud service tiers [v09]. *Prediction:* an AI repair entrant either (a) owns a layer the OEM structurally can't re-lock: owner-controlled data rights, regulator-compelled access (the 10-year Deere order), orphaned fleets the OEM has walked away from; or (b) is built to be acquired. "Fight the OEM on its current fleet" loses.

**Law 7. Cheap knowledge raises volume more than it cuts total cost (Jevons), so the scarce input becomes hands and capacity.** Examples: Apple batteries 11M vs 1–2M [s02]; radiologist demand rising after AI [d02]; software maintenance staying around 42% [h08]; auto repair cost rising after 2014 [k04]; downtime cost per hour doubling as downtime hours fall [z06, q02]. *Prediction:* value goes to whoever owns **certified technician-hours, shop and dock slots, rotable pools and pre-positioned parts**, and to whoever sells **outcome or risk contracts** priced on uptime (power-by-the-hour, Asurion-style protection plans, Mantle-style uptime operators) [o03, x06, x05].

**Law 8. Independents win at the end of the lifecycle, not the frontier.** The OEM monopoly decays on a clock of roughly 8–16 years, and the orphaned tail is where independents compound. Examples: FTAI [m05]; CFM56's 40 shops [m01]; gas turbines [e01]; Rochester [p01]; orphaned inverters (Fimer, SunPower, Powin) [e07]; dead e-bike brands [s07]; legacy PLCs [e05]; obsolete rail electronics [m12]. *Prediction:* the strongest company shape remains an **orphan or late-life fleet house**: approval track record, feedstock and teardown, records integrity, pooled spares, then an uptime contract on top. It expands one installed base at a time rather than as "an AI parts factory for everything".

## What this predicts in one table

| Likely winners | Likely losers |
|---|---|
| Approved-data and sign-off holders using AI internally (DER/DOA, Part 145, dedication labs) [i02, h07] | Standalone AI diagnosis or knowledge apps [h01, h08, x01, x07] |
| Verification and provenance infrastructure (signed certificates, POD-qualification-as-a-service) [p02, i01, i03] | Lead-gen and matching marketplaces (Angi spends about 49% of revenue on marketing; Homejoy, Handy) [s06, x07] |
| Parts liquidity, teardown and rotable pools with trusted records [m05, z09, h09] | Uncertified on-demand parts factories (Fast Radius, Shapeways) [l03, x04] |
| Risk-bearing uptime and outcome contractors [o03, x06, z05] | Horizontal predictive-maintenance platforms (Predix, Uptake, C3, AWS Monitron) [n01, n03] |
| Owners of closed-loop outcome data (symptom → fix → result) [u05, d02, z08] | Brute litigation against an OEM's current fleet without a legal unlock [v08] |

## Main caveats

- Many figures were recalled because search was unavailable: PMA market share and discounts, ANDA cost, the remanufacturing share of manufacturing, RCM man-hours, HEICO and TransDigm margins [o05, h11, h10, n02].
- The 2026 Deere settlements come from Wikipedia and still need docket confirmation [z01].
- The PIRG harm estimates come from an advocacy source, and CEI's estimate is about 7x lower [v07].

finalists.name: Approval Factory: an AI-native multi-regime design-approval holder for sole-source and orphaned parts
merged_from: Approval Factory: an AI-native design-approval holder for sole-source aero and defense parts
Equivalence Works: an AI-native qualification house that owns approvals
finalists.description: WHAT IT DOES: A certified design and qualification organisation (FAA DER and later ODA, DLA source approval and SAR, then nuclear commercial-grade dedication and rail ECM). It turns reverse-engineered or redesigned parts into regulator-approved part numbers and repair schemes. AI handles scan-to-geometry reconstruction, material and process identification, similarity and failure-mode analysis, test-plan generation, compliance-matrix and document assembly, and drafting responses to reviewers. An owned accredited lab plus automated CT and metrology produce the physical evidence. WHAT IT OWNS: The approval portfolio (PMA part numbers, DER repairs, STCs, SAR and source approvals, dedication packages), each a regulator-granted right to install, plus a track record with each regulator that speeds later filings. It also owns a material and process allowables database built coupon by coupon in its lab, which a rival would have to rebuild, and acceptance agreements with lessors and customers. Fabrication goes to a pre-qualified, process-agnostic network of CNC, casting and additive suppliers. The company holds the data package and the liability, not the factory. WEDGE: Start with DLA and depot sole-source items coded AMSC C/D/P whose prices have spiked, on legacy platforms (C-130, KC-135, H-60, A-10). There the government owns or can compel the data, the 25%-in-12-months sole-source price trigger produces a target list, and 10 USC 3243 reimburses small-business qualification testing. Approval cycles of 3-12 months build the track record. Next comes FAA PMA for cabin, landing-gear, component and non-hot-section engine parts on sunset CFM56/V2500-era fleets, where OEMs pay least attention. Later extend the same evidence engine to nuclear dedication and rail obsolete electronics. MARKET: Commercial aero aftermarket parts run about $40-50B a year inside about $119B of MRO, and DoD secondary items and spares add tens of billions a year. Nuclear, rail and industrial turbine obsolete spares add more. Capturing 1-3% at HEICO-like operating margins of 21-24% gives $1-5B of revenue. HEICO is valued at about $40B and TransDigm at about $70-80B, both built on this layer. COMPARABLES: HEICO Flight Support Group (about 20,000 PMAs, about 400-550 added a year, no material patents), TransDigm as the pricing benchmark (about 47% margin, its $2.2B purchase of Jet Parts Engineering and Victor Sierra in Jan 2026), Wencor, Rochester Electronics, StandardAero's 2,000+ proprietary repairs, and Paragraph IV first filers in generic drugs. KEY RISKS: OEM IP litigation (UTC v HEICO ran 10.5 years). Incumbents tend to buy whoever breaks their pricing (Law 6), so plan for a strategic exit unless the company reaches delegated authority (ODA/DOA) first. Regulators may accept AI-generated substantiation slowly.
finalists.why_finalist: This is the most direct expression of the C5 and C2 verdicts. The scarce layer is approval and substantiation, not making the part, and AI cuts exactly the engineering cost per approval that caps HEICO at about 500 approvals a year. Evidence is the strongest of any shape: HEICO and TransDigm margins, the $2.2B M&A that priced approval portfolios, and Law 4 on entrant-driven price falls. The moat is regulator-granted approvals with compounding track record. Novelty comes from a cost-per-approval curve steep enough to make 50-500-unit part numbers worth approving, and from serving several regulatory regimes with one engine. It also directly tests the sibling thread's 'HEICO for everything' hypothesis.

finalists.name: Late-Frame Turbine House: an AI-native independent owner-operator for mature gas turbine and aeroderivative fleets
merged_from: Late-Life Turbine House: FTAI-for-power for mature gas turbine and aeroderivative fleets
Late-Frame Turbine Works (AI-native independent gas turbine and aeroderivative service operator)
Gridstock: pre-positioned standardized spares for long-lead grid and generation equipment (gas-turbine HGP exchange-set component only)
finalists.description: WHAT IT DOES: An independent service operator and asset owner for mature gas-turbine frames (7F/7EA/9FA/6B, 501F) and aeroderivatives (LM2500/LM6000 and converted CFM56-class power units) that are leaving or have left OEM LTSAs. It buys retired engines and frames as teardown feedstock, runs pooled hot-gas-path and rotor exchange sets so parts come off the outage critical path, and develops its own approved repairs and non-OEM hot-section parts. It sells guaranteed-duration outages with liquidated damages and availability-based, interval-extension service contracts. AI cuts the engineering cost per repair qualification (borescope and NDE analysis, life modelling from operating data, dossier assembly). It lets a smaller certified workforce review more units, predicts emergent outage work from fleet history, and lets a small team underwrite availability risk across mixed fleets. WHAT IT OWNS: (1) A catalogue of approved repairs and parts with proven fleet hours. (2) Teardown feedstock and a cross-owner rotable exchange pool. (3) Qualification dossiers built on cross-owner condition data, accepted by insurers and lenders, which justify interval extensions. (4) The installed-base annuity of uptime contracts. Casting and fabrication are subcontracted. WEDGE: Behind-the-meter data-center, oilfield and merchant aeroderivative owners. They are new, outside LTSAs, and desperate for availability while OEM slots and new-unit lead times are sold out. Lead with a pooled exchange-engine and module program plus a time-to-restore guarantee. Then add combustion and transition-piece repairs and HGP exchange sets for out-of-LTSA 7FA/7EA owners (merchant IPPs, municipal utilities), one frame family at a time. MARKET: Gas turbine aftermarket services are about $20-35B a year globally. Only about 26% of GE's roughly 7,000 units are under LTSAs, which leaves a large transactional aftermarket. Siemens Energy cites about €400M of lifecycle value per GW. Data-center gas buildouts in 2025-2030 add tens of GW. Taking 5-15% of the mature-frame aftermarket gives $1-4B of revenue at 12-24% margins. COMPARABLES: FTAI Aviation and FTAI Power (aerospace revenue up about 3.5x in two years on 25-year-old engines), PSM (Hanwha) with 7F intervals extended from 24k to 32k+ hours, EthosEnergy, MD&A, Sulzer, AerSale (35-39% gross on owned parts against 17% on labour), StandardAero, and Calpine's insourced maintenance (26 GW at a 2.3% forced outage factor). KEY RISKS: OEM IP litigation. Concentrated superalloy casting supply. OEMs re-locking new frames through LTSAs, mitigated by targeting only frames the OEM is ceding (independents enter 8-16 years into a frame's life, Law 8). Insurer acceptance of non-OEM parts, which the company addresses by building the qualification layer IMIA says is missing.
finalists.why_finalist: Strongest demand tailwind of any shape: AI data-center load meets OEM capacity that is sold out. The moat sits in the layers the verdicts say keep the value: owned rotable pools, proven fleet hours, insurer- and lender-grade evidence, and uptime contracts (Laws 7 and 8). The EC record documents both the OEM lock and the clock on which it decays. The evidence is concrete (PSM, FTAI, AerSale margins, Calpine). This is the strongest energy-sector form of the sibling thread's orphan-parts hypothesis. It is capital-intensive, but the margin comes from owned assets, not labour.

finalists.name: Loopback Depot: an AI-native NFF-eliminating repair depot and data-package rebuilder for defense and aviation electronics
