Intermittent (AI-native avionics and defence electronics repair station)
Loopback Depot: high-throughput repair-loop capacity for defence and aviation electronics
finalists.description: WHAT IT DOES: A certificated component repair operator (FAA/EASA Part 145 station plus DoD Public-Private Partnership depot partner) for line-replaceable electronics: avionics, radar, EW, power and control units, later rail and wind converters and data-center GPU fleet RMA. It wins on turnaround and true first-time fix by eliminating no-fault-found removals. It uses its own environmental-stimulus intermittent-fault test rigs, AI fault isolation that fuses BITE logs, flight data and teardown findings, and a serial-number history across operators. It also reconstructs missing technical data packages, test procedures and repair specs with AI, including physical process characterization, because FOGBANK showed CAD alone is not enough. Pricing is per confirmed fault and per serviceable unit at turnaround SLAs, which reverses the incentive that keeps NFF at 30-60%. WHAT IT OWNS: (1) Repair-station certificates and capability lists, which carry legal return-to-service authority. (2) Proprietary stress-replay automated test equipment. (3) A cross-operator rogue-unit and shop-findings database that no single airline or service has. (4) A growing library of government-accepted reconstructed TDPs and DER repair approvals for obsolete boards. (5) PBH-style component availability contracts and an owned rotable pool, which supplies the margin (AerSale's 35-39% on owned parts against 17% on labour). WEDGE: A DoD PPP or OTA contract to clear one high-backlog LRU family where the government owns the data: legacy fighter, rotary or tanker avionics first, then F-35 common components as sustainment management transfers to the services by about 2027-28. Guarantee turnaround under 30 days and NFF re-removal below 5%. In parallel, sell NFF reduction for regional and narrowbody airline avionics pools. Each repaired line yields an accepted TDP that compounds into the library. MARKET: Commercial component MRO is about $20-21B, about 18% of $119B. US DoD depot maintenance is about $35-45B a year, F-35 sustainment about $1.3-1.58T over its life, and NFF waste over $2B a year at DoD. At 3-5% share, revenue is $1-4B. COMPARABLES: StandardAero (about $5B to $10.4B on licence-protected repair), AAR, VSE, HEICO Electronic Technologies, Universal Synaptics (intermittent-fault testers: about $62M saved and 4x MTBF), Lufthansa Technik Component Services, Gecko Robotics (the defense IDIQ path), and organic depots (OO-ALC, FRCs). KEY RISKS: Prime-contractor IP resistance (Lockheed). Slow DoD acceptance and procurement. Right-to-repair stripped from the FY26 NDAA, so the company must work through contracts on government-owned-data and orphaned items.
finalists.why_finalist: Electronics NFF is the one domain where the synthesis found that diagnosis itself drives parts and shop flow, so AI leverage is direct rather than marginal. The evidence is unusually quantified: 10,000+ F-35 components in backlog, 141-188 day OEM cycles against 72 days at government depots, 73% of work still going to the OEM, 93% latent wiring faults, and $2B+ a year of NFF. The buyer, the policy (F-35 sustainment transfer), and the moat (certificates, cross-operator serial data, accepted TDPs, owned rotables) all line up. Three proposals converged on this shape, which is a strong signal.

finalists.name: Provenant: the neutral equivalence standard and certificate authority for physical parts
merged_from: Equivalence and Provenance Gate: a neutral 'bioequivalence-for-parts' standard plus a signed-certificate network
Provenant: the certificate authority for physical parts
finalists.description: WHAT IT DOES: Trust infrastructure for regulated parts. It issues cryptographically signed digital release certificates (8130-3 / Form 1 equivalents, nuclear CoC, DFARS and AS6081 trace, NERC CIP-013 attestations) anchored to physical part fingerprints and markings. A verification API is checked at receiving, with AI vision, X-ray and XRF authentication cheap enough to run there. AI document forensics audit legacy paper trace packs and bring them into the system. Over time it authors and runs the per-part-family equivalence protocols (reference-part comparison and POD-qualified methods), executed by a network of independent accredited labs, that regulators, insurers, lessors and grid operators cite for non-OEM, used and AI-made parts: a 'bioequivalence for parts'. It also offers an authorization clearinghouse for pairing and calibration under compelled-access orders (FTC v Deere's 10-year order, Oregon pairing ban, EU 2024/1799), filling the 'independent entity' that Massachusetts and Maine mandated but nobody built. WHAT IT OWNS: The trust root (issuer keys and identities for approved organisations), the serial-level provenance graph across brokers, the forgery and anomaly corpus, the equivalence standards, and the lab network whose results count. It is built to be OEM-neutral and structurally independent of the inspected party, since Hubbard and credence-goods evidence show inspected-party-paid inspection drifts lenient and Ranbaxy showed a verification gate can be corrupted. WEDGE: Lessors and MROs handling CFM56/V2500 teardown USM and lease transitions after AOG Technics. Sell AI forensic audits of trace packs per engine or aircraft transition, and issue signed digital certificates for teardown houses that want a price premium for verified material. Lessors pay because records set residual value: an LLP without back-to-birth records is near-scrap. In parallel, run DFARS/AS6081 and CIP-013 authentication of obsolete ICS and power electronics for utilities and defense, and pairing credentialing for independents under the Deere order. Then expand into equivalence-protocol authorship for PMA and AM parts in rail and nuclear dedication. MARKET: TIC is about $250B globally and NDT about $11-18B. Aero aftermarket parts flow is about $50B+, ILSmart RFQ volume about $5-7B a year, and aviation USM about $7-8B a year. A per-certificate and per-verification toll plus enterprise contracts plus lab revenue could reach $1-3B revenue at partly software margins, with certificate-authority network effects. COMPARABLES: UL Solutions (the Part 68 / safety mark precedent), DigiCert/Verisign, CCC Intelligent Solutions (the data layer that captured collision), AutoAuth (a mandated lock collapsing into a $5-17.50/month credential), SGS, Bureau Veritas, FLYdocs/Bluetail/ProvenAir, SAE/ATA Spec 2000 Ch.16. KEY RISKS: The 'thin tool' trap, where it becomes a vendor rather than the gate unless it wins regulator, lessor-mandate or insurer endorsement early (C6 notes inspection mandates have historically entrenched incumbents). OEMs may build closed versions. Blockchain-era predecessors stalled because they could not stop forgery at the point of entry, which physical anchoring is meant to fix.
finalists.why_finalist: It captures Law 5, the most AI-specific dynamic in the review: AI makes both alternative parts and forged paperwork cheap, so verification becomes the binding scarce layer. Precedents for neutral gates opening markets are strong (Hatch-Waxman moved generics from 13% to 90% of prescriptions, Carterfone/Part 68). Pain is acute and documented (AOG Technics' 60,000 parts, GAO's 16 of 16 bogus parts, IMIA saying no independent qualifier exists). It has the most software-like economics and network effects of the set. It is also the complement every other finalist needs: approvals, orphan parts and turbine repairs all depend on accepted provenance.

finalists.name: Signet: the liable AI-native inspection and release authority for energy and defense assets
merged_from: Signet: the liable inspection-and-release authority for energy and defence assets
finalists.description: WHAT IT DOES: An AI-native inspection organisation built around certified sign-off. It is an accredited NDT and inspection body, an ASME/NBIC authorized inspection agency, and a Part 145 or class-recognised station. It combines robotic and sensor data capture, AI defect recognition qualified to MIL-HDBK-1823 probability-of-detection standards, and in-house Level III and authorized inspectors who review many sites remotely and sign. The signed return-to-service record becomes the accepted unit of evidence. Owning the inspection funnel then feeds repair work and risk-based interval extensions. WHAT IT OWNS: The legally accountable signature (accreditations and certificated staff). The regulator- and insurer-accepted method qualifications for each AI technique, which set the standard of proof (Law 2). The condition-data history that accumulates on every inspected asset. WEDGE: Power-plant boiler tubes, HRSGs, pressure vessels and tanks under ASME/NBIC jurisdiction, plus Navy hull and tank inspection. The asset owner pays, outage days are worth about $0.7-1.5M per GW-day, and the authorized-inspector slot is already licensable. The first deliverable is one AI ultrasonic/EMAT method qualified to an accepted POD standard, sold as 'outage critical-path inspection days cut in half, signed'. MARKET: NDT and inspection is about $11-18B globally, TIC about $250B+, and US authorized and in-service inspection for energy and defense is several billion. The repair spend inspection triggers is far larger. Bureau Veritas is valued at about €13B. Taking 2-5% of energy and defense TIC supports a $5B+ company. COMPARABLES: Gecko Robotics (data and capture plus a $300M Navy IDIQ, but it partners for sign-off), Mistras, Team Inc., HSB and TÜV (insurer-inspectors since 1866), Bureau Veritas, SGS, Waygate/Baker Hughes assisted defect recognition, and LegalZoom's move to owning a law firm as the 'be the licensed entity' precedent. KEY RISKS: Regulators may be slow to accept AI methods (EASA NPA 2025-07, ASNT NDE 4.0 are early), and outcome data is thin (C6 caveat). Incumbent TIC firms could buy or copy the approach. It must stay independent of the inspected party to keep its structural value.
finalists.why_finalist: C6 was the only claim mostly supported (95 of 108 agents): in regulated assets, certified sign-off decides return-to-service timing and becomes more valuable as diagnosis and parts get cheaper. The certified workforce is aging and capacity-bound (EDF's NDE analyst limit, the Vineyard Wind halt), so AI leverage is real but only counts once methods are qualified. That makes owning both the qualified AI method and the signature a novel, defensible combination that neither Gecko (data only) nor TIC incumbents (labour-heavy) have. It pairs naturally with Provenant but sells to a different buyer, asset owners during outages.

KEY RISKS: Fragmented SKUs could make onboarding expensive. Safety-certification cost for refurbished and replacement units. Lower per-event ticket sizes than aero. Possible IP claims from acquirers of bankrupt OEMs' assets.
finalists.why_finalist: This is the cleanest case where the Law 6 re-lock risk is structurally absent: the OEM no longer exists, so the knowledge and data blackout is real and AI reconstruction is the binding unlock. The orphan pool grows mechanically with every OEM bankruptcy and with the mismatch between electronics and asset lifetimes. Evidence fits well (inverters cause 43% of tickets and 36% of lost energy, and fault losses doubled while detection improved, so detection is not the bottleneck). It brings a novel combination to a fast-growing, under-served market: cheap acquisition of installed bases, a pooled spares layer, and risk transfer that financiers need. It is also the most consumer-adjacent finalist, giving portfolio diversity beyond aero and defense.

rejected.name: Grid Recovery Fleet: standardized pre-positioned transformers and switchgear as membership infrastructure
rejected.reason: This is the only shape with a demonstrated 10x (RecX), but it is an infrastructure-financed, capital-heavy spares fleet. AI is secondary (design configuration and risk ranking), and the business is exposed to the lead-time cycle (5-16 months in 2010), so it fits asset-backed financing better than venture equity.

rejected.name: Gridline Restoration (heavy electrical restoration and rewind operator)
rejected.reason: Duplicate of the grid recovery fleet with rewind depots added. It carries the same capital intensity and cyclicality, and its AI leverage, design reconstruction for rewinds, is too narrow to carry a venture case.

rejected.name: Gridstock: pre-positioned standardized spares for long-lead grid and generation equipment
rejected.reason: Merged into the grid cluster, which was rejected for capital intensity. Its gas-turbine HGP exchange-set idea was folded into the Late-Frame Turbine House finalist.

rejected.name: Fieldrun (multi-brand heavy-equipment uptime operator riding compelled access)
rejected.reason: A density-and-labour services business whose moat is a 10-year access order. OEMs can re-lock at telematics and data (Law 6), and dealers and Titan-style roll-ups can copy it. The AI copilot gains of 14-34% mostly benefit incumbents, so defensibility and margin structure are weak for venture scale.

finalist.name: Approval Factory: an AI-native multi-regime design-approval holder for sole-source and orphaned parts
merged_from: Approval Factory: an AI-native design-approval holder for sole-source aero and defense parts
Equivalence Works: an AI-native qualification house that owns approvals
finalist.description: WHAT IT DOES: A certified design and qualification organisation (FAA DER and later ODA, DLA source approval and SAR, then nuclear commercial-grade dedication and rail ECM). It turns reverse-engineered or redesigned parts into regulator-approved part numbers and repair schemes. AI handles scan-to-geometry reconstruction, material and process identification, similarity and failure-mode analysis, test-plan generation, compliance-matrix and document assembly, and drafting responses to reviewers. An owned accredited lab plus automated CT and metrology produce the physical evidence. WHAT IT OWNS: The approval portfolio (PMA part numbers, DER repairs, STCs, SAR and source approvals, dedication packages), each a regulator-granted right to install, plus a track record with each regulator that speeds later filings. It also owns a material and process allowables database built coupon by coupon in its lab, which a rival would have to rebuild, and acceptance agreements with lessors and customers. Fabrication goes to a pre-qualified, process-agnostic network of CNC, casting and additive suppliers. The company holds the data package and the liability, not the factory. WEDGE: Start with DLA and depot sole-source items coded AMSC C/D/P whose prices have spiked, on legacy platforms (C-130, KC-135, H-60, A-10). There the government owns or can compel the data, the 25%-in-12-months sole-source price trigger produces a target list, and 10 USC 3243 reimburses small-business qualification testing. Approval cycles of 3-12 months build the track record. Next comes FAA PMA for cabin, landing-gear, component and non-hot-section engine parts on sunset CFM56/V2500-era fleets, where OEMs pay least attention. Later extend the same evidence engine to nuclear dedication and rail obsolete electronics. MARKET: Commercial aero aftermarket parts run about $40-50B a year inside about $119B of MRO, and DoD secondary items and spares add tens of billions a year. Nuclear, rail and industrial turbine obsolete spares add more. Capturing 1-3% at HEICO-like operating margins of 21-24% gives $1-5B of revenue. HEICO is valued at about $40B and TransDigm at about $70-80B, both built on this layer. COMPARABLES: HEICO Flight Support Group (about 20,000 PMAs, about 400-550 added a year, no material patents), TransDigm as the pricing benchmark (about 47% margin, its $2.2B purchase of Jet Parts Engineering and Victor Sierra in Jan 2026), Wencor, Rochester Electronics, StandardAero's 2,000+ proprietary repairs, and Paragraph IV first filers in generic drugs. KEY RISKS: OEM IP litigation (UTC v HEICO ran 10.5 years). Incumbents tend to buy whoever breaks their pricing (Law 6), so plan for a strategic exit unless the company reaches delegated authority (ODA/DOA) first. Regulators may accept AI-generated substantiation slowly.
finalist.why_finalist: This is the most direct expression of the C5 and C2 verdicts. The scarce layer is approval and substantiation, not making the part, and AI cuts exactly the engineering cost per approval that caps HEICO at about 500 approvals a year. Evidence is the strongest of any shape: HEICO and TransDigm margins, the $2.2B M&A that priced approval portfolios, and Law 4 on entrant-driven price falls. The moat is regulator-granted approvals with compounding track record. Novelty comes from a cost-per-approval curve steep enough to make 50-500-unit part numbers worth approving, and from serving several regulatory regimes with one engine. It also directly tests the sibling thread's 'HEICO for everything' hypothesis.

killers.killer: The DLA wedge does not produce HEICO margins. Breaking a sole source is designed to make an item competitive, and a SAR approval is not exclusive.
killers.evidence: DLA source approval qualifies you as one more approved source. Once a sole-source NSN is opened up, DLA buys on lowest price, and other qualified small businesses can bid against you or file their own SARs. The 25%-in-12-months price-spike list is public, so competitors see the same targets. Many spiked items are bought only a few units a year, so each approval earns little. This is unlike PMA, where only the holder can make the part. The pitch borrows HEICO and TransDigm margins, but those come from proprietary PMAs and OEM positions, not from DLA competitive buys. Note: the web search budget for this run ran out before I could check this, so this and the other evidence come from background knowledge and should be verified.
killers.ai_answer: Partly. If AI cuts the cost of each package by a large factor, the business can win on cost per approval and volume rather than margin per part: hundreds of approvals a year, each with thin but positive margin. Better still, use DLA as the place to build the track record and the lab and allowables data, not as the profit pool. The profits come later from FAA PMA and orphan-part licensing, where the approval is exclusive.

killers.killer: The government's engineering reviewers are the bottleneck, not the applicant, and AI on the applicant side does not shorten their clock.
killers.evidence: In DoD, every SAR is reviewed by a service Engineering Support Activity, such as an Air Logistics Complex engineering office. In aviation, FAA certification offices oversee PMAs and DER findings. Both are understaffed. Industry often reports SAR reviews taking well over a year, many packages returned, and small-business SARs deprioritized. The pitch's 3-12 month figure is optimistic. Reviewers also sign under their own liability and will distrust substantiation generated by AI.
killers.ai_answer: Partial structural answer. First, packages that are complete the first time cut rework cycles, which are a large share of elapsed time. Second, the company can partner directly with ESAs and the Air Force Rapid Sustainment Office, or bid on their reverse-engineering contracts (OC-ALC already funds reverse engineering), so the government itself pulls the work. Third, in FAA, hire company DERs and aim for ODA so the company makes its own findings. ODA takes years, and the FAA grants it only after a long clean history.

killers.killer: Data rights and IP: on legacy platforms the government often does not own the data, and OEMs litigate.
killers.evidence: AMSC codes C, D and P usually mean the government lacks adequate data, lacks rights to it, or requires source approval by the design control activity. That is why reverse engineering is needed in the first place, which contradicts the pitch's claim that 'the government owns or can compel the data.' Clean-room reverse engineering must be documented carefully, and OEMs claim trade secrets on processes. UTC v HEICO ran about 10.5 years. Pratt & Whitney and GE have used warranty voids and service agreements to fight PMA.
killers.ai_answer: Yes, a good one. AI-assisted reconstruction from physical parts, with a full audit trail of the evidence, can be made provably clean-room, which is a litigation asset. The company should also license orphaned type-certificate and part data directly from OEMs that want to exit legacy support, as Ontic does. That replaces the IP fight with royalties.

killers.killer: Incumbents already do this at scale, and the AI tools are available to them too.
killers.evidence: HEICO Flight Support, which added Wencor in 2023, has roughly 20,000 PMAs and adds about 400-550 a year. TransDigm bought Jet Parts Engineering and Victor Sierra, PMA houses. Chromalloy and Kellstrom both run PMA and DER-repair businesses. StandardAero has more than 2,000 proprietary repairs. Ontic (CVC-owned) specializes in licensed orphan parts. In electronics obsolescence, Rochester Electronics and GDCA lead; in nuclear dedication, Curtiss-Wright, Paragon Energy Solutions and Westinghouse. On the government side, depots and the Air Force Rapid Sustainment Office do reverse engineering in house and work with vendors such as Physna, and Senvol sells additive allowables data. Scan-to-CAD and CT software are off the shelf from Geomagic, Oqton, Zeiss and Nikon. CFM56 and V2500 are among the most contested PMA markets, not neglected ones.
killers.ai_answer: The only answer is throughput and coverage of the long tail. Incumbents choose part numbers by return on engineering hours, so they skip the thousands of low-volume NSNs and PMAs that do not pay back. If AI cuts engineering hours per approval by 5-10x, a lower bar for what is worth approving opens a long tail they ignore. The moat is then an approval portfolio across that long tail, not the AI tools. Expect to be acquired, and that is an acceptable outcome.

killers.killer: Physics clocks and capital intensity: the evidence is coupons, fatigue tests and first-article inspection, and an accredited lab plus CT is expensive.
killers.evidence: ISO 17025 and Nadcap accreditation, an industrial CT system ($1-3M), test frames and coupon programs each cost millions and take 12-24 months to stand up. Fatigue and qualification tests run on fixed physical timelines. Public allowables already exist (MMPDS, CMH-17, NCAMP), so a proprietary allowables database is valuable only for unusual alloys or additive processes, and it is slow to build.
killers.ai_answer: Partial. Start with accredited third-party labs and only build an owned lab once test volume justifies it. Pick parts whose substantiation is mostly analysis plus a light test, such as cabin, brackets and non-critical structure. Use 10 USC 3243 and SBIR/STRATFI money for qualification testing. AI can cut the test plan to the minimum needed, but it cannot shorten the tests themselves.

killers.killer: Product liability and insurance: as the design approval holder, the company owns the failure.
killers.evidence: If a PMA or DER-repaired part is implicated in a crash or an engine event, the company faces unlimited product liability. Aviation products liability insurance for a young company with no loss history is expensive and hard to place. Lessors and airlines often restrict PMA and DER repairs in lease return conditions, which lowers their value to buyers.
killers.ai_answer: Structural. Begin with parts that are not flight-critical or that sit in defense programs, where government contracting rules and the government's own acceptance limit exposure. Build insurance on the record of evidence. Sign lessor acceptance agreements early: AerCap and others accept PMA when there is a cost case. AI does not help here.

killers.killer: Too many regimes for one startup: FAA, DLA, nuclear and rail ECM.
killers.evidence: Each regime has its own approval route, its own scarce credentialed people (DERs, ESA relationships, nuclear dedication under 10 CFR 21 and NQA-1, EU rail ECM), its own buyers and its own incumbents. A single seed-stage company cannot be credible in four regimes. YC will read this as a lack of focus.
killers.ai_answer: Yes: drop all but one regime for 3+ years. The 'evidence engine' carries across regimes, but the approvals and track record do not.

killers.killer: Scarce credentialed people: DERs and former ESA engineers.
killers.evidence: Every FAA finding needs a DER with the right delegation, and the DER workforce is old and shrinking. Signers are personally liable and slow to put their name on AI drafts. Talent is likely the binding constraint on scale, not engineering hours.
killers.ai_answer: Yes. This is where AI helps most: one DER signing 5-10x more well-prepared packages. Recruit retired DERs and depot engineers as consultants. The company's AI and evidence tools are what make them more productive.

attacks.who_already_does_it: FAA PMA and DER repair: HEICO Flight Support (about 20,000 PMAs, plus Wencor), TransDigm (Jet Parts Engineering and Victor Sierra, Jan 2026), Chromalloy, Kellstrom, StandardAero and AAR repair engineering. Orphan parts under OEM license: Ontic (CVC). DoD reverse engineering and SAR: in-house depot engineering at OC-ALC, WR-ALC and OO-ALC, the Air Force Rapid Sustainment Office, many small reverse-engineering and SAR job shops, Physna (geometric search and reverse engineering under DoD contracts), and Senvol (additive allowables data and machine learning). Electronics obsolescence: Rochester Electronics, GDCA. Nuclear commercial-grade dedication: Curtiss-Wright, Paragon Energy Solutions, Westinghouse. Scan-to-CAD and CT tools from Hexagon/Geomagic, Oqton, Zeiss and Nikon are sold to all of them. I found no AI-native company that holds the approvals itself, but every piece of the stack has an incumbent. Caveat: the web search budget for this run ran out, so this list comes from background knowledge and was not checked against current sources.
attacks.surviving_version: The surviving version is narrower: a single-regime approval house for the long tail. AI is a throughput engine that makes thousands of low-volume parts worth approving, parts that HEICO and the depots skip because they do not pay back their engineering hours. Phase 1: a DoD sustainment contractor that sells reverse-engineering and SAR packages, and ideally gets paid to produce them, under OC-ALC, WR-ALC or Rapid Sustainment Office contracts and SBIR/STRATFI. Revenue comes from engineering services plus being an approved source, not from margins on DLA competitive buys. Use accredited third-party labs at first. Phase 2: build the record and the DER bench, then move into exclusive approvals with real margin. That means FAA PMA for non-critical parts on legacy fleets and licensed orphan type-certificate and part data from OEMs exiting legacy support, as Ontic does. Pursue ODA status as the moat. Nuclear and rail come only after that. Plan to be acquired by HEICO, TransDigm or CVC/Ontic, which typically pay high multiples. Treat 'HEICO for everything' as the upside case, not the base case.
attacks.cheapest_first_test: Spend 6-8 weeks with about $50k and no lab. Pull 30-50 NSNs coded AMSC C/D/P whose prices spiked, using public DIBBS and FLIS data, and confirm what each code actually means for data rights. Take three to a retired ESA engineer or DER. Use AI-assisted reconstruction from purchased or surplus parts to produce full SAR-ready packages, and log engineering hours against the usual roughly 300-1,000 hours per package. Meanwhile, get one ALC engineering office or Rapid Sustainment Office program manager to agree in writing to review the packages, or to put them on contract, and get one DLA buyer to state the annual buy for those NSNs. Success means a 5x cut in hours, at least one ESA reviewing on a defined clock, and annual demand above $250k per approved item. If any of the three fails, drop the DLA wedge.

killers.killer: The government's engineering review step is the real bottleneck, not making the package. DLA source approval requests (SARs) go to the service's engineering support activity (ESA) for technical review, and that queue runs on government staff. Faster package production does not make the reviewers faster.
killers.evidence: 10 USC 3243 (read on Cornell LII) says the agency must give offerors a prompt chance to show they meet qualification standards, tell them promptly whether they qualified and why not, and pay testing and evaluation costs for small businesses that meet the standards. A 2025 amendment removed the old condition that this cost-sharing be justified by expected savings from more competition. So the law pays for the cost of testing and nudges toward speed, but nothing in it funds reviewer headcount. Long SAR review times are widely reported, but I could not check them this run because the shared web-search budget ran out. Treat the duration as unverified.
killers.ai_answer: Make the reviewer's job smaller, and get paid by the buyer for the package itself. (1) Send packages in the ESA's own checklist format, with a compliance matrix, a CT-versus-drawing deviation map and the test data mapped to each requirement. Measure review hours per package as the main KPI. (2) Sell tech data packages (TDPs) and SAR packages as a paid service to the depots, the Air Force Rapid Sustainment Office (RSO) and the program offices, which already fund reverse engineering. The government buying the data package also gives the company standing in the queue. (3) Ask for 10 USC 3243 reimbursement on every eligible filing.

killers.killer: Revenue per part number is small and spread out. Most AMSC C/D/P items sell a few units a year, so each approval brings in tens of thousands of dollars a year. Fixed qualification cost per NSN can exceed what the part earns over its life.
killers.evidence: This follows from how DLA demand is structured: thousands of low-volume NSNs. HEICO reached scale only by stacking about 20,000 PMAs, about 400-550 a year, over decades. That is the fact base in the brief; I did not re-check it.
killers.ai_answer: This is where AI matters most. The economics only work if engineering cost per approval falls about 5-10x, so the threshold of yearly demand times price spike that justifies a filing drops. Rank targets by demand value × price-spike × similarity to parts already approved. Then reuse the allowables database and family-level substantiation, so one coupon campaign covers many NSNs. Group target parts into families that share a material and process.

killers.killer: Asset-light is partly wrong. An FAA PMA is a production approval, not only a design approval. The holder must perform the inspections and tests that show conformity, run a quality system and control its suppliers. 'Hold the data and liability, not the factory' cannot mean having no manufacturing quality footprint.
killers.evidence: 14 CFR 21.303 (Cornell LII) requires design data, test reports and computations, and that the applicant perform all inspections and tests needed to confirm that materials, the article and its processes conform to the approved design. The page I read appears to be an older version of the rule; the current Subpart K adds formal quality-system rules (21.307/21.137) that I did not verify. Showing a part is identical to the OEM part requires a license, so a reverse-engineered PMA must go the test-and-computation route.
killers.ai_answer: Own receiving inspection and conformity (automated CT and metrology plus first-article inspection) and supplier quality control. Fabrication stays with the network. This is roughly HEICO's model. The CT and metrology cell is also what produces the evidence, so it does double duty.

killers.killer: OEMs and incumbents block the aviation stage through litigation, lock-in and acquisitions. OEMs sue, power-by-the-hour engine contracts and lessor return conditions keep PMA parts out, and TransDigm-style buyers absorb anyone who breaks their pricing.
killers.evidence: From the brief, not re-checked: UTC v HEICO ran 10.5 years, and TransDigm bought Jet Parts Engineering and Victor Sierra for $2.2B in Jan 2026. These cut both ways: the threat is real, and so is the exit.
killers.ai_answer: Run defense work first. There the government owns or can compel the data, and the litigation threat is far weaker. Enter commercial aviation only on sunset CFM56/V2500-era and cabin/landing-gear/component parts, where OEM PBH coverage is falling off. Use airlines and lessors that want a second source as anchor customers with acceptance agreements. Treat an exit to HEICO or TransDigm as a planned outcome, not a failure.

killers.killer: Regulators may be slow to accept AI-made substantiation, and the liability is personal. FAA DERs and DLA reviewers sign as individuals.
killers.evidence: Approval schemes depend on named signatories (DER, ODA unit members). No regulator has a category for AI-authored compliance findings.
killers.ai_answer: Never present the work as AI-made. AI writes drafts; employed DERs and qualified engineers review and sign. The pitch is human-certified packages produced at machine cost. Seek ODA only after a long clean record.

killers.killer: Doing too many regulatory regimes at once: FAA, DLA, NRC commercial-grade dedication and rail ECM. Each needs different credentials, quality programs (for example 10 CFR 50 Appendix B for nuclear) and buyers. A seed-stage company that tries all of them builds none.
killers.evidence: The brief's own sequencing already admits these are separate approval regimes, each with its own track record.
killers.ai_answer: Commit to defense aviation sustainment for about 3 years, then FAA PMA. Put nuclear and rail on the roadmap only as reuses of the evidence engine, and only once the aviation business pays for itself. One option is to license the evidence engine to existing nuclear dedicating entities rather than become one.

killers.killer: Small-business status may not survive venture funding. 10 USC 3243 cost reimbursement and many DLA set-asides need small-business certification, and venture ownership can trigger SBA affiliation questions.
killers.evidence: 10 USC 3243 limits the testing cost coverage to certified small businesses or their products (Cornell LII).
killers.ai_answer: Raise money in a structure that keeps SBA small-business eligibility, and plan for losing it once the business is profitable. The reimbursement is a bootstrap subsidy, not the business model.

attacks.who_already_does_it: Commercial PMA and DER repairs: HEICO Flight Support Group (including Wencor), TransDigm (now with Jet Parts Engineering and Victor Sierra), Chromalloy, StandardAero proprietary repairs, and many small DER and PMA shops. Defense: depot reverse-engineering cells at the Air Logistics Complexes, the Air Force Rapid Sustainment Office, DLA's own reverse-engineering and value-engineering programs, and many small DLA second-source manufacturers bidding on DIBBS. Obsolete electronics: Rochester Electronics. Nuclear dedication: established dedicating entities and nuclear supply-chain vendors. Nobody clearly sells AI-driven, multi-regime approval packages as its main product, but I could not check startups in this space: the shared web-search budget for this run ran out after the first queries. Only the two primary-source regulation pages cited here were read.
attacks.surviving_version: A defense-first approval house that sells approval packages, not parts, at first. Phase 1, years 0-2: be the AI-native producer of tech data packages and SAR/source-approval packages for depot and DLA sole-source items (AMSC C/D/P, price spikes of 25% or more, legacy C-130/KC-135/H-60/A-10). Get paid three ways: TDP and reverse-engineering contracts from depots, RSO and program offices; SBIR/AFWERX money; and 10 USC 3243 testing reimbursement, which the 2025 amendment made easier to get by dropping the savings-justification condition. Keep the approved sources and sell parts through a pre-qualified CNC, casting and additive supplier network. Own the conformity cell (CT and metrology plus first-article inspection) and the coupon-built allowables database. Main KPIs: engineering hours and reviewer hours per approval, and approvals per year. Pick NSNs by demand value × price-spike × similarity to parts already approved, so each coupon campaign covers a family of parts. Phase 2, years 2-4: buy a small PMA/DER shop that already has approvals and a quality system, which buys the FAA track record instead of waiting for it. Then file PMAs on sunset CFM56/V2500 component, cabin and landing-gear parts, with airline and lessor acceptance agreements signed up front. Phase 3: either reach ODA and become an independent HEICO-for-sunset-fleets, or sell to HEICO, TransDigm or a PE roll-up, valued on the approval portfolio. Nuclear and rail come only through licensing or reusing the evidence engine, never as day-one regimes.
attacks.cheapest_first_test: In 6-8 weeks, before YC. Pull DLA DIBBS award history for C-130 and KC-135 AMSC C/D/P NSNs and find the 30 with the largest price spikes and demand value. Run the AI pipeline on 5 of them using borrowed or bought parts and outsourced CT, to produce full SAR/TDP packages. Measure engineering hours per package against an industry baseline from a retired ESA engineer or DER. Submit at least 2 real SARs, and pitch the packages to one Air Logistics Complex reverse-engineering office or the RSO for a paid TDP pilot or an SBIR Phase I. Pass means two things: package cost at least 5x below baseline, and one government buyer willing to pay for packages or fast-track their review. Fail means reviewers will not take the packages or no one pays before approval.

finalist.name: Late-Frame Turbine House: an AI-native independent owner-operator for mature gas turbine and aeroderivative fleets
merged_from: Late-Life Turbine House: FTAI-for-power for mature gas turbine and aeroderivative fleets
Late-Frame Turbine Works (AI-native independent gas turbine and aeroderivative service operator)
Gridstock: pre-positioned standardized spares for long-lead grid and generation equipment (gas-turbine HGP exchange-set component only)
finalist.description: WHAT IT DOES: An independent service operator and asset owner for mature gas-turbine frames (7F/7EA/9FA/6B, 501F) and aeroderivatives (LM2500/LM6000 and converted CFM56-class power units) that are leaving or have left OEM LTSAs. It buys retired engines and frames as teardown feedstock, runs pooled hot-gas-path and rotor exchange sets so parts come off the outage critical path, and develops its own approved repairs and non-OEM hot-section parts. It sells guaranteed-duration outages with liquidated damages and availability-based, interval-extension service contracts. AI cuts the engineering cost per repair qualification (borescope and NDE analysis, life modelling from operating data, dossier assembly). It lets a smaller certified workforce review more units, predicts emergent outage work from fleet history, and lets a small team underwrite availability risk across mixed fleets. WHAT IT OWNS: (1) A catalogue of approved repairs and parts with proven fleet hours. (2) Teardown feedstock and a cross-owner rotable exchange pool. (3) Qualification dossiers built on cross-owner condition data, accepted by insurers and lenders, which justify interval extensions. (4) The installed-base annuity of uptime contracts. Casting and fabrication are subcontracted. WEDGE: Behind-the-meter data-center, oilfield and merchant aeroderivative owners. They are new, outside LTSAs, and desperate for availability while OEM slots and new-unit lead times are sold out. Lead with a pooled exchange-engine and module program plus a time-to-restore guarantee. Then add combustion and transition-piece repairs and HGP exchange sets for out-of-LTSA 7FA/7EA owners (merchant IPPs, municipal utilities), one frame family at a time. MARKET: Gas turbine aftermarket services are about $20-35B a year globally. Only about 26% of GE's roughly 7,000 units are under LTSAs, which leaves a large transactional aftermarket. Siemens Energy cites about €400M of lifecycle value per GW. Data-center gas buildouts in 2025-2030 add tens of GW. Taking 5-15% of the mature-frame aftermarket gives $1-4B of revenue at 12-24% margins. COMPARABLES: FTAI Aviation and FTAI Power (aerospace revenue up about 3.5x in two years on 25-year-old engines), PSM (Hanwha) with 7F intervals extended from 24k to 32k+ hours, EthosEnergy, MD&A, Sulzer, AerSale (35-39% gross on owned parts against 17% on labour), StandardAero, and Calpine's insourced maintenance (26 GW at a 2.3% forced outage factor). KEY RISKS: OEM IP litigation. Concentrated superalloy casting supply. OEMs re-locking new frames through LTSAs, mitigated by targeting only frames the OEM is ceding (independents enter 8-16 years into a frame's life, Law 8). Insurer acceptance of non-OEM parts, which the company addresses by building the qualification layer IMIA says is missing.
finalist.why_finalist: Strongest demand tailwind of any shape: AI data-center load meets OEM capacity that is sold out. The moat sits in the layers the verdicts say keep the value: owned rotable pools, proven fleet hours, insurer- and lender-grade evidence, and uptime contracts (Laws 7 and 8). The EC record documents both the OEM lock and the clock on which it decays. The evidence is concrete (PSM, FTAI, AerSale margins, Calpine). This is the strongest energy-sector form of the sibling thread's orphan-parts hypothesis. It is capital-intensive, but the margin comes from owned assets, not labour.

killers.killer: The wedge is already taken by well-funded aeroderivative pool operators
killers.evidence: ProEnergy's own site shows it rebuilding LM6000s as the PE6000, which is interchangeable with the LM6000PC. It runs leasing, depot overhauls promised in 120 days or less, CAPEX-free contracted power and 'Lifecycle Care' (parts, engines, predictive), and it has a 650 MW order of 13 PE6000 sets for Crusoe AI Factories. That is the exact behind-the-meter data-center wedge, with exchange engines and a restore guarantee already bundled. FTAI Power (from memory, 2025 announcements) converts CFM56 cores into power units for data centers and has a larger CFM56 feedstock base and module shops than any startup could build. Further players in the same space, from memory: GE Vernova's TM2500 and LM6000 rental and lease fleet, MTU Maintenance's industrial depot for LM2500 and LM6000, APR Energy, and Siemens Energy rental packages.
killers.ai_answer: AI does not answer this, because the binding constraint is owning engines and depot slots, not analysis. Structurally, the only openings are segments ProEnergy and FTAI underserve: older or less common aeroderivatives such as the LM2500 base or plus, LM1600 and RB211/Trent industrial units, plus non-GE frames. That is a much smaller market.

killers.killer: Teardown feedstock is scarce and its price keeps rising
killers.evidence: Retired LM6000s and LM2500s are being put back into service, not scrapped, because new-unit lead times are sold out. On CFM56 cores the company would bid against FTAI, AerSale and airlines, and airlines are flying 737NG/A320ceo fleets longer because Boeing and Airbus are delivering late. FTAI's results (25-year-old engines, aerospace revenue up about 3.5x) show who already holds the feedstock arbitrage.
killers.ai_answer: Partial. AI condition triage of borescope and records data can price used cores better and find salvageable modules others write off. That is an edge in buying, not a moat. Feedstock for orphan heavy frames (6B, 7EA, 501D5A, W251) is cheaper and less contested.

killers.killer: Capital intensity of the rotable pools before any revenue
killers.evidence: A spare LM6000-class engine costs roughly $10-25M. A 7FA hot-gas-path set or spare rotor costs roughly $10-30M per frame family. One credible pool for one family therefore needs $50-150M of assets before the first time-to-restore guarantee can be honoured. FTAI and AerSale fund this with public equity and asset-backed debt. A YC-stage company cannot.
killers.ai_answer: There is a structural answer: asset-backed lease financing with an infrastructure or aviation-lessor partner, or pooling assets the owners contribute (a co-op exchange) so the company runs the pool rather than owning it. It is feasible but dilutes the 'owns the feedstock' thesis.

killers.killer: Customers will not take liquidated damages from a startup
killers.evidence: Hyperscalers and IPP lenders want investment-grade counterparties on availability guarantees, because a lost data-center MW-day can cost far more than the outage contract. Calpine's 2.3% forced outage factor came from a 26 GW in-house fleet with decades of history. A new operator has no fleet history to underwrite with.
killers.ai_answer: Partial. Wrap the guarantees in an insurance or reinsurance product, which the AI life models could help price, and cap LDs at the contract value. Underwriters still want years of fleet hours first, so this is a physics clock that AI does not compress.

killers.killer: Qualifying non-OEM parts and repairs runs on fleet-hour physics clocks
killers.evidence: PSM took more than a decade of 7F fleet operation to support extending intervals from 24k to 32k+ hours. Chromalloy, Sulzer and Liburdi built their repair catalogues over decades. IMIA, the engineering insurers' association, notes that insurers lack a framework for accepting non-OEM parts. AI can speed up dossier assembly and NDE analysis, but the evidence insurers and lenders accept is hours run without failure. Land turbines need no FAA PMA, which helps, but insurer acceptance becomes the regulator in practice.
killers.ai_answer: A real but slow answer. The AI-built dossier lowers the engineering cost of each qualification, and reverse-engineered repair is legal for land turbines. Hours still have to accrue, so the catalogue moat takes 5-10 years. Start with lower-risk repairs (combustion liners, transition pieces) whose short intervals (8-12k hours) give quick feedback.

killers.killer: Superalloy casting capacity is captured by the OEMs
killers.evidence: PCC, Howmet, Doncasters and CPP are the industry's few superalloy casters, and they are booked out by aero and industrial OEM demand. A subcontracting startup queues behind GE, Siemens and Mitsubishi for new single-crystal or directionally-solidified blades and vanes. The non-OEM hot-section parts leg is likely blocked for years.
killers.ai_answer: There is a structural workaround: favour repair over replacement (coating strip and recoat, braze and weld repair of teardown parts), and treat newly made parts only as a later, narrower bet on equiaxed and fabricated parts such as combustion hardware and transition pieces. AI-guided adaptive repair and automated welding or braze cells help here.

killers.killer: Most units in the wedge are not actually outside an LTSA
killers.evidence: New behind-the-meter LM6000, LM2500XPRESS, SGT-800 and Titan units are sold with OEM CSAs or warranties, and financiers often require them. The prior thread's Law 8 says independents enter 8-16 years into a frame's life, which contradicts leading with brand-new data-center owners. The truly out-of-LTSA buyers are older merchant peakers, oilfield units and municipals, who are price-sensitive and slow to buy.
killers.ai_answer: No AI answer exists. Change the wedge to owners of 10-25-year-old units with no CSA who are now running them hard because power prices and capacity payments rose: merchant peakers, oilfield units and municipals. Data centers come later, as buyers of refurbished units with a restore guarantee.

killers.killer: Established independent service providers on mature 7F, 7EA and 501F frames
killers.evidence: PSM (Hanwha), EthosEnergy, MD&A, Sulzer, Allied Power Group, TurbineTech, Chromalloy and Liburdi already offer HGP exchange sets, combustion and transition-piece repairs, and interval extensions to out-of-LTSA 7FA, 7EA and 501F owners. They have catalogues, field crews and insurer acceptance today, and GE Vernova competes on transactional pricing for units leaving its LTSAs.
killers.ai_answer: Partial. The AI-native advantage would be lower engineering cost per repair, which makes long-tail frames economic that large independents skip (6B, Frame 5, W251, 501D5A, V84.2, GT11N, LM1600). That is an orphan-parts focus rather than a fight with PSM on 7FA.

killers.killer: OEM IP and trade-secret litigation risk
killers.evidence: Historically, OEMs have pursued trade-secret cases against people who moved between rivals, for example GE and Siemens over turbine bid materials. They also restrict tooling, software, and controls and data access. Reverse engineering itself is generally lawful for land turbines.
killers.ai_answer: Yes. Use clean-room reverse engineering from teardown hardware, keep documented provenance, and avoid hiring ex-OEM engineers with drawings. AI-assisted reverse engineering from 3D scans makes the clean room cheaper.

killers.killer: Access to condition data and a scarce certified workforce
killers.evidence: Cross-owner condition data sits with the OEM monitoring centers and with each owner. Field service engineers and borescope inspectors are scarce, and independents compete for the same people.
killers.ai_answer: Yes, partly. The data comes as a by-product of doing the service work, and AI borescope and NDE review lets fewer certified people sign off more units. The workforce leverage is the one place AI fits squarely.

attacks.who_already_does_it: For aeroderivative pools in the data-center wedge: ProEnergy (rebuilt PE6000/LM6000, lease fleet, depot overhauls in 120 days or less, 650 MW Crusoe order), FTAI Power (CFM56 conversion to power units), GE Vernova's TM2500/LM6000 rental and CSAs, MTU Maintenance (industrial LM depot), APR Energy and Siemens Energy rentals. For mature-frame HGP, repairs and interval extension: PSM (Hanwha), EthosEnergy, MD&A, Sulzer, Allied Power Group, Chromalloy, Liburdi and TurbineTech, plus Calpine-style insourcing at large IPPs. Models for owned parts and teardown: AerSale, HEICO, StandardAero. Caveat: the web search budget for this turn ran out after one direct page fetch (ProEnergy's homepage). The competitor list and figures come from that page plus my prior knowledge, and live verification of FTAI Power's current status, GE's LTSA share and pool asset prices is still needed.
attacks.surviving_version: The pitched version (data-center aeroderivative pools plus 7FA HGP sets, guaranteed with LDs) fails on its own: ProEnergy and FTAI own that wedge, and pools need $50-150M before revenue. What survives is a narrower, asset-light orphan-frame repair and qualification house. It would pick 1-2 frame families the OEM and large independents underserve: 6B, Frame 5, W251/501D5A, older LM2500 base/plus or LM1600. It would buy cheap teardown units from those fleets and earn first on repair, not new castings: combustion liners, transition pieces, recoat and braze of HGP parts. AI would cut engineering cost per repair, so long-tail frames become worth serving, and would assemble insurer-facing qualification dossiers. It would sell repaired parts and module exchanges transactionally to out-of-LTSA owners, and would sell to the large independents themselves where they skip the frame. Availability contracts come only after fleet hours accrue, wrapped by an insurance partner. A rotable pool comes later, financed off balance sheet with a lessor. This is the 'HEICO for orphan turbines' path, not a FTAI clone.
attacks.cheapest_first_test: Spend 4-6 weeks on three checks. (1) Interview 25 owners of out-of-LTSA 6B, 7EA, W251 or old LM units (municipals, merchant peakers, oilfield operators). Ask what was on their last outage's critical path, what lead time and price they were quoted, and whether they would sign an LOI for a repaired combustion set or exchange module at 60-70% of the OEM price. (2) Ask two engineering insurers (HSB/Munich Re, FM Global or an IMIA member) exactly what evidence would make them accept a non-OEM repaired part without a premium loading. (3) Get one quote on a retired orphan-frame teardown unit, and price its salvageable parts against current OEM part prices. If owners will not sign LOIs, insurers ask for more than about 8k hours of fleet evidence, or the teardown arbitrage is under 2x, the thesis dies cheaply.

killers.killer: Wedge collision: the behind-the-meter aeroderivative niche is already the most contested part of the market, and its customers are not 'outside service'. Data-center and oilfield buyers get refurbished units with uptime bundled in from vertically integrated players that already own the feedstock.
killers.evidence: From prior knowledge only; the shared web-search budget for this run (200 calls) was used up before this agent's queries ran, so none of this was re-checked live. ProEnergy (Sedalia, MO) refurbishes LM6000s into its PE6000 packages and runs its own exchange-engine and lease pool. It has reportedly sold more than 1 GW of these to data-center developers. FTAI Power (announced 2025) converts CFM56-7B cores into ~25 MW units and draws on FTAI's own stock of thousands of CFM56 modules, which a new entrant cannot match on feedstock cost. Solaris Energy Infrastructure leases Solar Titan 130 fleets to xAI with availability bundled in. GE Vernova sells LM2500XPRESS units, for example to Crusoe/Abilene, together with service. The wedge customers buy uptime as a product. They are not stranded owners looking for an MRO shop.
killers.ai_answer: Don't lead with aero. If aero stays in scope, enter as the independent multi-vendor layer that sits above the pools: an AI condition-monitoring and time-to-restore broker that covers mixed fleets (LM6000 from ProEnergy, CFM56 conversions from FTAI, Titans, older LM2500s in frac fleets). Rent exchange engines from the existing pools rather than owning them. The structural opening is the second-hand owner: a data center whose original supplier contract has lapsed, or an oilfield fleet that has changed hands, and that no single pool covers.

killers.killer: Capital intensity of owning exchange pools and feedstock doesn't fit a YC-stage company. Pool utilisation is unproven until a fleet exists.
killers.evidence: A 7FA hot-gas-path set is roughly $10-25M and an LM6000 spare engine roughly $8-15M (industry rules of thumb, not verified this run). FTAI, AerSale and Solaris all built their pools with public-market or asset-backed debt after they already had customers.
killers.ai_answer: Sequencing. Phase 1 owns no metal: sell AI outage scoping and qualification dossiers, and broker parts out of PSM, EthosEnergy, MD&A and surplus teardown inventory. Phase 2 finances a single 7EA or 7FA.03 HGP exchange set with asset-backed or insurer capital, secured against contracted outages. That mirrors aircraft lessors and Solaris, where the capital follows signed contracts. The company owns the dossiers and the contracts, and the balance sheet belongs to a capital partner.

killers.killer: Concentrated superalloy casting supply. PCC, Howmet and Doncasters prioritise OEMs and aero, so non-OEM new-make first-stage blades and vanes face very long lead times and qualification of each foundry.
killers.evidence: From prior knowledge: aero and IGT casting backlogs of 60-100+ weeks over 2024-26. Howmet and PCC report record aero backlogs. PSM and EthosEnergy survive mainly on combustion hardware, transition pieces and repairs, not on new-make rotating airfoils.
killers.ai_answer: Repair before new-make. The catalogue starts with combustion liners, transition pieces, fuel nozzles, and stage 2-3 nozzles and buckets returned to service by braze, weld, coating and additive tip repair. Teardown feedstock supplies the castings, which is exactly why harvesting retired frames matters. Use AI to grade harvested parts for life remaining, so a recovered blade becomes a qualified rotable without a new casting. Take on new-make only for orphan parts on frames the OEM has ceded (6B, 7EA, early 7FA, 501D5).

killers.killer: OEM IP and control-system lock-in. This means trade-secret and patent litigation, plus access to controls, software and fleet data such as Mark VIe and remote monitoring.
killers.evidence: Independents such as PSM (now Hanwha), EthosEnergy, MD&A and Sulzer have sold non-OEM 7F/7EA/501F hardware for decades. Interval extensions on 7FA (from 24k to 32k+ hours with PSM parts) show that reverse-engineered hardware is commercially defensible. Industrial gas turbines have no FAA-style PMA gate, so the barrier is IP and insurer comfort rather than regulation.
killers.ai_answer: Clean-room reverse engineering of teardown parts, with documented design provenance. AI makes producing that documentation cheap: scan to CAD, then life models built from cross-owner operating data rather than OEM drawings. Target only frames past year 8-16 of their life. Use independent controls retrofits (several firms offer Mark V/VI replacements) wherever the controls lock bites.

killers.killer: Underwriting liquidated damages and availability without fleet data. A single forced outage on an LD contract could wipe out a small balance sheet.
killers.evidence: Calpine's insourced fleet (about 26 GW at a ~2.3% forced outage factor) shows that availability risk can be managed at scale. But Calpine is now part of Constellation, so the best-known proof point has been absorbed into a large utility rather than serving third parties. A startup has neither the diversification nor the data.
killers.ai_answer: Cap and lay off the risk. Phase 1 sells a guaranteed duration only on outage scope, with capped LDs and the parts already staged. Wrap availability products in performance insurance or reinsurance from carriers such as HSB/Munich Re, using the cross-owner condition dataset as the underwriting input. The insurer takes the tail and the company keeps the data and the contract. This makes the qualification dossier the product, which is the gap IMIA flags.

killers.killer: AI is not proprietary to the startup. EthosEnergy, PSM, Sulzer, MD&A and the OEMs' own multi-vendor service arms can buy the same borescope and NDE AI, so AI alone doesn't shift share.
killers.evidence: This matches the sibling-thread finding: when AI levels knowledge, the monopoly moves to approvals, test evidence, installed fleets and scarce factories, and the leveller rarely keeps the value.
killers.ai_answer: Own the next scarce layer, not the AI. That layer is (a) qualification dossiers with accumulated fleet hours, accepted by insurers and lenders, which accrue on physics clocks and can't be bought quickly; (b) cross-owner condition data that single-owner incumbents structurally don't have; and (c) contracted installed-base annuities. AI lowers the cost of building those assets. The assets are the moat.

killers.killer: The out-of-LTSA customer base is consolidating into large owners who insource maintenance (Constellation-Calpine, Vistra, NRG), which shrinks the transactional mid-market.
killers.evidence: From prior knowledge: Constellation's acquisition of Calpine (closed around 2025-26). Big IPPs run their own turbine maintenance groups.
killers.ai_answer: Target the long tail that can't insource: PE-owned merchant plants (LS Power, Lightstone, Rockland-style owners), municipal utilities and co-ops, and new non-utility owners of second-hand frames. The large consolidators can still be customers for orphan parts and pool access.

killers.killer: Workforce and shop capacity. Certified field-service engineers and repair shops are scarce, and 'a smaller certified workforce' still needs physical shop throughput.
killers.evidence: From prior knowledge: industry-wide shortages of field-service technicians and long OEM outage-slot queues.
killers.ai_answer: Use AI-assisted remote borescope reviews so one certified engineer can review many units. For physical capacity, acquire or partner with one regional repair shop (a roll-up or search-fund style buy) once Phase 1 has shown demand, rather than building one.

attacks.who_already_does_it: Note on evidence: the shared web-search budget (200 calls per turn) was used up before this agent's searches ran, so everything below is from prior knowledge (to about mid-2026) and should be re-checked live. Mature heavy-frame independents: PSM (Hanwha; 7FA FlameTOP parts and interval extensions), EthosEnergy, MD&A, Sulzer, Chromalloy (coatings and castings repair), Liburdi, Doncasters (castings), and TurboCare, which was part of EthosEnergy. Aeroderivatives and conversions: ProEnergy (PE6000 refurbished LM6000s with its own exchange-engine and lease pool, selling to data centers), FTAI Power (CFM56-7B to ~25 MW conversions backed by FTAI's own module stock), Solaris Energy Infrastructure (leased Solar Titan fleets for xAI), GE Vernova's own LM2500XPRESS and LM6000 lease and service programs, Mitsubishi Power Aero FT8 MobilePac, and Boom's 'Superpower' turbine for Crusoe (announced). The OEMs themselves (GE Vernova, Siemens Energy, Mitsubishi) run multi-vendor service and are re-locking new frames through LTSAs. Calpine's insourced turbine maintenance group (now inside Constellation) is the availability proof point. What nobody clearly owns yet: a cross-owner condition-data and qualification-dossier layer accepted by insurers and lenders, combined with a financed HGP exchange pool, for the long tail of PE, municipal and second-hand frame owners.
attacks.surviving_version: It survives only in a narrower, re-sequenced form: an AI-native life-extension and qualification house for heavy frames the OEMs have ceded. Drop the aeroderivative wedge and don't start as an owner-operator. Why: aero data-center demand is real but already owned by vertically integrated players holding the feedstock (ProEnergy, FTAI Power, Solaris, GE's own pools). Heavy frames that are 8-20 years old are being run harder because load growth makes old capacity valuable. Those owners face sold-out OEM outage slots, and most of the installed base (around 74% of GE units on the stated figure) sits outside LTSAs. Phase 1 (0-18 months, capital-light, YC-compatible) targets PE-owned merchant plants, municipal utilities and co-ops running 7EA, 6B, 7FA.03 or 501D5/F units outside LTSAs. Sell AI outage scoping (borescope and NDE grading, emergent-work prediction from fleet history) for a fixed fee. Pair it with a parts and repair plan staged before the outage, sourced across PSM, EthosEnergy, MD&A and surplus teardown inventory. Offer guaranteed-duration outages with capped LDs, delivered by subcontracted shops. Every job feeds a cross-owner condition dataset. Phase 2 turns that data into qualification dossiers for interval and life extension that insurers (HSB/FM-type) and lenders accept. Owners pay for these because they unlock refinancing, capacity-market commitments and longer intervals. Phase 3 finances one HGP exchange set at a time, per frame family, with asset-backed or insurer capital against contracted outages, and buys retired frames as teardown feedstock to supply recovered, AI-graded rotating parts. That sidesteps the casting bottleneck. Phase 4 adds an orphan-parts catalogue of repairs and non-OEM combustion and transition-piece hardware, starting with repairs before any new-make, plus availability contracts with the tail reinsured. That is a slow-compounding path toward HEICO-like aftermarket margins. Value capture sits in what accrues on physics clocks (dossiers with fleet hours, contracted installed base, owned rotables), not in the AI, consistent with the sibling-thread hypothesis. Aero comes back later only as a multi-vendor time-to-restore broker for second-hand mixed fleets that no single pool covers.
attacks.cheapest_first_test: Within 6-8 weeks, at under $50k: (1) Get 8-10 out-of-LTSA 7EA, 7FA or 501F owners (PE-owned merchant plants and municipal utilities, found via CTOTF/7EA and 7F user-group contacts) to share their last two outage reports and borescope data. For 3 of them, deliver an AI-predicted scope and parts plan for their next outage. Charge $15-40k, or free in exchange for a signed LOI. Then measure whether the predicted emergent work matches what their incumbent finds. (2) Ask each owner what they would pay for a guaranteed-duration outage with capped LDs and a pooled HGP set staged on site. Target 2 LOIs. (3) Show a sample dossier to one equipment-breakdown insurer and one plant lender, and get a written list of what evidence they would accept to approve an interval extension. (4) Get quotes from teardown and surplus brokers for 2-3 retired 7EA hot-gas-path sets, to size feedstock cost against new OEM parts. Kill signal: fewer than 2 LOIs, or insurers refuse to engage on any non-OEM dossier.

finalist.name: Loopback Depot: an AI-native NFF-eliminating repair depot and data-package rebuilder for defense and aviation electronics
merged_from: Sovereign Depot: a commercial organic-depot operator that owns reconstructed technical data and certified repair capacity for contractor-locked defense components
Intermittent (AI-native avionics and defence electronics repair station)
Loopback Depot: high-throughput repair-loop capacity for defence and aviation electronics
finalist.description: WHAT IT DOES: A certificated component repair operator (FAA/EASA Part 145 station plus DoD Public-Private Partnership depot partner) for line-replaceable electronics: avionics, radar, EW, power and control units, later rail and wind converters and data-center GPU fleet RMA. It wins on turnaround and true first-time fix by eliminating no-fault-found removals. It uses its own environmental-stimulus intermittent-fault test rigs, AI fault isolation that fuses BITE logs, flight data and teardown findings, and a serial-number history across operators. It also reconstructs missing technical data packages, test procedures and repair specs with AI, including physical process characterization, because FOGBANK showed CAD alone is not enough. Pricing is per confirmed fault and per serviceable unit at turnaround SLAs, which reverses the incentive that keeps NFF at 30-60%. WHAT IT OWNS: (1) Repair-station certificates and capability lists, which carry legal return-to-service authority. (2) Proprietary stress-replay automated test equipment. (3) A cross-operator rogue-unit and shop-findings database that no single airline or service has. (4) A growing library of government-accepted reconstructed TDPs and DER repair approvals for obsolete boards. (5) PBH-style component availability contracts and an owned rotable pool, which supplies the margin (AerSale's 35-39% on owned parts against 17% on labour). WEDGE: A DoD PPP or OTA contract to clear one high-backlog LRU family where the government owns the data: legacy fighter, rotary or tanker avionics first, then F-35 common components as sustainment management transfers to the services by about 2027-28. Guarantee turnaround under 30 days and NFF re-removal below 5%. In parallel, sell NFF reduction for regional and narrowbody airline avionics pools. Each repaired line yields an accepted TDP that compounds into the library. MARKET: Commercial component MRO is about $20-21B, about 18% of $119B. US DoD depot maintenance is about $35-45B a year, F-35 sustainment about $1.3-1.58T over its life, and NFF waste over $2B a year at DoD. At 3-5% share, revenue is $1-4B. COMPARABLES: StandardAero (about $5B to $10.4B on licence-protected repair), AAR, VSE, HEICO Electronic Technologies, Universal Synaptics (intermittent-fault testers: about $62M saved and 4x MTBF), Lufthansa Technik Component Services, Gecko Robotics (the defense IDIQ path), and organic depots (OO-ALC, FRCs). KEY RISKS: Prime-contractor IP resistance (Lockheed). Slow DoD acceptance and procurement. Right-to-repair stripped from the FY26 NDAA, so the company must work through contracts on government-owned-data and orphaned items.
finalist.why_finalist: Electronics NFF is the one domain where the synthesis found that diagnosis itself drives parts and shop flow, so AI leverage is direct rather than marginal. The evidence is unusually quantified: 10,000+ F-35 components in backlog, 141-188 day OEM cycles against 72 days at government depots, 73% of work still going to the OEM, 93% latent wiring faults, and $2B+ a year of NFF. The buyer, the policy (F-35 sustainment transfer), and the moat (certificates, cross-operator serial data, accepted TDPs, owned rotables) all line up. Three proposals converged on this shape, which is a strong signal.

killers.killer: Return-to-service authority depends on data the company does not have. A Part 145 capability list for an avionics LRU needs acceptable data, usually the OEM's CMM. Collins, Honeywell, Thales and L3Harris restrict CMMs or license them only to their own or authorized shops. DER-approved alternative repairs are possible, but each one is slow work part by part. On the defense side, a new repair source needs a Source Approval Request approved by the Engineering Support Activity, and each SAR typically takes 1-3 years.
killers.evidence: GAO (GAO-23-105341, status as of March 2026): DOD still has not identified the technical data or IP it needs for F-35 sustainment, and transfer of tech data and maintenance to the services is pushed to the end of CY2028. Engineering sustainment stays with the JPO, which means Lockheed. OEM CMM restriction is well known in the industry and is why HEICO and StandardAero value licences. Note: the per-tool web search budget was used up, so these industry facts come from prior knowledge, not fresh citations.
killers.ai_answer: Partial. AI can cut the cost of drafting a reconstructed CMM, test procedure or TDP by an order of magnitude. It cannot shorten the approval step: a government ESA or FAA DER still has to accept it, and first-article and qualification testing still runs on physics clocks. The way to survive is to choose items where the approval holder has gone (orphaned, government-owned data, or OEM support ended), so that someone is actively asking for an alternate source. Buying an existing small avionics Part 145 shop gets the certificate and capability list on day one, instead of spending 12-18 months getting certified.

killers.killer: Defense depot workshare is fixed by statute and the PPP partner role is minor. Under 10 USC 2466 (the 50/50 rule) and 2464 (core logistics), at least half of depot maintenance funding must go to organic depots. Component work for F-35 was already assigned in 2014-15 to OO-ALC, FRC-East, FRC-SE and Warner Robins, together with the OEMs (Honeywell, Northrop, BAE, Lockheed). A PPP partner typically supplies parts, engineering or technicians to the depot, not depot-level repairs under its own name.
killers.evidence: The F-35 depot activation assignments, and GAO's 10,000+ components awaiting repair (GAO-23-105341), show the backlog sits inside an assigned organic plus OEM structure. The services take over sustainment management by October 2027, but GAO says most recommendations are only partially addressed.
killers.ai_answer: Yes, structurally: sell to the organic depot instead of competing with it. Offer NFF triage, intermittent-fault ATE and test program set (TPS) rehosting through a CRADA or PPP in which the depot keeps the workload credit. This fits 50/50 politics because the depot's throughput goes up. The cost is that you look like a tools and services vendor, not StandardAero.

killers.killer: Incumbents already own the NFF tools and the cross-operator data. Universal Synaptics (IFDIS/PIFD, used on USAF C-130 and F-16, holds an F-35 JPO ATO, claims about $63M saved on the 'Frankenjet' project) and Eclypse ESS already sell intermittent-fault ATE to depots. Airbus Skywise, Lufthansa Technik AVIATAR, Boeing AnalytX, Collins Ascentia and Honeywell Forge already pool reliability and removal data across operators, which weakens the 'database nobody has' moat on the commercial side. C3.ai (USAF PANDA), Uptake, Avathon/SparkCognition and Shift5 own predictive maintenance on the military side. AAR, StandardAero, HEICO ETG, LHT Component Services, AFI KLM E&M, Barfield and Satair already run avionics pools with PBH contracts.
killers.evidence: The usynaptics.com site lists IFDIS 2.0 with neural-network NFF remediation, C-130 EHSI and EIDS cases where faults were isolated in 30 minutes to 4 hours on aircraft grounded 11-18 months, and Navy F/A-18 AWTS work. It offers no repair services, so the gap is repair plus test plus pricing together, not the test technology. ARINC Report 672 has codified NFF reduction guidance since 2008.
killers.ai_answer: Partial. The open space is integration: combining a certified repair station, stress-replay testing, fault isolation that fuses findings from BITE logs and teardowns, and pricing on outcomes. Nobody combines all of these today. The defensibility claim should rest on per-serial-number teardown findings, which OEM analytics platforms do not see in detail for third-party shops, not on 'cross-operator data'. Universal Synaptics is a more likely partner or acquisition target than a competitor.

killers.killer: Capital intensity of the rotable pool and PBH contracts. Avionics and radar LRUs cost $50k-$1M+ each. A PBH availability contract for even one regional fleet's avionics needs a pool worth tens of millions of dollars, plus balance-sheet risk on reliability. AerSale's 35-39% margins come from used material it buys cheaply by tearing down aircraft, which is a distinct business from NFF repair.
killers.evidence: In standard industry pool economics, a component PBH requires the provider to own spares sized to the fleet's MTBUR. AAR and AerSale fund this with corporate debt and asset-backed lines. A seed-stage startup cannot.
killers.ai_answer: Structural. Defer the pool. Begin with repair and test fees billed per confirmed fault, on customer-owned units. Add a pool only after there are 12+ months of measured MTBUR improvement data to underwrite it, and fund it with asset-backed debt or a lessor partner. AI cannot remove this cost. It can only make reliability better to underwrite.

killers.killer: Sales cycles and procurement friction. DoD PPP or depot partnership agreements, ESA approvals, CMMC Level 2, ITAR registration and FedRAMP or IL-level hosting for fused BITE and flight data each add months. OTAs are meant for prototypes, so using one for repair-production sustainment needs a prototype framing first. Airlines buy component MRO through 3-7 year RFP-cycle contracts and rarely switch avionics pools in the middle of a contract.
killers.evidence: Gecko Robotics' Navy IDIQ took years and started from a commercial product already in service. GAO's 30 of 43 F-35 recommendations still open shows how slowly DoD sustainment changes. Commercial component MRO contracts are dominated by multi-year agreements with OEMs and large MROs.
killers.ai_answer: Partial. SBIR or AFWERX/NavalX open topics, plus the Rapid Sustainment Office and Navy NAVAIR obsolescence programs, give a sub-12-month entry for TPS rehosting, NFF triage and reverse engineering of orphaned boards. On the commercial side, regional, cargo and older-fleet operators (CRJ, ERJ, Dash 8, 737 Classic/NG and MD-80-era freighters) with orphaned avionics buy faster than majors.

killers.killer: Data access for fault isolation. BITE logs, flight data and maintenance records belong to the operator. Military data is CUI or classified and lives in systems such as ODIN/ALIS, REMIS and NALCOMIS. Airlines see shop findings as competitive data and will not let them flow into a shared database without contracts. The 'cross-operator serial-number history' moat needs many operators to sign up before it has any value: a cold-start problem.
killers.evidence: Lockheed's ODIN controls F-35 maintenance data. In GAO's account, DOD still has to identify which data it needs. Airbus Skywise works only because Airbus is the type-certificate holder with built-in leverage.
killers.ai_answer: Yes, partly. The repair shop generates its own teardown and stress-test findings for every unit that passes through. That data accrues without permission from anyone, and it is the highest-value signal for telling confirmed faults from NFF. Operator BITE data can be added later, contract by contract.

killers.killer: Prime and OEM IP resistance, and the loss of right-to-repair. Lockheed, Honeywell, Collins and RTX will resist third-party repair of current-production LRUs, using data rights, warranty voiding and parts denial (OEM-only piece parts and firmware keys). With repair-rights language stripped from the FY26 NDAA, there is no statutory lever.
killers.evidence: This is the founder's own stated risk. It fits GAO's finding that the government lacks the IP it needs for F-35 sustainment.
killers.ai_answer: Structural. Work only where the government owns the data, or where the item is orphaned or DMSMS-designated. That market is real: DoD obsolescence spending runs into billions a year, and aging platforms such as the C-130H, KC-135, F-16 legacy, H-60, E-3 and B-52 avionics have thousands of orphaned boards. F-35 should be a 2030+ option, not the wedge.

killers.killer: Pricing per confirmed fault cuts the depot's own revenue, and NFF often starts at the flight line. Line mechanics pull units because shotgun replacement is quicker than troubleshooting on the aircraft. A depot cannot stop those removals. It can only refuse to bill for them and lower re-removal rates, while each NFF unit still costs it test hours.
killers.evidence: In ARINC 672 and the NFF literature, line-level removal behaviour and MEL time pressure are the main drivers of NFF rates of 30-60%.
killers.ai_answer: Yes. Charge a triage fee for each unit tested and a premium on fleet-level MTBUR or availability outcomes, not just per confirmed fault. AI fault isolation offered back to the line (a troubleshooting assistant that runs before a unit is pulled) is the real lever on removals, and it can be bundled.

killers.killer: Physics clocks and skilled labour. Qualifying a reconstructed TDP needs first-article tests, environmental qualification and sometimes flight test. FOGBANK-type process characterization takes years. Avionics bench technicians and DERs are scarce.
killers.evidence: FOGBANK was reconstructed only after years and tens of millions of dollars. Industry surveys report shortages of avionics technicians across the board.
killers.ai_answer: Partial. AI cuts the cost of documentation and TPS generation and speeds up technicians. It does not shorten qualification. Pick electronics, where requalification is mostly bench, ESS and acceptance testing, over physical process items, where FOGBANK-type characterization is needed.

attacks.who_already_does_it: Test and NFF tools: Universal Synaptics (IFDIS/PIFD, USAF C-130/F-16, F-35 JPO ATO), Eclypse ESS, and the ARINC 672 practices adopted by large MROs. Avionics component MRO and pools: AAR, StandardAero, HEICO Electronic Technologies, Lufthansa Technik Component Services, AFI KLM E&M, Barfield, Satair, plus OEM shops at Collins, Honeywell, Thales and L3Harris. Cross-operator reliability data: Airbus Skywise, LHT AVIATAR, Boeing AnalytX, Collins Ascentia, Honeywell Forge. Military predictive maintenance: C3.ai (USAF PANDA), Uptake, Avathon/SparkCognition, Shift5. Organic depots: OO-ALC, WR-ALC 402nd, Tobyhanna, the FRCs. Defense obsolescence and reverse engineering: OEM DMSMS groups, the Air Force Rapid Sustainment Office, and many small Part 145 and AS9100 rebuild shops.
