F-35 component repair is already assigned to organic depots plus OEMs. Nobody offers the full bundle of a certified repair station, stress-replay testing, AI that fuses teardown findings with BITE and flight data, and outcome-based pricing. Note: the web search budget ran out after the first queries. Evidence came from direct fetches of GAO-23-105341, GAO-24-106703 and usynaptics.com, plus prior knowledge.
attacks.surviving_version: The full vision (an F-35 PPP depot with an owned rotable pool and PBH contracts) does not survive as a startup. It fails on 50/50 and core law, prime IP, pool capital, and DoD's own slow progress on deciding who does F-35 sustainment. A narrower company survives and can grow into it. (1) Acquire one small, existing avionics Part 145 shop (many shops with under $20M revenue are for sale) whose capability list covers legacy, orphaned or OEM-sunset LRUs on regional, cargo and older narrowbody fleets. That gives return-to-service authority on day one. (2) Run every unit through stress-replay intermittent-fault rigs (partner with or license Universal Synaptics-type ATE rather than rebuilding it). Log teardown findings by serial number, which builds the proprietary dataset without anyone's permission. (3) Charge a triage fee for each unit tested plus an outcome premium on re-removal rate and turnaround. Offer a line-level AI troubleshooting assistant that cuts removals before they happen. (4) In defense, sell to organic depots, not against them: TPS and test-procedure rehosting for obsolete ATE and NFF triage for one government-data, DMSMS-designated LRU family on aging platforms (C-130H, KC-135, H-60, legacy F-16), entered through SBIR, AFWERX or RSO and a CRADA. The depot keeps the workload credit. Each AI-drafted, ESA- or DER-accepted procedure or TDP goes into the library. That library is the real compounding asset, in line with the sibling-thread finding that value moves to approvals and test evidence. The rotable pool, PBH and F-35 come only after 2-3 years of measured MTBUR data, and the pool is debt-financed.
attacks.cheapest_first_test: Spend 4-6 weeks, under $25k. Get 12-24 months of removal and shop-findings records for one LRU family with a high NFF rate (for example a CRJ/ERJ display, FMS or air data unit) from one regional or cargo operator, or from an organic depot shop under a CRADA or SBIR Phase I. Then (a) show a model that flags rogue serials and predicts confirmed fault versus NFF better than the shop's current pass rate, and (b) run 20-30 units that were repeatedly returned as NFF through a borrowed or rented intermittent-fault tester with thermal and vibration cycling, and measure how many hidden faults it confirms. In parallel, call 10 depot shop chiefs and 10 regional-airline component managers and ask whether they would pay per tested unit for a guaranteed re-removal rate. Ask 3 avionics Part 145 brokers for asking prices on shops with legacy capability lists. If the tester confirms more than 20% of the repeat NFF units and two buyers sign LOIs, proceed.

killers.killer: The F-35 wedge is the wrong door: the data is not government-owned, and the prime controls the repair network
killers.evidence: GAO-23-105341 (verified by fetch): DoD relies heavily on Lockheed to manage F-35 sustainment, has not identified or obtained the technical data it needs, and has more than 10,000 parts waiting for repair. The services take over sustainment management by October 2027, but as of March 2026 most GAO recommendations are only 'partially addressed', several elements transfer by the end of 2028, and engineering sustainment stays with the JPO. Right-to-repair language was dropped from the FY26 NDAA (premise in the brief).
killers.ai_answer: Change the order. Do not start on F-35. Start on legacy platforms (C-130, KC-135, A-10, H-60, older F-16/F-15 blocks, E-3) where the government owns the data, has lost it, or the OEM has exited: orphan SRUs and circuit cards marked NRTS or backlogged at WR-ALC, OO-ALC or the FRCs. Treat F-35 as an option for 2029 and later, entered as a sub-tier repair source to an organic depot once the services hold the elements. Rebuilding a TDP with AI is the legal route in exactly the cases where the data was never delivered or the source is out of business.

killers.killer: Statutory limits on contractor depot work: 10 USC 2466 (the 50/50 rule) and 2464 (core depot capability)
killers.evidence: These are long-standing Title 10 rules: at most 50% of each service's depot maintenance funds can go to contractors, and core workloads must stay organic. Much of the $35-45B depot market is therefore closed to a private depot that wants to own the work outright.
killers.ai_answer: Structure the work as a 10 USC 2474 public-private partnership. Workshare done inside or credited to an ALC or FRC counts toward organic, so the depot commander has a reason to bring you in rather than resist. Sell intermittent-fault benches, AI isolation and rebuilt TDPs into the organic line, and keep the per-serviceable-unit fee and the orphan-board production yourself.

killers.killer: Intermittent-fault testing is not proprietary. The best-known vendor already sells to the same depots, and the depots own the testers
killers.evidence: Universal Synaptics (usynaptics.com, verified by fetch) sells IFDIS 2.0 (1,280 connection points) and the portable PIFD. PIFD got an F-35 JPO Authority to Operate in 2021. The company claims $63M in USAF savings, works with FRC Southwest, and cites C-130 harness faults isolated in 30 minutes to 4 hours after aircraft were grounded 11-18 months. Eclypse ESTAT and Astronics test systems sit in the same niche. The test rig is a feature, not a moat.
killers.ai_answer: Buy or partner for the stimulus hardware and do not try to win on the bench. The value worth owning is the closed loop that a tool vendor does not have: the outcome contract (paid per confirmed fault and per serviceable unit), serial-number history across operators, teardown findings, and the TDP or repair approval that each fixed fault produces. Universal Synaptics is a natural supplier or acquisition, not a competitor.

killers.killer: Commercial avionics is held by OEM CMM restrictions and OEM PBH pools (Collins, Honeywell, Thales)
killers.evidence: These OEMs sell avionics availability by flight hour and restrict component maintenance manuals and piece parts for current-production LRUs. Without approved data, a Part 145 capability list cannot list the unit. This is the same 'monopoly moves to the approval layer' pattern found in the sibling thread.
killers.ai_answer: Do not attack narrowbody avionics pools that OEMs control. On the commercial side, go after orphans: out-of-production avionics on freighter conversions, older regional jets and turboprops, and business jets where the OEM has ended support. Win DER-approved repairs (the HEICO model) and an owned rotable pool bought from teardown surplus, where the owned-parts margin sits (AerSale's mix is the comparable).

killers.killer: DoD contracting and acceptance run slower than a seed-stage runway
killers.evidence: Source approval, first-article test and engineering-authority sign-off on a rebuilt TDP usually take 12-36 months. Part 145 certification takes about 12-18 months. CMMC and ITAR compliance are required. Outcome-based pricing exists (PBL), but contracting officers default to time and materials.
killers.ai_answer: Run the steps in parallel and pick buyers with authority to move fast. Use AFWERX/SBIR open topics, the AF Rapid Sustainment Office and DLA reverse-engineering and obsolescence programs, then convert to an OTA production follow-on. Start on items where the engineering authority already wants a second source, which shortens the clock. Price per serviceable unit, which fits existing repair line-item structures, and keep PBH and availability contracts for after the record exists.

killers.killer: Nobody will contribute to a cross-operator rogue-unit database
killers.evidence: Airlines and services treat shop findings as competitive or classified. Existing data products such as Lufthansa Technik AVIATAR and OEM analytics get their data from units their owner maintains, not from data operators share.
killers.ai_answer: The database builds as a byproduct of units you repair and own: your rotable pool, plus every serial number that passes through the depot. It never depends on operators contributing.

killers.killer: Expanding too wide too early (rail, wind, GPU RMA) and the capital cost of a rotable pool
killers.evidence: Each vertical has its own certification regime and incumbents (Siemens and Alstom in rail, OEM service agreements in wind, ODMs and hyperscaler RMA flows for GPUs). A rotable pool needs tens of millions of dollars of inventory capital.
killers.ai_answer: Stay on defense and orphan aviation electronics until the TDP library and certificates are compounding. Finance the pool with asset-backed debt or through partners who hold surplus (the AerSale and Kellstrom model) once repair yields are proven.

attacks.who_already_does_it: Intermittent-fault and no-fault-found test equipment: Universal Synaptics (IFDIS 2.0, PIFD; F-35 JPO Authority to Operate; claims $63M in USAF savings), Eclypse International (ESTAT), Astronics test systems. Organic depots: OO-ALC, WR-ALC, OC-ALC, FRC Southwest and East, Tobyhanna. Commercial component repair: Lufthansa Technik Component Services (with AVIATAR analytics), AAR, VSE, StandardAero, Collins and Honeywell PBH programs. Reverse-engineered parts and DER repairs: HEICO (Flight Support plus Electronic Technologies), TransDigm aftermarket. Surplus and owned-pool margin: AerSale, Kellstrom. Government programs: AF Rapid Sustainment Office, DLA reverse engineering and DMSMS obsolescence programs, AFWERX. Adjacent startups: Gecko Robotics (inspection, on a defense IDIQ path), Lumafield (CT scanning for reverse engineering). No one I found combines an outcome-priced repair depot with an AI-rebuilt TDP library on orphan defense electronics.
attacks.surviving_version:
An orphan defense-electronics depot, built as 'HEICO Electronic Technologies plus a public-private depot partnership', with eliminating no-fault-found removals as the way in. This fits the sibling thread's thesis (the monopoly moves to approvals, test evidence and owned fleets), applied to electronics.

1. Owned assets: (a) accepted TDPs and engineering-authority or DER repair approvals for obsolete SRUs and circuit cards; (b) a Part 145 certificate and DoD repair-source approvals; (c) an owned rotable and surplus pool; (d) serial-number histories gathered from units that pass through the depot.

2. Wedge: one legacy platform (C-130 or KC-135 avionics or power units at WR-ALC or OK-ALC, or H-60 avionics at an FRC) where the government owns or has lost the data, or the OEM has exited. The deal is a 10 USC 2474 partnership with the organic depot, so workshare counts toward the 50/50 rule and the depot commander has a reason to want it. Price per serviceable unit, with a turnaround guarantee and a cap on re-removals.

3. AI's role: compress TDP reconstruction (teardown, X-ray/CT, netlist extraction, test-procedure generation) and fault isolation across BITE, test and teardown data. The value is captured in the approvals and the outcome contract, not in the software.

4. Commercial parallel: DER-approved repairs plus a surplus pool for out-of-production avionics on freighters, older regional jets, turboprops and business jets. Stay away from current-production pools that OEMs control.

5. Defer F-35 until the services hold the sustainment elements (2028+). Defer rail, wind and GPU RMA indefinitely. Buy test benches (Universal Synaptics as supplier or acquisition target) rather than building them.

Revenue math: a few hundred obsolete LRU families at $2-10M a year each gives $0.5-2B, with HEICO-like 20%+ operating margins on parts. That is smaller than the $1-4B pitch, but it holds up.
attacks.cheapest_first_test:
Within 60-90 days, before any certificate:

1. Get the top NRTS, backlog and no-fault-found SRU list from one organic depot (WR-ALC, OO-ALC or an FRC) through an AFWERX or RSO conversation or a CRADA. Pick one board or LRU family where the government owns the data, has lost it, or the vendor is defunct.

2. Buy 10-30 units of the same part as surplus through DLA Disposition or GSA auctions, or from commercial teardown brokers.

3. Run them through a rented or borrowed intermittent-fault bench and an environmental chamber, plus AI-assisted teardown and netlist capture.

4. Report three numbers: the share of 'no fault found' units with a real fault confirmed, the share returned to serviceable, and the hours needed to rebuild a test procedure or TDP draft against a human baseline.

Success means a signed letter of intent, an SBIR Phase I/II, or a depot sponsor for an OTA prototype on that one item.

Run a commercial mirror at the same time: buy five out-of-production avionics units and get one DER repair scheme drafted. This tests whether approvals move on the physics clock or on the paperwork clock.

Note: this turn's web search budget was already used up by sibling agents. Evidence here comes from two fetches (GAO-23-105341 and usynaptics.com) plus prior knowledge. A follow-up run could verify 50/50 rule headroom, OTA precedents for reverse-engineered SRUs, and AerSale margin figures.

finalist.name: Provenant: the neutral equivalence standard and certificate authority for physical parts
merged_from: Equivalence and Provenance Gate: a neutral 'bioequivalence-for-parts' standard plus a signed-certificate network
Provenant: the certificate authority for physical parts
finalist.description: WHAT IT DOES: Trust infrastructure for regulated parts. It issues cryptographically signed digital release certificates (8130-3 / Form 1 equivalents, nuclear CoC, DFARS and AS6081 trace, NERC CIP-013 attestations) anchored to physical part fingerprints and markings. A verification API is checked at receiving, with AI vision, X-ray and XRF authentication cheap enough to run there. AI document forensics audit legacy paper trace packs and bring them into the system. Over time it authors and runs the per-part-family equivalence protocols (reference-part comparison and POD-qualified methods), executed by a network of independent accredited labs, that regulators, insurers, lessors and grid operators cite for non-OEM, used and AI-made parts: a 'bioequivalence for parts'. It also offers an authorization clearinghouse for pairing and calibration under compelled-access orders (FTC v Deere's 10-year order, Oregon pairing ban, EU 2024/1799), filling the 'independent entity' that Massachusetts and Maine mandated but nobody built. WHAT IT OWNS: The trust root (issuer keys and identities for approved organisations), the serial-level provenance graph across brokers, the forgery and anomaly corpus, the equivalence standards, and the lab network whose results count. It is built to be OEM-neutral and structurally independent of the inspected party, since Hubbard and credence-goods evidence show inspected-party-paid inspection drifts lenient and Ranbaxy showed a verification gate can be corrupted. WEDGE: Lessors and MROs handling CFM56/V2500 teardown USM and lease transitions after AOG Technics. Sell AI forensic audits of trace packs per engine or aircraft transition, and issue signed digital certificates for teardown houses that want a price premium for verified material. Lessors pay because records set residual value: an LLP without back-to-birth records is near-scrap. In parallel, run DFARS/AS6081 and CIP-013 authentication of obsolete ICS and power electronics for utilities and defense, and pairing credentialing for independents under the Deere order. Then expand into equivalence-protocol authorship for PMA and AM parts in rail and nuclear dedication. MARKET: TIC is about $250B globally and NDT about $11-18B. Aero aftermarket parts flow is about $50B+, ILSmart RFQ volume about $5-7B a year, and aviation USM about $7-8B a year. A per-certificate and per-verification toll plus enterprise contracts plus lab revenue could reach $1-3B revenue at partly software margins, with certificate-authority network effects. COMPARABLES: UL Solutions (the Part 68 / safety mark precedent), DigiCert/Verisign, CCC Intelligent Solutions (the data layer that captured collision), AutoAuth (a mandated lock collapsing into a $5-17.50/month credential), SGS, Bureau Veritas, FLYdocs/Bluetail/ProvenAir, SAE/ATA Spec 2000 Ch.16. KEY RISKS: The 'thin tool' trap, where it becomes a vendor rather than the gate unless it wins regulator, lessor-mandate or insurer endorsement early (C6 notes inspection mandates have historically entrenched incumbents). OEMs may build closed versions. Blockchain-era predecessors stalled because they could not stop forgery at the point of entry, which physical anchoring is meant to fix.
finalist.why_finalist: It captures Law 5, the most AI-specific dynamic in the review: AI makes both alternative parts and forged paperwork cheap, so verification becomes the binding scarce layer. Precedents for neutral gates opening markets are strong (Hatch-Waxman moved generics from 13% to 90% of prescriptions, Carterfone/Part 68). Pain is acute and documented (AOG Technics' 60,000 parts, GAO's 16 of 16 bogus parts, IMIA saying no independent qualifier exists). It has the most software-like economics and network effects of the set. It is also the complement every other finalist needs: approvals, orphan parts and turbine repairs all depend on accepted provenance.

killers.killer: The aviation wedge is already crowded with records-trace and e-certificate players, and AI makes the forensic audit easy for them to copy
killers.evidence: ProvenAir (Cork) already sells AI and ML back-to-birth LLP trace reconstruction to lessors and teardown houses, which is exactly the proposed wedge. FLYdocs (Lufthansa Technik), Bluetail, AMOS and TRAX already hold the digital records layer. Moog VeriPart and Honeywell GoDirect Trade tried blockchain part provenance. ATA Spec 2000 Ch.16 already defines signed e-certificates, and OEMs and big MROs (GE, Boeing, Airbus Skywise, AAR, AerSale) issue their own e-releases. ASA-100 already accredits distributors. Caveat: the shared web-search budget ran out before this agent could search, so this list comes from prior knowledge and is not freshly verified for 2026.
killers.ai_answer: Partly. LLM and vision forensics can find forged or altered 8130-3 and Form 1 pages, signature reuse and certificate-number collisions across many brokers' packs. A single records vendor only sees its own customers, so a cross-broker anomaly corpus is a real edge. But the incumbents can add LLMs too, so the moat has to be the cross-broker data, not the model.

killers.killer: Regulators do not hand release authority or equivalence standards to a private certificate authority
killers.evidence: Under FAA and EASA rules only the approved production or repair organisation can issue an 8130-3 or Form 1. A third party cannot certify airworthiness. FAA approves PMA parts itself (test and computation or identicality), and lessors restrict PMA by contract whatever the evidence says. Nuclear commercial-grade dedication runs on EPRI guidance, licensee 10 CFR 21 responsibility and NUPIC audits, and dedicators such as Curtiss-Wright and Paragon already exist. UL took decades and fire-insurer backing to become a cited mark. The founder's own C6 note says inspection mandates entrench incumbents.
killers.ai_answer: No AI answer for the 'standard' ambition on a YC timescale. The structural workaround is a private-ordering mandate: get 2-3 major lessors or an aviation insurer to write 'Provenant-verified trace' into return conditions or underwriting. That is a contract wedge, not a regulatory one, and it takes years.

killers.killer: Physical anchoring cannot fix provenance for used parts, which were born before the system existed
killers.evidence: For teardown USM the fraud happens in the paper history (AOG Technics forged 8130-3s on real CFM56 parts). Fingerprinting the part at teardown only proves it has not been swapped since then. It cannot prove the back-to-birth history is true. Mandated physical authentication has failed before: DLA required Applied DNA SigNature marking for FSC 5962 microcircuits around 2012, and it stayed marginal with little revenue. Optical-fingerprint startups (Alitheon and similar) have stayed niche.
killers.ai_answer: Partial. For legacy parts the value is forensic, not cryptographic: checking packs against OEM shipment and serial records, LLP cycle consistency, and repair-station signature databases. Anchoring only pays off for parts certified from now on. That makes the trust root a 5-10 year build and only a wedge today.

killers.killer: Liability for a wrong signature is catastrophic and hard to insure
killers.evidence: If a Provenant-certified LLP fails or is later found suspect, the certifier is in the causal chain of an airworthiness event or grounding (AOG Technics forced fleet-wide inspections). Errors-and-omissions cover for this is costly. Labs and TIC firms survive by limiting liability to the fee, which makes their marks weaker evidence.
killers.ai_answer: Structural only. Sell an evidence report that scores risk, not a warranty, and cap liability the way TIC firms do. That weakens the 'gate' story into a 'vendor' story, which is the thin-tool trap again.

killers.killer: Neutrality conflicts with who pays
killers.evidence: The plan has teardown houses pay for certificates to earn a price premium, which is inspected-party-paid inspection. The founder's own cited Hubbard and credence-goods evidence says that drifts lenient. Brokers profit from opacity and will resist a cross-broker serial graph that exposes their sourcing.
killers.ai_answer: Yes, a structural fix exists. Let the relying party (the lessor, buyer or insurer) pay, and sell to the side that bears residual-value risk. That shrinks volume early, because lessors buy per transition, not per part.

killers.killer: Too many wedges with different slow sales cycles
killers.evidence: Aviation lessors, NERC CIP-013 utilities, DFARS and AS6081 defense electronics, Deere pairing and Massachusetts/Maine credentials, and nuclear dedication each have their own incumbents. CIP-013: Fortress Information Security and the utility Asset to Vendor network. DFARS: Exiger, Interos, ERAI, GIDEP, plus AS6171-accredited labs such as SMT and Integra. Automotive credentials: NASTF SDRM and AutoAuth. Utility and defense procurement takes 12-24 months. Building an ISO 17025 or Nadcap-grade lab network takes years.
killers.ai_answer: Focus is the only answer. Drop CIP-013, Deere and nuclear from the YC story and keep CFM56/V2500 trace forensics for lessors.

killers.killer: The right-to-repair clearinghouse may never exist, or the OEMs and NASTF will own it
killers.evidence: The Massachusetts 2020 data-access law has been stuck in Alliance for Automotive Innovation v. Campbell litigation. Maine's independent entity has moved slowly. NASTF's Secure Data Release Model already credentials locksmiths and repairers for vehicle security. Any Deere remedy is likely to run through Deere's own tools or a dealer-adjacent scheme. The status of the '10-year order' the pitch cites could not be checked because the search budget ran out.
killers.ai_answer: Weak. AI adds little to credentialing, and the AutoAuth precedent caps this at a $5-17.50 a month toll. Treat it as an option, not a pillar.

killers.killer: OEMs build closed versions and refuse to share serial data
killers.evidence: CFM and GE, Boeing and Airbus hold the birth records and shipment ledgers that make verification strong, and they profit from discouraging USM and PMA. OEM e-certificate and digital-twin programmes (Skywise, GE digital records) can verify their own new parts and leave used parts doubtful.
killers.ai_answer: Partial. OEMs do not cover the market the founder targets: USM and PMA from ageing CFM56/V2500 fleets, where OEMs are conflicted. Lessors want a neutral party, so OEM hostility is part of the pitch. The ceiling is still lower without birth-record access.

killers.killer: The real wedge pool is small next to the $1-3B claim
killers.evidence: Roughly a few thousand engine and aircraft lease transitions a year. Records work runs maybe tens of thousands of dollars per transition, much of it already done by records firms and in-house technical teams. That is a pool in the low hundreds of millions, against USM flow of about $7-8B. A per-certificate toll at broker volume needs network adoption that predecessors never got.
killers.ai_answer: AI lowers the cost per audit enough to price per serial or per pack, which opens broker and MRO receiving volume. But that only becomes large if some mandate makes verification required.

attacks.who_already_does_it: This list comes from prior knowledge, not fresh research: the shared search budget was spent before this agent could search. Aviation records and trace: ProvenAir (AI back-to-birth LLP trace for lessors), FLYdocs (Lufthansa Technik), Bluetail, AMOS/Swiss-AS, TRAX, plus records-service firms and lessors' in-house technical teams. E-certificates: ATA Spec 2000 Ch.16, which OEMs and large MROs implement for their own releases. Blockchain predecessors: Moog VeriPart, Honeywell GoDirect Trade. Accreditation: the ASA-100 distributor scheme. Counterfeit electronics: ERAI, GIDEP, AS6171 labs (SMT, Integra, Sentry), Exiger and Interos for DFARS supply-chain risk, Applied DNA (the failed DLA marking mandate). CIP-013: Fortress Information Security and the Asset to Vendor utility network. Automotive credentials: NASTF SDRM and AutoAuth. Nuclear: EPRI dedication guidance, NUPIC audits, dedicators such as Curtiss-Wright and Paragon. Physical fingerprinting and CT: Alitheon, Lumafield. TIC majors that could enter: SGS, Bureau Veritas, Intertek, UL Solutions.
attacks.surviving_version: Only a narrow version survives. Build cross-broker AI document forensics for CFM56/V2500 trace packs, paid by lessors and buyers (the relying party), not by teardown houses. It produces a risk-scored evidence report per engine or LLP set: forged-signature detection, certificate-number collisions, cycle and back-to-birth consistency checks, and a forgery corpus built from AOG Technics-type cases. Signed digital attestation comes later as an add-on for new certificates. The aim is to get 2-3 tier-1 lessors or an aviation insurer to write the report into lease return conditions or underwriting. That private mandate is the only realistic route to becoming 'the gate'. The certificate-authority, equivalence-standard, lab-network, CIP-013, DFARS, Deere-pairing and nuclear pieces should be dropped from the YC pitch and kept as long-term options. Expect it to start as a ProvenAir competitor. The moat has to be the cross-broker anomaly data, since the model itself can be copied. It also fits better as the trust and verification arm of an orphan-parts or HEICO-style business than as a standalone toll company.
attacks.cheapest_first_test: Collect 30-50 historical trace packs, seeded with publicly documented forged AOG Technics-style 8130-3s from court filings and EASA/FAA suspected-unapproved-parts notices. Run a prototype forensic pipeline over them and measure detection rate and false positives against a human records auditor. Then offer free audits on live transitions to 5 mid-tier lessors and asset managers, and ask two hard questions: (1) will you pay $5-20k per engine, and (2) will you require this report in your next lease return conditions? Also find out what ProvenAir charges and how lessors rate it. The idea is only worth pursuing if at least 2 lessors say yes to the contract-mandate question within 6-8 weeks.

killers.killer: The certificate-authority wedge is already taken by regulators and the approved organisations themselves
killers.evidence: Electronic signatures on release certificates are already allowed: FAA AC 120-78A and Order 8130.21, the EASA Part-21 e-Form 1 provisions, and ATA Spec 2000 Chapter 16 (digital ARC). The issuer of an 8130-3 or Form 1 has to be the approved production or repair organisation, and the regulators' certificate-holder registries are the real identity root. A private CA cannot hold issuer authority over approved organisations. It can only verify what they issue. (From prior knowledge; I could not re-check this because the shared search budget ran out.)
killers.ai_answer: Give up on being the issuing CA. Own verification at the receiving dock plus a cross-broker serial-level provenance graph that checks any signed or paper certificate against the regulator registry, the teardown source and the history of that part. Implement Spec 2000 Ch.16 rather than competing with it. The moat is the graph and the anomaly corpus, not the keys.

killers.killer: The 'thin tool' trap: AI trace-pack audit already exists and is being commoditised
killers.evidence: ProvenAir (fetched provenair.com) already sells AI/OCR back-to-birth trace and exception reports for engine, landing-gear and APU LLPs to lessors, airlines and MROs. It claims 'weeks to hours', more than 5,000 major assets analysed, an Allegiant testimonial, and shows logos including United, BA and AAR. Bluetail (fetched) does AI digital logbooks and FAA-form auto-tagging. FLYdocs (Lufthansa Technik) and the AerData/Boeing records tools cover lease transitions. ILSmart, the main parts marketplace, belongs to the Boeing/Aviall family, so an OEM already sits on the RFQ data layer.
killers.ai_answer: The audit alone does not make a company. What makes it defensible is a private mandate: get the top lessors (AerCap, SMBC, Avolon, ALC, BOC Aviation) to write 'independently verified trace dossier' into lease return conditions and USM purchase terms, and get hull and products-liability insurers to price it. A lease clause is the lessor-mandate version of a UL mark. It needs about 5 signatures, not a regulator.

killers.killer: Neutrality and who-pays paradox
killers.evidence: The pitch itself cites Hubbard and credence-goods evidence that inspected-party-paid inspection drifts lenient, and Ranbaxy as a captured verification gate. But the proposed wedge has teardown houses paying for certificates to earn a price premium, which is the inspected party paying. AOG Technics was forged paperwork on real used parts: the seller had both the incentive and the access.
killers.ai_answer: Have the buyer or lessor pay at the point of receipt or transition (an escrow-style fee per engine or LLP set). The seller can list 'verification-ready' but cannot buy the verdict. Publish false-accept rates and keep the lab network ISO 17025-accredited and rotated, the way blind proficiency testing works.

killers.killer: Scope sprawl across six regulated verticals with different regulators and buyers
killers.evidence: Aero FAA/EASA, nuclear CGD (10 CFR 21, EPRI guidance), DFARS 252.246-7008 / AS6081/AS6171, NERC CIP-013, the FTC v Deere order and state pairing laws, and AM/PMA equivalence each have their own standards body, sales cycle and liability regime. Electronics counterfeit detection already has incumbents: ERAI's reporting database, AS6171-accredited test labs, GIDEP.
killers.ai_answer: Pick one vertical. Aero USM and LLP trace has the clearest pain (after AOG Technics), the clearest payer (residual value) and the clearest data (back-to-birth records). Run DFARS/CIP-013 later as a second product on the same graph, and only after the aero lease clause exists.

killers.killer: Equivalence-protocol authorship ('bioequivalence for parts') runs on standards-body and regulator clocks
killers.evidence: Equivalence for non-OEM parts is decided through FAA PMA (14 CFR 21.303, test and computation or identicality), the EPRI commercial-grade dedication guidance plus NRC acceptance in nuclear, and AAR/FRA in rail. Those take a decade and favour incumbents (the pitch's C6 note). Drug bioequivalence worked because FDA wrote it into Hatch-Waxman, not because a private party authored it.
killers.ai_answer: Treat it as a year-5+ option. Feed the forgery and anomaly corpus and the measurement data into SAE G-19 and G-21, EPRI and ASTM F42 committees, so the company's methods become the cited ones. Don't sell protocol authorship as a product.

killers.killer: Liability for certifying a part that later fails
killers.evidence: An airworthiness-adjacent attestation that turns out wrong (for example a forged LLP passing) invites product-liability suits and regulator action. UL and TIC majors carry this risk with decades of balance sheet and insurance.
killers.ai_answer: Attest only to identity and documentary provenance ('this serial's records are complete, consistent and non-anomalous'), not to airworthiness, which stays with the certificated repair station. Carry E&O cover and cap fees per attestation.

killers.killer: Pairing and calibration clearinghouse captures little value
killers.evidence: AutoAuth (fetched autoauth.com, run by OmniTrust) sells mandated-access credentials for $5 a month Standard or $17.50 a month Plus. A legally compelled lock collapses into a cheap commodity credential. Nobody built the Massachusetts and Maine independent entity because OEMs fought it and no fee pool funds it.
killers.ai_answer: Drop it from the plan. At most, license the identity and credential layer to an AutoAuth-like operator later.

killers.killer: Physical anchoring does not catch the main fraud mode
killers.evidence: In AOG Technics, genuine used parts came with fabricated documents. X-ray, XRF or vision checks of a genuine part pass. Physical fingerprints help with counterfeit electronics and fake castings, but not with forged pedigree on a real part.
killers.ai_answer: Make the cross-document and cross-broker graph the main control: the same serial seen twice, cycle counts that are impossible, signatories who don't exist, mismatches with the regulator registry. Use physical fingerprints only to bind a serial at teardown so it cannot later be re-papered.

attacks.who_already_does_it: AI back-to-birth trace and lease-transition records: ProvenAir (lessors, MROs, Allegiant; logos include United, BA, AAR), FLYdocs (Lufthansa Technik), Bluetail, and the AerData/Boeing records tools. Parts marketplace and RFQ data: ILSmart (Boeing/Aviall family), plus ASA-100 distributor accreditation. Digital release-certificate format: ATA Spec 2000 Ch.16, with FAA and EASA e-signature acceptance. Electronics counterfeits: ERAI, GIDEP, and AS6171 test labs (for example SMT Corp). Nuclear dedication: EPRI guidance plus CGD vendors. Mandated access credentials: AutoAuth/OmniTrust at $5-17.50 a month. Large TIC players (UL Solutions, SGS, BV, Intertek, TÜV) could expand into this. Nobody owns a neutral, buyer-paid, cross-broker serial-level provenance graph tied to lease clauses. That gap is the opening.
attacks.surviving_version:
A narrow version survives, but not as a universal CA or equivalence authority. It survives as 'Carfax plus escrow for engine life-limited parts': a buyer- and lessor-paid verification service for CFM56, V2500 and later LEAP/GTF USM and LLP transactions.

(1) At each lease transition or USM purchase, AI forensics produce a back-to-birth dossier. Every serial is checked against a cross-broker provenance graph (duplicate serials, impossible cycles, non-existent signatories, regulator-registry mismatches) and the anomaly corpus.

(2) At teardown, serials are physically bound to the dossier (photo/marking fingerprint) so a part cannot be re-papered later. The dossier uses Spec 2000 Ch.16 signing rather than its own issuer keys.

(3) The mandate is private. Get 3-5 top lessors to name an 'independent verified trace dossier' in return conditions and USM purchase terms. Then take the clean-dossier versus no-dossier residual-value spread to appraisers (ISTAT) and insurers so it gets priced.

(4) Revenue: per-engine or per-LLP-set fees (roughly $10-50k a transition) plus per-serial verification at receipt. Rough sizing: thousands of engine transitions and teardowns a year gives a $100-300M core, not $1-3B. Upside comes from reusing the same graph for DFARS/AS6081 and CIP-013 obsolete electronics, and much later from data sold into equivalence standards.

It also fits the prior thread's thesis. A trust graph is a natural complement or acquisition target for an orphan-parts or 'HEICO-for-everything' house, or for a lessor consortium. That makes it a credible venture outcome even if it never becomes the gate.
attacks.cheapest_first_test: Get 10-20 historical engine LLP trace packs from one lessor or teardown house, including at least a few known-bad ones (an AOG-Technics-affected set if possible). Run the AI forensic plus cross-reference audit within a week, blind, and compare its findings, time and cost against their own back-to-birth review and against a ProvenAir quote. In the same calls, ask 3 lessor technical or asset-management heads two things: would they pay $15-25k per transition for a buyer-side, seller-independent dossier, and would they add an 'independently verified trace' clause to their next lease return conditions? Two signed paid pilots plus one clause commitment is the signal. Caveat: the shared web-search budget was used up before I could run new searches. Evidence here comes from directly fetched pages (provenair.com, bluetail.aero, autoauth.com) and prior knowledge. The regulatory citations (AC 120-78A, Spec 2000 Ch.16, EASA e-Form 1, FTC v Deere status) should be checked in a follow-up.

finalist.name: Signet: the liable AI-native inspection and release authority for energy and defense assets
merged_from: Signet: the liable inspection-and-release authority for energy and defence assets
finalist.description: WHAT IT DOES: An AI-native inspection organisation built around certified sign-off. It is an accredited NDT and inspection body, an ASME/NBIC authorized inspection agency, and a Part 145 or class-recognised station. It combines robotic and sensor data capture, AI defect recognition qualified to MIL-HDBK-1823 probability-of-detection standards, and in-house Level III and authorized inspectors who review many sites remotely and sign. The signed return-to-service record becomes the accepted unit of evidence. Owning the inspection funnel then feeds repair work and risk-based interval extensions. WHAT IT OWNS: The legally accountable signature (accreditations and certificated staff). The regulator- and insurer-accepted method qualifications for each AI technique, which set the standard of proof (Law 2). The condition-data history that accumulates on every inspected asset. WEDGE: Power-plant boiler tubes, HRSGs, pressure vessels and tanks under ASME/NBIC jurisdiction, plus Navy hull and tank inspection. The asset owner pays, outage days are worth about $0.7-1.5M per GW-day, and the authorized-inspector slot is already licensable. The first deliverable is one AI ultrasonic/EMAT method qualified to an accepted POD standard, sold as 'outage critical-path inspection days cut in half, signed'. MARKET: NDT and inspection is about $11-18B globally, TIC about $250B+, and US authorized and in-service inspection for energy and defense is several billion. The repair spend inspection triggers is far larger. Bureau Veritas is valued at about €13B. Taking 2-5% of energy and defense TIC supports a $5B+ company. COMPARABLES: Gecko Robotics (data and capture plus a $300M Navy IDIQ, but it partners for sign-off), Mistras, Team Inc., HSB and TÜV (insurer-inspectors since 1866), Bureau Veritas, SGS, Waygate/Baker Hughes assisted defect recognition, and LegalZoom's move to owning a law firm as the 'be the licensed entity' precedent. KEY RISKS: Regulators may be slow to accept AI methods (EASA NPA 2025-07, ASNT NDE 4.0 are early), and outcome data is thin (C6 caveat). Incumbent TIC firms could buy or copy the approach. It must stay independent of the inspected party to keep its structural value.
finalist.why_finalist: C6 was the only claim mostly supported (95 of 108 agents): in regulated assets, certified sign-off decides return-to-service timing and becomes more valuable as diagnosis and parts get cheaper. The certified workforce is aging and capacity-bound (EDF's NDE analyst limit, the Vineyard Wind halt), so AI leverage is real but only counts once methods are qualified. That makes owning both the qualified AI method and the signature a novel, defensible combination that neither Gecko (data only) nor TIC incumbents (labour-heavy) have. It pairs naturally with Provenant but sells to a different buyer, asset owners during outages.

killers.killer: The jurisdictional boiler/pressure-vessel inspection slot is bundled with equipment-breakdown insurance and is often a loss leader, so there is little standalone inspection revenue to win
killers.evidence: US in-service jurisdictional inspection is dominated by insurer AIAs (HSB/Munich Re, FM, Travelers, Zurich, etc.) and state inspectors. Insurers fund inspection out of boiler-and-machinery premiums as risk control, so the asset owner rarely pays a market price for the signature itself. In several states only a licensed boiler insurer or the jurisdiction can do the commissioned in-service inspection. A non-insurer AIA in that slot competes against something that is effectively free. (Based on prior knowledge of how NB-369 and state law are structured. The web search budget was used up, so I could not re-check this state by state.)
killers.ai_answer: Partial, and only structural. Signet would have to own the risk as well as the signature, by becoming an MGA or captive-backed equipment-breakdown insurer (an HSB-style model) whose cheaper AI inspection lowers loss ratios. That is a different company, a regulated insurer needing capital and a reinsurance partner. The other option is to sell the capture and AI layer to insurer AIAs, which turns Signet into a vendor, not the liable authority.

killers.killer: Independence rules make the 'inspection funnel feeds repair' thesis impossible
killers.evidence: ISO/IEC 17020 Type A inspection bodies must be independent of design, manufacture and repair. Under NBIC, an R-stamp repair organisation's work has to be accepted by a separate AIA or inspector. A body that finds the defect, sells the repair and then signs its release is the conflict of interest that accreditation exists to prevent. The pitch itself says Signet must stay independent, and that cuts against its own monetisation path.
killers.ai_answer: Structural only. Split into separately governed entities: a Type A inspection body plus a sister repair/parts company with firewalls, as TÜV and BV keep testing apart from advisory work. That reduces the cross-sell and invites regulator scrutiny. The cleaner answer is to make money from interval extensions (RBI) and data, not from repair referrals.

killers.killer: Incumbents get most of the AI benefit without method qualification by keeping a human in the loop
killers.evidence: Assisted defect recognition (Waygate/Baker Hughes InspectionWorks, Evident, Eddyfi) is already deployed with a certified Level II/III making the call. That needs no new POD qualification because the human stays the accountable examiner under SNT-TC-1A or CP-189. ASME Section V Article 14 and ENIQ/EPRI PDI-style performance demonstration already give anyone a path to qualify a system, so the 'standard of proof' is a published, open framework. HSB, Mistras, Team, TÜV, BV and Applus already hold every accreditation Signet would spend years getting, plus master service agreements (MSAs) at the same plants.
killers.ai_answer: Weak. The only durable edge is fully autonomous calls, where AI replaces the Level II rather than assisting them, qualified with a POD a90/95 below human performance on a specific damage mechanism (HRSG FAC, boiler waterwall thinning). That gives a real cost advantage, but it is copyable within 2-3 years by an incumbent that licenses or buys the model, as Gecko's partners could.

killers.killer: Gecko Robotics already owns the boiler-tube and Navy-hull wedge
killers.evidence: Gecko started on power-plant boiler tubes, raised at a reported ~$1.25B valuation in 2025, and its site cites a Navy sustainment deal grown from $71M to a $300M IDIQ with savings 'up to $8m per ship'. It sells the Cantilever data platform across power, oil and gas, and defense. Gecko works with class societies and AIAs for acceptance. Whenever sign-off becomes a bottleneck, Gecko can buy a small accredited inspection body or AIA, which is a cheap acquisition for it.
killers.ai_answer: Partial. Be the independent signer that Gecko's data and its rivals' data (ANYbotics, Square Robot, Voliro, Flyability) must pass through: robot-agnostic, the 'UL for robotic inspection data'. That positioning only lasts if Gecko does not vertically integrate first, and Gecko has the money to do it.

killers.killer: Outage critical-path value is overstated for the wedge
killers.evidence: On HRSG and boiler outages the critical path is usually turbine or generator overhaul, major pressure-part repairs, or scaffolding and access, not the UT/EMAT survey, which runs in parallel. Robotic crawlers already cut boiler-wall survey time a lot. The $0.7-1.5M per GW-day figure only applies when inspection is the binding constraint and only in high-price hours. Many coal units are retiring, although data-centre load has pushed some retirements back.
killers.ai_answer: Partial. Target the cases where inspection is the binding constraint: forced-outage tube-leak response, where diagnosis and return-to-service decisions are urgent; HRSG flow-accelerated-corrosion (FAC) and creep assessments that decide repair scope; and remote review to fix the shortage of commissioned inspectors and Level IIIs. Value the shortage and speed of the signature, not the scan.

killers.killer: Defense wedge has long sales cycles, technical-authority lock-in and in-house organic capacity
killers.evidence: Navy hull and tank inspection runs under NAVSEA technical authority and NAVSEA-specific personnel and procedure qualification (the T9074 series), with public shipyards doing much of the work in-house. Contracts arrive through primes and IDIQs that Gecko already holds. Clearances, ITAR and CMMC compliance add cost. Time from first meeting to revenue is often 2-4 years.
killers.ai_answer: Sequencing. Treat defense as phase two, entered through an SBIR/OTA, Gecko-style, once a commercial POD dataset exists. Navy demand for maintenance-delay reduction is real, and AI remote review fits a shipyard labour shortage.

killers.killer: Liability and capital intensity of being the signer
killers.evidence: An AIA or Type A body carries professional liability for missed defects. One boiler or vessel failure after a signed release can bring tort exposure, loss of accreditation and the end of the business. Insurers price that exposure for a startup with no loss history. Accreditation (NB-369/QAI-1, ISO 17020 via A2LA/ANAB, ASNT/NAS 410 staff) takes 12-24 months, and commissioned inspectors are scarce and expensive.
killers.ai_answer: Yes. Qualified POD data plus full-coverage scanning beats spot-check human sampling, so an AI-native body could have a better loss record and buy cheaper E&O cover over time. The scarcity of inspectors is the tailwind: one inspector reviewing 5-10 sites remotely is the real margin engine, if jurisdictions allow remote acceptance.

killers.killer: Regulatory acceptance of remote and AI sign-off is early and jurisdiction-by-jurisdiction
killers.evidence: There are about 50 US jurisdictions plus Canadian provinces, each adopting NBIC editions on its own schedule. Remote and digital inspection allowances are only starting to appear (NBIC remote-inspection discussion, ASNT NDE 4.0, EASA NPA 2025-07 on the aviation side). Outcome data for AI calls on in-service damage mechanisms is thin.
killers.ai_answer: Partial. Work through owner-user regimes where acceptance is internal (refinery and chemical API 510/570/653 programs, utility RBI programs), and through a single friendly jurisdiction's chief inspector plus a National Board committee item. Publish POD studies co-signed with EPRI to build the evidence. This is slow, measured in years per jurisdiction, and the same path is open to incumbents once it exists.

attacks.who_already_does_it: Insurer-inspectors HSB (Munich Re), FM Global, Travelers, Zurich and Allianz Risk Consulting, plus state jurisdictions, hold the US ASME/NBIC commissioned-inspector slot. TIC majors (Bureau Veritas, SGS, Intertek, TÜV SÜD/Rheinland, Applus, DNV, Element) hold ISO 17020 accreditation and class or notified-body status. NDT service firms Mistras (OneSuite data platform), Team Inc. and Acuren/NV5 do the field NDT. On capture and AI, Gecko Robotics already works boiler tubes and Navy hulls (Cantilever platform, Navy IDIQ grown to $300M per its site). Waygate/Baker Hughes (InspectionWorks ADR), Evident (Olympus), Eddyfi and Zetec sell assisted defect recognition. Robot vendors include Square Robot (in-service tank floors), ANYbotics, ExRobotics, Voliro and Flyability. EPRI runs performance-demonstration and POD programs, and ASME Section V Article 14 sets out system qualification. Nobody I could identify combines an AI-native POD-qualified method with owning the commissioned signature. That gap exists mainly because the signature is bundled with insurance.
attacks.surviving_version: The company only survives in narrowed form. Drop the US boiler commissioned-AIA slot, which insurers bundle with cover, and the inspect-then-repair funnel, which independence rules forbid. Start instead as an ISO 17020 Type A, AI-native inspection body for owner-user pressure equipment (refinery, chemical, LNG and utility vessels, piping, tanks under API 510/570/653 and utility RBI programs). Owners there already buy third-party inspection with signed reports and can accept new methods internally. The product is one damage mechanism (for example HRSG FAC/creep or boiler waterwall thinning) with an AI call qualified under ASME V Article 14 with POD a90/95, robot-agnostic data intake (Gecko, Square Robot, ANYbotics data), and API-certified inspectors and Level IIIs reviewing many sites remotely and signing. Revenue comes from per-asset fitness-for-service and RBI interval-extension sign-offs (API 579/580/581), priced on outage days and inspection intervals avoided, not on scanning hours. The condition-history dataset becomes the base for a later move into an equipment-breakdown MGA with a reinsurer. Owning the risk is how Signet finally enters the jurisdictional signature slot that HSB holds today. Repair and parts belong in a firewalled sister company, if at all. This fits the sibling thread's thesis: the scarce layer is the accepted signature plus the insurance behind it, not the AI.
attacks.cheapest_first_test: Spend 4-6 weeks and under $50k testing three things. (1) Interview 10 outage or reliability managers at combined-cycle and refinery sites, and get 3 actual outage schedules (Primavera) to check whether inspection or its sign-off is ever on the critical path, and what they pay per day for third-party API/NBIC sign-off. (2) Ask 2 state chief inspectors and one insurer AIA (HSB) in writing: would a commissioned inspector accept remotely reviewed robotic UT/EMAT thickness data with an AI call under the current NBIC Part 2, and what POD evidence would they need? (3) Run a blind POD pilot: get 50-100 pulled or retired HRSG/boiler tube samples with known wall loss (from EPRI or a utility scrap pile), scan them, and compare an AI call against Level II humans using the MIL-HDBK-1823A hit/miss method. Kill the idea if inspection is never on the critical path, or if no regulator or owner-user will accept AI-primary calls with a demonstrated a90/95.

killers.killer: Independence kills the inspection-to-repair funnel
killers.evidence: National Board rules split AIAs into new-construction agencies (NB-360, ASME-accredited, plus NB-381 for NBIC Part 3 repair work) and in-service agencies (a jurisdiction, or an entity accredited under NB-369/NB-381), per nationalboard.org pageID=66. The whole point of an AIA is to be independent of the R-stamp repair organization and of the owner's contractors. Bureau Veritas, TUV and SGS sell independence. They do not sell inspections that funnel into their own repairs.
killers.ai_answer: Drop owning repair. Make money downstream with no conflict: (a) risk-based interval extensions (NBIC/jurisdictional RBI, API 580/581), where the saved outage days are the product; (b) a neutral repair marketplace, with Signet paid only by the owner and never by the repairer; (c) insurer revenue share. Keep the repair business, if any, in a separately owned entity, or leave it out entirely.

killers.killer: In-service boiler and vessel inspection is often bundled free with equipment-breakdown insurance, so a standalone signature has little price power
killers.evidence: HSB (Munich Re) has done this since 1866: the insurer's inspectors do the jurisdictional inspections and the premium pays for them. FM Global, Zurich, Allianz and Travelers work the same way. Commissioned inspectors are billed at modest hourly rates, and the AIA signature fee is a small line item next to outage cost. (This is general knowledge of the industry. My search budget ran out before I could get a fresh citation.)
killers.ai_answer: Stop selling the signature and sell the outage days and the risk. Charge per outage-day saved, or a share of the interval extension. Better still, partner with or become the inspection arm of an equipment-breakdown insurer or MGA, so AI-derived condition data lowers loss ratios and earns underwriting economics. That is the HSB playbook rebuilt on sensor data.

killers.killer: Capture speed is the real outage lever, and Gecko already owns it. Sign-off alone does not halve critical-path days
killers.evidence: Gecko's site (fetched October 2026) shows a $71M Navy deal (March 2026), expanded to a $300M IDIQ (October 2026), and boiler, power and oil-and-gas customers. It mentions no code certifications or authorized inspectors, which supports the brief's claim that Gecko partners for sign-off. Most of the critical path is access, scaffolding, capture and repair. Interpretation and paperwork are a smaller slice.
killers.ai_answer: Be capture-agnostic and become the sign-off and qualification layer for every robot and drone company, including Gecko, ANYbotics, Voliro and Eddyfi crawlers. They have data and no signature, and Signet has the signature. The AI lever is remote Level III and AI review across sites on the same night, so the call on results arrives hours after capture rather than days, and data from many vendors gets one release decision. Wedge: the outage window where a delay in the release decision holds up the restart.

killers.killer: Qualifying an AI method to POD runs on a physics clock, and no regulator framework for AI-only acceptance exists yet
killers.evidence: I fetched EASA NPA 2025-07. It covers general AI trustworthiness under the EU AI Act (published November 2025, comments closed March 2026) and does not address NDT. That means aviation acceptance of AI-only inspection is years away. MIL-HDBK-1823 POD studies need flawed-specimen libraries and hit/miss or a-hat-versus-a trials. There is a precedent for automated analysis being accepted: EPRI's qualified automated data analysis for steam-generator eddy current in nuclear. I could not re-verify it because the search budget ran out.
killers.ai_answer: Sequence it so the AI never needs regulator acceptance first. AI screens, and a credentialed Level III or commissioned inspector signs. That is legal today, and the gain is reviewer throughput, about 10x. In parallel, build the flawed-specimen library and the POD dataset as a separate asset, and sell method qualification to other companies (a 'UL for AI-NDT'). Pursue code cases with ASME Section V and NBIC through committee participation. Leave aviation (Part 145) out until year 4 or later.

killers.killer: Liability for a missed defect is catastrophic and concentrated
killers.evidence: A signed return-to-service on a pressure vessel or HRSG that later ruptures means personal injury, property loss and a test case against AI-assisted inspection. Professional liability and E&O pricing for a new AIA with an AI method will be high or unavailable.
killers.ai_answer: Sign only inside the qualified envelope (the material, thickness, flaw type and probe combinations that have POD data). Get an insurer partner or fronting arrangement early, which ties back to the insurer channel above. Keep a human signature on every release. Use the condition-data history to show lower loss frequency, which brings the premium down over time.

killers.killer: Navy hull and tank work is not a licensable release authority
killers.evidence: The Navy keeps certification authority (NAVSEA, SUBSAFE and shipyard QA). Contractors capture data and report but do not sign return-to-service. Gecko already holds a $300M IDIQ, so it has the vehicle.
killers.ai_answer: Drop the Navy from the wedge. Return later as a qualification-evidence provider (POD studies for NAVSEA acceptance of robotic and AI methods), or as a Level III review subcontractor under the Gecko or HII vehicles. Do not lead with it.

killers.killer: The wedge market is narrowing, and incumbents can copy or buy
killers.evidence: The coal boiler fleet is retiring. The HRSG and combined-cycle fleet is busy, but Mistras, Team, BV, Applus and HSB serve it. Waygate/Baker Hughes already ships assisted defect recognition. A TIC major could buy a robotics company plus an ADR tool. BV's market value of about EUR 13B shows the category pays, but also that scale players dominate it.
killers.ai_answer: Expand the wedge to API 510/570/653 owner-user programs in refineries and chemicals plus HRSGs. RBI interval extension there is worth tens of millions per site-turnaround. Defensibility comes from the accumulated, signed condition history per asset and from POD-qualified method dossiers, not from the AI model itself. Being multi-vendor neutral is something a robot owner like Gecko or an OEM like Baker Hughes cannot credibly offer.

killers.killer: Scarce credentialed staff and the AIA employment requirement
killers.evidence: National Board commissioned inspectors must be employed by an AIA or a jurisdiction. ASNT Level IIIs are an aging, scarce workforce. Getting AIA accreditation (NB-369, ASME QAI-1) takes time and needs an existing quality program and inspection history.
killers.ai_answer: Scarcity here is the thesis, not just a risk: AI makes each Level III cover 10x as many sites. Acquire a small existing in-service AIA, NDT company or Level III shop to get the accreditation and certificates on day one. This is the LegalZoom-buys-a-law-firm move, and roll-up economics follow. Use remote-witness practices that became accepted after COVID to cover many sites.

attacks.who_already_does_it: Insurer-inspectors (HSB/Munich Re with IoT sensing, FM Global, Zurich, Allianz, Travelers) own US jurisdictional in-service boiler and vessel inspection, bundled with equipment-breakdown cover. TIC majors (Bureau Veritas, SGS, TUV SUD/Rheinland, Intertek, Applus+, DNV) and NDT service companies (Mistras with its PCMS data platform, Team Inc., Acuren) do inspection and sign-off. Gecko Robotics does robotic capture and the Cantilever data platform, holds a $71M Navy deal expanded to a $300M IDIQ in October 2026, and shows no code-certification role on its site. Waygate/Baker Hughes, Evident/Olympus, Eddyfi and Zetec ship AI-assisted defect recognition. In nuclear, EPRI and the OEMs (Westinghouse, Framatome) use qualified automated eddy-current analysis. Drone and robot capture companies (Voliro, ANYbotics, Zeitview, Percepto) have data but no signature. No one combines a neutral, multi-vendor AI review authority that is accredited to sign with qualified POD method dossiers. That gap is the opening.
attacks.surviving_version: Signet survives as a neutral, multi-vendor AI review and release authority. It is not a funnel into repair, and it does not do its own capture. Sequence: (1) Buy or partner with a small in-service AIA, NDT company or Level III shop, so the accreditation and certificated staff exist on day one. (2) Take inspection data from any robot or drone (Gecko, Eddyfi, ANYbotics, the owner's own crews) at HRSG, boiler and API 510/570 pressure-equipment outages. AI screens the data, and a Level III or commissioned inspector signs remotely and overnight. The product is 'release decision in hours, signed', priced per outage-day saved rather than per inspector-hour. (3) Build the flawed-specimen and POD library, and sell AI method qualification to capture vendors and owners as a separate line (a 'UL for AI-NDT'). Pursue ASME Section V and NBIC code cases through committee seats. (4) Use the signed, accumulated condition history to win risk-based interval extensions. Those are worth far more than the inspections, and owners pay for them as a share of the outage cost avoided. (5) Partner with, or later become, an equipment-breakdown insurer or MGA so the data earns underwriting economics. That is the HSB model rebuilt on sensors. Out of scope: owning repair (it breaks independence), the Navy as a release authority (NAVSEA keeps that authority), and aviation Part 145 until much later. This fits the sibling thread's finding that value moves to the approval and certification layer once AI makes knowledge cheap. It also suggests Signet could be the certification arm that a later orphan-parts or 'HEICO for everything' play needs, but only if the two companies are separate.
attacks.cheapest_first_test: Test it in 4-6 weeks. Get written answers from 3 combined-cycle or refinery outage managers, 1 state chief boiler inspector, and the inspection lead at 1 equipment-breakdown insurer (HSB, FM or Zurich). The questions: (a) how many critical-path hours in their last outage went to waiting on inspection interpretation and release, as opposed to capture or repair; (b) whether they would accept a Level III-signed, AI-screened UT/EMAT tube or vessel report from a third party at their spring 2027 outage; (c) what they would pay per outage-day saved. In parallel, run a blind retrospective: apply an off-the-shelf AI screen to an existing tube-thickness dataset that one owner provides and compare its calls with failures found later. If inspection release is under 10% of critical path, or the insurer bundles inspection for free and will not partner, pivot the wedge to RBI interval extension. Note: the web search budget for this run was used up early, so most of the evidence above comes from a few direct page fetches (National Board AIA rules, EASA NPA 2025-07, Gecko's site) plus industry knowledge. The insurer-bundling and EPRI automated-analysis claims need checking in a follow-up search round.

finalist.name: Last Resort Power Depot: service operator of last resort for orphaned power electronics and distributed machines
merged_from: Last Resort Power Depot (orphaned power-electronics and distributed-machine service operator)
finalist.description: WHAT IT DOES: A depot and field operator that takes over service of orphaned or failing-OEM power electronics and distributed machines: solar central and string inverters, BESS power conversion and controls, EV chargers, and later warehouse and service robot fleets and e-mobility batteries and BMS. It does board-level repair, refurbishment, form-fit-function replacement of discontinued boards, and hyperscaler-style batched repair: swap the module now from a pooled stock and repair the core later at the depot. It sells a fixed-fee 'warranty of last resort' and uptime contracts to owners, tax-equity and debt financiers, and insurers. AI isolates faults down to the board component, reconstructs schematics, analyses firmware, cuts per-SKU onboarding cost enough to support thousands of orphaned models, and automates warranty-claim evidence. WHAT IT OWNS: (1) Board-level repair and automated test capability plus a library of reverse-engineered replacements. (2) A cross-brand pool of harvested and refurbished modules with provenance. (3) Service contracts and installed bases taken over cheaply from bankrupt integrators and OEMs (Fimer, SunPower, Powin, Satcon). (4) Fleet failure data across brands. (5) Safety re-certification and fire-authority return-to-service packages (UL 2849/2271, BESS augmentation), which form the gate and the moat. WEDGE: Utility-scale and C&I solar owners and their financiers holding orphaned inverter fleets. Offer a guaranteed swap within 72 hours from pooled refurbished stock plus depot board repair. Then take over BESS PCS and controls service from failed integrators, then EV chargers and robot fleets for OEMs that cannot staff field service. MARKET: Solar plus storage O&M is about $15-25B a year on more than 1.5 TW installed, and inverter replacement cycles add a multi-billion pool. EV charger O&M and robot field service are emerging pools worth tens of billions by 2030. Orphaned and out-of-warranty assets are a growing majority of the installed base because 10-15 year electronics sit inside 30-40 year assets. A dominant independent at 5-10% of the after-warranty pool reaches $1-3B, with protection-plan underwriting on top. COMPARABLES: Mantle (outsourced uptime for new OEMs, not orphans), Asurion/Domestic & General (risk transfer plus owned fulfilment), Assurant, Rochester Electronics (licensed continuation), NovaSource and independent solar O&M, specialty board-repair houses, and hyperscaler fleet repair (repair cut from 5-15% of equipment value to 0.75%; Google's 29% refurbished components). KEY RISKS: Fragmented SKUs could make onboarding expensive. Safety-certification cost for refurbished and replacement units. Lower per-event ticket sizes than aero. Possible IP claims from acquirers of bankrupt OEMs' assets.
finalist.why_finalist: This is the cleanest case where the Law 6 re-lock risk is structurally absent: the OEM no longer exists, so the knowledge and data blackout is real and AI reconstruction is the binding unlock. The orphan pool grows mechanically with every OEM bankruptcy and with the mismatch between electronics and asset lifetimes. Evidence fits well (inverters cause 43% of tickets and 36% of lost energy, and fault losses doubled while detection improved, so detection is not the bottleneck). It brings a novel combination to a fast-growing, under-served market: cheap acquisition of installed bases, a pooled spares layer, and risk transfer that financiers need. It is also the most consumer-adjacent finalist, giving portfolio diversity beyond aero and defense.

killers.killer: Repowering beats repair. Inverter $/W has collapsed, so owners of 10-15 year-old orphaned string and central inverters often find it cheaper and safer to replace them with new units. New units come with a fresh 10-year warranty, higher efficiency, current grid-code support (IEEE 1547-2018, UL 1741 SB) and a bankable OEM. That caps what anyone will pay for a refurbished orphan swap.
killers.evidence: NovaSource's own case study (novasourcepower.com) shows its answer to 10-year-old inverters with no spare parts left: a retrofit to new three-phase inverters, with the old units kept as spares. That is the default incumbent playbook: replace, then cannibalize the old units for parts. Utility-scale inverters cost a few cents per watt, which is small next to lost energy plus truck rolls. (This $/W figure comes from prior knowledge. Its source could not be re-checked this run because the shared web search budget was used up.)
killers.ai_answer: There is a partial structural answer, not an AI one. Swapping a central inverter or BESS PCS like-for-like can preserve the existing interconnection agreement, utility witness test and MV skid. A different inverter can trigger a material-modification review, re-study and skid rework, which can take months. Repair wins only where the replacement triggers that re-study, or where downtime per day is high. AI does not change the economics of repair versus repowering.

killers.killer: The cheap, scarce resource is gone at the auction: IP and spares from a bankrupt OEM go to a strategic buyer, who then sells the service. Taking over installed bases 'cheaply' is a one-off auction, not a repeatable channel, and acquirers can assert firmware and IP rights against reverse-engineered boards.
killers.evidence: From prior knowledge, not re-verified this run: Powin's 2025 Chapter 11 assets reportedly went to FlexGen, which markets lifecycle services and a hardware-agnostic EMS (flexgen.com; the site does not mention Powin). SunPower's 2024 bankruptcy sent its brand to Complete Solaria, and lease servicing went to a separate servicer. ABB's solar inverter business went to Fimer, which then restructured. In each case a buyer with deeper pockets got the firmware, the service tooling and the spares.
killers.ai_answer: Partial. AI cuts the cost of clean-room schematic reconstruction and firmware analysis. Form-fit-function boards have legal precedent: HEICO-style PMA parts, and right-to-repair, including the DMCA 1201 repair exemptions. But the firmware and the grid-certification files stay with whoever owns the IP. The best structural answer is to bid at these auctions for the spares inventory and tooling, which needs capital and speed.

killers.killer: Safety certification and liability, especially for BESS. Fire authorities, insurers and lenders require listed equipment (UL 9540/9540A, NFPA 855). A refurbished or reverse-engineered board in a PCS or BMS can void the listing. One thermal-runaway event on a $50-300M asset is an existential liability for a startup.
killers.evidence: Post-Moss Landing (2025) scrutiny of BESS by fire authorities and insurers is rising. UL listings attach to a specific construction, so replacement components need re-evaluation by a testing lab. A recertification package for each SKU takes months and costs tens to hundreds of thousands of dollars. Physics clocks: thermal and abuse testing cannot be compressed.
killers.ai_answer: The moat thesis is right that whoever holds re-certification packages owns the gate. But that gate is slow and capital-heavy, and AI does not speed up lab testing or a fire authority's sign-off. The structural answer is to stay out of the cells and BMS at first. Start with PV inverters (where the field-repair norms are lower stakes), and partner with a testing lab (UL, TÜV, CSA) and a specialty insurer before touching BESS.

killers.killer: Incumbents already cover most of the pool. OEMs serve their own fleets (SMA, Sungrow, Power Electronics, Fluence, Tesla). Large independent O&M firms (NovaSource, plus the in-house O&M of NextEra, AES, Enel and others) handle the rest by swapping. Residential orphans already have 'warranty of last resort' players.
killers.evidence: Solar Insure (solarinsure.com): operating since 2006, 100k+ systems protected, an explicit 'Installer Out of Business' program, and 20-year inverter coverage on commercial systems. ChargerHelp (chargerhelp.com) already sells charger 'Reliability as a Service' with AI diagnostics across 60+ CMS and OEM brands, 500k+ field-service records and nationwide technicians, with customers including Autel and The Mobility House. The EV-charger expansion step is therefore already taken.
killers.ai_answer: Partial. What incumbents lack is board-level depot repair and form-fit-function replacement of discontinued central-inverter and PCS boards. Today they cannibalize old units or repower. A focused supplier of repaired cores and FFF boards to O&M firms (wholesale, not direct to owners) avoids competing with them and turns them into the channel.

killers.killer: Unit economics and capital intensity of a service business. A pooled cross-brand stock across thousands of SKUs is working capital that turns slowly. Field truck rolls and depot labour carry thin margins (typically 10-25% for O&M). A fixed-fee uptime guarantee is an underwriting risk that needs reinsurance, and the data on correlated failure modes is thin.
killers.evidence: Hyperscaler batched repair works because there are a few SKUs at enormous scale. Solar and BESS fleets are the opposite: many vintages and few units per SKU. The pitch lists 'fragmented SKUs' as a risk itself. The Asurion and Assurant analogs depend on huge homogeneous device volumes and carrier distribution.
killers.ai_answer: Real but bounded. AI-assisted fault isolation and schematic reconstruction can cut onboarding cost per SKU by perhaps 5-10x. Harvested modules from decommissioned or repowered plants give cheap inventory. Underwriting should come from a carrier partner (kWh Analytics-style) rather than the startup's own balance sheet. Margins can reach HEICO-like levels only on FFF parts sales, not on labour.

killers.killer: Sales cycle and buyer mismatch. IPPs buy O&M through RFPs on 1-5 year terms. Tax-equity and debt financiers do not buy service; they demand bankable counterparties. A seed-stage startup is not bankable as a guarantor of 'last resort'.
killers.evidence: Project finance lenders' independent engineers review O&M and warranty counterparties for credit. A startup guarantee carries little weight without insurance wrap. Utility-scale procurement cycles run 6-18 months.
killers.ai_answer: The structural answer is to sell transactionally first: fixed-price emergency board repair and core exchange, priced per event, to asset managers who are already suffering downtime on orphaned fleets. Build a track record and failure data, then wrap guarantees with a carrier.

killers.killer: Robots and e-mobility expansion is too early or too proprietary. Robot OEMs lock down firmware and parts, fleets are young and still under warranty, and e-mobility battery and BMS repair carries the same fire liability as BESS.
killers.evidence: The installed base of warehouse and service robots that are both out of warranty and orphaned is small in 2026. Most OEMs (Locus, Symbotic, Amazon Robotics) service their own fleets.
killers.ai_answer: This does not need answering now. Drop it from the YC pitch except as long-term optionality.

attacks.who_already_does_it: Utility and C&I O&M: NovaSource Power Services, which handles orphaned inverters by retrofitting to new units and cannibalizing old ones, plus owners' in-house O&M and OEM service (SMA, Sungrow, Power Electronics, Fluence). BESS: integrators and acquirers of bankrupt OEM assets. FlexGen offers lifecycle services and a hardware-agnostic EMS and reportedly took Powin's assets in 2025 (the Powin link is unverified this run). Residential warranty of last resort: Solar Insure (since 2006, 100k+ systems, an 'installer out of business' program). EV chargers: ChargerHelp (AI diagnostics, 60+ brands, 500k+ field records, reliability-as-a-service). Obsolete-electronics continuation: Rochester Electronics. There are also small independent central-inverter and industrial-electronics board-repair shops, not named here because they could not be verified. Caveat: the shared web search budget for this workflow ran out before this agent's searches executed. Evidence comes from direct fetches of chargerhelp.com, novasourcepower.com, solarinsure.com and flexgen.com, plus prior knowledge flagged as unverified.
attacks.surviving_version: The company survives only narrowed, not as a 'Last Resort Power Depot for everything'. The surviving version is a form-fit-function parts and repaired-core house for orphaned utility-scale central inverters and BESS PCS (power stage and controls only, never cells or BMS). It sells wholesale to O&M providers and asset managers, priced per event and by core exchange. Its wedge is the set of sites where like-for-like replacement avoids interconnection re-study, MV-skid rework and re-commissioning. On those sites repair beats repowering on time and on approval risk, not on hardware cost. AI is used for schematic reconstruction, fault isolation and per-SKU onboarding. Inventory comes from bidding on bankrupt-OEM spares at auction and harvesting units from repowered plants. Value accrues in a growing library of FFF boards with test evidence: the 'HEICO for power electronics' shape, where margin sits in the parts, not in labour or truck rolls. Uptime and 'warranty of last resort' products come later, wrapped by a carrier, once failure data exists. EV chargers (ChargerHelp already covers this) and robots are dropped. This is a credible niche business. Venture-scale upside depends on whether the FFF part library generalizes across grid-tied power electronics, and that is still unproven.
attacks.cheapest_first_test: In 2-3 weeks and for under $5k: (1) Interview 20-30 asset managers and O&M directors who run 2010-2016 vintage plants with orphaned or limping central inverters or PCS (Satcon, Advanced Energy, PV Powered, ABB/Fimer, Powin, plus early Chinese brands that exited the US). Ask what happened at their last failure: days down, cost, and whether they repaired, cannibalized or repowered. Ask whether a replacement would have triggered utility re-study. Then ask for a paid purchase order for a single board repair or core exchange. (2) In parallel, buy 10-20 failed boards from one orphaned model (liquidation, eBay, or a willing owner). Measure AI-assisted time-to-schematic and repair yield against a human technician baseline. Kill signals: owners repower by default, no one pays at least $10-20k per event, or the repair yield is under 60%.

killers.killer: Repair economics lose to replacement with new hardware. String inverters are commodity hardware at a few cents per watt, so an owner of an orphaned string fleet just swaps in new units. For central inverters, the independent O&M firms already sell retrofit and upgrade packages.
killers.evidence: NovaSource's own site describes a case study where a client's aging inverters 'lost replacement-part support' and NovaSource retrofitted them with newer three-phase units. That shows the default answer for an orphaned fleet is replace or retrofit, not repair (novasourcepower.com, fetched). New-inverter prices keep falling apart from tariffs.
killers.ai_answer: Don't sell repair. Sell 'keep the interconnection agreement and the financing model intact'. A like-for-like (form-fit-function) swap avoids re-studying interconnection under IEEE 1547/UL 1741, avoids changing the energy model the tax-equity and debt deals were underwritten on, and avoids civil and BOS rework. The buyer is the financier and asset manager who wants zero change to the model, not the O&M tech. Focus on central inverters and BESS PCS, where a module or stack swap is 10-30x the ticket of a string inverter, and skip residential and string inverters entirely. Tariffs and FEOC rules on new Chinese PCS also make repairing an existing compliant unit more attractive.

killers.killer: Fragmented SKUs make per-model onboarding too expensive. There are thousands of inverter, PCS and charger models, each with its own boards, firmware and failure modes.
killers.evidence: This comes from the prompt's own risk list and from the industry's structure: Satcon, Advanced Energy, Power-One/ABB/Fimer, Schneider, Solectria and several dozen BESS integrators each shipped multiple generations. I could not quantify fleet concentration because the search budget ran out. Fleet concentration by MW (EIA-860 plus the CEC inverter list) is the number to pull first.
killers.ai_answer: Use the installed MW of each model as a Pareto filter.
